Indicator System: General Theory

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

This chapter opens Part Two, "The Indicator System," and serves as the hinge that carries the transition from the L₁ layer (the ontological-epistemological framework layer) to the L₄ layer (the operational protocol layer). Part One has completed the argument for the New Three Views, Part Three will derive the normative principles, and the task of this part is to transform the abstract philosophical framework into operable measurement tools.

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The indicator system design of this chapter derives directly from the core propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{Indicator System} = f(\text{New Cosmological View}, \text{New View of Life}, \text{New View of Cognition})$$

Specifically:

  • The New Cosmological View (NC) → CDI (Civilizational Development Index), CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment)
  • The New View of Life (NL) → UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale), MBCL (Memetic Biosafety Containment Level)
  • The New View of Cognition (NK) → RFD (Recursive Freedom Degree), CRV (Commitment Reversibility Verifiability)

V. Reading Suggestions

  • If the reader is already familiar with the argument for the New Three Views in Part One, they may proceed directly to §6.1
  • If the reader has a particular interest in indicator design methodology, it is recommended to read §6.2 closely
  • If the reader wishes to quickly understand the six major indicators, they may first read §6.3 and then return to §6.1–6.2

VI. Boundary Statement

All indicators in this chapter are at the stage of "conceptual prototype," with a technology readiness level of TRL 2[1]. This means that:

  1. The theoretical frameworks of the indicators have been established, but the operationalization procedures have not yet been fully determined
  2. The indicators are suitable for academic research and thought experiments, but not for mandatory decision-making
  3. The specific parameters and weights of the indicators need to converge gradually through interdisciplinary collaboration

§6.1 Why an Indicator System Is Needed

§6.1.1 The Gap from Principle to Operation

I. Statement of the Problem

Part One completed the argument for the New Three Views and established the ontological-epistemological foundation for interstellar civilization governance. However, a fundamental question immediately arises:

Core question: How can abstract philosophical principles be transformed into operable governance tools?

This problem is not unique to this work. In the history of normative theory, the gap from principle to operation has always been a core difficulty[2].

Definition 6.1.1 (Principle-Operation Gap)

Let $P$ be a set of normative principles and $O$ a set of operational procedures. The Principle-Operation Gap (POG) is defined as:

$$\text{POG}(P, O) = 1 - \frac{|\{o \in O : o \text{ traceable to } P\}|}{|O|}$$

When $\text{POG} = 0$, all operational procedures can be traced back to the principles; when $\text{POG} = 1$, the operational procedures are entirely disconnected from the principles.

II. The Three Dimensions of the Gap

The principle-operation gap exhibits three dimensions in the context of interstellar civilization governance:

Table 6.1 The Three Dimensions of the Principle-Operation Gap

DimensionDescriptionManifestation in Traditional GovernanceAggravation in Interstellar Governance
Dimension of abstractnessThe tension between the universality of principles and the particularity of situationsLegal principles require judicial interpretationThe diversity of cross-civilizational situations makes interpretation more difficult
Dimension of measurabilityNormative concepts are difficult to quantify"Justice" is difficult to measureConcepts such as "consciousness" and "freedom" are even more difficult to measure
Dimension of temporalityThe tension between the stability of principles and the dynamism of operationsThe relation between constitutional principles and specific policiesDeep time scales make this tension even sharper

III. Analysis of the Dimension of Abstractness

The New Three Views provide the ontological-epistemological framework for interstellar civilization governance, but the abstractness of this framework makes it difficult to guide concrete decisions directly.

Take the core proposition of the New View of Life, NL-1 (consciousness is a fundamental feature of the universe), as an example:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Derivation: NL-1 to Operational Decision                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│ NL-1: consciousness yes basic feature of universe                │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Corollary: entities w/ consciousness have moral status           │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Problem: how to judge if entity yes/no has consciousness?        │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Problem: how to compare degrees of consciousness?                │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Problem: how does consciousness degree affect moral weight?      │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Operational need: measurable consciousness framework             │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This derivation chain reveals several "breakpoints" from abstract principle to operational decision. Each breakpoint requires additional conceptual tools to bridge.

IV. Analysis of the Dimension of Measurability

The measurement difficulty of normative concepts is an ancient philosophical problem. In the context of interstellar civilization governance, this difficulty is significantly amplified.

Definition 6.1.2 (Measurement Difficulty)

Let $C$ be a normative concept. Its Measurement Difficulty (MD) is defined as:

$$\text{MD}(C) = \alpha \cdot \text{Abstractness}(C) + \beta \cdot \text{Heterogeneity}(C) + \gamma \cdot \text{Temporality}(C)$$

where:

  • $\text{Abstractness}(C)$: the degree of abstractness of the concept
  • $\text{Heterogeneity}(C)$: the heterogeneity of the objects to which the concept applies
  • $\text{Temporality}(C)$: the temporal sensitivity of the concept
  • $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$: weight coefficients satisfying $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$

Table 6.2 Assessment of the Measurement Difficulty of Core Normative Concepts

ConceptAbstractnessHeterogeneityTemporal SensitivityComposite Difficulty
ConsciousnessHighExtremely highMediumExtremely high
FreedomHighHighHighHigh
ResponsibilityMediumHighExtremely highHigh
DevelopmentMediumHighHighMedium-high
SecurityLowMediumMediumMedium
ImpactMediumHighExtremely highHigh

V. Analysis of the Dimension of Temporality

Interstellar civilization governance involves deep time, which makes the temporal dimension of the principle-operation gap particularly prominent.

Proposition 6.1.1 (Amplification Effect of the Temporal Gap)

Let $T$ be the time span of a decision's impact. The principle-operation gap is amplified as the time span increases:

$$\text{POG}(T) = \text{POG}_0 \cdot (1 + \lambda \cdot \log T)$$

where $\text{POG}_0$ is the baseline gap and $\lambda$ is the amplification coefficient.

Argument:

  1. An increase in the time span leads to the accumulation of uncertainty
  2. The accumulation of uncertainty makes the concrete application of principles more difficult
  3. Therefore, the principle-operation gap is amplified as the time span increases

Boundary conditions:

  • This proposition assumes that the complexity of the decision environment increases over time
  • In highly stable environments, the amplification effect may weaken

Historical case: the principle-operation gap in environmental governance

The field of environmental governance provides a typical case of the principle-operation gap. The 1972 Stockholm Declaration established the principle of "sustainable development," but from this principle to concrete environmental policies, decades of conceptual operationalization elapsed.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Operationalization of Sustainable Development                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│ 1972 yr: Stockholm Declaration (principle level)                 │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ 1987 yr: Brundtland Report (concept clarity)                     │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ 1992 yr: Rio Declaration (principle refinement)                  │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ 2000 yr: MDGs (indicator attempt)                                │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ 2015 yr: SDGs (systematic indicator system)                      │
│                                                                 │
│ Time span: 43 yrs                                                │
│ principle to operational indicator: ~2 generations               │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This history shows that even in governance at the Earth scale, bridging the principle-operation gap requires a long time and sustained effort. In the context of interstellar civilization governance, this challenge will be even more formidable.

§6.1.2 Indicators as Bridges

I. Definition of the Bridging Function

The core function of an indicator system is to bridge the principle-operation gap, serving as a bridge from abstract principles to concrete operations. That is, to operationalize abstract normative principles[3].

Definition 6.1.3 (Indicator)

An indicator is a mapping function from an observation domain to a numerical domain:

$$I: \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n$$

where $\mathcal{O}$ is the observation domain (the set of observable phenomena) and $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the n-dimensional real number space.

An effective indicator must satisfy the following conditions:

  1. Traceability: the indicator can be traced back to normative principles
  2. Operationalizability: the indicator can be calculated through explicit procedures
  3. Interpretability: changes in the indicator's numerical value have clear normative meaning

Definition 6.1.4 (Indicator System)

An indicator system is a set of interrelated indicators:

$$\mathcal{I} = \{I_1, I_2, ..., I_m\}$$

satisfying the following conditions:

  1. Completeness: $\mathcal{I}$ covers all core normative concepts
  2. Consistency: the indicators in $\mathcal{I}$ do not contradict each other
  3. Hierarchy: the indicators in $\mathcal{I}$ have clear hierarchical relations

Formal expression of the bridging function

The bridging function of an indicator system can be formalized as:

$$\text{Bridge}(\mathcal{I}) = \text{POG}_{\text{before}} - \text{POG}_{\text{after}}$$

where $\text{POG}_{\text{before}}$ is the principle-operation gap before the introduction of the indicator system and $\text{POG}_{\text{after}}$ is the gap after its introduction.

An effective indicator system should satisfy:

$$\text{Bridge}(\mathcal{I}) > 0$$

that is, the introduction of the indicator system should reduce the principle-operation gap.

II. The Three Levels of the Bridging Function

The bridging function of an indicator system unfolds at three levels:

Table 6.3 The Bridging Function of the Indicator System

LevelFunctional DescriptionConcrete Manifestation
Conceptual levelTransform abstract concepts into measurable constructs"Consciousness" → the multi-dimensional construct of UCS
Methodological levelProvide standardized measurement proceduresExplicit data collection and calculation methods
Decision-making levelProvide quantitative grounds for decisionsThreshold setting, comparison benchmarks

III. The Bridging Function at the Conceptual Level

At the conceptual level, the indicator system transforms abstract normative concepts into measurable constructs.

Take the concept of "consciousness" as an example:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Operationalization path of "consciousness"                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│ Abstract concept: consciousness (Consciousness)                  │
│       ↓                                                         │
│                                                                  │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Construct: consciousness = f(info integration, global access,    │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Indicator design: UCS = w1*Phi + w2*G + w3*S                    │
│       ↓                                                         │
│ Measurement: concrete data collection and computation method     │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IV. The Bridging Function at the Methodological Level

At the methodological level, the indicator system provides standardized measurement procedures, enabling different observers to obtain comparable results.

Definition 6.1.5 (Measurement Procedure)

A measurement procedure is an algorithm from raw data to indicator values:

$$\text{MP}: \mathcal{D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n$$

where $\mathcal{D}$ is the raw data set.

An effective measurement procedure should satisfy:

  1. Reproducibility: identical data produce identical results
  2. Transparency: every step of the procedure can be audited
  3. Robustness: a certain tolerance for data noise

V. The Bridging Function at the Decision-Making Level

At the decision-making level, the indicator system provides quantitative grounds for governance decisions.

Definition 6.1.6 (Decision Threshold)

A decision threshold is a mapping rule between indicator values and decision actions:

$$\text{DT}: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$$

where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of decision actions.

For example, for MBCL (Memetic Biosafety Containment Level):

$$\text{DT}_{\text{MBCL}}(x) = \begin{cases} \text{Routine Monitoring} & \text{if } x \leq 2 \\ \text{Enhanced Monitoring} & \text{if } 2 < x \leq 4 \\ \text{Active Intervention} & \text{if } x > 4 \end{cases}$$

VI. Relation to the New Three Views

The bridging function of the indicator system directly embodies the core propositions of the New View of Cognition.

According to NK-2 (cognition is distributed), knowledge exists not only in individual minds but also in tools, symbol systems, and social practices. The indicator system is precisely a concrete embodiment of such distributed cognition: it "externalizes" abstract normative knowledge into operable tools, enabling this knowledge to be transmitted and applied among different subjects.

$$\text{Indicator System} \subseteq \text{distributed cognitive system}$$

According to NK-3 (cognition is participatory), cognition is not a passive reflection of the external world but an active interaction between subject and environment. The design and application of an indicator system is itself a participatory cognitive activity: by designing indicators, we participate in constructing the conceptual framework for understanding and evaluating interstellar civilization.

§6.1.3 The Functions and Limitations of Indicators

I. The Five Major Functions of Indicators

The indicator system performs five major functions in interstellar civilization governance:

Table 6.4 The Five Major Functions of the Indicator System

FunctionDescriptionConcrete ManifestationCorresponding New Three Views
Descriptive functionCharacterize the current state of a systemCDI describes the level of civilizational developmentNC (relational ontology)
Evaluative functionJudge whether a system meets normative requirementsUCS assesses the moral status of conscious entitiesNL (continuum of consciousness)
Early-warning functionIdentify potential risksMBCL warns of memetic propagation risksNK (participatory cognition)
Comparative functionCompare across different systemsRFD compares the freedom degrees of different entitiesNL (substrate independence)
Guiding functionGuide a system toward a desired directionCRV guides the verifiability of commitmentsNK (social knowledge)

(i) Descriptive function

The descriptive function is the most basic function of an indicator, namely, characterizing the current state of a system.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Describe}(I, S, t) = I(S, t)$$

where $S$ is the system, $t$ is the time point, and $I(S, t)$ is the value of the indicator for system $S$ at time $t$.

The effectiveness of the descriptive function depends on the validity of the indicator: whether the indicator truly measures the concept it claims to measure.

(ii) Evaluative function

The evaluative function is that of judging whether a system meets normative requirements.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Evaluate}(I, S, t, \theta) = \begin{cases} \text{Compliant} & \text{if } I(S, t) \geq \theta \\ \text{Non-compliant} & \text{if } I(S, t) < \theta \end{cases}$$

where $\theta$ is the normative threshold.

The effectiveness of the evaluative function depends on the legitimacy of the threshold setting: whether the threshold reflects genuine normative requirements.

(iii) Early-warning function

The early-warning function is that of identifying potential risks and issuing warnings before a problem deteriorates.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Alert}(I, S, t, \Delta t, \theta_{\text{alert}}) = \begin{cases} \text{Alert} & \text{if } \frac{dI(S, t)}{dt} \cdot \Delta t > \theta_{\text{alert}} \\ \text{Normal} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

where $\frac{dI(S, t)}{dt}$ is the rate of change of the indicator, $\Delta t$ is the prediction time window, and $\theta_{\text{alert}}$ is the warning threshold.

The effectiveness of the early-warning function depends on the predictive validity of the indicator: whether the current change of the indicator can predict future risks.

(iv) Comparative function

The comparative function is that of comparing across different systems.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Compare}(I, S_1, S_2, t) = I(S_1, t) - I(S_2, t)$$

The effectiveness of the comparative function depends on the cross-system comparability of the indicator: whether the indicator has the same meaning in different systems.

This function is particularly important in interstellar civilization governance, because we need to compare intelligent entities with different physical substrates.

(v) Guiding function

The guiding function is that of guiding a system toward a desired direction.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Guide}(I, S, t, I^) = I^ - I(S, t)$$

where $I^$ is the desired indicator value and $I^ - I(S, t)$ is the "development gap."

The effectiveness of the guiding function depends on the degree of alignment between the indicator and the desired goal: whether an improvement in the indicator truly means approaching the desired goal.

II. The Four Major Limitations of Indicators

Although the indicator system is powerful, it also has inherent limitations:

Table 6.5 The Four Major Limitations of the Indicator System

LimitationDescriptionRiskMitigation Strategy
Simplification limitationIndicators necessarily simplify complex realityOmission of important dimensionsMulti-indicator combination, qualitative supplementation
Measurement limitationCertain concepts are difficult to measure preciselyMeasurement error, biasMulti-method triangulation
Goodhart effectIndicators fail once they become goalsIndicator manipulation, goal displacementAnti-Goodhart design
Cultural limitationIndicators may reflect particular cultural biasesInapplicability across civilizationsCross-substrate applicability design

(i) Simplification limitation

Any indicator is a simplification of complex reality. Such simplification is necessary (otherwise the indicator would lose operability), but it is also dangerous (it may omit important dimensions).

Proposition 6.1.2 (Simplification-Operability Trade-off)

Let $C$ be the complexity of an indicator and $O$ its operability. There exists a trade-off relation:

$$O = f(C), \quad \frac{dO}{dC} < 0$$

that is, an increase in the complexity of the indicator reduces its operability.

Mitigation strategies:

  • Adopt a combination of multiple indicators, each capturing a different dimension
  • Preserve space for qualitative assessment alongside quantitative indicators
  • Explicitly state the coverage and blind spots of each indicator

(ii) Measurement limitation

Certain normative concepts are in principle difficult to measure precisely. For example, the measurement of "consciousness" faces the philosophical difficulty of the "problem of other minds."

Definition 6.1.7 (Measurement Uncertainty)

Measurement Uncertainty is defined as:

$$U(I) = \sqrt{U_{\text{random}}^2 + U_{\text{systematic}}^2 + U_{\text{conceptual}}^2}$$

where:

  • $U_{\text{random}}$: random error
  • $U_{\text{systematic}}$: systematic error
  • $U_{\text{conceptual}}$: conceptual uncertainty (arising from the vagueness of the concept itself)

In the context of interstellar civilization governance, $U_{\text{conceptual}}$ is often the dominant term.

Mitigation strategies:

  • Adopt methodological triangulation
  • Explicitly report measurement uncertainty
  • Take the influence of uncertainty into account in decision-making

(iii) The Goodhart effect

Goodhart's law states: when an indicator becomes a goal, it ceases to be a good indicator.

Definition 6.1.8 (Goodhart Effect)

Let $I$ be an indicator and $G$ the true goal that the indicator is intended to measure. The Goodhart effect occurs when:

$$\text{Corr}(I, G)_{t_0} > \text{Corr}(I, G)_{t_1}$$

where $t_0$ is before the indicator is set as a goal and $t_1$ is after.

That is, the correlation between the indicator and the true goal declines after the indicator is set as a goal.

The mechanism of the Goodhart effect:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Causal mechanism of the Goodhart effect                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│ Stage 1: indicator design                                        │
│ - indicator I designed to measure objective G                    │
│ - Corr(I, G) is high                                            │
│                                                                 │
│ Stage 2: indicator becomes objective                             │
│ - actors incentivized to optimize I                              │
│ - actors find "shortcuts" to optimize I                          │
│                                                                 │
│ Stage 3: indicator failure                                       │
│ - actors raise I via "shortcuts" w/o improving G                 │
│ - Corr(I, G) declines                                           │
│ - indicator loses measurement function                           │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Mitigation strategies:

  • Anti-Goodhart design (see §6.2.4 for details)
  • Regularly audit the alignment between indicators and goals
  • Maintain the capacity for dynamic adjustment of indicator design

(iv) Cultural limitation

Indicators may reflect the value biases of a particular culture and lose their applicability in a cross-civilizational context.

Proposition 6.1.3 (Cultural Embeddedness)

Any indicator $I$ is embedded in a particular cultural framework $F$:

$$I = I_F$$

When the indicator is applied to a different cultural framework $F'$, systematic bias may arise:

$$\text{Bias}(I_F, F') = I_F(S) - I_{F'}(S)$$

Mitigation strategies:

  • Cross-substrate applicability design (see §6.2.3 for details)
  • Incorporate multicultural perspectives into indicator design
  • Explicitly state the cultural assumptions of the indicator

III. Relation to the New Three Views

The limitations of indicators directly echo the core insights of the New View of Cognition.

According to NK-1 (cognition is participatory), our measurement activity is itself a kind of "participation" in the object being measured. This means that measurement cannot be entirely "objective"—the measurer's framework, tools, and purposes all influence the measurement results.

$$\text{Measurement Result} = f(\text{Object Measured}, \text{Measurement Framework}, \text{Measurement Instrument}, \text{Measurement Purpose})$$

This insight requires us to maintain epistemic humility about indicators: indicators are useful tools, but they are not perfect reflections of reality.

§6.2 The Principles of Indicator Design

§6.2.1 Anchoring to Normative Principles

I. The Necessity of Anchoring

The indicator system is not an arbitrarily designed technical tool but an operationalized expression of normative principles. Therefore, every indicator must be anchored to a specific normative principle.

Definition 6.2.1 (Normative Anchoring)

Let $I$ be an indicator and $P$ a normative principle. $I$ is anchored to $P$ (denoted $I \triangleleft P$) if and only if:

  1. The conceptual basis of $I$ can be traced back to $P$
  2. The numerical changes of $I$ have the normative meaning prescribed by $P$
  3. The application of $I$ serves the realization of $P$

Formal expression of anchoring

The anchoring relation can be formalized as a mapping:

$$\text{Anchor}: \mathcal{I} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}$$

where $\mathcal{I}$ is the set of indicators and $\mathcal{P}$ is the set of normative principles.

For the indicator system of this work, the anchoring relations are as follows:

Table 6.6 The Anchoring Relations between Indicators and Normative Principles

IndicatorAnchored Normative PrincipleAnchored New Three Views PropositionAnchoring Explanation
UCSPrinciple of Recursive FreedomNL-1, NL-3Measures subjecthood and determines whose freedom needs protection
RFDPrinciple of Recursive FreedomNC-2, NC-3Directly measures the degree of openness of the possibility space
CRVPrinciple of ReversibilityNK-1[12], NK-4Assesses the verifiability and reversibility of commitments
CDIPrinciple of Negentropy ResponsibilityNC-1, NL-2Measures the multi-dimensional state of development of a civilization
MBCLPrinciple of ReversibilityNK-1, NK-2Assesses the risk level of information propagation
CSIASynthesis of the three principlesThe New Three Views as a wholeComprehensively assesses the systemic impact of major actions

II. Methods of Verifying Anchoring

The anchoring relation needs to be verified through the following methods:

Method one: conceptual traceability verification

Examine whether the conceptual definition of the indicator can be traced back to the normative principle.

$$\text{Valid}_{\text{concept}}(I \triangleleft P) \Leftrightarrow \text{Def}(I) \subseteq \text{Implications}(P)$$

Method two: normative-meaning verification

Examine whether the numerical changes of the indicator have the meaning prescribed by the normative principle.

$$\text{Valid}_{\text{normative}}(I \triangleleft P) \Leftrightarrow \forall \Delta I, \text{Meaning}(\Delta I) \in \text{Normative-Space}(P)$$

Method three: functional-service verification

Examine whether the application of the indicator serves the realization of the normative principle.

$$\text{Valid}_{\text{functional}}(I \triangleleft P) \Leftrightarrow \text{Application}(I) \rightarrow \text{Realization}(P)$$

III. The Risk of Anchoring Failure

When the anchoring relation fails, the indicator loses its normative meaning and is reduced to a purely technical tool.

Definition 6.2.2 (Anchoring Failure)

Anchoring failure occurs when:

$$\text{Corr}(\Delta I, \Delta P_{\text{realization}}) \leq \theta_{\text{failure}}$$

where $\Delta P_{\text{realization}}$ is the change in the degree of realization of the normative principle and $\theta_{\text{failure}}$ is the failure threshold.

Prevention of anchoring failure:

  • Regularly audit the anchoring relations
  • Explicitly set out the anchoring chain in indicator design
  • Establish an early-warning mechanism for anchoring failure

§6.2.2 The Requirement of Operability

I. Definition of Operability

Operability is the capacity of an indicator to be actually calculated and applied.

Definition 6.2.3 (Operability)

The operability of an indicator $I$ is defined as:

$$\text{Op}(I) = f(\text{DataAvailability}, \text{ComputationalFeasibility}, \text{InterpretationalClarity})$$

where:

  • $\text{DataAvailability}$: the availability of the required data
  • $\text{ComputationalFeasibility}$: the feasibility of computation
  • $\text{InterpretationalClarity}$: the clarity of interpretation

II. The Three Dimensions of Operability

Table 6.7 The Three Dimensions of Operability

DimensionDescriptionEvaluation CriterionWeight
Data availabilityWhether the data required to compute the indicator is availableAccessibility of data sources, data quality, data cost0.4
Computational feasibilityWhether the computation of the indicator can be completed within reasonable time and resourcesComputational complexity, required resources, algorithm maturity0.3
Interpretational clarityWhether the numerical value of the indicator has a clear meaningClarity of the value range, interpretability of changes0.3

III. Data Availability

Data availability is the primary dimension of operability. Without data, the indicator cannot be calculated.

Definition 6.2.4 (Data Availability)

Data Availability is defined as:

$$\text{DA}(I) = \frac{\sum_{d \in D_I} w_d \cdot \text{Accessible}(d)}{\sum_{d \in D_I} w_d}$$

where $D_I$ is the set of data required to compute indicator $I$, $w_d$ is the weight of data $d$, and $\text{Accessible}(d) \in [0, 1]$ is the degree of accessibility of data $d$.

Challenges of data availability:

In the context of interstellar civilization governance, data availability faces particular challenges:

  1. Cross-substrate data: intelligent entities with different physical substrates may produce different types of data
  2. Deep-time data: data over long time scales is difficult to obtain
  3. Cross-civilizational data: different civilizations may use different data formats and standards

IV. Computational Feasibility

Computational feasibility is the capacity to complete the calculation of an indicator under reasonable time and resource constraints.

Definition 6.2.5 (Computational Feasibility)

Computational Feasibility is defined as:

$$\text{CF}(I) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } T(I) \leq T_{\max} \land R(I) \leq R_{\max} \\ \frac{T_{\max}}{T(I)} \cdot \frac{R_{\max}}{R(I)} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

where $T(I)$ is the computation time, $R(I)$ is the required resources, and $T_{\max}$ and $R_{\max}$ are the acceptable upper limits.

V. Interpretational Clarity

Interpretational clarity is that the numerical value of the indicator has a clear and consistent meaning.

Definition 6.2.6 (Interpretational Clarity)

Interpretational Clarity is defined as:

$$\text{IC}(I) = 1 - H(\text{Interpretation}(I))$$

where $H(\text{Interpretation}(I))$ is the entropy (uncertainty) of the indicator's interpretation.

Requirements of interpretational clarity:

  1. Clear value range: the value range of the indicator should be clearly defined
  2. Clear direction of change: the normative meaning of an increase or decrease in the indicator should be clear
  3. Clear meaning of thresholds: the normative meaning of key thresholds should be clear

VI. The Trade-off between Operability and Theoretical Depth

There exists a trade-off relation between operability and theoretical depth.

Proposition 6.2.1 (Operability-Depth Trade-off)

Let $\text{Op}(I)$ be the operability of an indicator and $\text{Depth}(I)$ its theoretical depth. There exists a trade-off relation:

$$\text{Op}(I) + \text{Depth}(I) \leq K$$

where $K$ is a constant.

Argument:

  1. An increase in theoretical depth usually means an increase in conceptual complexity
  2. An increase in conceptual complexity leads to an increase in measurement difficulty
  3. An increase in measurement difficulty leads to a decline in operability

Trade-off strategies:

  • Adopt indicator versions of different depths in different application scenarios
  • Establish a "streamlined version" and a "complete version" of the indicators
  • Explicitly state the scope of application of each version

Node No.Core ConclusionArgumentative Basis

§6.2.3 The Requirement of Cross-Substrate Applicability

I. The Necessity of Cross-Substrate Applicability

One of the core challenges of interstellar civilization governance is dealing with intelligent entities that have different physical substrates. The indicator system must be able to cross substrate differences and provide comparable measurement results.

Definition 6.2.7 (Physical Substrate)

A physical substrate is the mode of physical realization of an intelligent entity. Common substrate types include:

Substrate TypeDescriptionExample
Carbon-based biologyOrganisms based on carbon chemistryHumans, terrestrial organisms
Silicon-based computationComputing systems based on silicon chipsAI systems, robots
Quantum computationComputing systems based on quantum effectsQuantum computers
Hybrid systemsMixtures of multiple substratesBrain-computer interfaces, cyborgs
Unknown substrateSubstrate types not yet discoveredPossible extraterrestrial life

Definition 6.2.8 (Cross-Substrate Applicability)

The Cross-Substrate Applicability of an indicator $I$ is defined as:

$$\text{CSA}(I) = \frac{|\{s \in S : I \text{ applicable to } s\}|}{|S|}$$

where $S$ is the set of all possible substrate types.

II. The Challenges of Cross-Substrate Applicability

Cross-substrate applicability faces three core challenges:

Challenge one: conceptual equivalence

Intelligent entities with different substrates may realize the same function in different ways. How can we ensure that the indicator measures a functional equivalent rather than a substrate-specific realization?

Formal expression:

Let $F$ be a function and $R_1$ and $R_2$ two realizations with different substrates. Conceptual equivalence requires:

$$I(R_1) = I(R_2) \Leftrightarrow F(R_1) = F(R_2)$$

that is, the indicator values are equal if and only if the functions are equivalent.

Challenge two: data comparability

Intelligent entities with different substrates may produce different types of data. How can we ensure that this data can be converted into comparable indicator values?

Formal expression:

Let $D_1$ and $D_2$ be the data types produced by two substrates. Data comparability requires the existence of a conversion function:

$$T: D_1 \times D_2 \rightarrow D_{\text{common}}$$

such that $I(T(d_1)) \sim I(T(d_2))$ when $d_1$ and $d_2$ reflect the same underlying state.

Challenge three: normative equivalence

Intelligent entities with different substrates may have different normative statuses. How can we ensure that the indicator reflects this normative difference rather than substrate bias?

Formal expression:

Let $N(e)$ be the normative status of entity $e$. Normative equivalence requires:

$$I(e_1) > I(e_2) \Leftrightarrow N(e_1) > N(e_2)$$

that is, the ordering of the indicators is consistent with the ordering of the normative statuses.

III. Design Strategies for Cross-Substrate Applicability

Strategy one: functionalist definition

Adopt a functionalist conceptual definition[6], focusing on function rather than realization.

Example: the definition of UCS does not depend on a particular neural structure but focuses on functional features such as information integration and autonomy.

$$\text{UCS} = f(\Phi, A, T, M, V)$$

where each dimension is functionally defined.

Strategy two: multimodal data fusion

Design measurement procedures capable of fusing multiple data types.

Example: the measurement of RFD may be based on behavioral data, structural data, or self-report data, depending on the characteristics of the entity being measured.

$$\text{RFD} = g(\text{Behavioral}, \text{Structural}, \text{Self-Report})$$

Strategy three: calibration mechanism

Establish a cross-substrate calibration mechanism to ensure that the measurement results of different substrates are comparable.

Example: establish a set of "calibration entities" whose indicator values are known, used to calibrate the measurement procedures of different substrates.

$$\text{Calibrate}(I, s) = I(s) \cdot \frac{I_{\text{ref}}}{I_s(\text{calibration entity})}$$

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

Cross-substrate applicability directly embodies the core proposition of the New View of Life, NL-4 (substrate independence).

According to NL-4, the essence of life and consciousness lies not in a particular physical substrate but in the pattern of information processing. This proposition provides the ontological foundation for cross-substrate applicability: if consciousness is substrate-independent, then the indicator measuring consciousness should also be substrate-independent.

$$\text{NL-4} \Rightarrow \text{CSA}(I_{\text{consciousness}}) \approx 1$$

Argument Node 6.2-C

Node No.Core ConclusionArgumentative Basis
6.2-CCross-substrate applicability is a core requirement of interstellar civilization governance indicators and needs to be achieved through functionalist definition, multimodal data fusion, and calibration mechanismsAnalysis of cross-substrate challenges and argument for design strategies

§6.2.4 Anti-Goodhart Design

I. In-Depth Analysis of the Goodhart Effect

The Goodhart effect[7] is one of the most serious threats facing the indicator system. When an indicator becomes a goal, actors seek "shortcuts" to optimize the indicator, causing the indicator to become disconnected from the true goal.

Definition 6.2.9 (The Four Types of the Goodhart Effect)

According to the classification of Manheim and Garrabrant, the Goodhart effect has four types:

TypeDescriptionExample
RegressionalThe correlation between indicator and goal weakens at extreme valuesThe correlation between college entrance examination scores and academic ability weakens at very high scores
ExtremalOptimizing the indicator drives the system into an extreme stateOver-optimizing GDP leads to environmental destruction
CausalIntervening in the indicator destroys the causal relation between indicator and goalDirectly raising the thermometer reading cannot cure a disease
AdversarialActors actively manipulate the indicatorAcademic fraud increases citation counts

Formal model of the Goodhart effect

Let $I$ be an indicator, $G$ the true goal, and $A$ the action of an actor. The Goodhart effect can be modeled as:

$$\frac{\partial \text{Corr}(I, G)}{\partial \text{Optimize}(I, A)} < 0$$

that is, optimizing the indicator reduces the correlation between the indicator and the goal.

II. Principles of Anti-Goodhart Design

Principle one: multi-indicator combination

Use a combination of multiple indicators, such that manipulating a single indicator cannot yield an advantage.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Score} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot I_i$$

where $w_i$ is the weight, satisfying $\sum w_i = 1$.

Design requirements:

  • There should be a certain degree of independence among the indicators
  • The weights should be adjusted regularly
  • The weight-adjustment mechanism should be unpredictable

Principle two: process auditing

Assess not only results but also processes.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Valid}(I) = \text{Valid}_{\text{result}}(I) \land \text{Valid}_{\text{process}}(I)$$

Design requirements:

  • Establish an audit trail for indicator computation
  • Conduct process audits regularly
  • Investigate anomalous processes

Principle three: dynamic adjustment

Regularly adjust the definition and calculation method of the indicator, rendering manipulation strategies ineffective.

Formal expression:

$$I_{t+1} = f(I_t, \text{Feedback}_t, \text{Random}_t)$$

where $\text{Feedback}_t$ is feedback information and $\text{Random}_t$ is random perturbation.

Design requirements:

  • Establish a trigger mechanism for indicator adjustment
  • The adjustment should be based on the detection of manipulative behavior
  • The adjustment should keep the core meaning of the indicator unchanged

Principle four: meta-indicator monitoring

Establish "meta-indicators" that monitor the validity of the indicators.

Definition 6.2.10 (Meta-Indicator)

A meta-indicator is an indicator that measures the validity of an indicator:

$$\text{MI}(I) = \text{Corr}(I, G) \cdot \text{Stability}(I) \cdot (1 - \text{Manipulation}(I))$$

where:

  • $\text{Corr}(I, G)$: the correlation between the indicator and the goal
  • $\text{Stability}(I)$: the stability of the indicator
  • $\text{Manipulation}(I)$: the degree to which the indicator is manipulated

Design requirements:

  • Calculate the meta-indicator regularly
  • Trigger a review when the meta-indicator declines
  • The meta-indicator itself also requires anti-Goodhart design

IV. Implementation Framework of Anti-Goodhart Design

Anti-Goodhart design directly embodies the core proposition of the New View of Cognition, NK-4 (the negotiability of knowledge).

According to NK-4, cognitive standards are not fixed but can be adjusted through negotiation. This proposition provides the epistemological foundation for anti-Goodhart design: indicators are not fixed reflections of reality but cognitive tools that can be adjusted according to feedback.

$$\text{NK-4} \Rightarrow \text{indicator adjustability is legitimate}$$

The Universal Consciousness Scale (UCS) is a multi-dimensional indicator measuring the degree of consciousness of an entity.

$$\text{UCS}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]^5$$

where $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of entities and $[0, 1]^5$ is the five-dimensional unit hypercube.

§6.3.2 RFD: Recursive Freedom Degree

I. Conceptual Definition

Definition 6.3.2 (RFD)

The Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD) is an indicator measuring the impact of an action on the possibility space.

$$\text{RFD}: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{S} \rightarrow [-1, 1]$$

where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of actions and $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of states.

II. Numerical Meaning

RFD ValueMeaningNormative Evaluation
RFD > 0The action expands the possibility spacePositive
RFD = 0The action does not change the possibility spaceNeutral
RFD < 0The action compresses the possibility spaceNegative

Formal expression

$$\text{RFD}(a, s) = \frac{|\mathcal{P}(s')| - |\mathcal{P}(s)|}{|\mathcal{P}(s)|}$$

where:

  • $s$ is the state before the action
  • $s' = \text{Result}(a, s)$ is the state after the action
  • $\mathcal{P}(s)$ is the possibility space of state $s$

Definition of the possibility space

Definition 6.3.3 (Possibility Space)

The possibility space is the set of all future states reachable from a given state:

$$\mathcal{P}(s) = \{s' : \exists \text{path from } s \text{ to } s'\}$$

The "size" of the possibility space can be measured in various ways:

  • Number of states
  • Diversity of states
  • Reachability of states

The core concept of RFD, "recursive freedom"[11], refers to the idea that the exercise of freedom should not extinguish freedom itself, that is, the space of future choices should be protected

§6.3.6 CSIA: Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment

I. Conceptual Definition

Definition 6.3.7 (CSIA)

Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment (CSIA) is a framework for comprehensively assessing the systemic impact of major actions.

where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of actions, and the output is a composite score and a risk level.

§6.4 The Overall Architecture of the Indicator System

§6.4.1 The Logical Relations among Indicators

I. Types of Relations among Indicators

Various logical relations exist among the six major indicators:

Table 6.16 Types of Relations among Indicators

Type of RelationDescriptionExample
Prerequisite relationOne indicator is a prerequisite for anotherUCS is a prerequisite for RFD
Complementary relationTwo indicators measure related concepts from different anglesRFD and CRV are complementary
Integrative relationOne indicator integrates other indicatorsCSIA integrates the other indicators
Constraint relationOne indicator constitutes a constraint on anotherMBCL constrains information propagation

II. Prerequisite Relation

UCS provides the subject basis for the other indicators. Only after the degree of consciousness of an entity (UCS) is determined can one assess the impact of its actions on the possibility space (RFD), the quality of its commitments (CRV), and so on.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFD}(a, e) \text{ is meaningful} \Rightarrow \text{UCS}(e) > \theta_{\text{min}}$$

that is, only when the UCS of an entity exceeds the minimum threshold is it meaningful to assess the RFD of its actions.

II. Complementary Relation

RFD and CRV measure the normative character of an action from different angles:

  • RFD focuses on the impact of the action on the possibility space
  • CRV focuses on the verifiability and reversibility of the action (as a commitment)

Formal expression:

$$\text{ActionQuality}(a) = f(\text{RFD}(a), \text{CRV}(a))$$

III. Integrative Relation

CSIA integrates the other indicators and provides a comprehensive assessment:

$$\text{CSIA}(a) = g(\text{UCS}, \text{RFD}(a), \text{CRV}(a), \text{CDI}, \text{MBCL})$$

IV. Constraint Relation

MBCL constitutes a constraint on information propagation:

$$\text{MBCL}(m) \geq 3 \Rightarrow \text{dissemination requires special approval}$$

III. Detailed Explanation of Tier Functions

(i) Foundational tier functions

The foundational tier provides the subject basis and background information for assessment:

  1. UCS determines which entities have moral subjecthood and the degree of that subjecthood
  2. CDI provides background information on civilizational development, offering a frame of reference for assessment

Formal expression:

$$\text{Context} = (\text{UCS}(\mathcal{E}), \text{CDI}(\mathcal{V}))$$

where $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of relevant entities and $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of relevant civilizations.

(ii) Assessment tier functions

The assessment tier assesses concrete actions and information:

  1. RFD assesses the impact of an action on the possibility space
  2. CRV assesses the quality of a commitment
  3. MBCL assesses the risk of information propagation

Formal expression:

$$\text{Evaluation}(a, m) = (\text{RFD}(a), \text{CRV}(a), \text{MBCL}(m))$$

where $a$ is the action and $m$ is the relevant meme.

(iii) Integration tier functions

The integration tier integrates the information of the foundational and assessment tiers and provides a comprehensive assessment:

$$\text{CSIA}(a) = h(\text{Context}, \text{Evaluation}(a, m))$$

IV. Feedback Mechanisms between Tiers

Between the tiers there is not only bottom-up information flow but also top-down feedback:

  1. The results of CSIA may trigger a reassessment of UCS: if CSIA finds that the impact of certain entities has been underestimated, their UCS may need to be reassessed
  2. The results of the assessment tier may revise the parameters of the foundational tier: if RFD assessment finds certain patterns of action, the assessment criteria of CDI may need to be adjusted

IV. Root Causes of the Maturity Gap

The root causes of the low maturity of the indicators include:

  1. Novelty of the concepts: many concepts (such as "possibility space" and "memetic risk") are newly proposed and lack a mature measurement tradition
  2. Interdisciplinarity: the indicators involve multiple disciplines and require interdisciplinary collaboration to be refined
  3. Hypotheticality of application scenarios: many application scenarios (such as interstellar communication) are currently hypothetical and cannot be validated in practice
  4. Deep uncertainty: many of the problems involved have deep uncertainty and are difficult to validate through traditional methods

§6.5.2 Usage Restrictions

I. Classification of Usage Restrictions

Based on the maturity assessment, this work proposes the following restrictions on the use of the indicators:

Table 6.23 Usage Restrictions of the Indicators

Type of RestrictionDescriptionApplicable Indicators
Prohibitive restrictionProhibited in specific situationsAll indicators
Conditional restrictionUsable only when specific conditions are metAll indicators
Procedural restrictionSpecific procedures must be followed when usingAll indicators

II. Prohibitive Restrictions

Restriction P1: Prohibition of using the indicators for mandatory decisions

At the current level of maturity, the indicators may not be used for:

  • Legal judgments
  • Mandatory resource allocation
  • Irreversible major decisions

Formal expression:

$$\text{TRL}(I) < 5 \Rightarrow \neg \text{Mandatory}(I)$$

Restriction P2: Prohibition of using the indicators for discriminatory purposes

The indicators may not be used for:

  • Discrimination based on UCS
  • Hierarchical classification of civilizations based on CDI
  • Any form of improper discrimination

III. Conditional Restrictions

Restriction C1: Conditions for use in academic research

The indicators may be used in academic research, but it must:

  • Explicitly state the maturity of the indicators
  • Report measurement uncertainty
  • Discuss the limitations of the indicators

Restriction C2: Conditions for use in policy consultation

The indicators may be used in policy consultation, but it must:

  • Serve as a reference rather than a decisive basis
  • Be used in combination with other assessment methods
  • Be subject to independent review

Restriction C3: Conditions for use in thought experiments

The indicators may be used in thought experiments, but it must:

  • Explicitly state the assumptions
  • Explore multiple scenarios
  • Avoid excessive inference

IV. Procedural Restrictions

Restriction R1: Requirement for reporting uncertainty

When using the indicators, the following must be reported:

  • Measurement uncertainty
  • Model uncertainty
  • Conceptual uncertainty

Formal expression:

$$\text{Report}(I) = (I_{\text{value}}, U_{\text{measurement}}, U_{\text{model}}, U_{\text{conceptual}})$$

Restriction R2: Requirement for multi-method validation

When using the indicators in important decisions, the following must be done:

  • Use multiple methods to calculate the indicators
  • Compare the results of different methods
  • Explain the reasons for discrepancies

Restriction R3: Requirement for stakeholder participation

When using the indicators in situations involving multiple parties' interests, the following must be done:

  • Invite stakeholders to participate in the assessment process
  • Publicize the assessment methods and data
  • Establish an appeal mechanism

§6.5.3 Development Roadmap

I. Development Goals

The development goal of the indicator system is to gradually raise its maturity, ultimately reaching a level usable for actual governance.

Table 6.24 Development Goals of the Indicators

PhaseTime FrameTRL GoalMain Tasks
Near term1-3 yearsTRL 3Proof of concept, preliminary operationalization
Medium term3-10 yearsTRL 5Validation in a relevant environment, refinement of methods
Long term10-30 yearsTRL 7+Demonstration in an operational environment, practical application

(i) Near-term development tasks (1-3 years)

Task N1: Conceptual clarification and formalization

  • Further clarify the definitions of core concepts
  • Refine the formal expressions
  • Establish the logical relations among concepts

Task N2: Development of operationalization procedures

  • Develop measurement procedures for each indicator
  • Establish data collection standards
  • Design calculation algorithms

Task N3: Preliminary validation

  • Test the indicators on simulated data
  • Conduct sensitivity analysis
  • Identify the main problems

Task N4: Establishment of interdisciplinary collaboration

  • Establish an interdisciplinary research network
  • Organize academic workshops
  • Publish academic papers

(ii) Medium-term development tasks (3-10 years)

Task M1: Refinement of methods

  • Refine the methods based on preliminary validation results
  • Develop multiple measurement methods
  • Establish a framework for comparing methods

Task M2: Validation in a relevant environment

  • Validate the indicators in relevant scenarios at the Earth scale
  • Collect actual data
  • Assess the validity of the indicators

Task M3: Testing of cross-substrate applicability

  • Test UCS on different types of AI systems
  • Assess cross-substrate applicability
  • Develop calibration methods

Task M4: Refinement of anti-Goodhart mechanisms

  • Monitor the Goodhart effect of the indicators
  • Refine the anti-Goodhart design
  • Establish dynamic adjustment mechanisms

(iii) Long-term development tasks (10-30 years)

Task L1: Demonstration in an operational environment

  • Trial the indicators in actual governance scenarios
  • Collect feedback
  • Continuously improve

Task L2: Institutionalization

  • Establish an institutional framework for the use of the indicators
  • Train users
  • Establish a certification mechanism

Task L3: International coordination

  • Promote international recognition of the indicators
  • Establish international coordination mechanisms
  • Address cross-cultural differences

II. Uncertainty of Development

The development roadmap involves significant uncertainty:

  1. Technological uncertainty: some measurement methods may not be developable
  2. Resource uncertainty: the resources required for development may not be obtainable
  3. Social uncertainty: societal acceptance of the indicators is uncertain
  4. External uncertainty: external events (such as AI breakthroughs or extraterrestrial contact) may change the development path

Response strategies:

  • Maintain the flexibility of the development roadmap
  • Review and adjust regularly
  • Establish multiple development paths
  • Conduct scenario analysis of key uncertainties

Chapter Summary

I. Summary of Core Conclusions

As the opening of Part Two, "The Indicator System," this chapter has completed the following core tasks:

Conclusion one: identification and analysis of the principle-operation gap

Interstellar civilization governance faces a fundamental gap from abstract principles to concrete operations. This gap unfolds along the three dimensions of abstractness, measurability, and temporality, and is significantly amplified in the context of interstellar civilization governance. The indicator system is the core tool for bridging this gap.

Conclusion two: establishment of the four principles of indicator design

This chapter has established the four meta-principles of indicator design:

PrincipleCore RequirementImplementation Mechanism
Normative anchoringEvery indicator must be anchored to a specific normative principleClear traceability of the anchoring chain
OperabilityThe indicator must be actually calculable and applicableData availability, computational feasibility, interpretational clarity
Cross-substrate applicabilityThe indicator must be able to cross differences in physical substrateFunctionalist definition, multimodal data fusion, calibration mechanism
Anti-Goodhart designThe indicator must resist the Goodhart effectMulti-indicator combination, process auditing, dynamic adjustment, meta-indicator monitoring

Conclusion three: overview of the six major indicator systems

This chapter has provided an overview of the six major indicator systems:

IndicatorFull NameCore FunctionAnchored Principle
UCSUniversal Consciousness ScaleMeasure the degree of consciousness of an entityPrinciple of Recursive Freedom
RFDRecursive Freedom DegreeMeasure the impact of an action on the possibility spacePrinciple of Recursive Freedom
CRVCommitment Reversibility VerifiabilityAssess the quality of commitmentsPrinciple of Reversibility
CDICivilizational Development IndexMeasure the multi-dimensional state of development of a civilizationPrinciple of Negentropy Responsibility
MBCLMemetic Biosafety Containment LevelAssess the risk of information propagationPrinciple of Reversibility
CSIACosmic-Scale Impact AssessmentComprehensively assess the impact of major actionsSynthesis of the three principles

Conclusion four: the overall architecture of the indicator system

The six major indicators form an organic whole with a three-tier architecture:

  • Foundational tier (UCS, CDI): provides the subject basis and background information
  • Assessment tier (RFD, CRV, MBCL): assesses concrete actions and information
  • Integration tier (CSIA): integrates assessments and supports decisions

Conclusion five: maturity statement and development roadmap

The six major indicators are all at the conceptual prototype stage around TRL 2. This chapter has clarified the usage restrictions (prohibitive, conditional, procedural) and the development roadmap (near, medium, and long term), providing a framework for the responsible use and continuous development of the indicators.

[1] Technology Readiness Level (TRL): The technology readiness level is a systematic assessment method developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) to assess the degree of maturity of a technology from concept to practical application. TRL 1-3 is the conceptual stage, TRL 4-6 the technology development stage, and TRL 7-9 the system development and operation stage. This work adopts TRL to identify the development stage of the indicator system. See: Mankins, J. C. (1995). Technology Readiness Levels. NASA White Paper; Mankins, J. C. (2009). "Technology Readiness Assessments: A Retrospective." Acta Astronautica, 65(9-10), 1216-1223.

[2] Principle-operation gap: The difficulty of transforming normative theory into practice is a long-standing problem in political philosophy and applied ethics. Rawls distinguished between "ideal theory" and "nonideal theory," the former focusing on the justification of principles and the latter on the application of principles. See: Rawls, J. (1971). A Theory of Justice. Harvard University Press, Part Three; Simmons, A. J. (2010). "Ideal and Nonideal Theory." Philosophy & Public Affairs, 38(1), 5-36.

[3] Operationalization: Operationalization is a core concept in social science methodology, referring to the process of transforming abstract theoretical concepts into measurable empirical indicators. This concept originates from logical positivism, and Bridgman's "operationalism" is its philosophical foundation. See: Bridgman, P. W. (1927). The Logic of Modern Physics. Macmillan; Blalock, H. M. (1982). Conceptualization and Measurement in the Social Sciences. Sage.

[4] Human Development Index (HDI): The HDI is a comprehensive development indicator published by the United Nations Development Programme since 1990, covering the three dimensions of life expectancy, education, and per capita income. The HDI transcends the limitations of a single economic indicator (such as GDP) and provides an important reference for the multi-dimensional design of CDI. See: UNDP. (1990). Human Development Report 1990. Oxford University Press; Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Knopf.

[5] Integrated Information Theory (IIT): The IIT is a theory of consciousness proposed by Giulio Tononi, holding that consciousness is the quantity of integrated information (expressed by the value Φ). The IIT provides the theoretical basis for the graded measurement of consciousness and is a core reference for the design of UCS. See: Tononi, G. (2004). "An Information Integration Theory of Consciousness." BMC Neuroscience, 5, 42; Tononi, G., Boly, M., Massimini, M., & Koch, C. (2016). "Integrated Information Theory: From Consciousness to Its Physical Substrate." Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 17(7), 450-461.

[6] Functionalism: Functionalism is an important position in the philosophy of mind, holding that mental states are defined by their functional roles rather than their physical realization. This position supports the multiple realizability of mind on different physical substrates and provides the philosophical foundation for cross-substrate applicability. See: Putnam, H. (1967). "Psychological Predicates." In W. H. Capitan & D. D. Merrill (Eds.), Art, Mind, and Religion. University of Pittsburgh Press; Block, N. (1980). "Troubles with Functionalism." In N. Block (Ed.), Readings in Philosophy of Psychology, Vol. 1. Harvard University Press.

[7] Goodhart's law: Goodhart's law was originally proposed by the British economist Charles Goodhart in 1975 in relation to monetary policy, and has since been widely applied in various fields of indicator evaluation. The law reveals the distorting effects that arise when a measurement indicator is transformed into a goal. See: Goodhart, C. A. E. (1984). Monetary Theory and Practice: The UK Experience. Macmillan, p. 96; Strathern, M. (1997). "'Improving Ratings': Audit in the British University System." European Review, 5(3), 305-321.

[8] Negentropy: The concept of negentropy was proposed by Schrödinger in What Is Life? to describe the process by which living systems draw order from the environment to maintain their own organization. Prigogine's theory of dissipative structures further developed this concept. See: Schrödinger, E. (1944). What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell. Cambridge University Press; Prigogine, I. (1967). Introduction to Thermodynamics of Irreversible Processes. Wiley.

[9] Biosafety Level (BSL): The BSL is a laboratory safety standard established by the World Health Organization and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, divided into four levels, BSL-1 to BSL-4, to regulate the handling of pathogens of different degrees of danger. MBCL draws on this grading idea. See: WHO. (2004). Laboratory Biosafety Manual (3rd ed.). World Health Organization; CDC/NIH. (2009). Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (5th ed.).

[10] Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA): The EIA is a procedure for assessing the possible environmental impact of a proposed project. It originated in the 1969 National Environmental Policy Act of the United States and has now become an internationally accepted tool of environmental management. CSIA extends the framework of the EIA to the cosmic scale. See: Glasson, J., Therivel, R., & Chadwick, A. (2012). Introduction to Environmental Impact Assessment (4th ed.). Routledge; Morgan, R. K. (2012). "Environmental Impact Assessment: The State of the Art." Impact Assessment and Project Appraisal, 30(1), 5-14.

[11] Recursive freedom: The concept of recursive freedom emphasizes the self-referential character of freedom: true freedom is not only the capacity for present choice but also the capacity to protect the space of future choice. This concept has intellectual affinities with Sen's "capability approach" and Nussbaum's "list of capabilities." See: Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Knopf; Nussbaum, M. C. (2011). Creating Capabilities: The Human Development Approach. Harvard University Press.

[12] Participatory cognition: Participatory cognition is a core concept of the 4E cognition (embodied, embedded, extended, enactive) paradigm, emphasizing that cognition is not an internal computation of the brain but a process of interaction between organism and environment. This concept comes from the "enactivist" tradition of cognitive science. See: Varela, F. J., Thompson, E., & Rosch, E. (1991). The Embodied Mind: Cognitive Science and Human Experience. MIT Press; Thompson, E. (2007). Mind in Life: Biology, Phenomenology, and the Sciences of Mind. Harvard University Press.

[13] Negotiability: The negotiability of knowledge is a core view of social constructivist epistemology, emphasizing that cognitive standards and knowledge claims are products of social negotiation rather than being fixed and unchangeable. This position provides an epistemological defense for the dynamic adjustment of indicators. See: Kuhn, T. S. (1962). The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. University of Chicago Press; Bloor, D. (1991). Knowledge and Social Imagery (2nd ed.). University of Chicago Press; Longino, H. E. (2002). The Fate of Knowledge. Princeton University Press.

Universal Consciousness Scale

Chapter Introduction

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

This chapter is the core chapter of Part II, "The Indicator System," and undertakes the key task of operationalizing the New View of Life (NL) into measurable indicators. Chapter 6 established the overall framework of the indicator system; this chapter, by contrast, provides an in-depth argument for the most philosophically challenging of the six major indicators: the Universal Consciousness Scale (UCS).

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

UCS is directly anchored to the core propositions of the New View of Life:

$$\text{UCS} \triangleleft \{\text{NL-1}, \text{NL-3}\}$$

Specifically:

  • NL-1 (consciousness is a fundamental feature of the universe) → the object measured by UCS has ontological status
  • NL-3 (consciousness is a gradational continuum) → UCS adopts a continuous scale rather than a binary classification
  • NL-4 (consciousness is substrate-independent) → UCS has cross-substrate applicability

V. The Core Question

This chapter attempts to answer a fundamental question:

Core question: How can "consciousness," the most elusive concept, be transformed into an operational measurement tool while maintaining philosophical rigor?

The answer to this question will determine how the foundational question of "whose interests ought to be considered" is handled in the governance of interstellar civilization.

VI. Boundary Statement

All content in this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Positioning as a conceptual prototype: UCS is at TRL 2, applicable to academic research and thought experiments
  2. Prohibition of coercive application: UCS must not be used for coercive adjudication of moral status
  3. Open revision: the dimensional design and measurement methods of UCS may be revised in light of new evidence
  4. Acknowledgment of the problem of other minds: UCS cannot fully resolve the "problem of other minds" [1] and can only provide indirect inference

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • Readers with an in-depth understanding of consciousness science may focus on §7.2 and §7.3
  • Readers concerned with ethical applications are advised to focus on §7.5
  • Readers wishing to understand the limitations of UCS may read §7.6 directly

§7.1 The Theoretical Foundations of UCS

§7.1.1 From NL-3 to UCS

I. Review of the Core Propositions of the New View of Life

Chapter 2 established three core propositions of the New View of Life:

Table 7.1 Core propositions of the New View of Life

Proposition No.Proposition ContentRelation to UCS

NL-2Life is a particular form of negentropic organization, dependent on the continuous acquisition of negentropic flowProvides constraints for the physical basis of UCS
NL-3Consciousness is a gradational continuum, not a binary state of present/absentProvides the basis for the continuous scale design of UCS
NL-4The essence of consciousness does not lie in a particular physical substrateProvides the basis for the cross-substrate applicability of UCS

Derivation from NL-3 to UCS

NL-3 is the direct theoretical foundation for the design of UCS. The core claim of this proposition is:

Proposition NL-3 (continuum of consciousness)

Consciousness is not a binary property (present or absent), but a gradational property that exists on a continuum from extremely low to extremely high.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{Consciousness}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

where $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of entities and $[0, 1]$ is the continuous interval of degrees of consciousness.

Derivation chain:

└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Definition 7.1.1 (conceptual definition of UCS)

The Universal Consciousness Scale (UCS) is a mapping function from a set of entities to a multidimensional consciousness space:

$$\text{UCS}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]^n$$

where:

  • $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of entities (including humans, animals, AI systems, possible extraterrestrial life, etc.)
  • $[0, 1]^n$ is the n-dimensional unit hypercube, each dimension corresponding to one aspect of consciousness
  • This work adopts $n = 5$, i.e., a five-dimensional design

Design principles of UCS

The design of UCS follows these principles:

Principle One: the principle of theoretical anchoring

UCS must be anchored to the core propositions of the New View of Life, in particular NL-3.

$$\text{UCS} \triangleleft \text{NL-3}$$

Principle Two: the multidimensional principle

Consciousness is a complex multidimensional phenomenon that cannot be fully characterized by a single numerical value. UCS adopts a multidimensional design, with each dimension capturing one aspect of consciousness.

$$\text{UCS}(e) = (D_1(e), D_2(e), D_3(e), D_4(e), D_5(e))$$

Principle Three: the principle of cross-substrate applicability

According to NL-4, UCS must be able to traverse different physical substrates.

$$\forall s_1, s_2 \in \text{Substrates}: \text{UCS} \text{ can be applied to } s_1 \land s_2$$

Principle Four: the functionalist principle

UCS focuses on the functional features of consciousness rather than a particular physical implementation.

$$\text{UCS}(e) = f(\text{FunctionalProperties}(e))$$

Principle Five: the revisability principle

UCS is revisable; when new evidence from consciousness science emerges, the dimensional design and measurement methods can be adjusted.

§7.1.2 The Gradational Hypothesis of Consciousness

I. The Content of the Gradational Hypothesis

The gradational hypothesis of consciousness is the core premise of the design of UCS. This hypothesis claims:

Hypothesis H7.1 (gradational hypothesis of consciousness)

Consciousness is a gradational property that exists on a continuum from extremely low (approaching zero) to extremely high. Different entities may possess different degrees of consciousness, and these degrees can be compared.

Formalized statement:

Let $C: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$ be the consciousness function. The gradational hypothesis claims:

  1. Continuity: the range of $C$ is continuous, not discrete
  2. Comparability: for any $e_1, e_2 \in \mathcal{E}$, $C(e_1)$ and $C(e_2)$ can be compared
  3. Non-binarity: there exists $e$ such that $0 < C(e) < 1$

II. Empirical Support for the Gradational Hypothesis

The gradational hypothesis receives empirical support from multiple disciplines:

III. The Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI)

The Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) developed by Massimini et al. provides direct measurement evidence for the gradational nature of consciousness.

Definition 7.1.2 (perturbational complexity index)

$$\text{PCI} = \frac{L(Z)}{S}$$

where:

  • $L(Z)$ is the Lempel-Ziv complexity of the EEG response evoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
  • $S$ is the number of signal sources

The PCI value is positively correlated with the level of consciousness:

Deep sleep0.1-0.3Low

Awake0.4-0.7High
Minimally conscious state0.3-0.5Medium
Vegetative state0.1-0.3Low

Research in comparative psychology shows that different species display different degrees of cognitive ability, supporting the gradational hypothesis of consciousness.

V. Philosophical Defense of the Gradational Hypothesis

The gradational hypothesis has not only empirical support but also philosophical defenses:

Defense One: the functionalist argument

If consciousness is a certain kind of functional state, and function admits of differences in degree, then consciousness can also admit of differences in degree.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{Consciousness} = f(\text{Function}) \land \text{Function is gradational} \Rightarrow \text{Consciousness is gradational}$$

Defense Two: the information integration argument

According to Integrated Information Theory (IIT), consciousness is related to the degree of information integration (Φ). Since Φ is a continuous variable, consciousness should also be gradational.

$$\text{Consciousness} \propto \Phi \land \Phi \in \mathbb{R}^+ \Rightarrow \text{Consciousness is gradational}$$

Defense Three: the evolutionary continuity argument

If consciousness is a product of evolution, and evolution is gradual, then conscious capacity should also develop gradually rather than appearing suddenly.

$$\text{Evolution is gradual} \land \text{Consciousness is a product of evolution} \Rightarrow \text{Consciousness is gradational}$$

VI. Objections to the Gradational Hypothesis and Responses

Objection One: the unity-of-consciousness argument

Some hold that consciousness possesses unity, either fully present or fully absent, with no such thing as "partial consciousness."

Response: unity can itself be gradational. A system can possess degrees of unity, from highly fragmented to highly integrated.

Objection Two: the incomparability of subjectivity

Some hold that subjective experience is incomparable, and therefore degrees of consciousness are also incomparable.

Response: while the qualitative aspects of subjective experience may be incomparable, the functional aspects of consciousness (such as information integration and the complexity of the self-model) are comparable. UCS focuses on the functional aspects.

Objection Three: the impossibility of measurement

Some hold that consciousness is subjective and in principle cannot be objectively measured.

Response: UCS does not claim to directly measure subjective experience, but rather to measure functional features associated with consciousness. These functional features can be measured indirectly.

§7.1.3 The Challenge of Cross-Substrate Assessment

I. The Necessity of Cross-Substrate Assessment

One of the core challenges of interstellar civilization governance is dealing with intelligent entities possessing different physical substrates. UCS must be able to traverse substrate differences and provide comparable assessment results.

Definition 7.1.3 (cross-substrate assessment)

Cross-Substrate Assessment refers to the assessment of the degree of consciousness of entities possessing different physical substrates, such that the assessment results are comparable.

Formalized statement:

Let $S = \{s_1, s_2, ..., s_k\}$ be the set of substrate types. Cross-substrate assessment requires:

$$\forall s_i, s_j \in S, \forall e_i \in \mathcal{E}_{s_i}, e_j \in \mathcal{E}_{s_j}: \text{UCS}(e_i) \text{ and } \text{UCS}(e_j) \text{ are comparable}$$

II. Classification of Substrate Types

Table 7.4 Classification of substrate types

Substrate TypeDescriptionExampleCurrent Assessability
Carbon-based biologyOrganisms based on carbon chemistryHumans, animalsHigh
Silicon-based computationComputing systems based on silicon chipsCurrent AI systemsMedium
Quantum computingComputing systems based on quantum effectsQuantum computersLow
Hybrid systemsMixtures of multiple substratesBrain-computer interfacesMedium-low
Unknown substratesSubstrate types not yet discoveredPossible extraterrestrial lifeExtremely low

III. Three Major Challenges of Cross-Substrate Assessment

Challenge One: the problem of functional equivalence

Different substrates may implement the same function in different ways. How can we determine that two implementations are "functionally equivalent"?

Formalized statement:

Let $F$ be a function, and $R_1$ and $R_2$ be implementations in two different substrates. The problem of functional equivalence is:

$$R_1 \equiv_F R_2 \Leftrightarrow ?$$

that is, how to define the criterion for determining functional equivalence.

Response strategies:

  1. Behavioral equivalence: if two implementations produce the same behavioral output, they are regarded as functionally equivalent
  2. Causal-structural equivalence: if two implementations possess the same causal structure, they are regarded as functionally equivalent
  3. Information-processing equivalence: if two implementations perform the same information processing, they are regarded as functionally equivalent

This work adopts information-processing equivalence as the primary criterion, supplemented by behavioral equivalence for verification.

Challenge Two: the problem of data comparability

Entities with different substrates produce different types of data. How can these data be converted into comparable UCS values?

Formalized statement:

Let $D_1$ and $D_2$ be the data types produced by two substrates. The problem of data comparability is:

$$\exists T: D_1 \times D_2 \rightarrow D_{\text{common}} \text{ such that } \text{UCS}(T(d_1)) \sim \text{UCS}(T(d_2))$$

that is, whether there exists a valid data transformation function.

Response strategies:

  1. Abstraction-layer transformation: transform different types of data to a common abstraction layer
  2. Functional-indicator extraction: extract common functional indicators from different data
  3. Calibration entities: use entities with known UCS values for calibration

Challenge Three: the problem of normative equivalence

Entities with different substrates may possess different normative statuses. Should UCS reflect such differences?

Formalized statement:

Let $N(e)$ be the normative status of entity $e$. The problem of normative equivalence is:

$$\text{UCS}(e_1) = \text{UCS}(e_2) \Rightarrow N(e_1) = N(e_2) ?$$

that is, whether the same UCS value implies the same normative status.

Response strategies:

The position of this work is: UCS measures the degree of consciousness, whereas normative status is jointly determined by the degree of consciousness and other factors. Therefore:

$$N(e) = g(\text{UCS}(e), \text{OtherFactors}(e))$$

UCS is a necessary but not sufficient condition for normative status.

V. Relation to the New Three Views

The challenge of cross-substrate assessment directly echoes proposition NL-4 of the New View of Life (substrate independence).

According to NL-4, the essence of consciousness does not lie in a particular physical substrate, but in a pattern of information processing. This proposition provides the ontological basis for cross-substrate assessment:

$$\text{NL-4} \Rightarrow \text{consciousness can be implemented on different substrates} \Rightarrow \text{cross-substrate assessment is possible}$$

However, NL-4 also brings a methodological challenge: if consciousness is substrate-independent, how can we ensure that the measurement methods of UCS are not biased toward a particular substrate?

Response strategies:

  1. Functionalist definitions: each dimension of UCS is defined on the basis of functional properties rather than substrate-specific properties
  2. Multimodal measurement: develop multiple measurement methods for each dimension, applicable to different substrates
  3. Continuous calibration: continuously calibrate the measurement methods as understanding of different substrates deepens
