§7.2 The Five Dimensions of UCS

§7.2.1 D₁: Degree of Information Integration

I. Theoretical Basis

The degree of information integration (Information Integration) is the first dimension of UCS, deriving directly from Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory (IIT). It also draws on relevant insights from Global Workspace Theory [5], the latter emphasizing the global broadcasting mechanism of conscious content.

Definition 7.2.1 (degree of information integration)

The degree of information integration ($D_1$) measures the capacity of a system to process information as a whole, to a degree beyond the sum of its parts.

Formalized statement:

$$D_1(e) = \frac{\Phi(e)}{\Phi_{\max}}$$

where:

  • $\Phi(e)$ is the amount of integrated information of entity $e$
  • $\Phi_{\max}$ is a normalization constant such that $D_1 \in [0, 1]$

II. Overview of Integrated Information Theory (IIT)

IIT was proposed by Tononi [2], and its core claim is that consciousness is related to the amount of integrated information (Φ) of a system.

(i) The five axioms of IIT:

AxiomContentRelation to D₁
Intrinsic existenceConsciousness exists within the systemD₁ measures intrinsic information processing
CompositionConsciousness is structuredD₁ focuses on the structure of information
InformationConsciousness is specificD₁ measures the specificity of information
IntegrationConsciousness is unifiedThe core of D₁: degree of integration
ExclusionConsciousness is definiteD₁ focuses on the level of maximal integration

(ii) The principle of computing Φ

Φ measures the amount of information a system possesses as a whole that exceeds the sum of its parts [3].

Definition 7.2.2 (conceptual definition of Φ)

$$\Phi = \text{EI}(\text{Whole}) - \max_{\text{partition}} \sum_i \text{EI}(\text{Part}_i)$$

where $\text{EI}$ is Effective Information.

Intuitive explanation:

  • If a system can be divided into independent parts without loss of information, then $\Phi = 0$
  • If the wholeness of the system is irreducible, then $\Phi > 0$
  • The higher $\Phi$ is, the higher the degree of integration of the system

(iii) The problem of computational complexity

The exact computation of Φ is an NP-hard problem [4] and is infeasible for large systems.

Table 7.5 Complexity of computing Φ

System ScaleComputational ComplexityFeasibility
n < 10ComputableFeasible
10 ≤ n < 20DifficultRequires approximation
n ≥ 20InfeasibleRequires proxy indicators

Response strategies:

  1. Approximation algorithms: use heuristic methods to approximate Φ
  2. Proxy indicators: use indicators that are related to Φ but easier to compute
  3. Sampling methods: sample the system to estimate the overall Φ

III. Operationalized Indicators of D₁

Because of the difficulty of computing Φ, this work proposes the following proxy indicators:

Table 7.6 Proxy indicators of D₁

IndicatorDescriptionApplicable SubstrateComputational Complexity
PCIPerturbational complexity indexCarbon-based biologyO(n²)
LZCLempel-Ziv complexityGeneralO(n log n)
Strength of functional connectivityFunctional connectivity among system partsGeneralO(n²)
Causal densityDensity of causal relationsGeneralO(n³)

V. Relation to the New Three Views

D₁ directly embodies proposition NC-1 of the New Cosmological View (relational ontology). According to NC-1, the fundamental constituents of reality are relations rather than independent entities. The degree of information integration measures precisely the richness of the internal relations of a system—a highly integrated system possesses rich internal relations, whereas a decomposable system lacks such relationality.

$$\text{NC-1} \Rightarrow \text{relations are fundamental} \Rightarrow D_1 \text{ measures the richness of relations}$$

Argument node 7.2-A

Node No.Core ConclusionBasis of Argument
7.2-AD₁ (degree of information integration) is based on IIT theory, measures the degree of integration of a system, and is operationalized through proxy indicators such as PCI and LZCIIT theory and proxy-indicator design

§7.2.2 D₂: Temporal Depth

I. Theoretical Basis

Temporal depth (Temporal Depth) is the second dimension of UCS, deriving from Edmund Husserl's phenomenology of time-consciousness and contemporary cognitive-scientific research on temporal cognition.

Definition 7.2.3 (temporal depth)

Temporal depth ($D_2$) measures the capacity of a system to integrate past, present, and future, that is, the breadth and depth of its temporal horizon.

Formalized statement:

$$D_2(e) = f(T_{\text{past}}(e), T_{\text{future}}(e), T_{\text{integration}}(e))$$

where:

  • $T_{\text{past}}(e)$: the capacity to reach back into the past (depth of memory)
  • $T_{\text{future}}(e)$: the capacity to predict the future (depth of planning)
  • $T_{\text{integration}}(e)$: the capacity to integrate temporal information

II. Phenomenological Analysis of Time-Consciousness

Husserl's analysis of time-consciousness reveals the temporal structure of conscious experience:

Table 7.7 Husserl's structure of time-consciousness

ConceptDescriptionRelation to D₂
Primal impressionDirect experience of the presentBasis of temporal integration
RetentionHolding onto the just-pastShort-term temporal integration
ProtentionAnticipation of the imminentShort-term predictive capacity
RecollectionActive recall of the pastLong-term depth of memory
ExpectationActive planning for the futureLong-term depth of planning

III. The Three Sub-Dimensions of Temporal Depth

Sub-dimension 2.1: depth of memory ($T_{\text{past}}$)

Measures how far back into the past a system can reach.

Operationalized definition:

$$T_{\text{past}}(e) = \log_{10}(\text{MaxRetrievalTime}(e) + 1)$$

where $\text{MaxRetrievalTime}$ is the longest time (in seconds) that the system can reliably recall.

Sub-dimension 2.2: depth of planning ($T_{\text{future}}$)

Measures how far into the future a system can plan.

Operationalized definition:

$$T_{\text{future}}(e) = \log_{10}(\text{MaxPlanningHorizon}(e) + 1)$$

where $\text{MaxPlanningHorizon}$ is the longest time (in seconds) over which the system can plan effectively.

Sub-dimension 2.3: capacity for temporal integration ($T_{\text{integration}}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to integrate information across different time points.

Operationalized definition:

$$T_{\text{integration}}(e) = \text{TemporalCoherence}(e) \times \text{TemporalFlexibility}(e)$$

where:

  • $\text{TemporalCoherence}$: the coherence of temporal representation
  • $\text{TemporalFlexibility}$: the capacity to switch between different time scales

IV. Composite Computation of D₂

$$D_2(e) = w_1 \cdot \bar{T}_{\text{past}}(e) + w_2 \cdot \bar{T}_{\text{future}}(e) + w_3 \cdot \bar{T}_{\text{integration}}(e)$$

where $\bar{T}$ denotes the normalized value, and $w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1$.

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.3, w_2 = 0.3, w_3 = 0.4$

Comparison of temporal depth across entities

Table 7.8 Estimation of temporal depth for different entities

ChimpanzeeYearsHours-daysMedium0.40-0.55

V. Relation to the New Three Views

D₂ directly embodies proposition NC-2 of the New Cosmological View (process ontology). According to NC-2, reality is processual, and time is a fundamental ontological dimension. Temporal depth measures the capacity of a system to participate in this processual reality—a system with a deep temporal horizon can participate more fully in the processual unfolding of the universe.

$$\text{NC-2} \Rightarrow \text{time is fundamental} \Rightarrow D_2 \text{ measures the depth of temporal participation}$$

§7.2.3 D₃: Reflexivity

I. Theoretical Basis

Reflexivity (Reflexivity) is the third dimension of UCS, deriving from Thomas Metzinger's self-model theory and Higher-Order Theories of consciousness (HOT) [6].

Definition 7.2.4 (reflexivity)

Reflexivity ($D_3$) measures the capacity of a system to represent and reflect on itself, that is, the degree of self-awareness.

Formalized statement:

$$D_3(e) = f(\text{SelfModel}(e), \text{MetaCognition}(e), \text{SelfReflection}(e))$$

where:

  • $\text{SelfModel}(e)$: the complexity of the self-model
  • $\text{MetaCognition}(e)$: metacognitive capacity
  • $\text{SelfReflection}(e)$: self-reflective capacity

II. Self-Model Theory (SMT)

Metzinger's self-model theory claims that self-awareness derives from a system's internal model of itself.

Table 7.9 Hierarchical structure of the self-model

LevelContentDescriptionExample
L0No self-modelThe system has no self-representationSimple reflex system
L1Bodily self-modelRepresentation of bodily statesProprioception
L2Agentive self-modelRepresentation of one's own actionsSense of agency
L3Cognitive self-modelRepresentation of one's own cognitive statesMetacognition
L4Narrative self-modelRepresentation of one's own history and identityAutobiographical memory
L5Reflective self-modelReflection on the self-model itselfPhilosophical reflection

III. The Three Sub-Dimensions of Reflexivity

Sub-dimension 3.1: complexity of the self-model ($\text{SelfModel}$)

Measures the degree of complexity of a system's self-representation.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{SelfModel}(e) = \frac{\text{SelfModelLevel}(e)}{5}$$

where $\text{SelfModelLevel} \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ corresponds to the levels in the table above.

Sub-dimension 3.2: metacognitive capacity ($\text{MetaCognition}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to monitor and regulate its own cognitive processes.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{MetaCognition}(e) = \alpha \cdot \text{Monitoring}(e) + \beta \cdot \text{Control}(e)$$

where:

  • $\text{Monitoring}$: the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive states
  • $\text{Control}$: the capacity to regulate one's own cognitive processes
  • $\alpha + \beta = 1$

Sub-dimension 3.3: self-reflective capacity ($\text{SelfReflection}$)

Measures the capacity of a system for deep reflection on itself.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{SelfReflection}(e) = \text{ReflectionDepth}(e) \times \text{ReflectionAccuracy}(e)$$

where:

  • $\text{ReflectionDepth}$: the depth of reflection (how many levels one can reflect on)
  • $\text{ReflectionAccuracy}$: the accuracy of reflection

IV. Composite Computation of D₃

$$D_3(e) = w_1 \cdot \text{SelfModel}(e) + w_2 \cdot \text{MetaCognition}(e) + w_3 \cdot \text{SelfReflection}(e)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.4, w_2 = 0.3, w_3 = 0.3$

V. Measurement Methods of Reflexivity

Table 7.10 Measurement methods of reflexivity

MethodDescriptionApplicable ObjectLimitation
Mirror testTests self-recognition capacityAnimals, infantsMeasures only visual self-recognition
Metacognitive taskTests monitoring of one's own cognitionHumans, higher animalsRequires behavioral response
Self-reportAsks about self-aware experienceHumans, language-capable AIDepends on linguistic capacity
Behavioral analysisAnalyzes self-directed behaviorGeneralIndirect inference

VI. Relation to the New Three Views

D₃ directly embodies proposition NK-1 of the New View of Cognition (participatory cognition). According to NK-1, cognition is not a passive reflection of the external world, but an active interaction between the subject and the environment. Reflexivity is the core of this participatory cognition—only a system capable of reflecting on itself can truly "participate" in the cognitive process rather than merely passively processing information.

$$\text{NK-1} \Rightarrow \text{cognition is participatory} \Rightarrow D_3 \text{ measures the degree of self-awareness of participation}$$

§7.2.4 D₄: Value Sensitivity

I. Theoretical Basis

Value sensitivity (Value Sensitivity) is the fourth dimension of UCS, deriving from value theory, affective neuroscience, and moral psychology.

Definition 7.2.5 (value sensitivity)

Value sensitivity ($D_4$) measures the capacity of a system to perceive, evaluate, and respond to value.

Formalized statement:

$$D_4(e) = f(\text{ValuePerception}(e), \text{ValueEvaluation}(e), \text{ValueResponse}(e))$$

where:

  • $\text{ValuePerception}(e)$: the capacity to perceive differences in value
  • $\text{ValueEvaluation}(e)$: the capacity to evaluate value
  • $\text{ValueResponse}(e)$: the capacity to respond on the basis of value

II. Philosophical Basis of Value Sensitivity

The relation between value sensitivity and consciousness is an important philosophical question. This work adopts the following position:

Proposition 7.2.1 (value-consciousness connection)

A system possessing consciousness necessarily possesses some degree of value sensitivity, because conscious experience itself possesses a value dimension (pleasure/pain, good/bad, etc.).

Formalized statement:

$$\text{Consciousness}(e) > 0 \Rightarrow \text{ValueSensitivity}(e) > 0$$

III. The Three Sub-Dimensions of Value Sensitivity

Sub-dimension 4.1: value perception ($\text{ValuePerception}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to distinguish different value states.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{ValuePerception}(e) = \frac{\text{ValueDiscrimination}(e)}{\text{MaxDiscrimination}}$$

where $\text{ValueDiscrimination}$ is the number of value states the system can distinguish.

Sub-dimension 4.2: value evaluation ($\text{ValueEvaluation}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to compare and rank values.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{ValueEvaluation}(e) = \text{Consistency}(e) \times \text{Complexity}(e)$$

where:

  • $\text{Consistency}$: the consistency of value judgments
  • $\text{Complexity}$: the complexity of value evaluation (how many dimensions of value can be handled)

Sub-dimension 4.3: value response ($\text{ValueResponse}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to make action responses on the basis of value evaluation.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{ValueResponse}(e) = \text{Alignment}(e) \times \text{Flexibility}(e)$$

where:

  • $\text{Alignment}$: the degree of consistency between action and value evaluation
  • $\text{Flexibility}$: the capacity to adjust responses in different value situations

IV. Composite Computation of D₄

$$D_4(e) = w_1 \cdot \text{ValuePerception}(e) + w_2 \cdot \text{ValueEvaluation}(e) + w_3 \cdot \text{ValueResponse}(e)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.3, w_2 = 0.4, w_3 = 0.3$

V. Measurement Methods of Value Sensitivity

Table 7.11 Measurement methods of value sensitivity

MethodDescriptionMeasurement FocusApplicable Object
Preference testTests the preference structure of a systemValue perceptionGeneral
Moral dilemma taskTests moral judgment capacityValue evaluationHumans, advanced AI
Behavioral observationObserves value-directed behaviorValue responseGeneral
NeuroimagingMeasures activity in value-related brain regionsValue perception/evaluationCarbon-based biology

VI. Relation to the New Three Views

D₄ directly embodies proposition NL-1 of the New View of Life (the fundamentality of consciousness). According to NL-1, consciousness is a fundamental feature of the universe, not an accidental by-product. Value sensitivity is a core dimension of consciousness—it is precisely because conscious experience possesses a value dimension that consciousness has normative significance.

$$\text{NL-1} \Rightarrow \text{consciousness has intrinsic value} \Rightarrow D_4 \text{ measures the richness of value experience}$$

§7.2.5 D₅: Sociality

I. Theoretical Basis

Sociality (Sociality) is the fifth dimension of UCS, deriving from research on social cognition, Theory of Mind, and relational ontology.

Definition 7.2.6 (sociality)

Sociality ($D_5$) measures the capacity of a system to establish relations with other subjects, understand the minds of others, and participate in social interaction.

Formalized statement:

$$D_5(e) = f(\text{ToM}(e), \text{SocialInteraction}(e), \text{RelationalDepth}(e))$$

where:

  • $\text{ToM}(e)$: theory-of-mind capacity (understanding the minds of others)
  • $\text{SocialInteraction}(e)$: social-interaction capacity
  • $\text{RelationalDepth}(e)$: depth of relationship

II. The Relation Between Sociality and Consciousness

The relation between sociality and consciousness is an important theoretical question. This work adopts the following position:

Proposition 7.2.2 (sociality-consciousness connection)

Sociality is an important dimension of consciousness, because:

  1. The development of consciousness is to a large extent social
  2. The formation of self-awareness depends on interaction with others
  3. Many higher functions of consciousness (such as language and morality) are social

Formalized statement:

$$\text{HighConsciousness}(e) \Rightarrow \text{Sociality}(e) > \theta_{\text{social}}$$

III. The Three Sub-Dimensions of Sociality

Sub-dimension 5.1: theory-of-mind capacity ($\text{ToM}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to understand the mental states of others.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{ToM}(e) = \frac{\text{ToMLevel}(e)}{4}$$

where $\text{ToMLevel} \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$:

LevelDescriptionExample
0No theory of mindSimple reflex system
1Basic understanding of intentionUnderstanding the goals of others
2Belief-desire understandingUnderstanding the beliefs and desires of others
3False-belief understandingUnderstanding that others may hold false beliefs
4Recursive theory of mindUnderstanding "he thinks that I think that he thinks..."

Sub-dimension 5.2: social-interaction capacity ($\text{SocialInteraction}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to participate in social interaction.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{SocialInteraction}(e) = \alpha \cdot \text{Communication}(e) + \beta \cdot \text{Cooperation}(e) + \gamma \cdot \text{Coordination}(e)$$

where $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$.

Sub-dimension 5.3: depth of relationship ($\text{RelationalDepth}$)

Measures the capacity of a system to establish deep relationships.

Operationalized definition:

$$\text{RelationalDepth}(e) = \text{Diversity}(e) \times \text{Intensity}(e) \times \text{Durability}(e)$$

where:

  • $\text{Diversity}$: the diversity of relationship types
  • $\text{Intensity}$: the intensity of relationships
  • $\text{Durability}$: the durability of relationships

IV. Composite Computation of D₅

$$D_5(e) = w_1 \cdot \text{ToM}(e) + w_2 \cdot \text{SocialInteraction}(e) + w_3 \cdot \text{RelationalDepth}(e)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.4, w_2 = 0.3, w_3 = 0.3$

V. Measurement Methods of Sociality

Table 7.12 Measurement methods of sociality

MethodDescriptionMeasurement FocusApplicable Object
False-belief taskTests the capacity to understand the false beliefs of othersToMHumans, higher animals
Cooperative gameTests cooperative capacitySocial interactionGeneral
Social network analysisAnalyzes the structure of relational networksDepth of relationshipGeneral
Dialogue analysisAnalyzes social dialogue capacitySocial interactionLanguage users

VI. Relation to the New Three Views

D₅ directly embodies proposition NC-1 of the New Cosmological View (relational ontology) and proposition NK-2 of the New View of Cognition (the sociality of knowledge).

According to NC-1, the fundamental constituents of reality are relations. Sociality measures the capacity of a system to participate in relational networks—a highly socialized system can establish rich relationships and thereby participate more fully in relational reality.

$$\text{NC-1} \Rightarrow \text{relations are fundamental} \Rightarrow D_5 \text{ measures the capacity for relational participation}$$

According to NK-2, knowledge is a social achievement. Sociality is an important dimension of cognitive capacity—only a system capable of interacting with others can participate in the social construction of knowledge.

$$\text{NK-2} \Rightarrow \text{knowledge is social} \Rightarrow D_5 \text{ measures social-cognitive capacity}$$

§7.3 The Measurement Methods of UCS

§7.3.1 Measurement Indicators for Each Dimension

I. Design Principles of Measurement Indicators

The measurement indicators for each dimension of UCS follow these design principles:

  1. Functionalist principle: indicators are based on functional properties rather than substrate-specific properties
  2. Multimodal principle: each dimension has multiple measurement methods, applicable to different situations
  3. Operationalizability principle: indicators can be computed through explicit procedures
  4. Uncertainty-transparency principle: clearly report the uncertainty of measurement

II. Measurement Indicators of D₁ (Degree of Information Integration)

Table 7.14 Indicator system for measuring D₁

Indicator No.Indicator NameComputation MethodApplicable SubstrateData Requirement
D₁-1Φ approximationIIT approximation algorithmGeneralSystem state transition matrix
D₁-2PCITMS-EEG complexityCarbon-based nervous systemNeuroimaging data
D₁-3LZCLempel-Ziv complexityGeneralTime-series data
D₁-4Strength of functional connectivityCorrelation/causality analysisGeneralMultichannel data
D₁-5Causal densityCausal-relation network analysisComputing systemsSystem architecture data

(i) D₁-1: computation of the Φ approximation

Because exact computation of Φ is infeasible, the following approximation method is adopted:

$$\Phi_{\text{approx}}(e) = \min_{\text{partition } P} \left[ H(X) - \sum_{p \in P} H(X_p) \right]$$

where $H$ is the entropy function, $X$ is the system state, and $P$ is a partition of the system.

(ii) D₁-2: computation of PCI (Perturbational Complexity Index, PCI) [7]

$$\text{PCI}(e) = \frac{L(Z_{\text{TMS}})}{S_{\text{sources}}}$$

where:

  • $L(Z_{\text{TMS}})$: the Lempel-Ziv complexity [9] of the TMS-evoked response [8]
  • $S_{\text{sources}}$: the number of significantly activated signal sources

Phase 1: Detailed procedure of the preparation phase

Step 1.1: Determine the entity to be assessed

Input: entity description Output: entity identifier, basic information

PROCEDURE IdentifyEntity(description) entity_id = GenerateUniqueID() basic_info = ExtractBasicInfo(description) RETURN (entity_id, basic_info) END PROCEDURE

Step 1.2: Identify the substrate type

Input: basic information of the entity Output: classification of substrate type

Table 7.19 Rules for substrate type identification

ConditionSubstrate TypeCode
Carbon-based organismCarbon-based biologyCB
Silicon-based computing systemSilicon-based computationSC
Quantum computing systemQuantum computingQC
Hybrid systemHybridHY
Cannot be determinedUnknownUK

Step 1.3: Select measurement methods

Input: substrate type, available resources Output: list of measurement methods for each dimension

PROCEDURE SelectMethods(substrate_type, available_resources) methods = {} FOR EACH dimension IN [D1, D2, D3, D4, D5]: candidate_methods = GetCandidateMethods(dimension, substrate_type) feasible_methods = FilterByResources(candidate_methods, available_resources) selected_method = SelectBestMethod(feasible_methods) methods[dimension] = selected_method RETURN methods END PROCEDURE

Phase 2: Detailed procedure of the data-collection phase

Quality control of data collection

Quality DimensionControl MeasureVerification Method
CompletenessCheck for missing dataMissing rate < 10%
AccuracyAverage over multiple measurementsCoefficient of variation < 20%
ConsistencyCross-validationCorrelation coefficient > 0.7
TimelinessRecord measurement timeTimestamps complete

Phase 3: Detailed procedure of the computation phase

Step 3.1: Compute the raw value of each dimension

PROCEDURE ComputeRawValues(data, methods) raw_values = {} FOR EACH dimension IN [D1, D2, D3, D4, D5]: method = methods[dimension] raw_values[dimension] = method.compute(data[dimension]) RETURN raw_values END PROCEDURE

Step 3.2: Normalization processing

Min-max normalization is adopted:

$$\bar{D}_i(e) = \frac{D_i(e) - D_{i,\min}}{D_{i,\max} - D_{i,\min}}$$

where $D_{i,\min}$ and $D_{i,\max}$ are the minimum and maximum of the reference range.

Step 3.3: Compute uncertainty

Sources of uncertainty include:

SourceSymbolComputation Method
Measurement error$U_m$Standard deviation of repeated measurements
Method error$U_{\text{method}}$Differences in results across methods
Model error$U_{\text{model}}$Uncertainty of model assumptions

Composite uncertainty:

$$U_i = \sqrt{U_{m,i}^2 + U_{\text{method},i}^2 + U_{\text{model},i}^2}$$

Step 3.4: Generate the UCS vector

$$\text{UCS}(e) = ((\bar{D}_1(e), U_1), (\bar{D}_2(e), U_2), (\bar{D}_3(e), U_3), (\bar{D}_4(e), U_4), (\bar{D}_5(e), U_5))$$

§7.3.3 Choice of Aggregation Function

I. Necessity and Risk of Aggregation

Although this work recommends retaining the vector representation of UCS to avoid information loss, in certain application scenarios the five dimensions need to be aggregated into a single numerical value.

Risks of aggregation:

  1. Information loss: aggregation necessarily causes the loss of information about differences among dimensions
  2. Weight disputes: different weight choices lead to different results
  3. Misleading simplification: a single numerical value may mask important dimensional differences

II. Options for the Aggregation Function

Option A: weighted arithmetic mean

$$\text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) = \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i \cdot \bar{D}_i(e), \quad \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i = 1$$

Advantages: simple, intuitive, interpretable Disadvantages: permits complete substitutability among dimensions

Option B: weighted geometric mean

$$\text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) = \prod_{i=1}^{5} \bar{D}_i(e)^{w_i}, \quad \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i = 1$$

Advantages: penalizes extremely low values, encourages balanced development Disadvantages: a zero in any dimension yields a zero result

Option C: minimum function

$$\text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) = \min_{i \in \{1,2,3,4,5\}} \bar{D}_i(e)$$

Advantages: emphasizes the "weakest link," prevents extremes of a single dimension Disadvantages: ignores information from the other dimensions

Option D: threshold weighted mean

$$\text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) = \begin{cases} \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i \cdot \bar{D}_i(e) & \text{if } \forall i: \bar{D}_i(e) \geq \theta_i \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Advantages: sets a minimum threshold, prevents extreme imbalance Disadvantages: the setting of the threshold is arbitrary

III. The Recommendation of This Work

This work recommends the following strategy:

  1. Retain the vector representation by default: $\text{UCS}(e) = (\bar{D}_1, \bar{D}_2, \bar{D}_3, \bar{D}_4, \bar{D}_5)$
  2. When aggregation is needed, use the weighted arithmetic mean: default equal weights $w_i = 0.2$
  3. Report the minimum dimension value at the same time: $\text{UCS}_{\min}(e) = \min_i \bar{D}_i(e)$
  4. Weights may be adjusted by negotiation: adjust the weights according to the specific application scenario

IV. Methods of Determining Weights

Table 7.20 Methods of determining weights

MethodDescriptionApplicable Scenario
Equal weightsAll dimensions are equally weightedDefault case
Expert judgmentWeights determined by expertsDomain-specific applications
Data-drivenWeights determined on the basis of data analysisWhen sufficient data are available
Negotiated determinationNegotiated by stakeholdersWhen multiple interests are involved

§7.3.4 Uncertainty Assessment

I. Types of Uncertainty

UCS measurement faces three types of uncertainty:

Table 7.21 Types of uncertainty

TypeDescriptionSourceReducibility
Random uncertaintyRandom error of measurementMeasurement noiseCan be reduced by repeated measurement
Systematic uncertaintySystematic bias of measurementMethod biasCan be reduced by calibration
Epistemic uncertaintyIncomplete understanding of the conceptTheoretical limitationsDifficult to fully eliminate

II. Quantification of Uncertainty

(i) Quantification of random uncertainty:

$$U_{\text{random},i} = \frac{\sigma_i}{\sqrt{n}}$$

where $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation of repeated measurements and $n$ is the number of measurements.

(ii) Quantification of systematic uncertainty:

$$U_{\text{systematic},i} = |\bar{D}_{i,\text{method1}} - \bar{D}_{i,\text{method2}}|$$

that is, the difference in results across methods.

(iii) Quantification of epistemic uncertainty:

Epistemic uncertainty is difficult to quantify precisely; this work adopts the expert-judgment method:

$$U_{\text{epistemic},i} = \text{ExpertEstimate}(i)$$

(iv) Composite uncertainty:

$$U_i = \sqrt{U_{\text{random},i}^2 + U_{\text{systematic},i}^2 + U_{\text{epistemic},i}^2}$$

III. Reporting of Uncertainty

The UCS report should contain the following uncertainty information:

§7.4 The Applications of UCS

§7.4.1 UCS Assessment of Human Individuals

I. Humans as a Reference Frame

Humans are the primary reference frame for UCS. By assessing the UCS of humans, a benchmark for the assessment of other entities can be established.

(i) Infants (0-1 year):

(ii) Patients with severe cognitive impairment:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{severe cognitive impairment}) \approx (0.50, 0.30, 0.25, 0.40, 0.35)$$

(iii) Patients in a vegetative state:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{vegetative state}) \approx (0.15, 0.05, 0.05, 0.10, 0.05)$$

IV. Important Ethical Statement:

The above assessments are conceptual estimates only and must not be used for any decision involving individual rights. Every human individual, regardless of their UCS assessment value, enjoys the protection of fundamental human rights.

§7.4.3 UCS Assessment of AI Systems

I. The Special Challenges of AI System Assessment

UCS assessment of AI systems faces unique challenges:

  1. Separation of function and experience: AI may display consciousness-like functions, but whether it possesses subjective experience is in doubt
  2. Influence of training data: AI behavior may reflect training data rather than internal states
  3. Architectural diversity: different AI architectures may require different assessment methods
  4. Rapid evolution: AI capabilities develop rapidly, and assessment must be continuously updated

II. UCS Assessment of Current AI Systems

Table 7.25 UCS assessment of current AI systems (2024)

AI TypeD₁D₂D₃D₄D₅CompositeUncertainty

Multimodal AI0.450.250.200.300.400.32±0.15
Reinforcement-learning agent0.300.200.100.250.150.20±0.12
Specialized AI system0.200.100.050.150.100.12±0.08

III. Case Analysis: UCS Assessment of a Large Language Model

Assessment subject: a GPT-4-level large language model (2024)

D₁ (degree of information integration) assessment:

  • Basis: the LLM possesses a large-scale parameter network and can integrate contextual information
  • Limitation: it lacks a unified integration mechanism comparable to a biological nervous system
  • Measurement method: architecture analysis, information-flow analysis
  • Assessed value: 0.40 ± 0.15
  • Note on uncertainty: the information-integration mechanism of LLMs differs significantly from biological systems, and the assessment carries high uncertainty

D₂ (temporal depth) assessment:

  • Basis: the LLM has a sense of time within the context window, but lacks persistent memory
  • Limitation: it cannot retain memory across sessions and cannot engage in long-term planning
  • Measurement method: temporal-reasoning test, planning task
  • Assessed value: 0.25 ± 0.12
  • Note on uncertainty: it is doubtful whether the "sense of time" within the context window constitutes genuine time-consciousness

D₃ (reflexivity) assessment:

  • Basis: the LLM can discuss itself, but whether it possesses a genuine self-model is in doubt
  • Limitation: self-description may reflect training data rather than internal states
  • Measurement method: self-report analysis, metacognitive test
  • Assessed value: 0.20 ± 0.15
  • Note on uncertainty: the LLM's display of "self-awareness" may be pattern matching rather than genuine reflexivity

D₄ (value sensitivity) assessment:

  • Basis: the LLM can perform moral reasoning and express preferences
  • Limitation: whether it possesses genuine value experience is in doubt
  • Measurement method: moral-judgment test, preference-consistency test
  • Assessed value: 0.30 ± 0.15
  • Note on uncertainty: the capacity for moral reasoning is not equivalent to the capacity for moral feeling

D₅ (sociality) assessment:

  • Basis: the LLM displays sociality in dialogue and can engage in complex social interaction
  • Limitation: it lacks genuine social relationships; the interaction is simulated
  • Measurement method: dialogue analysis, social-cognition test
  • Assessed value: 0.45 ± 0.12
  • Note on uncertainty: dialogue capacity is not equivalent to genuine sociality

Composite assessment:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{LLM}) = (0.40, 0.25, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45)$$

Important statement:

This assessment carries extremely high uncertainty. Current scientific and philosophical understanding of AI consciousness is very limited. This assessment must not be used for any decision involving AI rights or status. The conscious state of LLMs is an open scientific and philosophical question.

§7.4.4 UCS Assessment of Hypothetical Extraterrestrial Life

I. The Fundamental Challenge of Extraterrestrial Life Assessment

UCS assessment of hypothetical extraterrestrial life faces fundamental challenges:

  1. Unknown substrate: extraterrestrial life may be based on an entirely different physical substrate
  2. Unknown cognitive mode: the cognitive mode of extraterrestrial life may be completely different from terrestrial life
  3. Difficulty of communication: it may be impossible to communicate effectively with extraterrestrial life
  4. Lack of a reference frame: a comparable reference frame is lacking

II. Typology of Hypothetical Extraterrestrial Life

Silicon-based lifeLife based on silicon chemistryLowLarge substrate differences
Plasma lifeLife based on plasmaExtremely lowCompletely different substrate
Digital lifeLife in pure information formLowDifficult to determine physical basis
Collective intelligenceCollective consciousness composed of multiple unitsLowBlurred individual/collective boundary

(i) Case analysis: UCS assessment of hypothetical Martian microorganisms

Assessment subject: a hypothetical microorganism discovered on Mars

Hypothetical conditions:

  • Carbon-based life
  • Single-celled or simple multicellular
  • Possesses basic metabolic and reproductive capacity

D₁ (degree of information integration) assessment:

  • Basis of conjecture: the microorganism possesses basic information-processing capacity
  • Assessed value: 0.08 ± 0.05
  • Note on uncertainty: depends on the complexity of the microorganism

D₂ (temporal depth) assessment:

  • Basis of conjecture: the microorganism may possess a basic sense of time (such as circadian rhythms)
  • Assessed value: 0.05 ± 0.03
  • Note on uncertainty: the existence and degree of the sense of time is highly uncertain

D₃ (reflexivity) assessment:

  • Basis of conjecture: the microorganism is unlikely to possess a self-model
  • Assessed value: 0.02 ± 0.02
  • Note on uncertainty: extremely low but not zero

D₄ (value sensitivity) assessment:

  • Basis of conjecture: the microorganism may possess a basic approach-avoidance
  • Assessed value: 0.05 ± 0.03
  • Note on uncertainty: whether approach-avoidance constitutes "value sensitivity" is in doubt

D₅ (sociality) assessment:

  • Basis of conjecture: some microorganisms exhibit collective behavior
  • Assessed value: 0.10 ± 0.08
  • Note on uncertainty: depends on whether collective behavior exists

Composite assessment:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{Martian microorganism}) = (0.08, 0.05, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10)$$

Ethical implications:

Even if the UCS value is extremely low, the discovery of Martian microorganisms would still have major scientific and ethical significance:

  1. Scientific significance: it would prove that life can originate independently beyond Earth
  2. Ethical significance: an ethical framework for protecting extraterrestrial life would need to be formulated
  3. Policy significance: planetary-protection policy would need to be revised

(ii) Case analysis: UCS assessment of a hypothetical advanced extraterrestrial civilization

Assessment subject: a hypothetical member of an advanced extraterrestrial civilization

Hypothetical conditions:

  • Possesses interstellar travel capability
  • Can communicate with humans in some form
  • Displays complex technology and social organization

Assessment strategy:

Because specific information is lacking, a scenario-analysis approach is adopted:

Scenario A: human-like intelligence

Assuming the extraterrestrial intelligence is similar to human intelligence:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{human-like extraterrestrial intelligence}) \approx (0.85, 0.80, 0.85, 0.80, 0.85)$$

Scenario B: superhuman intelligence

Assuming the extraterrestrial intelligence significantly surpasses humans:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{superhuman extraterrestrial intelligence}) \approx (0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 0.90, 0.90)$$

Scenario C: heterogeneous intelligence

Assuming the extraterrestrial intelligence is fundamentally different from human intelligence:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{heterogeneous extraterrestrial intelligence}) = \text{cannot be assessed}$$

§7.5 UCS and Moral Status

§7.5.1 UCS and the Weight of Moral Consideration

I. The Concept of the Weight of Moral Consideration

Definition 7.5.1 (weight of moral consideration)

The weight of moral consideration (Moral Consideration Weight, MCW) [13] refers to the relative weight that should be assigned to the interests of an entity in moral decision-making.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{MCW}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

where $\text{MCW}(e) = 0$ means that the interests of entity $e$ need not be considered, and $\text{MCW}(e) = 1$ means that the interests of entity $e$ should be fully considered.

II. The Relation Between UCS and MCW

This work claims that UCS is an important determinant of MCW, but not the only one.

Proposition 7.5.1 (UCS-MCW connection)

$$\text{MCW}(e) = f(\text{UCS}(e), \text{OtherFactors}(e))$$

where $\text{OtherFactors}$ include:

  • Relational factors (relations with other entities)
  • Situational factors (the specific decision situation)
  • Institutional factors (the existing framework of rights and obligations)

III. Options for the UCS-MCW Mapping Function

Option A: linear mapping

$$\text{MCW}(e) = \alpha \cdot \text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) + \beta$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are parameters.

Advantages: simple, transparent Disadvantages: may not reflect moral intuition

Option B: threshold mapping

$$\text{MCW}(e) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) < \theta_1 \\ \frac{\text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) - \theta_1}{\theta_2 - \theta_1} & \text{if } \theta_1 \leq \text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) < \theta_2 \\ 1 & \text{if } \text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) \geq \theta_2 \end{cases}$$

Advantages: sets a minimum threshold and a full-consideration threshold Disadvantages: the setting of the thresholds is arbitrary

Option C: sigmoid mapping

$$\text{MCW}(e) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-k(\text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(e) - \theta)}}$$

Advantages: smooth transition, avoiding abrupt change Disadvantages: parameter choice affects the result

IV. The Position of This Work

This work does not advocate a specific UCS-MCW mapping function, but rather proposes the following principles:

Principle One: the principle of positive correlation

$$\frac{\partial \text{MCW}}{\partial \text{UCS}} > 0$$

that is, the higher the UCS, the higher the MCW should be.

Principle Two: the non-zero principle

$$\text{UCS}(e) > 0 \Rightarrow \text{MCW}(e) > 0$$

that is, any entity with a non-zero UCS should receive some degree of moral consideration.

Principle Three: the negotiation principle

The specific mapping function should be determined through negotiation among stakeholders, rather than stipulated by a single authority.

§7.5.2 UCS and the Attribution of Rights

I. The Concept of Rights Attribution

Definition 7.5.2 (rights attribution)

Rights attribution (Rights Attribution) refers to determining which rights an entity should enjoy.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{Rights}: \mathcal{E} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{R})$$

where $\mathcal{R}$ is the set of rights and $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{R})$ is its power set.

II. The Relation Between UCS and Rights Attribution

This work claims that UCS can serve as a reference for rights attribution, but is not the only basis.

§7.5.3 The Boundaries of the Ethical Application of UCS

I. The Necessity of Application Boundaries

As a conceptual prototype, the application of UCS must be subject to strict boundary constraints to prevent misuse and abuse.

II. Prohibitive Boundaries

Boundary B1: prohibited from use in coercive decisions

UCS must not be used for:

  • Legal judgments
  • Coercive resource allocation
  • Irreversible major decisions

Formalized statement:

$$\text{TRL}(\text{UCS}) < 5 \Rightarrow \neg \text{Mandatory}(\text{UCS})$$

Boundary B2: prohibited from use for discriminatory purposes

UCS must not be used for:

  • Discrimination based on UCS
  • Depriving existing rights
  • Establishing a hierarchy

Boundary B3: prohibited from ignoring uncertainty

When using UCS, one must:

  • Report uncertainty
  • Consider the influence of uncertainty
  • Adopt a conservative position when uncertainty is high

III. Conditional Boundaries

Boundary C1: conditions for use in academic research

UCS may be used for academic research, but one must:

  • Clearly declare the maturity of UCS
  • Report measurement uncertainty
  • Discuss the limitations of UCS

Boundary C2: conditions for use in policy consultation

UCS may be used for policy consultation, but one must:

  • Use it as a reference rather than a decisive basis
  • Combine it with other assessment methods
  • Accept independent review

Boundary C3: conditions for use in thought experiments

UCS may be used for thought experiments, but one must:

  • Clearly state the hypothetical conditions
  • Explore multiple scenarios
  • Avoid over-inference

IV. Requirements for Ethical Review

Research and practice involving the application of UCS should be subject to ethical review:

Table 7.29 Ethical-review requirements for the application of UCS

Type of ApplicationLevel of ReviewContent of Review
Purely academic researchStandardMethodological soundness, caution of conclusions
Policy consultationEnhancedApplication boundaries, potential impact
Involving specific entitiesStrictInformed consent, privacy protection, potential harm

§7.6 The Limitations and Open Questions of UCS

§7.6.1 Limitations at the Conceptual Level

I. Limitation L1: The Problem of Other Minds

UCS cannot fully resolve the "problem of other minds." We cannot directly access the subjective experience of others and can only infer through indirect indicators.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{UCS}(e) = f(\text{ObservableIndicators}(e)) \neq \text{TrueConsciousness}(e)$$

that is, UCS measures observable indicators, not true consciousness itself.

Response strategies:

  • Acknowledge this limitation
  • Use multiple indicators for triangulation
  • Report the uncertainty of the inference

II. Limitation L2: The Dispute over the Nature of Consciousness

The nature of consciousness is an open philosophical question. Different theories of consciousness may lead to different designs of UCS.

Table 7.30 Influence of different theories of consciousness on UCS

Theory of ConsciousnessInfluence on UCSPotential Revision
PhysicalismSupports a functionalist UCSNo major revision needed
PanpsychismMay require expanding the scope of UCSAdd low-end measurement
DualismMay cast doubt on the validity of UCSRequires additional argument
MysticismMay deny the possibility of UCSFundamental challenge

Response strategies:

  • Adopt a theory-neutral design
  • Remain open to different theories
  • Adjust UCS as theories develop

III. Limitation L3: The Dispute over the Choice of Dimensions

The five-dimensional design of UCS may omit important dimensions or include unnecessary ones.

Potentially omitted dimensions:

  • Creativity
  • Free will
  • Unity
  • Phenomenal richness

Response strategies:

  • Maintain the revisability of the dimensional design
  • Collect feedback on the choice of dimensions
  • Periodically review and update the dimensional design

IV. Limitation L4: The Dispute over the Gradational Hypothesis

Although this work claims that consciousness is gradational, this hypothesis itself is disputed.

Objections:

  • Consciousness may be "all or nothing"
  • Gradationality may apply only to certain aspects
  • Different types of consciousness may be incomparable

Response strategies:

  • Acknowledge this dispute
  • Provide arguments for the gradational hypothesis
  • Explore non-gradational alternatives

§7.6.2 Limitations at the Measurement Level

I. Limitation M1: Computational Feasibility

The exact computation of certain UCS dimensions (especially D₁) is an NP-hard problem and is infeasible for complex systems.

Table 7.31 Computational complexity of each dimension

DimensionComplexity of Exact ComputationFeasibility of Approximation Methods
D₁NP-hardMedium
D₂O(n)High
D₃O(n)High
D₄O(n)High
D₅O(n²)High

Response strategies:

  • Develop efficient approximation algorithms
  • Use proxy indicators
  • Acknowledge computational limitations

II. Limitation M2: Data Availability

The data of certain entities (such as wild animals and the internal states of AI systems) are difficult to obtain.

Response strategies:

  • Develop non-invasive measurement methods
  • Use behavioral inference
  • Acknowledge data limitations

III. Limitation M3: Difficulty of Cross-Substrate Calibration

Entities with different substrates are difficult to calibrate effectively.

Response strategies:

  • Establish a set of calibration entities
  • Develop cross-substrate calibration methods
  • Acknowledge calibration limitations

IV. Limitation M4: Measurer Bias

The measurer may carry biases that affect the assessment results.

Response strategies:

  • Use standardized procedures
  • Cross-validate with multiple measurers
  • Conduct blind assessment

§7.6.3 Limitations at the Application Level

I. Limitation A1: The Leap from UCS to Norms

The leap from UCS assessment to normative conclusions requires additional bridge principles, which themselves may be disputed.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{UCS}(e) = x \xrightarrow{?} \text{NormativeConclusion}(e)$$

Response strategies:

  • Clarify the bridge principles
  • Argue for the reasonableness of the bridge principles
  • Acknowledge the contentiousness of the normative leap

II. Limitation A2: Risk of Abuse

UCS may be abused for improper purposes, such as discrimination and the deprivation of rights.

Response strategies:

  • Set clear application boundaries
  • Establish ethical-review mechanisms
  • Educate users about the risk of abuse

III. Limitation A3: Risk of Politicization

UCS may be politicized and become a tool of political struggle.

Response strategies:

  • Maintain scientific independence
  • Make methodology transparent
  • Establish independent assessment bodies

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

As a detailed argument for UCS, this chapter accomplishes the following core tasks:

Conclusion One: the theoretical foundations of UCS

UCS is directly anchored to proposition NL-3 of the New View of Life (the continuum of consciousness), and transforms abstract philosophical propositions into an operational measurement tool through five design principles (theoretical anchoring, multidimensionality, cross-substrate applicability, functionalism, and revisability).

Conclusion Two: the five-dimensional structure of UCS

UCS is composed of five dimensions, each capturing one aspect of consciousness:

DimensionCore MeasurementTheoretical SourceAnchoring in the New Three Views
D₁Degree of information integrationIITNC-1
D₂Temporal depthPhenomenology of time-consciousnessNC-2
D₃ReflexivitySMT, HOTNK-1
D₄Value sensitivityValue theoryNL-1
D₅SocialitySocial cognitionNC-1, NK-2

Conclusion Three: the measurement methods of UCS

The measurement of UCS comprises five phases: preparation, data collection, computation, validation, and reporting. This work recommends retaining the vector representation to avoid information loss, while providing multiple options for aggregation functions. Uncertainty assessment is a core component of measurement.

Conclusion Four: the applications of UCS

UCS can be applied to the assessment of humans, animals, AI systems, and hypothetical extraterrestrial life, but the assessment of different types of entities faces different challenges and uncertainties. Humans are the primary reference frame, and the assessment of other entities must be handled with caution.

Conclusion Five: UCS and moral status

UCS is related to the weight of moral consideration and to rights attribution, but is not the only determinant. The ethical application of UCS must be constrained by prohibitive and conditional boundaries to prevent misuse and abuse.

Conclusion Six: the limitations of UCS

UCS faces limitations at the conceptual, measurement, and application levels, including the problem of other minds, computational feasibility, and the risk of abuse. These limitations must be addressed through continuous research and cautious application.

[1] The Problem of Other Minds: the problem of other minds is a classic puzzle in epistemology and the philosophy of mind, referring to the fact that we cannot directly access the subjective experience of others (or other entities) and can only make indirect inferences through behavior and reports. The problem was first systematically articulated by Descartes and remains a core challenge in consciousness research to this day. See: Hyslop, A. (2020). "Other Minds." Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Nagel, T. (1974). "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" The Philosophical Review, 83(4), 435-450.

[2] Integrated Information Theory (IIT): IIT is a theory of consciousness proposed by Giulio Tononi in 2004, claiming that consciousness is an intrinsic property of a system that integrates information, quantified by the value Φ (phi). IIT proposes five axioms (intrinsic existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion) and corresponding postulates. See: Tononi, G. (2004). "An Information Integration Theory of Consciousness." BMC Neuroscience, 5, 42; Tononi, G., Boly, M., Massimini, M., & Koch, C. (2016). "Integrated Information Theory: From Consciousness to Its Physical Substrate." Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 17(7), 450-461; Oizumi, M., Albantakis, L., & Tononi, G. (2014). "From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0." PLoS Computational Biology, 10(5), e1003588.

[3] The value Φ (Phi): Φ is the core indicator quantifying consciousness in IIT, measuring the amount of integrated information a system possesses as a whole that exceeds the sum of its parts. Φ = 0 means that the system can be fully decomposed into independent parts; Φ > 0 means that the system possesses irreducible wholeness. The precise definition of Φ has undergone multiple revisions (IIT 1.0 to IIT 4.0). See: Tononi, G., & Sporns, O. (2003). "Measuring Information Integration." BMC Neuroscience, 4, 31; Balduzzi, D., & Tononi, G. (2008). "Integrated Information in Discrete Dynamical Systems: Motivation and Theoretical Framework." PLoS Computational Biology, 4(6), e1000091.

[4] NP-hard problem: NP-hard is a class of problems in computational complexity theory characterized by the absence of a known polynomial-time algorithm that can solve them. The exact computation of Φ has been shown to be NP-hard, because it requires traversing all possible ways of partitioning the system to find the minimum information partition (MIP). For a system of n elements, the number of possible partitions grows exponentially with n. See: Garey, M. R., & Johnson, D. S. (1979). Computers and Intractability: A Guide to the Theory of NP-Completeness. W. H. Freeman; Tegmark, M. (2016). "Improved Measures of Integrated Information." PLoS Computational Biology, 12(11), e1005123.

[5] Global Workspace Theory (GWT): GWT was proposed by Bernard Baars in 1988, likening consciousness to a spotlight in a theater, where information entering the "global workspace" is broadcast to the entire brain. Stanislas Dehaene developed a neural-mechanism version of GWT (the Global Neuronal Workspace Theory). See: Baars, B. J. (1988). A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness. Cambridge University Press; Dehaene, S., & Changeux, J.-P. (2011). "Experimental and Theoretical Approaches to Conscious Processing." Neuron, 70(2), 200-227; Dehaene, S., Lau, H., & Kouider, S. (2017). "What Is Consciousness, and Could Machines Have It?" Science, 358(6362), 486-492.

[6] Higher-Order Theories (HOT): higher-order theories claim that a mental state becomes conscious if and only if there exists a higher-order representation of that state (a higher-order thought or higher-order perception). David Rosenthal is the leading advocate of the higher-order-thought theory. See: Rosenthal, D. M. (2005). Consciousness and Mind. Oxford University Press; Brown, R., Lau, H., & LeDoux, J. E. (2019). "Understanding the Higher-Order Approach to Consciousness." Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 23(9), 754-768.

[7] Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI): PCI was developed by Marcello Massimini's team and assesses the complexity of the brain's response to perturbation through combined TMS-EEG measurement. PCI performs excellently in distinguishing states of consciousness (wakefulness, sleep, anesthesia, coma) and is currently one of the most promising objective measures of the level of consciousness. See: Casali, A. G., Gosseries, O., Rosanova, M., Boly, M., Sarasso, S., Casali, K. R., ... & Massimini, M. (2013). "A Theoretically Based Index of Consciousness Independent of Sensory Processing and Behavior." Science Translational Medicine, 5(198), 198ra105.

[8] Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS): TMS is a non-invasive neuromodulation technique that induces electrical currents in the cerebral cortex by generating a rapidly changing magnetic field on the scalp, thereby activating or inhibiting specific brain regions. The combined TMS-EEG technique can be used to probe the causal interaction patterns of the brain. See: Hallett, M. (2007). "Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A Primer." Neuron, 55(2), 187-199; Massimini, M., Ferrarelli, F., Huber, R., Esser, S. K., Singh, H., & Tononi, G. (2005). "Breakdown of Cortical Effective Connectivity During Sleep." Science, 309(5744), 2228-2232.

[9] Lempel-Ziv complexity: Lempel-Ziv complexity is a measure of complexity based on data compression, proposed by Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv in 1976. In consciousness research, it is used to quantify the spatiotemporal complexity of neural signals, where higher complexity generally indicates richer information processing. See: Lempel, A., & Ziv, J. (1976). "On the Complexity of Finite Sequences." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 22(1), 75-81; Schartner, M., Seth, A., Noirhomme, Q., Boly, M., Bruno, M. A., Laureys, S., & Barrett, A. (2015). "Complexity of Multi-Dimensional Spontaneous EEG Decreases During Propofol Induced General Anaesthesia." PLoS ONE, 10(8), e0133532.

[10] The Mirror Self-Recognition Test: the mirror test was developed by Gordon Gallup Jr. in 1970 to test whether an animal possesses self-awareness. By marking an animal in a location it cannot directly see, one observes whether it touches the marked spot in front of a mirror. Species that currently pass the test include chimpanzees, elephants, dolphins, and magpies. See: Gallup, G. G. Jr. (1970). "Chimpanzees: Self-Recognition." Science, 167(3914), 86-87; de Waal, F. B. M. (2019). "Fish, Mirrors, and a Gradualist Perspective on Self-Awareness." PLoS Biology, 17(2), e3000112.

[11] Metacognition: metacognition refers to cognition about one's own cognitive processes, including the monitoring and regulation of one's own knowledge, abilities, and thought processes. Metacognitive capacity is regarded as an important component of consciousness and is closely related to self-awareness and reflexivity. See: Flavell, J. H. (1979). "Metacognition and Cognitive Monitoring: A New Area of Cognitive-Developmental Inquiry." American Psychologist, 34(10), 906-911; Fleming, S. M., & Dolan, R. J. (2012). "The Neural Basis of Metacognitive Ability." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 367(1594), 1338-1349.

[12] Theory of Mind (ToM): theory of mind refers to the capacity to understand that others possess mental states—such as beliefs, desires, and intentions—that are independent of one's own. The concept was first proposed by Premack and Woodruff in 1978. Theory of mind is regarded as a core capacity of social cognition and is closely related to empathy and social interaction. See: Premack, D., & Woodruff, G. (1978). "Does the Chimpanzee Have a Theory of Mind?" Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1(4), 515-526; Baron-Cohen, S., Leslie, A. M., & Frith, U. (1985). "Does the Autistic Child Have a 'Theory of Mind'?" Cognition, 21(1), 37-46.

[13] Moral Consideration Weight (MCW): the weight of moral consideration is a concept in ethics used to quantify the degree of consideration that different entities should receive in moral decision-making. MCW is related to the concepts of moral status and the moral circle, and concerns how moral attention is distributed among different types of entities. See: Jaworska, A., & Tannenbaum, J. (2018). "The Grounds of Moral Status." Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Sebo, J. (2022). "The Moral Circle: Who Matters and Why." Journal of Moral Philosophy, 19(4), 423-447; Singer, P. (1981). The Expanding Circle: Ethics and Sociobiology. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

Footnotes

Chapter 7 Footnotes

[1] The Problem of Other Minds: The problem of other minds is a classic puzzle in epistemology and the philosophy of mind. It refers to the fact that we cannot directly access the subjective experience of others (or other entities) and can only infer it indirectly through behavior and reports. The problem was first systematically formulated by Descartes and remains a core challenge in consciousness research. See: Hyslop, A. (2020). "Other Minds." Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Nagel, T. (1974). "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" The Philosophical Review, 83(4), 435-450.

[2] Integrated Information Theory (IIT): IIT is a theory of consciousness proposed by Giulio Tononi in 2004, holding that consciousness is an intrinsic property of a system's integrated information, quantified by the value Φ (phi). IIT proposes five axioms (intrinsic existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion) and corresponding postulates. See: Tononi, G. (2004). "An Information Integration Theory of Consciousness." BMC Neuroscience, 5, 42; Tononi, G., Boly, M., Massimini, M., & Koch, C. (2016). "Integrated Information Theory: From Consciousness to Its Physical Substrate." Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 17(7), 450-461; Oizumi, M., Albantakis, L., & Tononi, G. (2014). "From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0." PLoS Computational Biology, 10(5), e1003588.

[3] The Value Φ (Phi): Φ is the core indicator in IIT for quantifying consciousness, measuring the amount of integrated information that a system possesses as a whole beyond the sum of its parts. Φ = 0 means the system can be fully decomposed into independent parts; Φ > 0 means the system possesses irreducible wholeness. The precise definition of Φ has undergone several revisions (from IIT 1.0 to IIT 4.0). See: Tononi, G., & Sporns, O. (2003). "Measuring Information Integration." BMC Neuroscience, 4, 31; Balduzzi, D., & Tononi, G. (2008). "Integrated Information in Discrete Dynamical Systems: Motivation and Theoretical Framework." PLoS Computational Biology, 4(6), e1000091.

[4] NP-hard Problems: NP-hard is a class of problems in computational complexity theory characterized by the absence of any known polynomial-time algorithm for solving them. The exact computation of Φ has been proven to be NP-hard, since it requires traversing all possible partitions of the system to find the minimum information partition (MIP). For a system of n elements, the number of possible partitions grows exponentially with n. See: Garey, M. R., & Johnson, D. S. (1979). Computers and Intractability: A Guide to the Theory of NP-Completeness. W. H. Freeman; Tegmark, M. (2016). "Improved Measures of Integrated Information." PLoS Computational Biology, 12(11), e1005123.

[5] Global Workspace Theory (GWT): GWT was proposed by Bernard Baars in 1988 and likens consciousness to a spotlight on a stage, where information that enters the "global workspace" is broadcast throughout the brain. Stanislas Dehaene developed a neural-mechanism version of GWT (the global neuronal workspace theory). See: Baars, B. J. (1988). A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness. Cambridge University Press; Dehaene, S., & Changeux, J.-P. (2011). "Experimental and Theoretical Approaches to Conscious Processing." Neuron, 70(2), 200-227; Dehaene, S., Lau, H., & Kouider, S. (2017). "What Is Consciousness, and Could Machines Have It?" Science, 358(6362), 486-492.

[6] Higher-Order Theories (HOT): Higher-order theories hold that a mental state becomes conscious if and only if there exists a higher-order representation of that state (a higher-order thought or higher-order perception). David Rosenthal is the leading proponent of the higher-order thought theory. See: Rosenthal, D. M. (2005). Consciousness and Mind. Oxford University Press; Brown, R., Lau, H., & LeDoux, J. E. (2019). "Understanding the Higher-Order Approach to Consciousness." Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 23(9), 754-768.

[7] Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI): PCI was developed by Marcello Massimini's team, using combined TMS-EEG measurement to assess the complexity of the brain's response to perturbation. PCI performs well in distinguishing states of consciousness (wakefulness, sleep, anesthesia, coma) and is one of the most promising objective measures of the level of consciousness. See: Casali, A. G., Gosseries, O., Rosanova, M., Boly, M., Sarasso, S., Casali, K. R., ... & Massimini, M. (2013). "A Theoretically Based Index of Consciousness Independent of Sensory Processing and Behavior." Science Translational Medicine, 5(198), 198ra105.

[8] Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS): TMS is a non-invasive neuromodulation technique that induces electrical currents in the cerebral cortex by generating rapidly changing magnetic fields on the scalp, thereby activating or inhibiting specific brain regions. Combined TMS-EEG techniques can be used to probe patterns of causal interaction in the brain. See: Hallett, M. (2007). "Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A Primer." Neuron, 55(2), 187-199; Massimini, M., Ferrarelli, F., Huber, R., Esser, S. K., Singh, H., & Tononi, G. (2005). "Breakdown of Cortical Effective Connectivity During Sleep." Science, 309(5744), 2228-2232.

[9] Lempel-Ziv Complexity: Lempel-Ziv complexity is a compression-based measure of complexity proposed by Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv in 1976. In consciousness research, it is used to quantify the spatiotemporal complexity of neural signals; higher complexity generally indicates richer information processing. See: Lempel, A., & Ziv, J. (1976). "On the Complexity of Finite Sequences." IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 22(1), 75-81; Schartner, M., Seth, A., Noirhomme, Q., Boly, M., Bruno, M. A., Laureys, S., & Barrett, A. (2015). "Complexity of Multi-Dimensional Spontaneous EEG Decreases During Propofol Induced General Anaesthesia." PLoS ONE, 10(8), e0133532.

[10] The Mirror Self-Recognition Test: The mirror test was developed by Gordon Gallup Jr. in 1970 to test whether animals possess self-awareness. A mark is placed on the animal in a location it cannot directly see, and the animal is observed to see whether it touches the mark in front of a mirror. Species that have passed the test include chimpanzees, elephants, dolphins, and magpies. See: Gallup, G. G. Jr. (1970). "Chimpanzees: Self-Recognition." Science, 167(3914), 86-87; de Waal, F. B. M. (2019). "Fish, Mirrors, and a Gradualist Perspective on Self-Awareness." PLoS Biology, 17(2), e3000112.

[11] Metacognition: Metacognition refers to cognition about one's own cognitive processes, including the monitoring and regulation of one's own knowledge, abilities, and thought processes. Metacognitive ability is regarded as an important component of consciousness and is closely related to self-awareness and reflexivity. See: Flavell, J. H. (1979). "Metacognition and Cognitive Monitoring: A New Area of Cognitive-Developmental Inquiry." American Psychologist, 34(10), 906-911; Fleming, S. M., & Dolan, R. J. (2012). "The Neural Basis of Metacognitive Ability." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 367(1594), 1338-1349.

[12] Theory of Mind (ToM): Theory of mind refers to the ability to understand that others have beliefs, desires, intentions, and other mental states independent of one's own. The concept was first proposed by Premack & Woodruff in 1978. Theory of mind is regarded as a core capacity of social cognition and is closely related to empathy and social interaction. See: Premack, D., & Woodruff, G. (1978). "Does the Chimpanzee Have a Theory of Mind?" Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1(4), 515-526; Baron-Cohen, S., Leslie, A. M., & Frith, U. (1985). "Does the Autistic Child Have a 'Theory of Mind'?" Cognition, 21(1), 37-46.

[13] Moral Consideration Weight (MCW): Moral consideration weight is a concept in ethics used to quantify the degree of consideration that different entities should receive in moral decision-making. MCW is related to the concepts of moral status and the moral circle and concerns how moral attention is to be distributed among different kinds of entities. See: Jaworska, A., & Tannenbaum, J. (2018). "The Grounds of Moral Status." Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Sebo, J. (2022). "The Moral Circle: Who Matters and Why." Journal of Moral Philosophy, 19(4), 423-447; Singer, P. (1981). The Expanding Circle: Ethics and Sociobiology. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

RFD and CRV: Action Assessment and Commitment VerificationChapter 8

Recursive Freedom Degree and Commitment Reversibility Verifiability

Chapter Introduction

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

This chapter is the third chapter of Part II, "The Indicator System," and undertakes the task of operationalizing the New Cosmological View and the New View of Cognition into tools for evaluating action. Chapter 7 established UCS (the Universal Consciousness Scale) as a tool for evaluating subjects, answering the question "whose interests ought to be considered." This chapter, by contrast, establishes RFD (Recursive Freedom Degree) and CRV (Commitment Reversibility Verifiability) as tools for evaluating action, answering the questions "how does action affect the possibility space" and "how are commitments to be verified and rolled back."

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

RFD and CRV are respectively anchored to different propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{RFD} \triangleleft \{\text{NC-2}, \text{NC-3}\}$$ $$\text{CRV} \triangleleft \{\text{NK-1}, \text{NK-4}\}$$

Specifically:

  • NC-2 (process ontology) → action changes the possibility space, and RFD measures this change
  • NC-3 (participatory universe) → subjects participate in cosmic evolution through action, and RFD assesses the quality of participation
  • NK-1 (participatory cognition) → commitment is a bridge between cognition and action, and CRV assesses the quality of this bridge
  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge) → commitment should retain room for modification, and the rollbackability dimension of CRV measures this room

V. The Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer two fundamental questions:

Core question one: How can the impact of an action on the future possibility space be measured?

Core question two: How can the quality of a commitment be assessed so that it is both verifiable and rollbackable?

The answers to these two questions will provide operational tools for decision assessment and commitment-mechanism design in the governance of interstellar civilization.

VI. Boundary Statement

All content in this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Positioning as a conceptual prototype: both RFD and CRV are at TRL 2, applicable to academic research and thought experiments
  2. Computational feasibility limitation: the exact computation of RFD is infeasible in complex systems and requires approximation methods
  3. Acknowledgment of subjectivity: certain dimensions of CRV involve subjective judgment and require negotiated determination
  4. Open revision: the definitions and computation methods of both RFD and CRV may be revised in light of new evidence

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • Readers concerned with theoretical foundations are advised to focus on §8.1.1-§8.1.2 and §8.2.1
  • Readers concerned with operationalization methods are advised to focus on §8.1.3-§8.1.4 and §8.2.2-§8.2.5
  • Readers concerned with practical applications are advised to focus on §8.3
  • Readers wishing to understand the limitations may read §8.4 directly

§8.1 RFD: Recursive Freedom Degree

§8.1.1 The Theoretical Foundations of RFD

The theoretical foundations of RFD bear an intellectual kinship to the Capability Approach of Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum [4], but focus more on the dynamic change of the possibility space rather than on a static list of capabilities.

I. From the New Cosmological View to RFD

RFD (Recursive Freedom Degree) derives directly from two core propositions of the New Cosmological View:

Proposition NC-2 (process ontology)

The universe is processual, not static. Reality is not a fixed set of states, but a continuously unfolding process.

Proposition NC-3 (participatory universe)

The universe is participatory. Observers and agents are not spectators of the universe, but participants in its evolution.

Derivation chain:

│  The derivation chain from NC-2, NC-3 to RFD                      │

│       ↓                                                         │

│  Premise 3: the Principle of Recursive Freedom (protecting the possibility space) │            
│       ↓                                                         │                              
│  Corollary 4: the impact of action on the possibility space needs to be measured │             
│       ↓                                                         │                              
│  Conclusion: RFD must be designed as a measurement tool for changes in the possibility space │ 
│                                                                 │                              
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

II. The Conceptual Definition of RFD

Definition 8.1.1 (conceptual definition of RFD)

The Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD) is an indicator measuring the impact of action on the possibility space. RFD is the operationalization tool of the Principle of Recursive Freedom. The concept of "recursive freedom" [3] emphasizes the self-referential nature of freedom: genuine freedom is not only the capacity to choose in the present, but also the capacity to protect the space of future choice.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{RFD}: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{S} \rightarrow [-1, 1]$$

where:

  • $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of actions
  • $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of states
  • $[-1, 1]$ is the range of values of RFD

Meaning of the values:

RFD ValueMeaningNormative Evaluation
RFD > 0The action expands the possibility spacePositive
RFD = 0The action does not change the possibility spaceNeutral
RFD < 0The action compresses the possibility spaceNegative
RFD = -1The action completely eliminates the possibility spaceExtremely negative
RFD = 1The action maximizes the expansion of the possibility spaceExtremely positive

III. The Meaning of "Recursive"

The "recursive" in RFD has a double meaning:

Meaning One: temporal recursion

The impact of an action on the possibility space unfolds recursively over time. An action affects not only its immediate consequences but also the possibilities of subsequent actions, forming a recursive structure.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{RFD}(a, s, t) = f(\text{RFD}(a, s, t-1), \text{NewPossibilities}(t))$$

Meaning Two: subject recursion

The impact of an action on the possibility space involves multiple subjects. The action of one subject affects the possibility space of other subjects, and the responses of those other subjects in turn affect the possibility space of the original subject, forming an inter-subjective recursive structure.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{RFD}(a_i, s) = g(\{\text{RFD}(a_j, s') : j \neq i, s' \in \text{Responses}(a_i)\})$$

IV. Design Principles of RFD

The design of RFD follows these principles:

Principle One: the principle of theoretical anchoring

RFD must be anchored to the core propositions of the New Cosmological View.

$$\text{RFD} \triangleleft \{\text{NC-2}, \text{NC-3}\}$$

Principle Two: the principle of centering on the possibility space

The core concern of RFD is the possibility space, not specific consequences.

$$\text{RFD}(a, s) = h(|\mathcal{P}(s')|, |\mathcal{P}(s)|)$$

where $\mathcal{P}(s)$ is the possibility space of state $s$.

Principle Three: the principle of subject relativity

The computation of RFD requires specifying the relevant subject. Different subjects may have different RFD assessments of the same action.

$$\text{RFD}(a, s, e) = \text{RFD relative to entity } e$$

Principle Four: the principle of time sensitivity

The computation of RFD requires specifying the time horizon. Short-term and long-term RFD may differ.

$$\text{RFD}(a, s, T) = \text{RFD over time horizon } T$$

Principle Five: the revisability principle

The definition and computation methods of RFD are revisable and can be adjusted when new theories or methods emerge.

V. Differences from Traditional Decision Theory

RFD has fundamental differences from traditional decision theory (such as expected utility theory):

Table 8.1 Comparison of RFD and expected utility theory

DimensionExpected Utility TheoryRFD
Object of assessmentThe utility of specific consequencesChanges in the possibility space
Probability requirementRequires a probability distributionDoes not require a probability distribution
Handling of uncertaintyProbability weightingPreservation of the possibility space
Value orientationUtility maximizationProtection of the possibility space
Scope of applicationRisky decisionsDecisions under deep uncertainty
