§8.1.2 The Definition of the Possibility Space

I. The Concept of the Possibility Space

The possibility space (Possibility Space) [1] is the core concept of RFD. It refers to the set of all future states reachable from a given state. The concept of the possibility space draws on the concept of phase space in physics [2], but makes important extensions.

Definition 8.1.2 (possibility space)

The possibility space (Possibility Space) is the set of all future states reachable from a given state:

$$\mathcal{P}(s) = \{s' : \exists \text{ path from } s \text{ to } s'\}$$

where "path" refers to a path from state $s$ to state $s'$ via a series of actions.

Formalization of the possibility space

The possibility space can be formalized through a state transition graph:

Definition 8.1.3 (state transition graph)

The state transition graph $G = (S, A, T)$ is composed of the following elements:

  • $S$: the set of states
  • $A$: the set of actions
  • $T: S \times A \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(S)$: the transition function, where $T(s, a)$ is the set of states possibly reached after executing action $a$ from state $s$

II. Computation of the Possibility Space:

$$\mathcal{P}(s) = \bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathcal{P}_n(s)$$

where:

  • $\mathcal{P}_0(s) = \{s\}$
  • $\mathcal{P}_{n+1}(s) = \bigcup_{s' \in \mathcal{P}_n(s)} \bigcup_{a \in A} T(s', a)$

III. Measurement of the Possibility Space

The evolution of the possibility space can be modeled with a Markov chain [5]. Let the state transition probability be $P(s'|s,a)$, denoting the probability of transitioning to state $s'$ after taking action $a$ in state $s$. The "size" of the possibility space can be measured in several ways:

Measure One: number of states

$$|\mathcal{P}(s)| = \text{number of states in } \mathcal{P}(s)$$

Advantages: simple, intuitive Disadvantages: does not consider the differences among states

Measure Two: state diversity

$$\text{Diversity}(\mathcal{P}(s)) = H(\mathcal{P}(s))$$

where $H$ is the entropy function, measuring the diversity of the state distribution.

Advantages: considers the distribution of states Disadvantages: requires a probability distribution

Measure Three: state accessibility

$$\text{Accessibility}(\mathcal{P}(s)) = \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{P}(s)} \text{Reach}(s, s')$$

where $\text{Reach}(s, s')$ is the accessibility from $s$ to $s'$ (such as the number of paths or the reciprocal of the shortest path length).

Advantages: considers differences in accessibility Disadvantages: computationally complex

Measure Four: value coverage

$$\text{ValueCoverage}(\mathcal{P}(s)) = \text{Volume}(\{V(s') : s' \in \mathcal{P}(s)\})$$

where $V(s')$ is the value vector of state $s'$ and $\text{Volume}$ is the coverage volume in value space.

Advantages: considers the value dimension Disadvantages: requires a value function

The recommendation of this work

This work recommends using state diversity as the primary measure, supplemented by value coverage:

$$|\mathcal{P}(s)|_{\text{eff}} = \alpha \cdot \text{Diversity}(\mathcal{P}(s)) + (1-\alpha) \cdot \text{ValueCoverage}(\mathcal{P}(s))$$

where $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ is a weight parameter, with a default of $\alpha = 0.5$.

IV. The Time Horizon of the Possibility Space

The definition of the possibility space requires specifying the time horizon:

Definition 8.1.4 (finite-time possibility space)

The finite-time possibility space $\mathcal{P}(s, T)$ is the set of all states reachable from state $s$ within the time horizon $T$:

$$\mathcal{P}(s, T) = \bigcup_{n=0}^{T} \mathcal{P}_n(s)$$

Choice of time horizon:

Time HorizonDescriptionApplicable Scenario
Short term (T < 10 years)Immediate consequencesEveryday decisions
Medium term (10-100 years)Intergenerational impactPolicy decisions
Long term (100-1000 years)Civilization-scale impactMajor technological decisions
Deep time (> 1000 years)Cosmic-scale impactInterstellar civilization decisions

V. Subject Relativity of the Possibility Space

The possibility space is subject-relative. Different subjects may have different possibility spaces:

Definition 8.1.5 (subject-relative possibility space)

The possibility space $\mathcal{P}_e(s)$ of subject $e$ is the set of all states reachable by subject $e$ starting from state $s$:

$$\mathcal{P}_e(s) = \{s' : \exists \text{ path from } s \text{ to } s' \text{ accessible to } e\}$$

Sources of subject relativity:

  1. Differences in ability: different subjects have different action capacities
  2. Differences in resources: different subjects have different resource constraints
  3. Differences in knowledge: different subjects possess different knowledge and information

Hierarchical structure of the possibility space

VI. The possibility space has a hierarchical structure:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Hierarchical structure of the possibility space                 │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Level 1: Physical possibility space                             │
│  ├─ Determined by physical laws                                  │
│  └─ The largest possibility space                                │
│       ↓                                                         │ 
│  Level 2: Technological possibility space                        │
│  ├─ Determined by the current level of technology                │
│  └─ A subset of the physical possibility space                   │
│       ↓                                                         │ 
│  Level 3: Economic possibility space                             │
│  ├─ Determined by economic resources                             │
│  └─ A subset of the technological possibility space              │
│       ↓                                                         │ 
│  Level 4: Institutional possibility space                        │
│  ├─ Determined by institutional rules                            │
│  └─ A subset of the economic possibility space                   │
│       ↓                                                         │

│  ├─ Determined by individual capacity and choice                 │

│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

§8.1.3 The Computation Methods of RFD

I. The Basic Computation Formula of RFD

Definition 8.1.6 (basic definition of RFD)

The recursive freedom degree of action $a$ in state $s$ is defined as:

$$\text{RFD}(a, s) = \frac{|\mathcal{P}(s')|_{\text{eff}} - |\mathcal{P}(s)|_{\text{eff}}}{|\mathcal{P}(s)|_{\text{eff}}}$$

where:

  • $s' = \text{Result}(a, s)$ is the state after executing action $a$
  • $|\mathcal{P}(s)|_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective size of the possibility space of state $s$

Interpretation of the values:

  • $\text{RFD} = 0.5$ means the possibility space has expanded by 50%
  • $\text{RFD} = -0.3$ means the possibility space has compressed by 30%
  • $\text{RFD} = 0$ means the possibility space is unchanged

II. Extended Definitions of RFD

The basic definition can be extended to consider more factors:

Extension One: time-weighted RFD

$$\text{RFD}_T(a, s) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \gamma^{t-1} \cdot \text{RFD}(a, s, t)$$

where $\gamma \in (0, 1)$ is the time discount factor and $\text{RFD}(a, s, t)$ is the RFD at time $t$.

Extension Two: subject-weighted RFD

$$\text{RFD}_E(a, s) = \sum_{e \in E} w_e \cdot \text{RFD}_e(a, s)$$

where $E$ is the set of relevant subjects, $w_e$ is the weight of subject $e$ (which may be determined on the basis of UCS), and $\text{RFD}_e(a, s)$ is the RFD of subject $e$.

Extension Three: uncertainty-weighted RFD

When the outcome of an action is uncertain:

$$\text{RFD}_U(a, s) = \sum_{s' \in \text{Outcomes}(a, s)} p(s'|a, s) \cdot \text{RFD}(a, s \rightarrow s')$$

where $p(s'|a, s)$ is the probability of reaching state $s'$ after executing action $a$ from state $s$.

III. The Computation Procedure of RFD

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  RFD computation procedure                                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Input:                                                          │
│  - action a                                                      │
│  - current state s                                               │
│  - time horizon T                                                │
│  - set of relevant subjects E                                    │
│  - subject weights {w_e}                                         │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Output: RFD(a, s) ∈ [-1, 1]                                    │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 1: Compute the current possibility space                   │
│  P_current = ComputePossibilitySpace(s, T)                      │ 
│  size_current = MeasureSize(P_current)                          │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 2: Simulate the execution of the action                    │
│  s_prime = SimulateAction(a, s)                                 │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 3: Compute the possibility space after the action          │
│  P_after = ComputePossibilitySpace(s_prime, T)                  │ 
│  size_after = MeasureSize(P_after)                              │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 4: Compute the basic RFD                                   │
│  RFD_basic = (size_after - size_current) / size_current         │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 5: Subject weighting (if needed)                           │
│  RFD_weighted = 0                                               │ 
│  FOR EACH e IN E:                                               │ 
│      RFD_e = ComputeRFD_ForEntity(a, s, e, T)                   │ 
│      RFD_weighted += w_e  RFD_e                                │  
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 6: Normalization                                           │
│  RFD_final = Normalize(RFD_weighted, [-1, 1])                   │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 7: Uncertainty assessment                                  │
│  uncertainty = EstimateUncertainty(a, s, T)                     │ 
│                                                                 │ 
│  Return: (RFD_final, uncertainty)                                │
│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Computation StepComplexityBottleneck

Measurement of the possibility spaceO(P)Linear
Subject weightingO(E)Linear
Uncertainty assessmentO(Outcomes)Depends on the number of outcomes

Total complexity: O(|A|^T · |S|), infeasible in large-scale systems.

§8.1.4 Approximate Computation of RFD

I. The Necessity of Approximate Computation

Because the exact computation of RFD is infeasible in complex systems, approximation methods need to be developed. This section introduces four approximation methods.

Method A: Monte Carlo [6] sampling

Basic idea: estimate the size of the possibility space through random sampling.

Algorithm:

PROCEDURE MonteCarloRFD(a, s, T, N) // N: number of samples

// Step 1: Sample the current possibility space samples_current = [] FOR i = 1 TO N: path = RandomWalk(s, T) samples_current.append(path.final_state) diversity_current = EstimateDiversity(samples_current)

// Step 2: Simulate the action s_prime = SimulateAction(a, s)

// Step 3: Sample the possibility space after the action samples_after = [] FOR i = 1 TO N: path = RandomWalk(s_prime, T) samples_after.append(path.final_state) diversity_after = EstimateDiversity(samples_after)

// Step 4: Compute RFD RFD = (diversity_after - diversity_current) / diversity_current

// Step 5: Estimate uncertainty uncertainty = EstimateMonteCarloUncertainty(N)

RETURN (RFD, uncertainty) END PROCEDURE

Complexity: O(N · T)

Advantages:

  • Applicable to arbitrary state spaces
  • Can handle continuous state spaces
  • Uncertainty can be quantified

Disadvantages:

  • Requires a large number of samples to be accurate
  • May miss rare but important states

Method B: local linearization

Basic idea: linearize the system dynamics near the current state, and compute the reachable set of the linearized system.

Algorithm:

Let the system dynamics be $s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t)$, linearized at $(s_0, a_0)$:

$$s_{t+1} \approx f(s_0, a_0) + J_s (s_t - s_0) + J_a (a_t - a_0)$$

where $J_s = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}|_{(s_0, a_0)}$ and $J_a = \frac{\partial f}{\partial a}|_{(s_0, a_0)}$.

The reachable set of the linearized system can be computed through an ellipsoid approximation:

$$\mathcal{P}_{\text{linear}}(s, T) \approx \text{Ellipsoid}(\mu_T, \Sigma_T)$$

where $\mu_T$ and $\Sigma_T$ are the mean and covariance after $T$ steps.

Complexity: O(d³ · T), where $d$ is the dimension of the state space.

Advantages:

  • High computational efficiency
  • Applicable to continuous systems
  • Has theoretical guarantees

Disadvantages:

  • Valid only locally
  • Not applicable to highly nonlinear systems

Method C: expert-judgment method

Basic idea: invite experts to assess the impact of an action on the possibility space, and aggregate opinions using the Delphi method.

Procedure:

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Expert-judgment method procedure                                │                     
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │                      
│  Step 1: Expert selection                                        │                     
│  - Select k experts from relevant fields                         │                     
│  - Ensure diversity of expert backgrounds                        │                     
│                                                                 │                      
│  Step 2: First round of assessment                               │                     
│  - Provide experts with the action description and background information │            
│  - Ask experts to independently assess the RFD value (-1 to 1)   │                     
│  - Ask experts to provide reasons for their assessment           │                     
│                                                                 │                      
│  Step 3: Feedback and revision                                   │                     
│  - Summarize the results of the first round (mean, variance, reasons) │                
│  - Feed the summary back to the experts                          │                     
│  - Ask experts to revise their assessments                       │                     
│                                                                 │                      
│  Step 4: Iteration (repeat Step 3 until convergence)             │                     
│                                                                 │                      
│  Step 5: Final aggregation                                       │                     
│  - Compute the final RFD = weighted mean (weights may be based on expert credibility) │
│  - Compute uncertainty = standard deviation of expert assessments │                    
│                                                                 │                      
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Complexity: O(k · r), where $k$ is the number of experts and $r$ is the number of iteration rounds.

Advantages:

  • Can handle situations difficult to formalize
  • Integrates multiple perspectives
  • Applicable to situations of deep uncertainty

Disadvantages:

  • Highly subjective
  • May involve bias
  • Relatively costly

Method D: proxy-indicator method

Basic idea: use proxy indicators that are related to the possibility space but easier to compute.

Proxy-indicator system:

Table 8.3 Proxy indicators of RFD

Proxy IndicatorSymbolDescriptionRelation to RFD
Resource availability$R_s$The diversity and quantity of available resourcesPositive correlation
Technological capacity$T_c$The number and quality of technological optionsPositive correlation
Environmental carrying capacity$E_c$The capacity of the environment to support future developmentPositive correlation
Institutional flexibility$I_f$The capacity of institutions to adapt to changePositive correlation
Knowledge stock$K_s$The richness of knowledge and informationPositive correlation

Formula for the proxy indicators:

$$\text{RFD}_{\text{proxy}}(a, s) = \sum_{i} w_i \cdot \frac{\Delta X_i(a, s)}{X_i(s)}$$

where $X_i$ is the $i$-th proxy indicator, $\Delta X_i(a, s) = X_i(s') - X_i(s)$, and $w_i$ is the weight.

Default weights:

IndicatorWeight
$R_s$0.20
$T_c$0.25
$E_c$0.25
$I_f$0.15
$K_s$0.15

Complexity: O(m), where $m$ is the number of proxy indicators.

Advantages:

  • Simple computation
  • High operability
  • Good interpretability

Disadvantages:

  • May omit important factors
  • The proxy relations may be unstable

II. Guide to Choosing an Approximation Method

§8.1.5 Examples of the Application of RFD

Example One: Renewable Energy Transition Decision

Background: a country considers large-scale investment in renewable energy infrastructure.

Action description: invest 1 trillion USD over the next 10 years to build solar and wind power generation facilities.

RFD assessment:

Step 1: Determine the changes in the proxy indicators

Proxy IndicatorBefore the ActionAfter the ActionRate of Change
Resource availability ($R_s$)0.600.75+25%
Technological capacity ($T_c$)0.650.80+23%
Environmental carrying capacity ($E_c$)0.500.70+40%
Institutional flexibility ($I_f$)0.700.700%
Knowledge stock ($K_s$)0.700.75+7%

Step 2: Compute RFD

$$\text{RFD} = 0.20 \times 0.25 + 0.25 \times 0.23 + 0.25 \times 0.40 + 0.15 \times 0 + 0.15 \times 0.07$$

$$\text{RFD} = 0.05 + 0.0575 + 0.10 + 0 + 0.0105 = 0.218$$

Step 3: Uncertainty assessment

Sources of uncertainty:

  • Uncertainty of technological development: ±0.05
  • Uncertainty of policy implementation: ±0.03
  • Uncertainty of economic conditions: ±0.04

Composite uncertainty: $U = \sqrt{0.05^2 + 0.03^2 + 0.04^2} \approx 0.07$

Conclusion: $\text{RFD} = 0.22 \pm 0.07$

Interpretation: this action is expected to expand the possibility space by about 22%, which is a positive evaluation. Execution is recommended.

Example Two: Deployment of Gene-Editing Technology

Background: considering the approval of clinical application of human embryo gene-editing technology.

Action description: permit human embryo gene editing under strict regulation to prevent genetic diseases.

RFD assessment (using the expert-judgment method):

Results of expert assessment:

ExpertRFD AssessmentReason
Expert A (bioethicist)-0.15May lead to irreversible genetic changes, closing certain possibilities
Expert B (geneticist)+0.10Expands therapeutic options, but caution is needed
Expert C (sociologist)-0.20May exacerbate social inequality, closing the possibility of equitable development
Expert D (medical ethicist)-0.05Risks and benefits are roughly balanced
Expert E (futurist)+0.05May expand human capacities in the long run

Aggregation result:

$$\text{RFD} = \frac{-0.15 + 0.10 - 0.20 - 0.05 + 0.05}{5} = -0.05$$

Uncertainty: $\sigma = 0.13$

Conclusion: $\text{RFD} = -0.05 \pm 0.13$

Interpretation: the RFD of this action is close to zero but slightly negative, with relatively large uncertainty. Recommendations:

  1. Suspend large-scale deployment
  2. Conduct more research to reduce uncertainty
  3. Establish a strict regulatory framework
  4. Design rollback mechanisms

Example Three: Interstellar Communication Decision

Background: considering sending a signal to an identified potentially habitable planet.

§8.2 CRV: Commitment Reversibility Verifiability

§8.2.1 The Theoretical Foundations of CRV

The core concept of CRV (Commitment Reversibility Verifiability) is "commitment" (Commitment) [7]. The theoretical foundations of CRV derive in part from the theory of commitment in game theory [12]. Thomas Schelling's theory of strategic commitment shows that credible commitments can change the equilibrium structure of a game.

I. From the New View of Cognition to CRV

CRV (Commitment Reversibility Verifiability) derives directly from two core propositions of the New View of Cognition:

Proposition NK-1 (participatory cognition)

Cognition is not a passive reflection of the external world, but an active interaction between the cognizer and the environment. The cognizer participates through action in shaping the knowable reality.

Proposition NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge)

Knowledge is not fixed and immutable, but can be adjusted through negotiation. The standards of cognition themselves are revisable.

Derivation chain:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  The derivation chain from NK-1, NK-4 to CRV                      │                  
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │                    
│  Premise 1: NK-1 (cognition is participatory)                    │                   
│       ↓                                                         │                    
│  Corollary 1: the cognizer transforms cognition into action through commitment │     
│       ↓                                                         │                    
│  Corollary 2: commitment is the bridge between cognition and action │                
│       ↓                                                         │                    
│  Premise 2: NK-4 (knowledge is negotiable)                       │                   
│       ↓                                                         │                    
│  Corollary 3: commitment should retain room for modification     │                   
│       ↓                                                         │                    
│  Premise 3: the Principle of Reversibility (prefer reversible actions) │             
│       ↓                                                         │                    
│  Corollary 4: the reversibility and verifiability of commitment need to be assessed │
│       ↓                                                         │                    
│  Conclusion: CRV must be designed as a tool for assessing the quality of commitment │
│                                                                 │                    
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

II. The Conceptual Definition of CRV

Definition 8.2.1 (conceptual definition of CRV)

The first dimension of CRV is verifiability (Verifiability) [8]. Commitment Reversibility Verifiability (CRV) is a three-dimensional indicator for assessing the quality of commitment. Verifiability can be achieved through a variety of technical means, including smart contracts [9], third-party auditing, distributed ledgers, and so on. Smart contracts automatically execute the terms of a commitment through code, providing a high degree of verifiability.

Formalized statement:

$$\text{CRV}: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow [0, 1]^3$$

where:

  • $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of commitments
  • $[0, 1]^3$ is the three-dimensional unit cube

Three-dimensional structure:

$$\text{CRV}(c) = (V_{\text{obs}}(c), V_{\text{enf}}(c), V_{\text{rev}}(c))$$

where:

  • $V_{\text{obs}}$: observability (Observability)
  • $V_{\text{enf}}$: enforceability (Enforceability)
  • $V_{\text{rev}}$: rollbackability (Reversibility)

III. The Concept of Commitment

Definition 8.2.2 (commitment)

A commitment (Commitment) is a subject's declaration regarding future action or state that carries binding force.

Formalized statement:

$$c = (A, P, \phi, T, \text{Conditions})$$

where:

  • $A$: the committing subject
  • $P$: the object of the commitment (the recipient of the commitment)
  • $\phi$: the content of the commitment (the action or state committed to)
  • $T$: the time horizon of the commitment
  • $\text{Conditions}$: the conditions of the commitment

Types of commitment:

TypeDescriptionExample
Action commitmentCommits to performing a specific action"I will reduce carbon emissions by 10% next year"
State commitmentCommits to reaching a specific state"I will ensure the system is secure"
Constraint commitmentCommits not to perform a specific action"I will not be the first to use nuclear weapons"
Conditional commitmentA commitment under specific conditions"If you cooperate, I will cooperate too"

III. Design Principles of CRV

The design of CRV follows these principles:

Principle One: the principle of theoretical anchoring

CRV must be anchored to the core propositions of the New View of Cognition.

$$\text{CRV} \triangleleft \{\text{NK-1}, \text{NK-4}\}$$

Principle Two: the three-dimensional principle

CRV focuses on three key aspects of commitment: observability, enforceability, and rollbackability.

Principle Three: the game-theoretic foundation principle

The design of CRV takes into account the problem of commitment in game theory, in particular how to make commitment credible.

Principle Four: the operationalizability principle

Each dimension of CRV should be assessable through explicit procedures.

IV. The Relation Between CRV and Game Theory

The design of CRV draws on research on the problem of commitment in game theory:

Table 8.5 Correspondence between CRV and game-theoretic concepts

CRV DimensionGame-Theoretic ConceptRelation
$V_{\text{obs}}$Information structureHigh observability means that action can be observed
$V_{\text{enf}}$Punishment mechanismHigh enforceability means that defection can be punished
$V_{\text{rev}}$RenegotiationHigh rollbackability means that commitment can be modified

§8.2.2 V_obs: Observability

I. The Concept of Observability

Definition 8.2.3 (observability)

Observability ($V_{\text{obs}}$) measures the degree to which the fulfillment of a commitment can be observed and verified.

Formalized statement:

$$V_{\text{obs}}: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

where $V_{\text{obs}}(c) = 1$ means that the fulfillment of the commitment is fully observable, and $V_{\text{obs}}(c) = 0$ means that it is completely unobservable.

II. Sub-Dimensions of Observability

Observability can be decomposed into three sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimension 1: outcome observability ($V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{outcome}}$)

Whether the outcome of the commitment can be observed.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{outcome}}(c) = \frac{\text{number of observable outcome indicators}}{\text{total number of outcome indicators}}$$

Sub-dimension 2: process observability ($V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{process}}$)

Whether the process of fulfilling the commitment can be observed.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{process}}(c) = \frac{\text{number of observable process steps}}{\text{total number of process steps}}$$

Sub-dimension 3: attribution observability ($V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{attribution}}$)

Whether the outcome can be attributed to the action of the committing subject.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{attribution}}(c) = 1 - \text{attribution ambiguity}$$

III. Composite Computation of Observability

$$V_{\text{obs}}(c) = w_1 \cdot V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{outcome}}(c) + w_2 \cdot V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{process}}(c) + w_3 \cdot V_{\text{obs}}^{\text{attribution}}(c)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.4, w_2 = 0.3, w_3 = 0.3$

IV. Assessment Procedure of Observability

│                                                                 │

│  - List all outcome indicators involved in the commitment        │                                         
│  - Assess the observability of each indicator                    │

│                                                                 │

│  - Assess the observability of each step                         │

│                                                                 │                                          
│  Step 3: Assess the clarity of attribution                       │

│  - Consider confounding factors                                  │

§8.2.3 V_enf: Enforceability

I. The Concept of Enforceability

Definition 8.2.4 (enforceability)

Enforceability ($V_{\text{enf}}$) measures the degree to which the violation of a commitment can be punished or corrected.

Formalized statement:

$$V_{\text{enf}}: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

where $V_{\text{enf}}(c) = 1$ means that a violation of the commitment is necessarily punished, and $V_{\text{enf}}(c) = 0$ means that a violation has no consequences whatsoever.

II. Sub-Dimensions of Enforceability

Enforceability can be decomposed into four sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimension 1: detection capacity ($V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{detect}}$)

The probability that an act violating the commitment can be detected.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{detect}}(c) = P(\text{detect violation} | \text{violation occurs})$$

Sub-dimension 2: punishment capacity ($V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{punish}}$)

The capacity to impose punishment after a violation has been detected.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{punish}}(c) = P(\text{impose punishment} | \text{detect violation})$$

Sub-dimension 3: punishment severity ($V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{severity}}$)

The severity of the punishment relative to the gain from the violation.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{severity}}(c) = \min\left(1, \frac{\text{cost of punishment}}{\text{gain from violation}}\right)$$

Sub-dimension 4: punishment credibility ($V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{credibility}}$)

The degree of credibility of the threat of punishment.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{credibility}}(c) = P(\text{the punisher will carry out the punishment})$$

III. Composite Computation of Enforceability

$$V_{\text{enf}}(c) = V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{detect}}(c) \times V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{punish}}(c) \times \sqrt{V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{severity}}(c) \times V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{credibility}}(c)}$$

The multiplicative form is adopted because the various links of enforceability are in series: the failure of any one link reduces the overall enforceability.

IV. Assessment Procedure of Enforceability

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Enforceability assessment procedure                             │  
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │   
│  Input: commitment c                                             │  
│  Output: V_enf(c) ∈ [0, 1]                                       │  
│                                                                 │   
│  Step 1: Assess detection capacity                               │  
│  - Identify possible modes of violation                          │  
│  - Assess the detection probability of each mode of violation    │  
│  - Compute the weighted average V_enf^detect                     │  
│                                                                 │   
│  Step 2: Assess punishment capacity                              │  
│  - Identify available punishment mechanisms                      │  
│  - Assess the feasibility of implementing the punishment mechanism │
│  - Compute V_enf^punish                                          │  
│                                                                 │   
│  Step 3: Assess punishment severity                              │  
│  - Estimate the potential gain from violating the commitment     │  
│  - Estimate the cost of punishment                               │  
│  - Compute V_enf^severity                                        │  
│                                                                 │   
│  Step 4: Assess punishment credibility                           │  
│  - Assess the willingness and capacity of the punisher           │  
│  - Consider track record and reputation                          │  
│  - Compute V_enf^credibility                                     │  
│                                                                 │   
│  Step 5: Composite computation                                   │  
│  V_enf = V_enf^detect × V_enf^punish                           │    
│          × sqrt(V_enf^severity × V_enf^credibility)            │    
│                                                                 │   
│  Return: V_enf(c)                                                │  
│                                                                 │   
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

VI. Enforceability and Game Theory

Enforceability is closely related to the concept of "credible commitment" in game theory. According to game theory, for a commitment to be credible, it must satisfy:

$$\text{cost of violation} > \text{gain from violation}$$

This is precisely what $V_{\text{enf}}^{\text{severity}}$ measures.

§8.2.4 V_rev: Rollbackability

I. The Concept of Rollbackability [10]

Definition 8.2.5 (rollbackability)

Rollbackability ($V_{\text{rev}}$) measures the degree to which a commitment can be modified, withdrawn, or rolled back.

Formalized statement:

$$V_{\text{rev}}: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$

where $V_{\text{rev}}(c) = 1$ means the commitment can be fully rolled back, and $V_{\text{rev}}(c) = 0$ means the commitment is completely non-rollbackable.

II. The Importance of Rollbackability

Rollbackability is the most distinctive dimension of CRV, directly embodying proposition NK-4 of the New View of Cognition (the negotiability of knowledge) and the Principle of Reversibility.

Sources of the importance of rollbackability:

  1. Epistemic humility: our knowledge is limited, and commitments may be based on erroneous information
  2. Environmental change: the environment may change, rendering the original commitment no longer appropriate
  3. Value evolution: values may evolve, rendering the original commitment no longer consistent with current values
  4. Error correction: mechanisms are needed to correct erroneous commitments

III. Sub-Dimensions of Rollbackability

Rollbackability can be decomposed into three sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimension 1: modifiability ($V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{modify}}$)

The degree to which the content of the commitment can be modified.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{modify}}(c) = \frac{\text{number of modifiable clauses}}{\text{total number of clauses}} \times \text{feasibility of the modification procedure}$$

Sub-dimension 2: withdrawability ($V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{withdraw}}$)

The degree to which the commitment can be fully withdrawn.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{withdraw}}(c) = P(\text{withdrawal is accepted}) \times (1 - \text{cost of withdrawal}/\text{value of commitment})$$

Sub-dimension 3: impact reversibility ($V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{impact}}$)

The degree to which the impact already produced by the commitment can be reversed.

Operationalized definition:

$$V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{impact}}(c) = \frac{\text{reversible impact}}{\text{total impact}}$$

Composite computation of rollbackability

$$V_{\text{rev}}(c) = w_1 \cdot V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{modify}}(c) + w_2 \cdot V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{withdraw}}(c) + w_3 \cdot V_{\text{rev}}^{\text{impact}}(c)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.3, w_2 = 0.3, w_3 = 0.4$

The weight of impact reversibility is higher because it measures the reversibility of actual consequences, not merely the modifiability of the commitment itself.

IV. Assessment Procedure of Rollbackability

│  Rollbackability assessment procedure                            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │ 
│  Input: commitment c                                             │
│  Output: V_rev(c) ∈ [0, 1]                                       │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 1: Assess modifiability                                    │
│  - Identify the various clauses of the commitment                │
│  - Assess the modifiability of each clause                       │
│  - Assess the feasibility of the modification procedure          │
│  - Compute V_rev^modify                                          │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 2: Assess withdrawability                                  │
│  - Assess the procedural requirements for withdrawal             │
│  - Assess the cost of withdrawal                                 │
│  - Assess the probability that withdrawal is accepted            │
│  - Compute V_rev^withdraw                                        │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 3: Assess impact reversibility                             │
│  - Identify the impact that the commitment may produce           │
│  - Assess the reversibility of each impact                       │
│  - Compute the weighted average V_rev^impact                     │
│                                                                 │ 
│  Step 4: Composite computation                                   │
│  V_rev = w1  V_rev^modify + w2  V_rev^withdraw               │    
│          + w3  V_rev^impact                                    │  
│                                                                 │ 
│  Return: V_rev(c)                                                │
│                                                                 │ 
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

VI. The Relation Between Rollbackability and RFD

Rollbackability is closely related to RFD:

Proposition 8.2.1 (rollbackability-RFD connection)

All else being equal, commitments with high rollbackability tend to preserve a higher RFD.

Formalized statement:

$$\frac{\partial \text{RFD}}{\partial V_{\text{rev}}} > 0$$

Intuitive explanation: a rollbackable commitment retains the possibility of modification and therefore does not excessively close the possibility space.

§8.2.5 Integrated Assessment of CRV

I. The Vector Representation of CRV

The complete assessment result of CRV is a three-dimensional vector:

$$\text{CRV}(c) = (V_{\text{obs}}(c), V_{\text{enf}}(c), V_{\text{rev}}(c))$$

Advantages of the vector representation:

  • Preserves the information of each dimension
  • Allows analysis targeted at different dimensions
  • Avoids over-simplification

II. The Aggregate Score of CRV

In certain application scenarios, CRV needs to be aggregated into a single score:

Aggregation method one: weighted average

$$\text{CRV}_{\text{score}}(c) = w_{\text{obs}} \cdot V_{\text{obs}}(c) + w_{\text{enf}} \cdot V_{\text{enf}}(c) + w_{\text{rev}} \cdot V_{\text{rev}}(c)$$

Default weights: $w_{\text{obs}} = 0.35, w_{\text{enf}} = 0.35, w_{\text{rev}} = 0.30$

Aggregation method two: geometric mean

$$\text{CRV}_{\text{score}}(c) = \sqrt[3]{V_{\text{obs}}(c) \cdot V_{\text{enf}}(c) \cdot V_{\text{rev}}(c)}$$

Advantage: penalizes extremely low values in any dimension.

Aggregation method three: minimum

$$\text{CRV}_{\text{score}}(c) = \min(V_{\text{obs}}(c), V_{\text{enf}}(c), V_{\text{rev}}(c))$$

Advantage: emphasizes the "weakest-link" effect.

The recommendation of this work

This work recommends:

  1. Retain the vector representation by default
  2. Use the weighted average when aggregation is needed
  3. Report the minimum dimension value at the same time

III. Threshold Constraints of CRV

To ensure the quality of commitment, threshold constraints may be set:

Table 8.9 Threshold constraints of CRV

Minimum observability$V_{\text{obs}} \geq \theta_{\text{obs}}$Commitments requiring verification
Minimum enforceability$V_{\text{enf}} \geq \theta_{\text{enf}}$Commitments requiring enforcement
Minimum rollbackability$V_{\text{rev}} \geq \theta_{\text{rev}}$Situations of deep uncertainty [11]
Composite threshold$\text{CRV}_{\text{score}} \geq \theta_{\text{CRV}}$General quality requirement

Suggested default thresholds:

§8.3 The Integrated Application of RFD and CRV

§8.3.1 The Complementary Relationship Between the Two Indicators

I. Complementarity at the Conceptual Level

RFD and CRV are complementary at the conceptual level:

Table 8.10 Conceptual complementarity of RFD and CRV

DimensionRFDCRV
Object of assessmentThe consequences of actionThe quality of commitment
Temporal focusFuture possibilitiesThe current decision process
Core concernProtection of the possibility spaceThe credibility and flexibility of commitment
Theoretical anchoringNC-2, NC-3NK-1, NK-4
Normative relationThe Principle of Recursive FreedomThe Principle of Reversibility

II. Complementarity at the Computational Level

RFD and CRV are also complementary at the computational level:

  1. RFD assesses the impact of action: does the action keep the possibility space open?
  2. CRV assesses the quality of the decision: is the decision process consistent with epistemic humility?

III. Formalized Relation

There is a formalized relation between RFD and CRV:

Proposition 8.3.1 (CRV-RFD connection)

All else being equal:

  1. High $V_{\text{rev}}$ (high rollbackability) tends to lead to high RFD
  2. High $V_{\text{obs}}$ (high observability) allows timely error correction, thereby protecting RFD
  3. High $V_{\text{enf}}$ (high enforceability) ensures that the commitment is fulfilled, and the RFD impact is predictable

Formalized statement:

$$\text{RFD}(a) = g(\text{CRV}(c_a), \text{OtherFactors})$$

where $c_a$ is the commitment related to action $a$.

II. Detailed Procedure of Integrated Application

PROCEDURE IntegratedRFD_CRV_Assessment(decision_problem)

// Phase 1: Problem definition actions = IdentifyActions(decision_problem) commitments = IdentifyCommitments(decision_problem) time_horizon = DetermineTimeHorizon(decision_problem) risk_level = AssessRiskLevel(decision_problem)

// Phase 2: RFD assessment RFD_results = {} FOR EACH action IN actions: method = SelectRFDMethod(action, time_horizon) RFD_value, uncertainty = ComputeRFD(action, method) RFD_results[action] = (RFD_value, uncertainty)

// Phase 3: CRV assessment CRV_results = {} FOR EACH commitment IN commitments: CRV_vector = EvaluateCRV(commitment) CRV_score = ComputeCRVScore(CRV_vector) constraints_met = CheckConstraints(CRV_vector, risk_level) CRV_results[commitment] = (CRV_vector, CRV_score, constraints_met)

// Phase 4: Integrated analysis integrated_results = {} FOR EACH action IN actions: related_commitments = GetRelatedCommitments(action, commitments) RFD_value = RFD_results[action][0] avg_CRV = AverageCRV(related_commitments, CRV_results) assessment = JointAssessment(RFD_value, avg_CRV) integrated_results[action] = assessment

// Phase 5: Decision recommendations recommendations = GenerateRecommendations(integrated_results)

RETURN (RFD_results, CRV_results, integrated_results, recommendations)

END PROCEDURE

§8.4 The Limitations of RFD and CRV

§8.4.1 The Problem of the Computational Feasibility of RFD

Limitation R1: the curse of dimensionality of the state space

The exact computation of RFD requires enumerating the possibility space, but the state space of real systems is usually high-dimensional, rendering computation infeasible.

Formalized statement:

Let the dimension of the state space be $d$, with each dimension having $n$ possible values; then the size of the state space is $n^d$. When $d$ is large, enumeration is infeasible.

Example:

SystemState-Space DimensionState-Space SizeFeasibility
Simple game10$10^{10}$Difficult
Economic system1000$10^{1000}$Infeasible
Ecosystem10000$10^{10000}$Completely infeasible

Response strategies:

  1. Use approximation methods (§8.4.1)
  2. Dimensionality reduction
  3. Focus on key dimensions
  4. Acknowledge computational limitations

Limitation R2: the undecidability of reachability

In certain systems, determining whether a state is reachable may be undecidable.

Formalized statement:

For Turing-complete systems, the reachability problem is equivalent to the halting problem and is undecidable.

Response strategies:

  1. Limit the complexity of the system
  2. Use approximate reachability
  3. Set time bounds

Limitation R3: the arbitrariness of the choice of measure

The "size" of the possibility space depends on the choice of measure, and different measures may lead to different RFD values.

Example:

MeasurePossibility Space APossibility Space BA vs B
Number of states10050A > B
State diversity0.50.8A < B
Value coverage0.60.7A < B

Response strategies:

  1. Clarify the rationale for the choice of measure
  2. Use multiple measures for sensitivity analysis
  3. Report the influence of the choice of measure

Limitation R4: the uncertainty of long-term prediction

RFD involves predicting the future possibility space, but long-term prediction carries fundamental uncertainty.

Sources of uncertainty:

  1. Model uncertainty: our model may be wrong
  2. Parameter uncertainty: parameter estimates may be inaccurate
  3. Structural uncertainty: the structure of the system may change
  4. Black-swan events: major events that cannot be foreseen

Response strategies:

  1. Use scenario analysis
  2. Report the range of uncertainty
  3. Periodically update the assessment
  4. Adopt conservative estimates

§8.4.2 The Subjectivity Problem of CRV

Limitation C1: the subjectivity of sub-dimension assessment

Many sub-dimensions of CRV involve subjective judgment, and different assessors may give different scores.

Sources of subjectivity:

Sub-DimensionDegree of SubjectivityMain Source
Outcome observabilityMediumThe definition of "observable"
Process observabilityMediumThe delimitation of "process"
Attribution observabilityHighThe complexity of causal judgment
Punishment credibilityHighInference about intention
Impact reversibilityHighThe definition of "reversible"

Response strategies:

  1. Establish standardized assessment procedures
  2. Use multi-assessor cross-validation
  3. Report inter-assessor differences
  4. Establish calibration mechanisms

Limitation C2: disputes over the determination of weights

The determination of the weights of the various dimensions and sub-dimensions of CRV is disputed, and different weights may lead to different conclusions.

Examples of weight disputes:

PositionRecommended WeightReason
Transparency firstHigh weight for $V_{\text{obs}}$Observability is the foundation
Enforcement firstHigh weight for $V_{\text{enf}}$A commitment without enforceability is meaningless
Flexibility firstHigh weight for $V_{\text{rev}}$Retaining room for modification is most important

Response strategies:

  1. Provide default weights but allow adjustment
  2. Conduct weight sensitivity analysis
  3. Determine weights through negotiation
  4. Report the results under different weights

Limitation C3: the vagueness of the boundaries of commitment

The boundaries of a commitment are sometimes vague, making it difficult to clearly delimit the object of assessment.

Sources of vagueness:

  1. Content vagueness: the content of the commitment is not clear enough
  2. Condition vagueness: the conditions of the commitment are not clear enough
  3. Temporal vagueness: the time horizon of the commitment is not clear
  4. Subject vagueness: the subject of the commitment is not clear enough

Response strategies:

  1. Require that commitments be made explicit
  2. Assess using the broadest interpretation
  3. Annotate vagueness
  4. Suggest improvements to the formulation of the commitment

Limitation C4: the difficulty of capturing dynamic change

CRV is a static assessment and has difficulty capturing the dynamic change of commitment quality.

Sources of dynamic change:

  1. Environmental change: changes in the external environment affect CRV
  2. Capacity change: changes in the capacity of the committing subject
  3. Relationship change: changes in the relationships among the parties to the commitment
  4. Institutional change: changes in the relevant institutions

Response strategies:

  1. Periodic reassessment
  2. Establish dynamic monitoring mechanisms
  3. Design conditions that trigger reassessment
  4. Consider the time series of CRV

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

As a detailed argument for RFD and CRV, this chapter accomplishes the following core tasks:

Conclusion One: the theoretical foundations and computation methods of RFD

RFD is directly anchored to NC-2 (process ontology) and NC-3 (participatory universe) of the New Cosmological View, and measures the impact of action on the possibility space. The possibility space is the set of all future states reachable from a given state, and possesses multiple modes of measurement. The exact computation of RFD is infeasible in complex systems, and approximation methods such as Monte Carlo sampling, local linearization, the expert-judgment method, or the proxy-indicator method must be used.

Conclusion Two: the three-dimensional structure of CRV

CRV is directly anchored to NK-1 (participatory cognition) and NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge) of the New View of Cognition, and assesses the quality of commitment through three dimensions:

DimensionCore MeasurementSub-Dimensions
$V_{\text{obs}}$ObservabilityOutcome, process, attribution
$V_{\text{enf}}$EnforceabilityDetection, punishment, severity, credibility
$V_{\text{rev}}$RollbackabilityModification, withdrawal, impact reversibility

Conclusion Three: the integrated application of RFD and CRV

RFD and CRV are complementary at the conceptual and computational levels. High CRV tends to protect RFD. The integrated application comprises five phases: problem definition, RFD assessment, CRV assessment, integrated analysis, and decision recommendations. The joint assessment matrix provides decision guidance.

Conclusion Four: limitations and directions for improvement

RFD faces problems of computational feasibility (the curse of dimensionality, undecidability, arbitrariness of measure, long-term uncertainty), and CRV faces problems of subjectivity (assessment subjectivity, weight disputes, boundary vagueness, dynamic change). Directions for improvement include improved computation methods, standardized assessment, deepened theory, and accumulated practice.

[1] Possibility Space: the possibility space is a concept describing the set of all future states reachable by a system from its current state. This concept is widely applied in modal logic, decision theory, and complex-systems science. In modal logic, the possibility space is related to the concept of "possible worlds"; in decision theory, it is related to the concepts of "decision trees" and "state spaces." See: Kripke, S. (1963). "Semantical Considerations on Modal Logic." Acta Philosophica Fennica, 16, 83-94; Kauffman, S. A. (1993). The Origins of Order: Self-Organization and Selection in Evolution. Oxford University Press.

[2] Phase Space: phase space is the mathematical space in physics that describes all possible states of a dynamical system. In classical mechanics, phase space is constituted by the generalized coordinates and generalized momenta of the system. The concept of phase space was developed by Joseph Liouville and Henri Poincaré. This work extends the concept of phase space from physical systems to more general state spaces. See: Arnold, V. I. (1989). Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (2nd ed.). Springer; Strogatz, S. H. (2015). Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (2nd ed.). Westview Press.

[3] Recursive Freedom: the concept of recursive freedom emphasizes the self-referential nature of freedom: genuine freedom is not only the capacity to choose in the present, but also the capacity to protect the space of future choice. This concept bears an intellectual kinship to Sen's "capability approach" and Nussbaum's "list of capabilities," but places more emphasis on the dynamic and recursive nature of freedom. See the detailed argument in Chapter 11 of this work; see also: Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Knopf; Pettit, P. (1997). Republicanism: A Theory of Freedom and Government. Oxford University Press.

[4] Capability Approach: the capability approach is a normative framework developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, focusing on what people are actually able to do and to be, rather than only on resources or utility. The capability approach emphasizes the intrinsic value of freedom and choice, and provides an important reference for the theoretical foundations of RFD. See: Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Knopf; Nussbaum, M. C. (2011). Creating Capabilities: The Human Development Approach. Harvard University Press; Robeyns, I. (2017). Wellbeing, Freedom and Social Justice: The Capability Approach Re-Examined. Open Book Publishers.

[5] Markov Chain: a Markov chain is a stochastic process characterized by "memorylessness": the future state of the system depends only on the current state and is independent of past states. The Markov chain was introduced by the Russian mathematician Andrey Markov in 1906 and is now widely applied in physics, biology, economics, and computer science. See: Norris, J. R. (1997). Markov Chains. Cambridge University Press; Levin, D. A., Peres, Y., & Wilmer, E. L. (2009). Markov Chains and Mixing Times. American Mathematical Society.

[6] Monte Carlo Method: the Monte Carlo method is a class of computational algorithms based on random sampling, used to estimate numerical values that are difficult to compute exactly. The method is named after the Monte Carlo casino in Monaco and was developed by Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann during the Manhattan Project. See: Metropolis, N., & Ulam, S. (1949). "The Monte Carlo Method." Journal of the American Statistical Association, 44(247), 335-341; Robert, C. P., & Casella, G. (2004). Monte Carlo Statistical Methods (2nd ed.). Springer.

[7] Commitment: in game theory and social-contract theory, a commitment is a binding declaration by a subject regarding future action. Thomas Schelling's theory of strategic commitment shows that credible commitments can change the equilibrium structure of a game, giving the committer a strategic advantage. The credibility of a commitment depends on the cost of default and the observability of the commitment. See: Schelling, T. C. (1960). The Strategy of Conflict. Harvard University Press; Elster, J. (2000). Ulysses Unbound: Studies in Rationality, Precommitment, and Constraints. Cambridge University Press.

[8] Verifiability: verifiability is the degree to which the truth value of a proposition or commitment can be independently confirmed. In logical positivism, verifiability is the criterion of meaning; in contract theory, verifiability is a prerequisite for the enforceability of a commitment. Verifiability is closely related to observability and measurability. See: Ayer, A. J. (1936). Language, Truth and Logic. Victor Gollancz; Hart, O., & Moore, J. (1999). "Foundations of Incomplete Contracts." The Review of Economic Studies, 66(1), 115-138.

[9] Smart Contract: a smart contract is a self-executing program stored on a blockchain that automatically executes contract terms when preset conditions are met. The concept was proposed by Nick Szabo in 1994 and later widely implemented on blockchain platforms such as Ethereum. Smart contracts provide a high degree of verifiability and automatic execution capability. See: Szabo, N. (1997). "Formalizing and Securing Relationships on Public Networks." First Monday, 2(9); Buterin, V. (2014). "A Next-Generation Smart Contract and Decentralized Application Platform." Ethereum White Paper.

[10] Rollbackability: rollbackability refers to the capacity of a system or decision to be withdrawn or restored to a previous state. This concept is widely applied in database systems, software engineering, and decision theory. Rollbackability is the operationalized embodiment of the Principle of Reversibility and is directly related to the New View of Cognition of this work (NK-4, the negotiability of knowledge). See: Gray, J., & Reuter, A. (1993). Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann; Chapter 13 of this work (the Principle of Reversibility).

[11] Deep Uncertainty: deep uncertainty refers to situations in which decision-makers cannot enumerate all possible outcomes, cannot assign probabilities to outcomes, or do not know which model is correct. Deep uncertainty is distinguished from risk (assignable probabilities) and uncertainty (enumerable outcomes). See: Knight, F. H. (1921). Risk, Uncertainty and Profit. Houghton Mifflin; Marchau, V. A., Walker, W. E., Bloemen, P. J., & Popper, S. W. (Eds.). (2019). Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty: From Theory to Practice. Springer; Taleb, N. N. (2007). The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable. Random House.

[12] Game Theory: game theory is the mathematical theory that studies strategic interaction among rational agents. It was founded by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern in 1944 and later developed by John Nash, Thomas Schelling, and others. The theory of commitment in game theory provides an important theoretical foundation for CRV. See: von Neumann, J., & Morgenstern, O. (1944). Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Princeton University Press; Osborne, M. J., & Rubinstein, A. (1994). A Course in Game Theory. MIT Press.

Footnotes

Chapter 8 Footnotes

[1] Possibility Space: A possibility space is the concept describing the set of all future states reachable by a system from its current state. The concept is widely applied in modal logic, decision theory, and complex systems science. In modal logic, the possibility space is related to the concept of "possible worlds"; in decision theory, it is related to the concepts of "decision trees" and "state spaces." See: Kripke, S. (1963). "Semantical Considerations on Modal Logic." Acta Philosophica Fennica, 16, 83-94; Kauffman, S. A. (1993). The Origins of Order: Self-Organization and Selection in Evolution. Oxford University Press.

[2] Phase Space: Phase space is the mathematical space in physics that describes all possible states of a dynamical system. In classical mechanics, phase space is constituted by the system's generalized coordinates and generalized momenta. The concept of phase space was developed by Joseph Liouville and Henri Poincaré. This work extends the concept of phase space from physical systems to more general state spaces. See: Arnold, V. I. (1989). Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (2nd ed.). Springer; Strogatz, S. H. (2015). Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (2nd ed.). Westview Press.

[3] Recursive Freedom: The concept of recursive freedom emphasizes the self-referential character of freedom: genuine freedom is not only the capacity to choose in the present but also the capacity to protect the space of future choice. This concept is intellectually affiliated with Sen's "capability approach" and Nussbaum's "list of capabilities," but it places greater emphasis on the dynamic and recursive character of freedom. See the detailed argument in Chapter 11 of this work; see also: Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Knopf; Pettit, P. (1997). Republicanism: A Theory of Freedom and Government. Oxford University Press.

[4] The Capability Approach: The capability approach is a normative framework developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum that focuses on what people are actually able to do and to be, rather than on resources or utility alone. The capability approach emphasizes the intrinsic value of freedom and choice and provides an important reference for the theoretical foundations of the RFD. See: Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Knopf; Nussbaum, M. C. (2011). Creating Capabilities: The Human Development Approach. Harvard University Press; Robeyns, I. (2017). Wellbeing, Freedom and Social Justice: The Capability Approach Re-Examined. Open Book Publishers.

[5] Markov Chains: A Markov chain is a stochastic process characterized by "memorylessness": the future state of the system depends only on the current state and not on past states. The Markov chain was introduced by the Russian mathematician Andrey Markov in 1906 and is now widely applied in physics, biology, economics, and computer science. See: Norris, J. R. (1997). Markov Chains. Cambridge University Press; Levin, D. A., Peres, Y., & Wilmer, E. L. (2009). Markov Chains and Mixing Times. American Mathematical Society.

[6] The Monte Carlo Method: The Monte Carlo method is a class of computational algorithms based on random sampling, used to estimate numerical values that are difficult to compute exactly. Named after the Monte Carlo casino in Monaco, the method was developed by Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann during the Manhattan Project. See: Metropolis, N., & Ulam, S. (1949). "The Monte Carlo Method." Journal of the American Statistical Association, 44(247), 335-341; Robert, C. P., & Casella, G. (2004). Monte Carlo Statistical Methods (2nd ed.). Springer.

[7] Commitment: In game theory and social contract theory, a commitment is a binding statement by an agent regarding its future actions. Thomas Schelling's theory of strategic commitment shows that credible commitments can alter the equilibrium structure of a game, giving the committer a strategic advantage. The credibility of a commitment depends on the cost of defection and the observability of the commitment. See: Schelling, T. C. (1960). The Strategy of Conflict. Harvard University Press; Elster, J. (2000). Ulysses Unbound: Studies in Rationality, Precommitment, and Constraints. Cambridge University Press.

[8] Verifiability: Verifiability is the degree to which the truth value of a proposition or commitment can be independently confirmed. In logical positivism, verifiability is the criterion of meaning; in contract theory, verifiability is a precondition for the enforceability of commitments. Verifiability is closely related to observability and measurability. See: Ayer, A. J. (1936). Language, Truth and Logic. Victor Gollancz; Hart, O., & Moore, J. (1999). "Foundations of Incomplete Contracts." The Review of Economic Studies, 66(1), 115-138.

[9] Smart Contracts: A smart contract is a self-executing program stored on a blockchain that automatically executes the terms of a contract when preset conditions are satisfied. The concept was proposed by Nick Szabo in 1994 and was later widely implemented on blockchain platforms such as Ethereum. Smart contracts provide a high degree of verifiability and automatic executability. See: Szabo, N. (1997). "Formalizing and Securing Relationships on Public Networks." First Monday, 2(9); Buterin, V. (2014). "A Next-Generation Smart Contract and Decentralized Application Platform." Ethereum White Paper.

[10] Rollbackability: Rollbackability refers to the capacity of a system or decision to be undone or restored to a previous state. The concept is widely applied in database systems, software engineering, and decision theory. Rollbackability is the operational expression of the Reversibility Principle and is directly related to the New Epistemic View of this work (NK-4, the negotiability of knowledge). See: Gray, J., & Reuter, A. (1993). Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann; Chapter 13 of this work (the Reversibility Principle).

[11] Deep Uncertainty: Deep uncertainty refers to situations in which decision-makers cannot enumerate all possible outcomes, cannot assign probabilities to outcomes, or do not know which model is correct. Deep uncertainty is distinguished from risk (assignable probabilities) and from uncertainty (enumerable outcomes). See: Knight, F. H. (1921). Risk, Uncertainty and Profit. Houghton Mifflin; Marchau, V. A., Walker, W. E., Bloemen, P. J., & Popper, S. W. (Eds.). (2019). Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty: From Theory to Practice. Springer; Taleb, N. N. (2007). The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable. Random House.

[12] Game Theory: Game theory is the mathematical theory of strategic interaction among rational agents. It was founded by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern in 1944 and later developed by John Nash, Thomas Schelling, and others. The theory of commitment in game theory provides an important theoretical foundation for the CRV. See: von Neumann, J., & Morgenstern, O. (1944). Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Princeton University Press; Osborne, M. J., & Rubinstein, A. (1994). A Course in Game Theory. MIT Press.

CDI, MBCL and CSIA: Civilizational and Impact AssessmentChapter 9

Civilization Development Index, Memetic Biosafety Containment Level, and Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment

Chapter Opening Guide

I. Position of This Chapter in the Book

This chapter is the fourth chapter of Part II, "The Indicator System," and undertakes the task of operationalizing the New Three Views into tools for civilizational assessment and impact assessment. Chapter 7 established the UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) as a subject-assessment tool, and Chapter 8 established the RFD (Recursive Freedom Degree) and the CRV (Commitment Reversibility Verifiability) as action-assessment tools. This chapter, in turn, establishes the CDI (Civilization Development Index), the MBCL (Memetic Biosafety Containment Level), and the CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment) as assessment tools at the civilizational level and the cosmic scale.

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

CDI, MBCL, and CSIA are anchored respectively to different propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{CDI} \triangleleft \{\text{NC-1}, \text{NC-2}, \text{NL-2}\}$$ $$\text{MBCL} \triangleleft \{\text{NL-2}, \text{NL-3}, \text{NK-3}\}$$ $$\text{CSIA} \triangleleft \{\text{NC-2}, \text{NK-3}, \text{NK-4}\}$$

Specifically:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology) → CDI measures the relational-network complexity of a civilization
  • NC-2 (process ontology) → CDI measures the processual development of a civilization, and CSIA assesses the processual impact of actions
  • NL-2 (negentropic organization) → CDI measures the negentropic capacity of a civilization, and MBCL assesses the negentropic risk of information systems
  • NL-3 (continuum of consciousness) → MBCL considers the risks at different levels of consciousness
  • NK-3 (deep uncertainty) → MBCL and CSIA handle situations of deep uncertainty
  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge) → The assessment results of CSIA are negotiable

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer three fundamental questions:

Core Question One: How can the level of civilizational development be assessed beyond energy consumption?

Core Question Two: How can the safety risks of information systems (including memes and AI) be assessed?

Core Question Three: How can the cosmic-scale impact of actions be assessed?

The answers to these three questions will provide operationalized tools for civilizational assessment, risk management, and impact assessment in interstellar civilization governance.

VI. Boundary Statement

All content of this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Conceptual-prototype positioning: CDI, MBCL, and CSIA are all at TRL 2, suitable for academic research and thought experiments
  2. Data-availability constraints: The measurement of certain dimensions depends on data that are not yet obtainable
  3. Cross-civilizational applicability challenges: These indicators are mainly based on human civilizational experience, and cross-civilizational applicability requires further verification
  4. Open revision: All definitions and calculation methods may be revised in light of new evidence

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • Readers concerned with civilizational assessment are advised to focus on §9.1
  • Readers concerned with risk management are advised to focus on §9.2
  • Readers concerned with impact assessment are advised to focus on §9.3
  • Readers concerned with integrated application are advised to focus on §9.4

§9.1 CDI: The Civilization Development Index

§9.1.1 Theoretical Foundations of CDI

I. From the New Three Views to CDI

The CDI (Civilization Development Index) derives directly from several core propositions of the New Three Views:

Proposition NC-1 (relational ontology)

The basic constitution of reality is relations rather than independent entities. As a complex system, a civilization's level of development is manifested in the complexity and quality of its relational network.

Proposition NC-2 (process ontology)

The universe is processual. A civilization is not a static state but a continuously evolving process. Civilizational development should be assessed from a processual perspective.

Proposition NL-2 (negentropic organization)

Life is a negentropy[2] organization. As the collective form of life, a civilization's level of development is manifested in its capacity to acquire, utilize, and maintain negentropy.

Derivation chain:

I. The Conceptual Definition of CDI

Definition 9.1.1 (Conceptual Definition of CDI)

The Civilization Development Index (CDI) is a multidimensional indicator for assessing the level of civilizational development.

Formal statement:

$$\text{CDI}: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow [0, 1]^5$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of civilizations
  • $[0, 1]^5$ is the five-dimensional unit hypercube

Five-dimensional structure:

$$\text{CDI}(c) = (E(c), I(c), S(c), R(c), T(c))$$

Where:

  • $E$: Energy Efficiency
  • $I$: Information Processing
  • $S$: Social Complexity
  • $R$: Environmental Relationship
  • $T$: Temporal Horizon

II. Design Principles of CDI

The design of the CDI follows these principles:

Principle One: Theoretical anchoring principle

The CDI must be anchored to the core propositions of the New Three Views.

$$\text{CDI} \triangleleft \{\text{NC-1}, \text{NC-2}, \text{NL-2}\}$$

Principle Two: Multidimensionality principle

The CDI adopts a multidimensional design, avoiding the simplification of a single dimension.

Principle Three: Processuality principle

The CDI focuses on the processual development of a civilization, rather than a static state.

Principle Four: Relationality principle

The CDI focuses on the quality of a civilization's relations with its environment and with other civilizations.

Principle Five: Revisability principle

The definitions and calculation methods of the CDI are revisable.

III. Differences Between CDI and Traditional Civilizational Assessment

The CDI is fundamentally different from traditional civilizational assessment methods:

§9.1.2 The Five Dimensions of CDI

Dimension One: Energy Efficiency (E)

Definition 9.1.2 (Energy Efficiency)

Energy efficiency ($E$) measures the efficiency with which a civilization acquires and utilizes energy, rather than the absolute quantity—for example, giant structures such as the Dyson Sphere[6] of a Kardashev Type II civilization.

Formal statement:

$$E(c) = \frac{\text{Effective Work Output}}{\text{Total Energy Input}} \times \text{Energy Diversity Coefficient}$$

Sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimensionSymbolDescription
Energy conversion efficiency$E_{\text{conv}}$Efficiency of the energy conversion process
Energy diversity$E_{\text{div}}$Diversity of energy sources
Energy sustainability$E_{\text{sus}}$Degree of sustainability of energy use

Comprehensive calculation:

$$E(c) = w_1 \cdot E_{\text{conv}}(c) + w_2 \cdot E_{\text{div}}(c) + w_3 \cdot E_{\text{sus}}(c)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.4, w_2 = 0.3, w_3 = 0.3$

Relation to the New Three Views:

Energy efficiency directly embodies NL-2 (negentropic organization). Efficient energy utilization means a better capacity to acquire and maintain negentropy.

Dimension Two: Information Processing (I)

Definition 9.1.3 (Information Processing)

Information processing ($I$) measures a civilization's capacity to acquire, store, process, and transmit information. The concept of information entropy[3] provides the theoretical foundation for quantifying information processing.

Formal statement:

$$I(c) = f(I_{\text{acq}}, I_{\text{store}}, I_{\text{proc}}, I_{\text{trans}})$$

Sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimensionSymbolDescription
Information acquisition capacity$I_{\text{acq}}$Capacity to acquire information from the environment
Information storage capacity$I_{\text{store}}$Capacity to store and preserve information
Information processing capacity$I_{\text{proc}}$Capacity to process and analyze information
Information transmission capacity$I_{\text{trans}}$Capacity to transmit and share information

Comprehensive calculation:

$$I(c) = \sqrt[4]{I_{\text{acq}}(c) \cdot I_{\text{store}}(c) \cdot I_{\text{proc}}(c) \cdot I_{\text{trans}}(c)}$$

The geometric mean is adopted because the various links in information processing are mutually dependent, and weakness in any one link affects the overall capacity.

Relation to the New Three Views:

Information processing directly embodies NC-1 (relational ontology). Information is the carrier of relations, and information processing reflects a civilization's capacity to participate in relational networks.

Dimension Three: Social Complexity (S)

Definition 9.1.4 (Social Complexity)

Social complexity ($S$) measures the degree and quality of the complexity of a civilization's social organization. The concept of social complexity[4] comes from sociology and complex-systems science and involves social differentiation, integration, and adaptive capacity.

Formal statement:

$$S(c) = f(S_{\text{struct}}, S_{\text{div}}, S_{\text{coop}}, S_{\text{adapt}})$$

Sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimensionSymbolDescription
Structural complexity$S_{\text{struct}}$Degree of hierarchy and differentiation of the social structure
Diversity$S_{\text{div}}$Diversity of social roles and functions
Cooperative capacity$S_{\text{coop}}$Capacity for large-scale cooperation
Adaptive capacity$S_{\text{adapt}}$Capacity of the society to adapt to change

Comprehensive calculation:

$$S(c) = w_1 \cdot S_{\text{struct}}(c) + w_2 \cdot S_{\text{div}}(c) + w_3 \cdot S_{\text{coop}}(c) + w_4 \cdot S_{\text{adapt}}(c)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.25, w_2 = 0.25, w_3 = 0.25, w_4 = 0.25$

Relation to the New Three Views:

Social complexity directly embodies NC-1 (relational ontology) and NC-2 (process ontology). A complex society is the expression of a rich relational network, and social adaptive capacity embodies processual development.

Dimension Four: Environmental Relationship Quality (R)

Definition 9.1.5 (Environmental Relationship Quality)

Environmental relationship quality ($R$) measures the quality of a civilization's relations with its environment (both the natural environment and the cosmic environment).

Formal statement:

$$R(c) = f(R_{\text{sus}}, R_{\text{regen}}, R_{\text{expand}}, R_{\text{harm}})$$

Sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimensionSymbolDescription
Sustainability$R_{\text{sus}}$Degree of sustainability of resource use
Regenerative capacity$R_{\text{regen}}$Capacity for environmental regeneration and repair
Expansion capacity$R_{\text{expand}}$Capacity to expand into new environments
Harm minimization$R_{\text{harm}}$Degree of minimization of harm to the environment

Comprehensive calculation:

$$R(c) = w_1 \cdot R_{\text{sus}}(c) + w_2 \cdot R_{\text{regen}}(c) + w_3 \cdot R_{\text{expand}}(c) + w_4 \cdot (1 - R_{\text{harm}}(c))$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.30, w_2 = 0.25, w_3 = 0.20, w_4 = 0.25$

Relation to the New Three Views:

Environmental relationship quality directly embodies NC-1 (relational ontology) and NL-2 (negentropic organization). The relation between a civilization and its environment is one of the core relations, and a sustainable environmental relation is a condition for the persistence of negentropic organization.

Dimension Five: Temporal Horizon (T)

Definition 9.1.6 (Temporal Horizon)

Temporal horizon ($T$) measures the time span considered by a civilization in its decisions. Research on temporal discounting[5] shows that humans tend to underestimate the value of the future, which limits long-term planning capacity.

Formal statement:

$$T(c) = f(T_{\text{past}}, T_{\text{future}}, T_{\text{integ}})$$

Sub-dimensions:

Sub-dimensionSymbolDescription
Historical consciousness$T_{\text{past}}$Capacity to understand and learn from history
Future planning$T_{\text{future}}$Capacity and practice of long-term planning
Temporal integration$T_{\text{integ}}$Capacity to integrate past, present, and future

Comprehensive calculation:

$$T(c) = w_1 \cdot T_{\text{past}}(c) + w_2 \cdot T_{\text{future}}(c) + w_3 \cdot T_{\text{integ}}(c)$$

Default weights: $w_1 = 0.30, w_2 = 0.40, w_3 = 0.30$

The weight of future planning is higher because it is directly related to the long-term survival of a civilization.

Relation to the New Three Views:

Temporal horizon directly embodies NC-2 (process ontology). A processual cosmological view requires a civilization to possess a deep temporal horizon, enabling it to consider long-term consequences in its decisions.

IV. Standardization Methods

Each indicator needs to be standardized to the interval [0, 1]:

Method One: Min-Max standardization

$$\bar{x}_i = \frac{x_i - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}$$

Method Two: Reference-frame standardization

$$\bar{x}_i = \frac{x_i}{x_{\text{ref}}}$$

Where $x_{\text{ref}}$ is a reference value (such as a theoretical maximum or the current value of human civilization).

Recommendation of this work: Use reference-frame standardization for indicators with a clear theoretical upper bound, and Min-Max standardization for indicators without a clear upper bound.

V. Aggregate Score of CDI

Although this work recommends retaining the vector representation of the CDI, an aggregate score is needed in certain application scenarios:

Aggregation Method One: Weighted arithmetic mean

$$\text{CDI}_{\text{score}}(c) = \sum_{i \in \{E,I,S,R,T\}} w_i \cdot D_i(c)$$

Default weights: $w_E = 0.20, w_I = 0.20, w_S = 0.20, w_R = 0.20, w_T = 0.20$

Aggregation Method Two: Weighted geometric mean

$$\text{CDI}_{\text{score}}(c) = \prod_{i \in \{E,I,S,R,T\}} D_i(c)^{w_i}$$

Advantage: It penalizes extreme low values in any dimension and encourages balanced development.
