§9.1.4 Applications of CDI

Application One: Assessment of Human Civilizational Development

Case: CDI assessment of current human civilization (2024)

E (Energy Efficiency) assessment:

Sub-dimensionAssessed ValueExplanation
$E_{\text{conv}}$0.35Global average energy conversion efficiency is about 35%
$E_{\text{div}}$0.40Moderate diversity of energy sources
$E_{\text{sus}}$0.25Renewable energy share is about 25%

$$E = 0.4 \times 0.35 + 0.3 \times 0.40 + 0.3 \times 0.25 = 0.335$$

I (Information Processing) assessment:

Sub-dimensionAssessed ValueExplanation
$I_{\text{acq}}$0.50Moderate scientific observation capacity
$I_{\text{store}}$0.45Rapidly growing data storage capacity
$I_{\text{proc}}$0.40Rapidly growing computing capacity
$I_{\text{trans}}$0.55Well-developed global communication network

$$I = \sqrt[4]{0.50 \times 0.45 \times 0.40 \times 0.55} = 0.472$$

S (Social Complexity) assessment:

Sub-dimensionAssessed ValueExplanation
$S_{\text{struct}}$0.55Complex global social structure
$S_{\text{div}}$0.60High occupational differentiation
$S_{\text{coop}}$0.45Limited global cooperative capacity
$S_{\text{adapt}}$0.40Moderate institutional adaptive capacity

$$S = 0.25 \times (0.55 + 0.60 + 0.45 + 0.40) = 0.50$$

R (Environmental Relationship Quality) assessment:

Sub-dimensionAssessed ValueExplanation
$R_{\text{sus}}$0.30Low sustainability of resource use
$R_{\text{regen}}$0.25Limited environmental regenerative capacity
$R_{\text{expand}}$0.15Nascent space-expansion capacity
$R_{\text{harm}}$0.60Considerable environmental harm

$$R = 0.30 \times 0.30 + 0.25 \times 0.25 + 0.20 \times 0.15 + 0.25 \times (1-0.60) = 0.28$$

T (Temporal Horizon) assessment:

Sub-dimensionAssessed ValueExplanation
$T_{\text{past}}$0.50Moderate historical consciousness
$T_{\text{future}}$0.30Limited long-term planning capacity
$T_{\text{integ}}$0.35Limited temporal integration capacity

$$T = 0.30 \times 0.50 + 0.40 \times 0.30 + 0.30 \times 0.35 = 0.375$$

Comprehensive assessment:

$$\text{CDI}(\text{human civilization 2024}) = (0.335, 0.472, 0.50, 0.28, 0.375)$$

$$\text{CDI}_{\text{score}} = 0.20 \times (0.335 + 0.472 + 0.50 + 0.28 + 0.375) = 0.392$$

Interpretation: Human civilization is relatively developed in social complexity (S) and information processing (I), but relatively lagging in environmental relationship quality (R) and energy efficiency (E). The temporal horizon (T) is at a moderate level.

§9.1.5 Comparison of CDI and the Kardashev Scale

I. Review of the Kardashev Scale

The Kardashev Scale, proposed by the Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev in 1964, classifies civilizations into three types based on energy consumption:

Table 9.8 The Kardashev Scale

TypeEnergy ConsumptionDescription
Type I~10¹⁶ WUtilization of all the energy of the home planet
Type II~10²⁶ WUtilization of all the energy of the home star
Type III~10³⁶ WUtilization of all the energy of the home galaxy

Limitations of the Kardashev Scale

LimitationDescriptionImprovement in CDI
Single dimensionBased only on energy consumptionMultidimensional comprehensive assessment
ExpansionismImplies that more energy consumption is betterEmphasizes efficiency and sustainability
Ignores relationsDoes not consider the relation with the environmentThe R dimension measures it specifically
Ignores timeDoes not consider the temporal horizonThe T dimension measures it specifically
TechnocentricFocuses only on technological capacityIncludes social and cognitive dimensions

Type III0.80-1.00Galactic energy utilization

Important distinction: CDI-E measures energy utilization efficiency, not the quantity of energy consumed. A civilization that efficiently utilizes a small amount of energy may have a higher CDI-E than a civilization that inefficiently utilizes a large amount.

§9.2.1 Theoretical Foundations of MBCL

I. From the New Three Views to MBCL

The MBCL (Memetic Biosafety Containment Level) derives directly from several core propositions of the New Three Views:

Proposition NL-2 (negentropic organization)

Life is a negentropic organization. Information systems (including memes) can enhance or disrupt the capacity for negentropic organization.

Proposition NL-3 (continuum of consciousness)

Consciousness is a matter of degree. Systems at different levels of consciousness have different vulnerabilities to information hazards.

Proposition NK-3 (deep uncertainty)

Deep uncertainty exists. The impacts of information systems often involve deep uncertainty and need to be managed prudently.

Derivation chain:

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Derivation Chain from NL-2, NL-3, NK-3 to MBCL                  │                                     
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │                                      
│  Premise 1: NL-2 (life is a negentropic organization)           │                                      
│       ↓                                                         │                                      
│  Corollary 1: Information systems can affect the capacity for negentropic organization │               
│       ↓                                                         │                                      
│  Premise 2: NL-3 (consciousness is a matter of degree)          │                                      
│       ↓                                                         │                                      
│  Corollary 2: Different levels of consciousness have different vulnerabilities to information hazards │
│       ↓                                                         │                                      
│  Premise 3: NK-3 (deep uncertainty exists)                      │                                      
│       ↓                                                         │                                      
│  Corollary 3: The impacts of information systems involve deep uncertainty │                            
│       ↓                                                         │                                      
│  Corollary 4: Information systems require risk-graded management │                                     
│       ↓                                                         │                                      
│  Conclusion: The MBCL needs to be designed as an information-risk grading tool │                       
│                                                                 │                                      
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

II. The Conceptual Definition of MBCL

Definition 9.2.1 (Conceptual Definition of MBCL)

The Memetic Biosafety Containment Level (MBCL) is a classification system for assessing the risk level of information systems (including memes, AI systems, etc.).

Formal statement:

$$\text{MBCL}: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{M}$ is the set of information systems
  • $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ are the risk levels

III. The Concept of "Meme"

Definition 9.2.2 (Meme)

The concept of the meme[7] was proposed by Richard Dawkins and refers to the basic unit of cultural transmission, analogous to the role of the gene in biological evolution. It refers to a replicable and transmissible unit of information, including ideas, beliefs, behavior patterns, and so on.

Characteristics of memes:

CharacteristicDescription
ReplicabilityCan be copied from one carrier to another
VariabilityMay mutate during replication
SelectivitySubject to selection pressure; some memes spread more easily
InfluenceCan affect the behavior and cognition of the carrier

IV. Analogy Between MBCL and BSL

The design of the MBCL draws on the Biosafety Level (BSL)[8] system:

BSL classifies pathogens into four levels according to their degree of danger, and the MBCL likewise classifies information-system risk into four levels for management.

Table 9.11 Analogy Between MBCL and BSL

BSLBiohazardMBCLInformation Hazard
BSL-1Low-risk pathogensMBCL-1Low-risk information
BSL-2Moderate-risk pathogensMBCL-2Moderate-risk information
BSL-3High-risk pathogensMBCL-3High-risk information
BSL-4Extremely high-risk pathogensMBCL-4Extremely high-risk information

§9.2.2 The Four Levels of MBCL

Certain memes can exploit human cognitive biases[9], such as confirmation bias and the availability heuristic, in order to spread. Such memes may lead to systematic cognitive distortion and need to be considered in MBCL assessment.

MBCL-1 applies to low-risk information systems whose transmission is unlikely to cause significant harm.

§9.2.3 The MBCL Assessment Procedure

I. Overall Framework of the Assessment Procedure

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Overall Framework of the MBCL Assessment Procedure             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Stage 1: Information-System Identification                     │
│  ├─ Identify the information system to be assessed              │
│  ├─ Describe the characteristics of the information system      │
│  └─ Determine the assessment scope                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Stage 2: Risk-Factor Assessment                                │
│  ├─ Assess propagation potential                                │
│  ├─ Assess depth of impact                                      │
│  ├─ Assess degree of harm                                       │
│  └─ Assess reversibility                                        │
│                                                                 │
│  Stage 3: Comprehensive Rating                                  │
│  ├─ Synthesize the risk factors                                 │
│  ├─ Determine the MBCL level                                    │
│  └─ Assess uncertainty                                          │
│                                                                 │
│  Stage 4: Control Recommendations                               │
│  ├─ Determine control measures according to the level           │
│  ├─ Formulate a specific implementation plan                    │
│  └─ Establish a monitoring mechanism                            │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

II. Risk-Factor Assessment

Factor One: Propagation Potential (P)

$$P = f(P_{\text{speed}}, P_{\text{range}}, P_{\text{persist}})$$

Sub-factorSymbolDescriptionScore Range
Propagation speed$P_{\text{speed}}$Speed of information transmission1-5
Propagation range$P_{\text{range}}$Range that the information may reach1-5
Persistence$P_{\text{persist}}$Persistence of the information in carriers1-5

Factor Two: Depth of Impact (D)

$$D = f(D_{\text{cog}}, D_{\text{behav}}, D_{\text{social}})$$

Sub-factorSymbolDescriptionScore Range
Cognitive impact$D_{\text{cog}}$Depth of impact on the cognitive system1-5
Behavioral impact$D_{\text{behav}}$Depth of impact on behavior1-5
Social impact$D_{\text{social}}$Depth of impact on the social structure1-5

Factor Three: Degree of Harm (H)

$$H = f(H_{\text{indiv}}, H_{\text{group}}, H_{\text{civ}})$$

Sub-factorSymbolDescriptionScore Range
Individual harm$H_{\text{indiv}}$Degree of harm to individuals1-5
Group harm$H_{\text{group}}$Degree of harm to groups1-5
Civilizational harm$H_{\text{civ}}$Degree of harm to civilization1-5

Factor Four: Reversibility (R)

$$R = f(R_{\text{correct}}, R_{\text{recover}}, R_{\text{prevent}})$$

Sub-factorSymbolDescriptionScore Range
Correctability$R_{\text{correct}}$Degree to which misinformation can be corrected1-5
Recoverability$R_{\text{recover}}$Degree to which affected systems can recover1-5
Preventability$R_{\text{prevent}}$Degree to which harm can be prevented1-5

III. Comprehensive Rating Method

Step 1: Calculate the score for each factor

$$P_{\text{total}} = \frac{P_{\text{speed}} + P_{\text{range}} + P_{\text{persist}}}{3}$$

$$D_{\text{total}} = \frac{D_{\text{cog}} + D_{\text{behav}} + D_{\text{social}}}{3}$$

$$H_{\text{total}} = \max(H_{\text{indiv}}, H_{\text{group}}, H_{\text{civ}})$$

$$R_{\text{total}} = \frac{R_{\text{correct}} + R_{\text{recover}} + R_{\text{prevent}}}{3}$$

Step 2: Calculate the comprehensive risk score

$$\text{Risk} = \frac{P_{\text{total}} + D_{\text{total}} + H_{\text{total}} + (6 - R_{\text{total}})}{4}$$

Note: Reversibility is inverted, because high reversibility means low risk.

Step 3: Determine the MBCL level

Comprehensive Risk ScoreMBCL Level
1.0-2.0MBCL-1
2.1-3.0MBCL-2
3.1-4.0MBCL-3
4.1-5.0MBCL-4

IV. Detailed Flow of the Assessment Procedure

PROCEDURE MBCL_Assessment(information_system)

// Stage 1: Information-system identification description = DescribeSystem(information_system) scope = DetermineScope(information_system)

// Stage 2: Risk-factor assessment P = EvaluatePropagationPotential(information_system) D = EvaluateImpactDepth(information_system) H = EvaluateHarmSeverity(information_system) R = EvaluateReversibility(information_system)

// Stage 3: Comprehensive rating Risk = (P + D + H + (6 - R)) / 4

IF Risk <= 2.0 THEN level = MBCL-1 ELSE IF Risk <= 3.0 THEN level = MBCL-2 ELSE IF Risk <= 4.0 THEN level = MBCL-3 ELSE level = MBCL-4 END IF

uncertainty = EstimateUncertainty(P, D, H, R)

// Stage 4: Control recommendations controls = DetermineControls(level) implementation = DesignImplementation(controls) monitoring = EstablishMonitoring(level)

RETURN (level, Risk, uncertainty, controls)

END PROCEDURE

§9.3 CSIA: Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment

§9.3.1 Theoretical Foundations of CSIA

I. From the New Three Views to CSIA

The CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment) derives directly from several core propositions of the New Three Views:

Proposition NC-2 (process ontology)

The universe is processual. The impact of an action unfolds in time and needs to be assessed from a processual perspective.

Proposition NK-3 (deep uncertainty)

Deep uncertainty exists. The impacts of major actions often involve deep uncertainty and need to be assessed prudently.

Proposition NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge)

Knowledge is negotiable. The results of impact assessment should be negotiable and revisable.

Derivation chain:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Derivation Chain from NC-2, NK-3, NK-4 to CSIA                  │                        
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │                         
│  Premise 1: NC-2 (the universe is processual)                   │                         
│       ↓                                                         │                         
│  Corollary 1: The impact of an action unfolds in time and requires processual assessment │
│       ↓                                                         │                         
│  Premise 2: NK-3 (deep uncertainty exists)                      │                         
│       ↓                                                         │                         
│  Corollary 2: The impacts of major actions involve deep uncertainty │                     
│       ↓                                                         │                         
│  Premise 3: NK-4 (knowledge is negotiable)                      │                         
│       ↓                                                         │                         
│  Corollary 3: Impact assessment should be negotiable and revisable │                      
│       ↓                                                         │                         
│  Corollary 4: Traditional EIA is insufficient for assessing cosmic-scale impacts │        
│       ↓                                                         │                         
│  Conclusion: The CSIA needs to be designed as a cosmic-scale impact assessment tool │     
│                                                                 │                         
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

II. The Conceptual Definition of CSIA

Definition 9.3.1 (Conceptual Definition of CSIA)

The Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment (CSIA) is a comprehensive framework for assessing the cosmic-scale impact of major actions.

Formal statement:

$$\text{CSIA}: \mathcal{A} \rightarrow [0, 100] \times \{L1, L2, L3, L4\}$$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of actions
  • $[0, 100]$ is the comprehensive score
  • $\{L1, L2, L3, L4\}$ are the risk levels

III. Differences Between CSIA and Traditional EIA

The design of the CSIA draws on the procedural framework of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)[10], but fundamentally expands it in terms of assessment scope, temporal scale, and subject coverage:

Table 9.13 Comparison of CSIA and EIA

DimensionTraditional EIACSIA
Assessment scopeEnvironmental impactImpact on cosmic systems
Temporal scaleProject cycleDeep time (centuries or more)
Spatial scaleLocal/regionalPlanetary/interstellar
Subject scopeHumansMultiple intelligent agents
Uncertainty handlingProbabilistic methodsDeep-uncertainty methods
Reversibility considerationLimitedCore dimension

§9.3.2 The Six Dimensions of CSIA

Dimension One: Scope of Impact (D₁)

Definition 9.3.2 (Scope of Impact)

Scope of impact ($D_1$) measures the spatial scope of an action's impact.

Formal statement:

$$D_1(a) = \log_{10}(\text{Impact Area}/\text{Reference Area})$$

Scoring standard:

ScoreScope of ImpactExample
0-0.2LocalA single facility
0.2-0.4RegionalCity/province
0.4-0.6NationalNational level
0.6-0.8GlobalGlobal level
0.8-1.0InterstellarPlanetary system/interstellar

Dimension Two: Depth of Impact (D₂)

Definition 9.3.3 (Depth of Impact)

Depth of impact ($D_2$) measures the temporal depth of an action's impact.

Formal statement:

$$D_2(a) = \log_{10}(\text{Impact Duration}/\text{Reference Time})$$

Scoring standard:

ScoreDepth of ImpactExample
0-0.2Short-term< 10 years
0.2-0.4Medium-term10-100 years
0.4-0.6Long-term100-1000 years
0.6-0.8Deep time1000-10000 years
0.8-1.0Geological time> 10000 years

Dimension Three: Severity of Impact (D₃)

Definition 9.3.4 (Severity of Impact)

Severity of impact ($D_3$) measures the severity of an action's impact.

Formal statement:

$$D_3(a) = f(\text{Number of Affected Subjects}, \text{Degree of Impact}, \text{Subject UCS})$$

Scoring standard:

ScoreSeverity of ImpactExample
0-0.2SlightNegligible impact
0.2-0.4ModerateManageable impact
0.4-0.6SeriousSignificant negative impact
0.6-0.8MajorMajor negative impact
0.8-1.0CatastrophicUnacceptable impact

Dimension Four: Reversibility (D₄)

Definition 9.3.5 (Reversibility)[13]

Reversibility ($D_4$) measures the degree to which an action's impact is reversible.

Formal statement:

$$D_4(a) = 1 - \text{Degree of Irreversibility}$$

Scoring standard:

ScoreReversibilityExample
0.8-1.0Fully reversibleCan be fully restored
0.6-0.8Mostly reversibleCan be mostly restored
0.4-0.6Partially reversibleCan be partially restored
0.2-0.4Mostly irreversibleMostly cannot be restored
0-0.2Fully irreversibleCompletely cannot be restored

Dimension Five: Uncertainty (D₅)

Definition 9.3.6 (Uncertainty)

Uncertainty ($D_5$) measures the degree of uncertainty in the assessment of an action's impact.

Formal statement:

$$D_5(a) = f(\text{Knowledge Uncertainty}, \text{Model Uncertainty}, \text{Parameter Uncertainty})$$

Scoring standard:

ScoreUncertaintyExample
0-0.2LowImpact can be accurately predicted
0.2-0.4Medium-lowImpact can be roughly predicted
0.4-0.6ModerateImpact involves significant uncertainty
0.6-0.8HighImpact is highly uncertain
0.8-1.0Extremely highDeep uncertainty[11]

Note: Deep Uncertainty refers to situations in which it is impossible to enumerate all possible outcomes or to assign probabilities to outcomes, which is especially common in cosmic-scale impact assessment.

Dimension Six: Cascade Risk (D₆)

Definition 9.3.7 (Cascade Risk)

Cascade risk ($D_6$) measures the risk that an action triggers cascading effects.

Formal statement:

$$D_6(a) = f(\text{Trigger Probability}, \text{Cascade Scale}, \text{Cascade Speed})$$

Scoring standard:

ScoreCascade RiskExample
0-0.2LowUnlikely to trigger a cascade
0.2-0.4Medium-lowMay trigger a limited cascade
0.4-0.6ModerateMay trigger a significant cascade
0.6-0.8HighMay trigger a large-scale cascade
0.8-1.0Extremely highMay trigger a systemic cascade

Overview of the Six Dimensions

When faced with high uncertainty and potentially irreversible impacts, the CSIA recommends adopting the Precautionary Principle[12]. The Precautionary Principle requires precautionary measures to be taken when there is a threat of serious or irreversible harm.

I. Overall Framework of the Assessment Procedure

II. Calculation of the Comprehensive Score

Formula 9.3.1 (CSIA Comprehensive Score)

$$\text{CSIA}_{\text{score}} = 100 \times \sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i \cdot D_i^$$

Where:

  • $D_i^ = D_i$ for $i \in \{1, 2, 3, 5, 6\}$
  • $D_4^ = 1 - D_4$ (reversibility is inverted, because high reversibility means low risk)
  • $w_i$ are the weights, with $\sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i = 1$

Default weights:

DimensionWeightRationale
D₁0.15Scope of impact
D₂0.15Depth of impact
D₃0.20Severity of impact (core)
D₄0.20Reversibility (core)
D₅0.15Uncertainty
D₆0.15Cascade risk

III. Determination of the Risk Level

Table 9.15 CSIA Risk Levels

Comprehensive ScoreRisk LevelDescriptionRecommended Action
0-25L1Low riskRoutine review
26-50L2Moderate riskEnhanced monitoring
51-75L3High riskStrict review
76-100L4Extremely high riskSpecial review/prohibition

IV. Detailed Flow of the Assessment Procedure

PROCEDURE CSIA_Assessment(action)

// Stage 1: Action description description = DescribeAction(action) scope = DetermineScope(action) stakeholders = IdentifyStakeholders(action)

// Stage 2: Six-dimension assessment D1 = EvaluateSpatialScope(action) D2 = EvaluateTemporalDepth(action) D3 = EvaluateSeverity(action) D4 = EvaluateReversibility(action) D5 = EvaluateUncertainty(action) D6 = EvaluateCascadeRisk(action)

// Stage 3: Comprehensive score D4_star = 1 - D4 // reversibility inverted

CSIA_score = 100 (0.15D1 + 0.15D2 + 0.20D3 + 0.20D4_star + 0.15D5 + 0.15D6)

// Determine the risk level IF CSIA_score <= 25 THEN level = L1 ELSE IF CSIA_score <= 50 THEN level = L2 ELSE IF CSIA_score <= 75 THEN level = L3 ELSE level = L4 END IF

overall_uncertainty = AggregateUncertainty(D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6)

// Stage 4: Recommendation generation recommendations = GenerateRecommendations(level, CSIA_score) further_analysis = IdentifyFurtherAnalysis(D5, D6) mitigation = ProposeMitigation(D3, D4, D6)

RETURN (CSIA_score, level, recommendations, mitigation)

END PROCEDURE

§9.3.4 Applications of CSIA

Application One: Assessment of Large-Scale Geoengineering

Case: Stratospheric Aerosol Injection (SAI)

Action description: Injecting sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere to reflect solar radiation and lower global temperatures.

Six-dimension assessment:

DimensionScoreExplanation
D₁ (scope of impact)0.80Global impact
D₂ (depth of impact)0.60Impact lasts decades to centuries
D₃ (severity of impact)0.65May alter global climate patterns
D₄ (reversibility)0.50Impact can gradually dissipate after injection stops, but with a lag
D₅ (uncertainty)0.70Regional impacts are highly uncertain
D₆ (cascade risk)0.60May trigger regional climate anomalies

Comprehensive score calculation:

$$D_4^ = 1 - 0.50 = 0.50$$

$$\text{CSIA}_{\text{score}} = 100 \times (0.15 \times 0.80 + 0.15 \times 0.60 + 0.20 \times 0.65 + 0.20 \times 0.50 + 0.15 \times 0.70 + 0.15 \times 0.60)$$

$$= 100 \times (0.12 + 0.09 + 0.13 + 0.10 + 0.105 + 0.09) = 63.5$$

Conclusion: L3 (high risk)

Recommendations:

  • Requires strict international review and approval
  • Establish a global monitoring system
  • Formulate emergency-stop procedures
  • Conduct more research on regional impacts
  • Establish an international governance framework

Application Two: Assessment of an Interstellar Probe Mission

Action description: Actively sending signals containing information about human civilization to identified potentially habitable planets.

Six-dimension assessment:

DimensionScoreExplanation
D₁ (scope of impact)0.90Interstellar impact
D₂ (depth of impact)0.85Impact may last thousands of years
D₃ (severity of impact)0.70May expose Earth's location
D₄ (reversibility)0.10Once sent, the signal cannot be withdrawn
D₅ (uncertainty)0.90The response of extraterrestrial civilizations is entirely unknown
D₆ (cascade risk)0.75May trigger unforeseen consequences

Comprehensive score calculation:

$$D_4^ = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90$$

$$\text{CSIA}_{\text{score}} = 100 \times (0.15 \times 0.90 + 0.15 \times 0.85 + 0.20 \times 0.70 + 0.20 \times 0.90 + 0.15 \times 0.90 + 0.15 \times 0.75)$$

$$= 100 \times (0.135 + 0.1275 + 0.14 + 0.18 + 0.135 + 0.1125) = 83.0$$

Conclusion: L4 (extremely high risk)

Recommendations:

  • Requires global consultation and approval
  • Establish an international decision-making mechanism
  • Conduct more risk analysis
  • Consider alternatives (such as passive listening)
  • Formulate an emergency-response plan

§9.4.3 Cases of Integrated Application

Case: Assessment of the AI Development Path of Human Civilization

Background: Assessing different path choices for human civilization in AI development.

Step 1: Current-State Assessment (CDI)

According to the assessment in §9.1.4, the CDI of current human civilization is:

$$\text{CDI}(\text{human civilization 2024}) = (0.335, 0.472, 0.50, 0.28, 0.375)$$

Key findings:

  • Information processing capacity (I = 0.472) is relatively high
  • Environmental relationship quality (R = 0.28) is relatively low
  • Temporal horizon (T = 0.375) is moderate

Step 2: Development-Path Design

Design three possible AI development paths:

Path A: Rapid-development path

  • Characteristics: Rapidly advancing AI capabilities, with minimal regulation
  • Expected CDI change: A large increase in I, with S and R possibly declining

Path B: Prudent-development path

  • Characteristics: Gradual development, with an emphasis on safety and regulation
  • Expected CDI change: A steady increase in I, with S and T increasing in tandem

Path C: Pause-development path

  • Characteristics: Pausing high-risk AI research and focusing on safety research
  • Expected CDI change: Slower growth in I, with R and T possibly increasing

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

As a detailed justification of CDI, MBCL, and CSIA, this chapter has accomplished the following core tasks:

Conclusion One: The multidimensional design of CDI

The CDI is directly anchored to the New Cosmological View (NC-1, NC-2) and the New View of Life (NL-2), assessing the level of civilizational development through five dimensions:

DimensionCore MeasurementAnchoring to the New Three Views
E (energy efficiency)Efficiency of energy acquisition and utilizationNL-2
I (information processing)Acquisition, storage, processing, and transmission of informationNC-1
S (social complexity)Degree and quality of complexity of social organizationNC-1, NC-2
R (environmental relationship quality)Quality of the relation with the environmentNC-1, NL-2
T (temporal horizon)Time span considered in decisionsNC-2

The CDI transcends the single energy-consumption dimension of the Kardashev Scale, providing a more comprehensive and more balanced assessment of civilizational development.

Conclusion Two: The four-level classification of MBCL

The MBCL is directly anchored to the New View of Life (NL-2, NL-3) and the New View of Cognition (NK-3), assessing the risk of information systems through four levels:

LevelDegree of RiskControl Measures
MBCL-1Low riskRoutine correction
MBCL-2Moderate riskControlled transmission
MBCL-3High riskStrict restriction
MBCL-4Extremely high riskMaximum protection

The MBCL draws on the BSL system in its design and provides an operationalized tool for information risk management.

Conclusion Three: The comprehensive assessment framework of CSIA

The CSIA is directly anchored to the New Cosmological View (NC-2) and the New View of Cognition (NK-3, NK-4), assessing the cosmic-scale impact of actions through six dimensions:

DimensionCore Measurement
D₁ (scope of impact)Spatial scope
D₂ (depth of impact)Temporal depth
D₃ (severity of impact)Degree of severity
D₄ (reversibility)Degree of reversibility
D₅ (uncertainty)Degree of uncertainty
D₆ (cascade risk)Cascading effects

The CSIA extends the traditional EIA and is applicable to cosmic-scale impact assessment.

Conclusion Four: The integrated application of the three indicators

CDI, MBCL, and CSIA have different but complementary functional positioning and can be applied in an integrated manner to scenarios such as new-technology deployment assessment, interstellar-contact readiness assessment, and civilizational development path planning.

[1] Kardashev Scale: The Kardashev Scale is a civilizational classification method proposed by the Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev in 1964, which classifies civilizations into three types based on the total amount of energy a civilization can utilize: Type I (planetary scale, about 10¹⁶ W), Type II (stellar scale, about 10²⁶ W), and Type III (galactic scale, about 10³⁶ W). The scale was later extended into a continuous scale by Carl Sagan and others. See: Kardashev, N. S. (1964). "Transmission of Information by Extraterrestrial Civilizations." Soviet Astronomy, 8, 217-221; Sagan, C. (1973). The Cosmic Connection: An Extraterrestrial Perspective. Anchor Press.

[2] Negentropy: The concept of negentropy was proposed by Schrödinger in What Is Life? to describe the process by which living systems draw order from the environment to maintain their own organization. Negentropy is the negative of entropy, indicating the degree of order of a system. Prigogine's theory of dissipative structures further developed this concept, explaining how open systems far from equilibrium maintain and increase complexity through negentropy flows. See: Schrödinger, E. (1944). What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell. Cambridge University Press; Brillouin, L. (1956). Science and Information Theory. Academic Press.

[3] Information Entropy: Information entropy is a concept proposed by Claude Shannon in 1948 to quantify the uncertainty or amount of information. The formula for information entropy is $H = -\sum p_i \log p_i$, where $p_i$ is the probability of each state. Information entropy provides the theoretical foundation for quantifying information processing. See: Shannon, C. E. (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication." Bell System Technical Journal, 27(3), 379-423; Cover, T. M., & Thomas, J. A. (2006). Elements of Information Theory (2nd ed.). Wiley-Interscience.

[4] Social Complexity: Social complexity is a concept in sociology and anthropology used to describe the degree of complexity of social organization, involving such dimensions as differentiation, integration, hierarchy, and specialization. Complex societies typically have more social roles, more complex institutional arrangements, and higher coordination capacity. See: Tainter, J. A. (1988). The Collapse of Complex Societies. Cambridge University Press; Turchin, P. (2003). Historical Dynamics: Why States Rise and Fall. Princeton University Press.

[5] Temporal Discounting: Temporal discounting is a concept in behavioral economics and psychology referring to the tendency of people to underestimate the value of future rewards relative to immediate rewards. A higher temporal discount rate indicates a lower degree of emphasis on the future. This phenomenon has an important influence on long-term planning and intergenerational equity. See: Frederick, S., Loewenstein, G., & O'Donoghue, T. (2002). "Time Discounting and Time Preference: A Critical Review." Journal of Economic Literature, 40(2), 351-401; Ainslie, G. (2001). Breakdown of Will. Cambridge University Press.

[6] Dyson Sphere: The Dyson Sphere is a hypothetical giant structure proposed by the physicist Freeman Dyson in 1960, referring to a structure that surrounds a star to capture most or all of its energy output. The Dyson Sphere is regarded as the signature technology of a Kardashev Type II civilization. Dyson himself preferred the concept of a "Dyson swarm," namely a large number of independent energy collectors. See: Dyson, F. J. (1960). "Search for Artificial Stellar Sources of Infrared Radiation." Science, 131(3414), 1667-1668.

[7] Meme: The concept of the meme was proposed by Richard Dawkins in The Selfish Gene (1976), referring to the basic unit of cultural transmission, analogous to the role of the gene in biological evolution. Memes spread from person to person through imitation and include ideas, behaviors, styles, and so on. Memetics studies the transmission, variation, and selection of memes. See: Dawkins, R. (1976). The Selfish Gene. Oxford University Press; Blackmore, S. (1999). The Meme Machine. Oxford University Press; Dennett, D. C. (1995). Darwin's Dangerous Idea. Simon & Schuster.

[8] Biosafety Level (BSL): BSL is a laboratory safety standard established by the World Health Organization and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which classifies pathogens into four levels according to their degree of danger: BSL-1 (low risk), BSL-2 (moderate risk), BSL-3 (high risk), and BSL-4 (extremely high risk). Each level corresponds to different protective measures and operating procedures. See: WHO. (2004). Laboratory Biosafety Manual (3rd ed.). World Health Organization; CDC/NIH. (2009). Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (5th ed.).

[9] Cognitive Biases: Cognitive biases are systematic errors of thinking that affect people's judgments and decisions. Common cognitive biases include confirmation bias, the availability heuristic, and the anchoring effect. The study of cognitive biases was initiated by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky. See: Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow. Farrar, Straus and Giroux; Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). "Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases." Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131.

[10] Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA): EIA is a procedure for assessing the possible environmental impacts of a proposed project. It originated from the U.S. National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) of 1969 and has now become an internationally accepted environmental management tool. EIA typically includes such steps as screening, scoping, impact prediction, mitigation measures, and public participation. See: Glasson, J., Therivel, R., & Chadwick, A. (2012). Introduction to Environmental Impact Assessment (4th ed.). Routledge; Morgan, R. K. (2012). "Environmental Impact Assessment: The State of the Art." Impact Assessment and Project Appraisal, 30(1), 5-14.

[11] Deep Uncertainty: Deep uncertainty refers to situations in which decision-makers cannot enumerate all possible outcomes, cannot assign probabilities to outcomes, or do not know which model is correct. Deep uncertainty differs from risk (assignable probabilities) and uncertainty (enumerable outcomes). Under deep uncertainty, the traditional method of expected-utility maximization fails. See: Knight, F. H. (1921). Risk, Uncertainty and Profit. Houghton Mifflin; Marchau, V. A., Walker, W. E., Bloemen, P. J., & Popper, S. W. (Eds.). (2019). Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty: From Theory to Practice. Springer.

[12] Precautionary Principle: The Precautionary Principle is an important principle in the fields of environmental law and public health, advocating that precautionary measures should be taken when there is a threat of serious or irreversible harm, even if the causal relationship has not been fully established scientifically. The 1992 Rio Declaration is an important source of international law for the Precautionary Principle. See: Raffensperger, C., & Tickner, J. (Eds.). (1999). Protecting Public Health and the Environment: Implementing the Precautionary Principle. Island Press; Sunstein, C. R. (2005). Laws of Fear: Beyond the Precautionary Principle. Cambridge University Press.

[13] Reversibility: Reversibility refers to the degree to which an action or process can be undone or restored to its original state. In thermodynamics, a reversible process is an ideal process in which entropy does not increase; in decision theory, reversibility is an important dimension for assessing the risk of an action. Highly reversible actions allow correction when errors are discovered. See: Chapter 13 of this work (The Principle of Reversibility); Gray, J., & Reuter, A. (1993). Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann.

Footnotes

Chapter 9 Footnotes

[1] The Kardashev Scale: The Kardashev scale is a method of classifying civilizations proposed by the Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev in 1964, dividing civilizations into three types based on the total energy they are able to utilize: Type I (planetary, about 10¹⁶ W), Type II (stellar, about 10²⁶ W), and Type III (galactic, about 10³⁶ W). The scale was later extended into a continuous measure by Carl Sagan and others. See: Kardashev, N. S. (1964). "Transmission of Information by Extraterrestrial Civilizations." Soviet Astronomy, 8, 217-221; Sagan, C. (1973). The Cosmic Connection: An Extraterrestrial Perspective. Anchor Press.

[2] Negentropy: The concept of negentropy was proposed by Schrödinger in What Is Life? to describe the process by which living systems draw order from their environment to maintain their own organization. Negentropy is the negative of entropy and indicates the degree of order of a system. Prigogine's theory of dissipative structures further developed this concept, explaining how open systems far from equilibrium maintain and increase complexity through negentropy flows. See: Schrödinger, E. (1944). What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell. Cambridge University Press; Brillouin, L. (1956). Science and Information Theory. Academic Press.

[3] Information Entropy: Information entropy is a concept proposed by Claude Shannon in 1948 to quantify the uncertainty or the amount of information. The formula for information entropy is $H = -\sum p_i \log p_i$, where $p_i$ is the probability of each state. Information entropy provides the theoretical foundation for quantifying information-processing capacity. See: Shannon, C. E. (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication." Bell System Technical Journal, 27(3), 379-423; Cover, T. M., & Thomas, J. A. (2006). Elements of Information Theory (2nd ed.). Wiley-Interscience.

[4] Social Complexity: Social complexity is a concept in sociology and anthropology used to describe the degree of complexity of social organization, involving the dimensions of social differentiation, integration, hierarchy, and specialization. Complex societies generally possess more social roles, more complex institutional arrangements, and higher coordination capacity. See: Tainter, J. A. (1988). The Collapse of Complex Societies. Cambridge University Press; Turchin, P. (2003). Historical Dynamics: Why States Rise and Fall. Princeton University Press.

[5] Temporal Discounting: Temporal discounting is a concept in behavioral economics and psychology referring to people's tendency to undervalue future rewards relative to immediate rewards. A higher temporal discount rate indicates a lower regard for the future. This phenomenon has important implications for long-term planning and intergenerational fairness. See: Frederick, S., Loewenstein, G., & O'Donoghue, T. (2002). "Time Discounting and Time Preference: A Critical Review." Journal of Economic Literature, 40(2), 351-401; Ainslie, G. (2001). Breakdown of Will. Cambridge University Press.

[6] The Dyson Sphere: The Dyson sphere is a hypothetical megastructure proposed by the physicist Freeman Dyson in 1960, referring to a structure that encloses a star to capture most or all of its energy output. The Dyson sphere is regarded as the signature technology of a Kardashev Type II civilization. Dyson himself favored the concept of a "Dyson swarm," namely a large number of independent energy collectors. See: Dyson, F. J. (1960). "Search for Artificial Stellar Sources of Infrared Radiation." Science, 131(3414), 1667-1668.

[7] Meme: The concept of the meme was proposed by Richard Dawkins in The Selfish Gene (1976), referring to the basic unit of cultural transmission, analogous to the role of the gene in biological evolution. Memes spread from person to person through imitation and include ideas, behaviors, styles, and the like. Memetics studies the spread, variation, and selection of memes. See: Dawkins, R. (1976). The Selfish Gene. Oxford University Press; Blackmore, S. (1999). The Meme Machine. Oxford University Press; Dennett, D. C. (1995). Darwin's Dangerous Idea. Simon & Schuster.

[8] Biosafety Level (BSL): BSL is a laboratory safety standard established by the World Health Organization and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which classifies pathogens into four levels according to their degree of danger: BSL-1 (low risk), BSL-2 (moderate risk), BSL-3 (high risk), and BSL-4 (extreme risk). Each level corresponds to different protective measures and operating procedures. See: WHO. (2004). Laboratory Biosafety Manual (3rd ed.). World Health Organization; CDC/NIH. (2009). Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (5th ed.).

[9] Cognitive Biases: Cognitive biases are systematic errors of thought that affect people's judgment and decision-making. Common cognitive biases include confirmation bias, the availability heuristic, and the anchoring effect. Research on cognitive biases was pioneered by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky. See: Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow. Farrar, Straus and Giroux; Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). "Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases." Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131.

[10] Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA): EIA is a procedure for assessing the potential environmental impacts of a proposed project. It originated in the U.S. National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) of 1969 and has since become an internationally standard environmental management tool. EIA typically includes steps such as screening, scoping, impact prediction, mitigation measures, and public participation. See: Glasson, J., Therivel, R., & Chadwick, A. (2012). Introduction to Environmental Impact Assessment (4th ed.). Routledge; Morgan, R. K. (2012). "Environmental Impact Assessment: The State of the Art." Impact Assessment and Project Appraisal, 30(1), 5-14.

[11] Deep Uncertainty: Deep uncertainty refers to situations in which decision-makers cannot enumerate all possible outcomes, cannot assign probabilities to outcomes, or do not know which model is correct. Deep uncertainty is distinguished from risk (assignable probabilities) and from uncertainty (enumerable outcomes). Under deep uncertainty, the traditional expected-utility-maximization approach fails. See: Knight, F. H. (1921). Risk, Uncertainty and Profit. Houghton Mifflin; Marchau, V. A., Walker, W. E., Bloemen, P. J., & Popper, S. W. (Eds.). (2019). Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty: From Theory to Practice. Springer.

[12] The Precautionary Principle: The precautionary principle is an important principle in environmental law and public health, holding that when there is a threat of serious or irreversible harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if the causal relationship has not yet been fully established scientifically. The 1992 Rio Declaration is an important source of the precautionary principle in international law. See: Raffensperger, C., & Tickner, J. (Eds.). (1999). Protecting Public Health and the Environment: Implementing the Precautionary Principle. Island Press; Sunstein, C. R. (2005). Laws of Fear: Beyond the Precautionary Principle. Cambridge University Press.

[13] Reversibility: Reversibility refers to the degree to which an action or process can be undone or restored to its original state. In thermodynamics, a reversible process is an ideal process in which entropy does not increase; in decision theory, reversibility is an important dimension in assessing the risk of an action. Highly reversible actions allow correction when errors are discovered. See: Chapter 13 of this work (the Reversibility Principle); Gray, J., & Reuter, A. (1993). Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann.

Consistency and Boundaries of the Indicator SystemChapter 10

Consistency and Boundaries of the Indicator System

Chapter Opening Guide

I. Position of This Chapter in the Book

This chapter is the concluding chapter of Part II, "The Indicator System." Chapter 6 established the methodological foundations of indicator design, and Chapters 7 through 9 respectively argued the theoretical foundations, calculation methods, and application scenarios of the six major indicators (UCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, CSIA). The task of this chapter is to subject this indicator system to a holistic examination: to test its internal consistency (Consistency)[1], to identify potential conflicts, to specify the boundaries of applicability, and to establish an evolution mechanism.

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The consistency testing of this chapter takes the New Three Views as its anchor:

$$\text{ConsistencyTesting} = f(\text{NC-anchoring}, \text{NL-anchoring}, \text{NK-anchoring})$$

Specifically:

  • NC anchoring: test whether the indicators consistently embody relationality, processuality, and participatoriness
  • NL anchoring: test whether the indicators consistently embody negentropic organization and the continuum of consciousness
  • NK anchoring: test whether the indicators consistently embody participatory cognition and deep uncertainty

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer four fundamental questions:

Core Question One: Are the six major indicators internally consistent at the conceptual, methodological, and application levels? Core Question Two: Are there potential conflicts among the indicators? How are they resolved? Core Question Three: Where are the boundaries of applicability of the indicator system? Core Question Four: How does the indicator system evolve as knowledge advances?

The answers to these four questions will provide a guarantee for the reliable application of the indicator system and lay the foundation for its continuous improvement.

VI. Boundary Statement

All content of this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Meta-level[2] positioning: this chapter is a meta-level examination of the indicator system, not an application of the indicators themselves
  2. Openness commitment: the results of consistency testing are provisional and may require revision as theory develops
  3. Acknowledgment of incompleteness: this chapter cannot exhaust all possible conflicts and boundary problems
  4. Versioning constraint: the content of this chapter applies to version v0.9.0 of the indicator system

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • Readers concerned with theoretical consistency are advised to focus on §10.1
  • Readers concerned with practical application are advised to focus on §10.2 and §10.3
  • Readers concerned with long-term development are advised to focus on §10.4

§10.1 Consistency Testing of the Six Major Indicators

§10.1.1 Conceptual Consistency

I. Definition of Conceptual Consistency

Definition 10.1.1 (Conceptual Consistency)

Conceptual consistency means that the indicators in the indicator system exhibit no logical contradiction at the conceptual level and are jointly anchored to a unified theoretical framework.

Formal statement:

Let the indicator set be $\mathcal{I} = \{I_1, I_2, ..., I_n\}$ and the theoretical framework be $\mathcal{T}$. Then conceptual consistency is defined as:

$$\text{ConceptualConsistency}(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{T}) \iff \forall I_i, I_j \in \mathcal{I}: \neg(\text{Def}(I_i) \land \text{Def}(I_j) \vdash \bot) \land \forall I_i \in \mathcal{I}: I_i \triangleleft \mathcal{T}$$

where:

  • $\text{Def}(I_i)$ is the definition of indicator $I_i$
  • $\bot$ is contradiction
  • $I_i \triangleleft \mathcal{T}$ means that $I_i$ is anchored to $\mathcal{T}$

II. Dimensions of Conceptual Consistency Testing

Conceptual consistency testing comprises three dimensions:

Dimension One: Definitional Consistency

No logical contradiction exists among the definitions of the indicators.

Dimension Two: Anchoring Consistency

The indicators are consistently anchored to the framework of the New Three Views.

Dimension Three: Terminological Consistency

The core terms used by the indicators have consistent meanings.

V. Clarification of Potential Relations:

(1) The relation between RFD and CSIA:

RFD measures the impact of action on the possibility space, while CSIA measures the comprehensive impact of action at the cosmic scale. The relation between the two is:

$$\text{RFD} \subseteq \text{CSIA}$$

RFD can serve as one input dimension of CSIA, but CSIA contains more dimensions (scope of impact, depth of impact, severity, etc.).

(2) The relation between CRV and CSIA:

The rollback dimension of CRV ($V_{\text{rev}}$) and the reversibility dimension of CSIA ($D_4$) measure similar concepts, but at different levels:

  • $V_{\text{rev}}$: measures the rollbackability of commitment
  • $D_4$: measures the reversibility of the impact of action

The relation between the two is:

$$V_{\text{rev}}(\text{commitment}) \rightarrow D_4(\text{impact of action})$$

A commitment with high rollbackability tends to produce action impacts with high reversibility.

Conclusion: The six major indicators exhibit no logical contradiction at the definitional level; the relations that exist are complementary rather than contradictory.

§10.1.2 Methodological Consistency

I. Definition of Methodological Consistency

Definition 10.1.2 (Methodological Consistency)

Methodological consistency means that the indicators in the indicator system follow consistent methodological principles at the level of calculation methods.

Formal statement:

Let the set of methodological principles be $\mathcal{P} = \{P_1, P_2, ..., P_m\}$. Then methodological consistency is defined as:

$$\text{MethodologicalConsistency}(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{P}) \iff \forall I_i \in \mathcal{I}, \forall P_j \in \mathcal{P}: \text{Method}(I_i) \models P_j$$

where $\text{Method}(I_i) \models P_j$ means that the calculation method of indicator $I_i$ satisfies principle $P_j$.

II. Methodological Principles

Based on the indicator design methodology established in Chapter 6, methodological consistency testing rests on the following principles:

P2Principle of operabilityThe calculation method must be operable
P3Principle of uncertainty quantificationThe calculation result must be accompanied by an uncertainty estimate
P4Principle of revisabilityThe calculation method must be revisable
P5Principle of transparencyThe calculation process must be transparent and auditable

IV. Explanation of Partial Satisfaction:

(1) Operability of UCS (△):

The precise calculation of UCS requires measuring the integrated information of consciousness, and current technical means are limited. This work provides approximate methods (behavioral inference, structural analysis), but precise measurement still faces challenges.

Directions for improvement:

  • Develop more proxy indicators
  • Interface with consciousness science research
  • Establish a calibration mechanism

(2) Operability of RFD (△):

The precise calculation of RFD requires enumerating the possibility space, and in complex systems the computational complexity is exponential. This work provides approximate methods (Monte Carlo sampling, local linearization, expert judgment, proxy indicators), but precise calculation remains infeasible.

Directions for improvement:

  • Develop more efficient approximation algorithms
  • Utilize machine learning methods
  • Establish a standardized proxy indicator system

(3) Uncertainty quantification of MBCL (△):

MBCL uses discrete grading (levels 1-4), and its uncertainty quantification is less refined than that of continuous indicators. At present, uncertainty is estimated by reporting inter-rater differences.

Directions for improvement:

  • Develop a continuous version of MBCL
  • Establish a more refined method of uncertainty quantification
  • Add inter-rater consistency testing

§10.1.3 Application Consistency

I. Definition of Application Consistency

Definition 10.1.3 (Application Consistency)

Application consistency means that the indicators in the indicator system produce consistent decision orientations in actual application and do not lead to mutually contradictory recommendations.

Formal statement:

Let the decision scenario be $\sigma$, the indicator set be $\mathcal{I}$, and the decision-recommendation function be $\text{Rec}: \mathcal{I} \times \sigma \rightarrow \mathcal{D}$. Then application consistency is defined as:

$$\text{ApplicationConsistency}(\mathcal{I}, \sigma) \iff \forall I_i, I_j \in \mathcal{I}: \neg(\text{Rec}(I_i, \sigma) \perp \text{Rec}(I_j, \sigma))$$

where $\text{Rec}(I_i, \sigma) \perp \text{Rec}(I_j, \sigma)$ means that the two recommendations are mutually contradictory.

II. Method of Application Consistency Testing

Application consistency testing is carried out through test cases:

  1. Design a typical decision scenario
  2. Perform assessments using each indicator
  3. Test whether the assessment results lead to consistent decision recommendations

§10.2 Potential Conflicts Among the Indicators

§10.2.1 Types of Conflict

The commensurability[9] of different indicators is a fundamental problem. This work acknowledges that the indicators measure different dimensions of value and does not claim to reduce them to a single scale of value.

I. Classification of Conflict Types

Although the consistency testing in §10.1 shows that the six major indicators possess relatively high consistency at the conceptual, methodological, and application levels, conflicts may still arise in specific scenarios. This section identifies and classifies these potential conflicts.

Definition 10.2.1 (Indicator Conflict)

An indicator conflict is a situation in which, under a specific scenario, the assessment results of different indicators lead to mutually contradictory decision recommendations.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Conflict}(I_i, I_j, \sigma) \iff \text{Rec}(I_i, \sigma) \perp \text{Rec}(I_j, \sigma)$$

II. Classification of Conflict Types:

Table 10.10 Classification of Conflict Types

Conflict TypeDescriptionExample
Level conflictConflict between indicators at different levelsIndividual UCS vs. civilization CDI
Dimensional conflictConflict between different dimensions of the same indicatorThe E dimension vs. the R dimension of CDI
Temporal conflictConflict between short-term and long-term assessmentShort-term RFD vs. long-term RFD
Subject conflictConflict between the perspectives of different subjectsThe RFD of subject A vs. the RFD of subject B
Weight conflictConflict caused by different weight settingsCSIA scores under different weights

(1) Level conflict

Definition 10.2.2 (Level Conflict)

A level conflict is a conflict that arises between indicators assessing objects at different levels.

Examples:

ScenarioIndividual-level assessmentCivilization-level assessmentConflict description

Minority groupHigh UCS of the minority groupCDI of the majority group improvesMinority vs. majority

A dimensional conflict is a conflict that arises between different dimensions of the same indicator.

Examples:

CSIA$D_1$ (scope of impact) large$D_4$ (reversibility) highBroad but reversible impact

Definition 10.2.4 (Temporal Conflict)

A temporal conflict is a conflict that arises between assessments at different time scales.

Examples:

Environmental protectionShort-term CDI decline (economic cost)Long-term CDI improvement (sustainability)Short-term loss vs. long-term benefit

(4) Subject conflict

A subject conflict is a conflict that arises between assessments from the perspectives of different subjects.

A weight conflict is a conflict of assessment results caused by different weight settings.

§10.2.3 Resolution of Conflicts

I. Principles of Conflict Resolution

Principle One: Principle of level priority

In a level conflict, the interest of the higher level is given priority, but a protection floor must be set.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Priority}(\text{civilization}) > \text{Priority}(\text{group}) > \text{Priority}(\text{individual})$$

Constraint:

$$\forall \text{individual} e: \text{UCS}(e) > \theta_{\text{min}} \Rightarrow \text{protect}(e)$$

where $\theta_{\text{min}}$ is the minimum protection threshold.

Principle Two: Principle of temporal discounting[7]

In a temporal conflict, long-term impacts should receive appropriate weight, but short-term impacts should not be entirely neglected.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Weight}(t) = \gamma^t, \quad \gamma \in (0.9, 1.0)$$

where $\gamma$ is the temporal discounting factor; a value close to 1 indicates emphasis on long-term impacts.

Principle Three: Principle of reversibility priority

Other things being equal, the option with higher reversibility is preferred.

Formal statement:

$$\text{if } \text{other conditions are equal}, \text{then } \text{choose } \arg\max_a V_{\text{rev}}(a)$$

Principle Four: Principle of negotiated resolution

In a subject conflict, consensus is preferentially reached through negotiation.

Formal statement:

$$\text{resolution plan} = \text{Negotiate}(\text{subject A}, \text{subject B}, ..., \text{subject N})$$

Principle Five: Principle of sensitivity analysis

In a weight conflict, sensitivity analysis is performed to identify the key weights.

Formal statement:

$$\text{sensitivity}(w_i) = \frac{\partial \text{result}}{\partial w_i}$$

§10.3 Boundaries of the Indicator System

§10.3.1 Boundary of Scope of Applicability

I. Definition of the Boundary of Scope of Applicability

Definition 10.3.1 (Boundary of Scope of Applicability)

The boundary of scope of applicability is the boundary of the set of scenarios in which the indicator system can be effectively applied.

Formal statement:

Let the scenario space be $\Sigma$ and the scope of applicability be $\Sigma_{\text{valid}} \subseteq \Sigma$. Then the boundary of scope of applicability is defined as:

$$\partial \Sigma_{\text{valid}} = \{\sigma \in \Sigma : \sigma \in \text{cl}(\Sigma_{\text{valid}}) \cap \text{cl}(\Sigma \setminus \Sigma_{\text{valid}})\}$$

where $\text{cl}(\cdot)$ denotes closure.

§10.3.2 Boundary of Precision

I. Definition of the Boundary of Precision

Definition 10.3.2 (Boundary of Precision)

The boundary of precision is the limit on the degree of reliability of the measurement results of the indicators.

Formal statement:

Let the true value be $v^$ and the measured value be $\hat{v}$. Then precision is defined as:

$$\text{Precision} = 1 - \frac{|\hat{v} - v^|}{|v^|}$$

The boundary of precision is the lower limit of precision:

$$\text{PrecisionBound} = \inf_{\sigma \in \Sigma_{\text{valid}}} \text{Precision}(\sigma)$$

§10.3.3 Boundary of Validity

I. Definition of the Boundary of Validity

Definition 10.3.3 (Boundary of Validity)

The boundary of validity is the limit on the degree to which an indicator can effectively measure its target concept.

Formal statement:

Let the target concept be $C$ and the indicator be $I$. Then validity is defined as:

$$\text{Validity}(I, C) = \text{Corr}(I, C)$$

where $\text{Corr}$ denotes correlation.

The boundary of validity is the lower limit of validity:

$$\text{ValidityBound} = \inf_{C \in \mathcal{C}} \text{Validity}(I, C)$$

II. Types of Validity

Table 10.19 Types of Validity

TypeDescriptionTesting Method
Content validityWhether the indicator covers all aspects of the target conceptExpert review
Construct validityWhether the indicator measures the concept it claims to measureTheoretical analysis, factor analysis
Criterion validityWhether the indicator correlates with an external criterionCorrelation analysis
Predictive validityWhether the indicator can predict future outcomesLongitudinal study

  1. The validity of each indicator has inherent limits. Construct Validity[3] refers to whether an indicator truly measures the concept it claims to measure. Owing to the abstractness of concepts such as consciousness and the possibility space, construct validity faces challenges.
  2. Criterion Validity[4] refers to the degree of correlation between an indicator and an external standard. Owing to the lack of historical data on cosmic-scale impact, the verification of the criterion validity of indicators such as CSIA faces difficulties.
  3. Content Validity[5] refers to whether an indicator covers all important aspects of the concept. The dimension design of each indicator strives for comprehensiveness, but dimensions may be omitted.

§10.4 Evolution of the Indicator System

§10.4.1 Versioned Management

I. Necessity of Versioned Management

The indicator system requires versioned management, for the following reasons:

  1. Knowledge progress: as scientific knowledge advances, the definitions and calculation methods of the indicators may need to be updated
  2. Application feedback: problems discovered in actual application need to be resolved through revision
  3. Scenario change: new scenarios may require new indicators or adjustment of existing indicators
  4. Traceability: versioned management ensures the traceability of assessment results

II. Version-Number Specification

Semantic Versioning[8] is adopted:

$$\text{version number} = \text{major version}.\text{minor version}.\text{patch version}$$

Table 10.22 Version-Number Specification

Version TypeType of ChangeExample
Major versionIncompatible major change1.0.0 → 2.0.0
Minor versionBackward-compatible feature addition1.0.0 → 1.1.0
Patch versionBackward-compatible bug fix1.0.0 → 1.0.1

Current version:

$$\text{indicator system version} = \text{v0.9.0}$$

Version history

Table 10.23 Version History Template

VersionDateType of ChangeContent of ChangeReason for Change
v0.9.02025-12Initial versionEstablished the six major indicator systemInitial release
v0.9.1TBDPatch[To be determined][To be determined]
v1.0.0TBDMajor version[To be determined][To be determined]

III. Version Compatibility Rules

Rule One: Backward compatibility

Changes in minor versions and patch versions must be backward compatible, that is:

$$\forall \sigma: \text{Result}(I, \sigma, v_{n+1}) \approx \text{Result}(I, \sigma, v_n)$$

where $\approx$ means that the results are consistent within an acceptable range.

Rule Two: Change notification

Major version changes must be notified in advance, and a migration guide must be provided.

Rule Three: Version coexistence

During the transition period, the old and new versions may coexist, allowing users to choose the version to use.

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

As a meta-level examination of the indicator system, this chapter accomplished the following core tasks:

Conclusion One: The indicator system possesses internal consistency

The six major indicators (UCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, CSIA) possess internal consistency at three levels:

LevelConsistency ConclusionMain Basis
Conceptual levelConsistentDefinitions non-contradictory, anchoring consistent, terminology consistent
Methodological levelRelatively high consistencyFollow common methodological principles, similar structure
Application levelRelatively high consistencyProduce consistent decision orientations in typical scenarios

This consistency derives from:

  • Common theoretical anchoring (the New Three Views)
  • Consistent methodological principles
  • A coordinated design of information flow

Conclusion Two: Manageable potential conflicts exist among the indicators

The potential conflicts among the indicators can be divided into five types:

Conflict TypeDescriptionResolution Principle
Level conflictConflict between indicators at different levelsPrinciple of level priority
Dimensional conflictConflict between different dimensions of the same indicatorPrinciple of Pareto improvement
Temporal conflictConflict between short-term and long-term assessmentPrinciple of temporal discounting
Subject conflictConflict between the perspectives of different subjectsPrinciple of negotiated resolution
Weight conflictConflict caused by different weight settingsPrinciple of sensitivity analysis

Through systematic conflict identification and resolution procedures, these conflicts are manageable.

Conclusion Three: The indicator system has clear boundaries

The boundaries of the indicator system include three aspects:

Boundary TypeContentHandling Method
Boundary of scope of applicabilityBoundaries along the four dimensions of subject, action, time, and scenarioSpecify boundary conditions; not applicable outside the boundary
Boundary of precisionPrecision limits of each indicatorReport uncertainty, sensitivity analysis
Boundary of validityValidity limits of each indicatorMulti-method verification, continuous improvement

Conclusion Four: The indicator system is evolvable

The indicator system adopts versioned management and supports orderly evolution:

Evolution MechanismContent
Versioned managementSemantic version numbers, version history
Revision procedureSix-stage procedure (proposal, assessment, negotiation, decision, implementation, rollback)
Directions of developmentShort-term (precision improvement), mid-term (international standardization), long-term (cross-civilizational applicability)

[1] Consistency: In logic and philosophy, consistency means that a set of propositions or a theory contains no contradiction. In measurement theory, consistency refers to the degree to which a measurement instrument produces similar results under different conditions. The "consistency" used in this chapter mainly refers to the coherence and non-contradictoriness among conceptual definitions, methodological principles, and application orientations. See: Tarski, A. (1944). "The Semantic Conception of Truth and the Foundations of Semantics." Philosophy and Phenomenological Research, 4(3), 341-376; Nunnally, J. C., & Bernstein, I. H. (1994). Psychometric Theory (3rd ed.). McGraw-Hill.

[2] Meta-level: The meta-level refers to a higher level that describes, analyzes, or assesses a given level. Meta-level analysis is concerned not with the object itself but with the theory, method, or language about the object. The examination of the indicator system in this chapter is meta-level because it assesses the properties of the indicators themselves, not the objects that the indicators measure. See: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books; Bateson, G. (1972). Steps to an Ecology of Mind. University of Chicago Press.

[3] Construct Validity: Construct validity is a core concept in psychometrics and refers to whether a measurement instrument truly measures the theoretical construct it claims to measure. The assessment of construct validity includes convergent validity (correlation with related constructs) and discriminant validity (independence from unrelated constructs). See: Cronbach, L. J., & Meehl, P. E. (1955). "Construct Validity in Psychological Tests." Psychological Bulletin, 52(4), 281-302; Messick, S. (1995). "Validity of Psychological Assessment." American Psychologist, 50(9), 741-749.

[4] Criterion Validity: Criterion validity refers to the degree of correlation between a measurement instrument and an external standard (criterion). Criterion validity is divided into concurrent validity (correlation with a current criterion) and predictive validity (correlation with a future criterion). The assessment of criterion validity requires a reliable external standard, which is often a challenge in a new field. See: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education. (2014). Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing. AERA.

[5] Content Validity: Content validity refers to whether a measurement instrument covers all important aspects of the construct being measured. Content validity is usually assessed through expert judgment, examining whether the measurement items comprehensively represent the content domain of the construct. See: Haynes, S. N., Richard, D. C. S., & Kubany, E. S. (1995). "Content Validity in Psychological Assessment: A Functional Approach to Concepts and Methods." Psychological Assessment, 7(3), 238-247.

[6] Pareto Improvement: Pareto improvement is a core concept in welfare economics and refers to a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off. Pareto optimality refers to a state in which there is no room for Pareto improvement. This concept is named after the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto. See: Pareto, V. (1906). Manuale di Economia Politica. Società Editrice Libraria; Sen, A. (1970). Collective Choice and Social Welfare. Holden-Day.

[7] Temporal Discounting: Temporal discounting refers to the depreciation of future value relative to present value. In economics, the discount rate determines the present value of future benefits. The choice of the social discount rate has a major impact on the assessment of long-term projects. This work advocates adopting a relatively low social discount rate to reflect responsibility toward future generations. See: Ramsey, F. P. (1928). "A Mathematical Theory of Saving." The Economic Journal, 38(152), 543-559; Stern, N. (2007). The Economics of Climate Change: The Stern Review. Cambridge University Press.

[8] Semantic Versioning: Semantic versioning is a standard specification for software version management, in the format "major version number.minor version number.patch number." A change in the major version number indicates an incompatible API modification, a change in the minor version number indicates a backward-compatible feature addition, and a change in the patch number indicates a backward-compatible bug fix. See: Preston-Werner, T. (2013). Semantic Versioning 2.0.0. https://semver.org/; this specification has been widely applied in the fields of software development and standards management.

[9] Commensurability: Commensurability refers to the property by which different things can be compared using a common standard. In the philosophy of science, Kuhn (Thomas Kuhn) proposed the concept of "incommensurability" between paradigms. In value theory, the problem of commensurability concerns whether different types of value can be reduced to a single scale. This work acknowledges the existence of partial incommensurability among the value dimensions measured by different indicators. See: Kuhn, T. S. (1962). The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. University of Chicago Press; Chang, R. (Ed.). (1997). Incommensurability, Incomparability, and Practical Reason. Harvard University Press.

Part V: Institutional Design

Part V. Institutional Design

The Protocol-Stack MethodologyChapter 16

Protocol Stack Methodology

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

This chapter opens Part Five, "Institutional Design," and undertakes the task of transforming normative principles into an institutional architecture. Part Three established the Principle of Recursive Freedom, the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility, and the Principle of Reversibility as the normative foundations of interstellar civilization governance; Part Four established the indicator system as an operationalization tool. The task of this chapter is to answer a key question: how can these principles and tools be organized into a coherent institutional architecture?

Traditional institutional design faces a fundamental tension: the contradiction between the stability of principles and the flexibility of operations. Institutions that are too rigid are difficult to adapt to change, while institutions that are too flexible lose their normative binding force. This chapter proposes the "protocol stack" (Protocol Stack) as a methodological framework for resolving this tension, drawing on the layered design idea of computer networks to achieve the unity of "stable principles" and "flexible operations."

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The protocol stack methodology is directly anchored in the core propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{Protocol Stack} \triangleleft \{\text{NC-1}, \text{NC-2}, \text{NK-4}\}$$

Specifically:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology) → the protocol stack emphasizes inter-layer relations rather than independent entities
  • NC-2 (process ontology) → the protocol stack supports dynamic evolution rather than static fixation
  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge) → the upper-layer rules of the protocol stack are negotiably revisable

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer four fundamental questions:

Core Question One: What is a protocol stack? What is its essential difference from traditional institutional design? Core Question Two: What design principles should the protocol stack follow? Core Question Three: What advantages and limitations does the protocol stack have relative to traditional governance models? Core Question Four: To what situations does the protocol stack apply? Where are its boundaries?

VI. Boundary Statement

All content of this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Methodological positioning: the protocol stack is a methodological framework for institutional design, not a concrete institutional scheme
  2. Limits of the analogy: the analogy from network protocols to governance protocols is heuristic, not an isomorphic mapping
  3. Conceptual prototype stage: the protocol stack methodology is at the TRL 2 stage, applicable to academic research and thought experiments
  4. Open revision: the protocol stack itself is revisable, following its own versioning principle

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • If the reader has a background in computer science, it is suggested to focus on the analogy analysis in §16.1.1
  • If the reader is concerned with institutional theory, it is suggested to focus on the comparative analysis in §16.3
  • If the reader is concerned with practical application, it is suggested to focus on the applicability assessment in §16.4

§16.1 The Concept of the Protocol Stack

§16.1.1 From Network Protocols to Governance Protocols

I. The Basic Structure of the Network Protocol Stack

The protocol stack of computer networks is one of the most important architectural innovations in information technology of the twentieth century. Represented by the seven-layer OSI model and the four-layer TCP/IP model, protocol stack design enabled heterogeneous networks to achieve interconnection and interoperability, laying the foundation for the development of the global Internet.

Definition 16.1.1 (Network Protocol Stack)

A network protocol stack is a set of hierarchically organized communication protocols, in which each layer provides services to the upper layer while using the services provided by the lower layer.

Formal statement:

Let the protocol stack be $\mathcal{P} = \{P_0, P_1, ..., P_n\}$, where $P_i$ is the protocol of the $i$-th layer; then the protocol stack satisfies:

$$\forall i \in [1, n]: P_i \text{ uses } \text{Service}(P_{i-1}) \land P_i \text{ provides } \text{Service}(P_i)$$

The seven-layer OSI model:

LayerNameFunctionTypical Protocols
L7Application LayerUser interfaceHTTP, FTP
L6Presentation LayerData formatSSL, JPEG
L5Session LayerSession managementNetBIOS
L4Transport LayerEnd-to-end transmissionTCP, UDP
L3Network LayerRouting and addressingIP
L2Data Link LayerFrame transmissionEthernet
L1Physical LayerBit transmissionCable, optical fiber

Core design principles of the network protocol stack:

  1. Layer encapsulation: each layer interacts only with adjacent layers, without cross-layer calls
  2. Interface standardization: inter-layer interfaces are clearly defined and replaceable
  3. Separation of concerns: each layer focuses on a specific function
  4. Lower-layer stability: lower-layer protocols are more stable than upper-layer protocols

II. The Analogy from Network Protocols to Governance Protocols

This work proposes applying the design ideas of the network protocol stack to governance institutional design, establishing a "governance protocol stack."

Definition 16.1.2 (Governance Protocol Stack)

A governance protocol stack is a set of hierarchically organized governance rules, in which each layer provides a constraint framework for the upper layer while operating within the constraint framework of the lower layer.

Formal statement:

Let the governance protocol stack be $\mathcal{G} = \{G_0, G_1, ..., G_n\}$, where $G_i$ is the governance rule of the $i$-th layer; then the governance protocol stack satisfies:

$$\forall i \in [1, n]: G_i \subseteq \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1}) \land G_i \text{ constrains } G_{i+1}$$

Analogy mapping:

Table 16.1 Analogy mapping between the network protocol stack and the governance protocol stack

Data Link LayerL₁ Ontological-Epistemological LayerFoundational conceptual framework
Network LayerL₂ Normative Principle LayerCore normative principles

Application LayerL₄ Operational Protocol LayerConcrete operating procedures
