III. Validity and Limits of the Analogy

The analogy from network protocols to governance protocols is heuristic, but important differences also exist:

Table 16.2 Validity and limits of the analogy

DimensionNetwork Protocol StackGovernance Protocol StackDifference Explanation
DeterminacyHighly determinateUncertainty existsGovernance involves value judgments
VerifiabilityPrecisely verifiablePartially verifiableNormativity is difficult to fully verify
SubjecthoodNo subjecthoodInvolves subjectsGovernance involves conscious subjects
PurposivenessFunctional purposeNormative purposeGovernance involves ought-questions
Evolution MechanismTechnology-drivenNegotiation-drivenGovernance rules require negotiation

IV. Boundary Statement of the Analogy:

Boundary Statement 16.1: The analogy from network protocols to governance protocols is structural rather than isomorphic. The layered design idea of the network protocol stack can inspire governance institutional design, but the governance protocol stack cannot simply replicate all characteristics of the network protocol stack. In particular, the governance protocol stack must handle problems such as value judgments, subjecthood, and normativity that the network protocol stack does not involve.

V. Relation to the New Three Views

The relation of the protocol stack methodology to the New Three Views is reflected in:

Reflection of NC-1 (relational ontology):

The protocol stack emphasizes inter-layer relations rather than independent entities. The meaning of each layer lies not in itself but in its relations with other layers.

$$\text{Layer}_i = f(\text{Constraint}(\text{Layer}_{i-1}), \text{Service}(\text{Layer}_{i+1}))$$

Reflection of NC-2 (process ontology):

The protocol stack supports dynamic evolution. The protocol stack is not a static set of rules but a process of continuous evolution.

$$\mathcal{G}(t+1) = \text{Evolve}(\mathcal{G}(t), \text{Feedback}(t), \text{Context}(t))$$

Reflection of NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge):

The upper-layer rules of the protocol stack are negotiably revisable. The higher the layer, the greater the space for negotiation.

$$\text{NegotiationSpace}(G_i) \propto i$$

§16.1.2 Core Characteristics of the Protocol Stack

Characteristic One: Layering

Definition 16.1.3 (Layering)

Layering means that the protocol stack is composed of multiple layers, each with a clear functional positioning and boundary.

Formal statement:

$$\mathcal{G} = \bigcup_{i=0}^{n} G_i, \quad G_i \cap G_j = \emptyset \text{ for } i \neq j$$

Requirements for realizing layering:

RequirementDescriptionFormal Statement
CompletenessThe layers cover all governance functions$\bigcup_{i=0}^{n} \text{Function}(G_i) = \text{AllFunctions}$
Mutual exclusivityFunctions do not overlap between layers$\text{Function}(G_i) \cap \text{Function}(G_j) = \emptyset$
OrderingThere is a clear order between layers$G_0 \prec G_1 \prec ... \prec G_n$

Characteristic Two: Constraint Propagation

Definition 16.1.4 (Constraint Propagation)

Constraint propagation means that the lower layer imposes constraints on the upper layer, and upper-layer rules must operate within the lower-layer constraint framework.

Formal statement:

$$\forall i \in [1, n]: G_i \models \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1})$$

where $G_i \models \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1})$ means that $G_i$ satisfies the constraint imposed by $G_{i-1}$.

Characteristic Three: Revision Difficulty Gradient

Definition 16.1.5 (Revision Difficulty Gradient)

The revision difficulty gradient means that the lower the layer, the more difficult it is to revise, and the higher the layer, the easier it is to revise.

Formal statement:

$$\text{RevisionDifficulty}(G_i) > \text{RevisionDifficulty}(G_j) \text{ for } i < j$$

Quantification of revision difficulty:

LayerRevision DifficultyRevision CycleRevision Procedure

L₁Extremely difficult (0.9)CentennialParadigm revolution
L₂Difficult (0.7)DecadalMajor negotiation
L₃Moderate (0.5)AnnualRoutine negotiation
L₄Easy (0.3)MonthlyTechnical update

Reasons for the revision difficulty gradient:

  1. Stability requirement: lower-layer rules provide a stable foundation for upper layers, and frequent revision would cause system instability
  2. Dependency relation: upper-layer rules depend on lower-layer rules, and lower-layer revision triggers cascading revision of upper layers
  3. Consensus cost: lower-layer rules involve more foundational consensus, and revision requires broader negotiation

Characteristic Four: Interface Standardization

Definition 16.1.6 (Interface Standardization)

Interface standardization means that inter-layer interaction proceeds through standardized interfaces, and interface definitions are clear and stable.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Interface}(G_i, G_{i+1}) = \langle \text{Input}_i, \text{Output}_i, \text{Protocol}_i \rangle$$

Characteristic Five: Rollbackability

Definition 16.1.7 (Rollbackability)

Rollbackability means that when a problem arises in upper-layer rules, one can roll back to a previous version without affecting lower-layer rules.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Rollback}(G_i, v_n \rightarrow v_{n-1}) \Rightarrow G_j \text{ unchanged for } j < i$$

Conditions for realizing rollbackability:

Inter-layer independenceRollback does not affect other layers$\text{Rollback}(G_i) \perp G_j$ for $j \neq i$

§16.1.3 Advantages of the Protocol Stack

Advantage One: Unity of Stability and Flexibility

Traditional institutional design faces the dilemma of stability versus flexibility: too much stability makes adaptation to change difficult, while too much flexibility loses normative binding force. The protocol stack resolves this dilemma through layered design.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Stability}(\mathcal{G}) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} w_i \cdot \text{Stability}(G_i)$$

$$\text{Flexibility}(\mathcal{G}) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} w_i \cdot \text{Flexibility}(G_i)$$

where lower layers have higher weights and upper layers have lower weights.

Hierarchical distribution of stability and flexibility:

LayerStabilityFlexibilityExplanation
L₀1.00.0Physical laws cannot be changed
L₁0.90.1The ontological framework is highly stable
L₂0.70.3Normative principles are relatively stable
L₃0.50.5Institutional design is adjustable
L₄0.30.7Operating procedures are highly flexible

Advantage Two: Traceability

The layered design of the protocol stack enables the rules of each layer to be traced back to the constraints of the next lower layer, forming a complete chain of argument.

Formal statement:

$$\forall r \in G_i: \exists c \in G_{i-1}: r \text{ is justified by } c$$

Realization of traceability:

│  Traceability example: from operating procedures to physical constraints │                           
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │                                    
│  L₄ Operating procedure: CSIA assessment procedure               │                                   
│       ↑ trace                                                   │                                    
│  L₃ Institutional design: the review function of the Cosmic-Scale IRB │                              
│       ↑ trace                                                   │                                    
│  L₂ Normative principle: the Principle of Reversibility requires assessment of irreversible impacts │
│       ↑ trace                                                   │                                    
│  L₁ Ontology: NC-2 (process ontology) emphasizes the processual consequences of action │             
│       ↑ trace                                                   │                                    
│  L₀ Physical constraint: the second law of thermodynamics limits irreversible processes │            
│                                                                 │                                    
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Advantage Three: Modular Revision

The layered design of the protocol stack enables revision to be conducted at a specific layer without affecting other layers.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Revise}(G_i) \Rightarrow G_j \text{ unchanged for } j \neq i \text{ (under certain conditions)}$$

Conditions for modular revision:

ConditionDescriptionFormal Statement
Interface compatibilityAfter revision, the inter-layer interface is still satisfied$G_i' \models \text{Interface}(G_{i-1}, G_i)$
Constraint satisfactionAfter revision, the lower-layer constraint is still satisfied$G_i' \models \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1})$
Service preservationAfter revision, services can still be provided to the upper layer$\text{Service}(G_i') \supseteq \text{Required}(G_{i+1})$

Advantage Four: Fault Tolerance

The rollbackability of the protocol stack gives the system fault-tolerant capability. When a problem arises in the rules of a certain layer, one can roll back to a previous version.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Error}(G_i, v_n) \Rightarrow \text{Rollback}(G_i, v_n \rightarrow v_{n-1}) \Rightarrow \text{System Restored}$$

Advantage Five: Auditability

The standardized interfaces and traceability of the protocol stack give the system auditability. Any decision can be traced back to its normative basis.

Formal statement:

$$\forall d \in \text{Decisions}: \exists \text{AuditTrail}(d) = \langle r_4, r_3, r_2, r_1, r_0 \rangle$$

where $r_i \in G_i$ is the normative basis of decision $d$ at the $i$-th layer.

§16.2 Design Principles of the Protocol Stack

§16.2.1 The Principle of Layer Separation

I. Statement of the Principle

Design Principle 16.1 (Principle of Layer Separation)

The layers of the protocol stack should be functionally separated, with each layer focusing on a specific type of problem and not handling problems of other layers across layers.

Formal statement:

$$\forall i, j \in [0, n], i \neq j: \text{Function}(G_i) \cap \text{Function}(G_j) = \emptyset$$

II. Reasons for Layer Separation

Reason One: Complexity Management

Layer separation decomposes complex governance problems into multiple relatively simple sub-problems, reducing the cognitive complexity of the system.

$$\text{Complexity}(\mathcal{G}) < \sum_{i=0}^{n} \text{Complexity}(G_i) \text{ (without separation)}$$

Reason Two: Specialization

Each layer can be handled by subjects with the corresponding professional knowledge, improving governance quality.

LayerRequired Professional KnowledgeTypical Responsible Subject
L₀Physics, information theoryScientists
L₁Philosophy, cognitive sciencePhilosophers, scientists
L₂Ethics, lawEthicists, jurists
L₃Institutional design, political scienceInstitutional designers, policymakers
L₄Technology, operationsTechnical experts, operators

Reason Three: Maintainability

Layer separation enables revision to be conducted at a specific layer without affecting other layers, improving the maintainability of the system.

III. Requirements for Realizing Layer Separation

Requirement One: Clear Functional Boundaries

The functional boundary of each layer must be clearly defined.

Table 16.5 Functional boundaries of each layer

LayerFunctional ScopeProblems Not Handled
L₀Identification and statement of physical constraintsValue judgments, institutional design
L₁Ontological and epistemological frameworkConcrete norms, operating procedures
L₂Core normative principlesInstitutional details, operating procedures
L₃Institutional architecture designPhysical constraints, operational details
L₄Concrete operating proceduresPrinciple formulation, institutional design

Requirement Two: Mechanism for Handling Cross-Layer Problems

When a problem involves multiple layers, it should be decomposed into sub-problems for each layer and handled separately.

Cross-layer problem handling procedure:

PROCEDURE HandleCrossLayerIssue(issue)

// Step 1: problem decomposition sub_issues = DecomposeByLayer(issue)

// Step 2: processing at each layer FOR EACH layer_i, sub_issue_i IN sub_issues: solution_i = ProcessAtLayer(layer_i, sub_issue_i) END FOR

// Step 3: integration of solutions integrated_solution = IntegrateSolutions(solutions)

// Step 4: consistency check IF NOT ConsistencyCheck(integrated_solution) THEN RETURN ConflictResolution(integrated_solution) END IF

RETURN integrated_solution

END PROCEDURE

Requirement Three: Institutionalization of Layer Responsibilities

The responsibilities of each layer should be clarified through institutionalized means.

Table 16.6 Institutionalization of layer responsibilities

LayerResponsible SubjectContent of ResponsibilityAccountability Mechanism
L₀Scientific communityIdentify and state physical constraintsPeer review
L₁Philosophy-Science CommitteeMaintain the ontological-epistemological frameworkAcademic review
L₂Normative Principles CommitteeMaintain and interpret normative principlesNegotiated deliberation
L₃Institutional Design CommitteeDesign and revise the institutional architectureDemocratic accountability
L₄Operating Procedures CommitteeFormulate and update operating proceduresTechnical audit

§16.2.2 The Principle of Lower-Layer Constraint

I. Statement of the Principle

Design Principle 16.2 (Principle of Lower-Layer Constraint)

Upper-layer rules must operate within the lower-layer constraint framework and must not violate lower-layer rules.

Formal statement:

$$\forall i \in [1, n]: G_i \models \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1})$$

Equivalent statement:

$$\forall r \in G_i: \neg(r \vdash \neg c) \text{ for any } c \in G_{i-1}$$

That is, upper-layer rules cannot derive conclusions that contradict lower-layer rules.

II. The Hierarchical Structure of Lower-Layer Constraint

(i) L₀'s constraint on L₁:

The physical constraints of the L₀ layer impose constraints on the ontological-epistemological framework of the L₁ layer.

L₀ ConstraintRequirement on L₁Example
Second law of thermodynamicsOntology must acknowledge the trend of entropy increaseNL-2 (negentropic organization) cannot violate thermodynamics
Information-theoretic boundsEpistemology must acknowledge the limits of information processingNK-3 (deep uncertainty) is consistent with information theory
Causal structureOntology must respect causal relationsNC-2 (process ontology) is consistent with causal structure

(ii) L₁'s constraint on L₂:

The ontological-epistemological framework of the L₁ layer imposes constraints on the normative principles of the L₂ layer.

L₁ ConstraintRequirement on L₂Example
NC-1 (relational ontology)Normative principles must consider relationalityThe Principle of Recursive Freedom considers inter-subject relations
NL-2 (negentropic organization)Normative principles must consider negentropy maintenanceThe Principle of Negentropy Responsibility derives directly from NL-2
NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge)Normative principles must allow negotiated revisionThe Principle of Reversibility supports the revisability of rules

(iii) L₂'s constraint on L₃:

The normative principles of the L₂ layer impose constraints on the institutional design of the L₃ layer.

L₂ ConstraintRequirement on L₃Example
Principle of Recursive FreedomInstitutions must protect the space of possibilitiesThe Multi-Intelligence Tribunal protects the options of all parties
Principle of Negentropy ResponsibilityInstitutions must promote negentropy maintenanceThe Cosmic-Scale IRB assesses negentropy impact
Principle of ReversibilityInstitutions must support reversible decisionsVersioned rollback mechanism

(iv) L₃'s constraint on L₄:

The institutional design of the L₃ layer imposes constraints on the operating procedures of the L₄ layer.

L₃ ConstraintRequirement on L₄Example
Multi-Intelligence TribunalOperating procedures must conform to tribunal proceduresDispute resolution procedure
Cosmic-Scale IRBOperating procedures must conform to IRB review requirementsCSIA assessment procedure
Versioned governanceOperating procedures must support versioningVersion identification specification

III. Inspection Procedure for Lower-Layer Constraint

PROCEDURE ConstraintCheck(rule, layer)

// Obtain lower-layer constraints lower_layer = layer - 1 constraints = GetConstraints(lower_layer)

// Check each constraint FOR EACH constraint IN constraints: IF Contradicts(rule, constraint) THEN RETURN (FALSE, constraint, "Violation detected") END IF END FOR

RETURN (TRUE, NULL, "All constraints satisfied")

END PROCEDURE

IV. Handling of Constraint Violations

When an upper-layer rule is detected to violate a lower-layer constraint, one should:

  1. Identify the violation: clarify which upper-layer rule violates which lower-layer constraint
  2. Analyze the cause: analyze the cause of the violation (misunderstanding, negligence, intent)
  3. Revise the upper layer: revise the upper-layer rule to eliminate the violation
  4. Record and archive: record the violation and the revision process

StepContentResponsible Subject

AnalysisAnalyze the cause of the violationRelevant layer committee
RevisionRevise the upper-layer ruleUpper-layer rule-maker
VerificationVerify consistency after revisionConsistency check system
ArchivingRecord the entire processArchive management system

§16.2.3 The Principle of Upper-Layer Flexibility

I. Statement of the Principle

Design Principle 16.3 (Principle of Upper-Layer Flexibility)

Under the premise of satisfying lower-layer constraints, upper-layer rules should maintain flexibility, allowing adjustment according to context.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Flexibility}(G_i) = \max \text{ subject to } G_i \models \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1})$$

II. Reasons for Upper-Layer Flexibility

Reason One: Contextual Adaptability

Upper-layer rules need to adapt to diverse contexts, and excessive rigidity would lead to inapplicability.

$$\text{Applicability}(G_i) \propto \text{Flexibility}(G_i)$$

Reason Two: Space for Innovation

The flexibility of upper-layer rules provides space for institutional innovation.

$$\text{InnovationSpace}(G_i) \propto \text{Flexibility}(G_i)$$

Reason Three: Possibility of Negotiation

The flexibility of upper-layer rules enables stakeholders to adjust rules through negotiation.

$$\text{NegotiationPossibility}(G_i) \propto \text{Flexibility}(G_i)$$

III. Hierarchical Distribution of Flexibility

Table 16.8 Hierarchical distribution of flexibility

LayerDegree of FlexibilityManifestation of Flexibility
L₀0 (no flexibility)Physical laws cannot be changed
L₁0.1 (extremely low)The ontological framework is rarely adjusted
L₂0.3 (low)Normative principles can be adjusted in boundary cases
L₃0.5 (moderate)Institutional design can be adjusted according to context
L₄0.7 (high)Operating procedures can be frequently adjusted

IV. Mechanisms for Realizing Flexibility

Mechanism One: Parametric Design

Upper-layer rules adopt parametric design, and parameters can be adjusted according to context.

Example: weight parameters in the CSIA assessment procedure

$$\text{CSIA}_{\text{score}} = \sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i \cdot D_i$$

The weights $w_i$ can be adjusted according to context, but must satisfy $\sum w_i = 1$.

Mechanism Two: Exception Clauses

Upper-layer rules include exception clauses, allowing deviation from general rules under specific circumstances.

Example: simplified procedure under emergency conditions

IF EmergencyCondition THEN ApplySimplifiedProcedure() ELSE ApplyStandardProcedure() END IF

Mechanism Three: Negotiated Revision Procedure

Upper-layer rules include a negotiated revision procedure, allowing stakeholders to propose revisions.

Negotiated revision procedure:

PROCEDURE NegotiatedRevision(rule, layer)

// Step 1: proposal proposal = SubmitRevisionProposal(rule)

// Step 2: assessment assessment = AssessProposal(proposal)

// Step 3: negotiation IF assessment.requires_negotiation THEN consensus = Negotiate(proposal, stakeholders) END IF

// Step 4: constraint check IF NOT ConstraintCheck(consensus, layer) THEN RETURN ReviseProposal(consensus) END IF

// Step 5: implementation ImplementRevision(consensus)

RETURN SUCCESS

END PROCEDURE

V. Balance between Flexibility and Stability

The Principle of Upper-Layer Flexibility must be balanced against the Principle of Lower-Layer Constraint. Flexibility cannot come at the cost of sacrificing lower-layer constraints.

Balancing principle:

$$\text{Flexibility}(G_i) = \max \text{ subject to } G_i \models \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1})$$

Realization of balance:

SituationHandling Method
Flexibility compatible with constraintAllow flexible adjustment
Flexibility conflicts with constraintConstraint takes priority, flexibility is limited
The constraint itself needs revisionInitiate the lower-layer revision procedure

§16.2.4 The Principle of Cross-Layer Consistency

I. Statement of the Principle

Design Principle 16.4 (Principle of Cross-Layer Consistency)

Consistency must be maintained among the layers of the protocol stack, with no cross-layer contradictions.

Formal statement:

$$\forall i, j \in [0, n]: \neg(G_i \cup G_j \vdash \bot)$$

That is, the rules of any two layers, when combined, cannot derive a contradiction.

II. Types of Cross-Layer Consistency

Type One: Vertical Consistency

Consistency between adjacent layers.

$$\text{VerticalConsistency}(G_i, G_{i+1}) \iff \neg(G_i \cup G_{i+1} \vdash \bot)$$

Type Two: Horizontal Consistency

Consistency within the same layer.

$$\text{HorizontalConsistency}(G_i) \iff \neg(G_i \vdash \bot)$$

Type Three: Global Consistency

Consistency of the entire protocol stack.

$$\text{GlobalConsistency}(\mathcal{G}) \iff \neg(\bigcup_{i=0}^{n} G_i \vdash \bot)$$

III. Consistency Inspection Procedure

PROCEDURE GlobalConsistencyCheck(protocol_stack)

// Step 1: horizontal consistency check FOR EACH layer IN protocol_stack: IF NOT HorizontalConsistencyCheck(layer) THEN RETURN (FALSE, "Horizontal inconsistency in " + layer) END IF END FOR

// Step 2: vertical consistency check FOR i = 0 TO n-1: IF NOT VerticalConsistencyCheck(layer[i], layer[i+1]) THEN RETURN (FALSE, "Vertical inconsistency between L" + i + " and L" + (i+1)) END IF END FOR

// Step 3: global consistency check all_rules = UnionAllLayers(protocol_stack) IF ContainsContradiction(all_rules) THEN RETURN (FALSE, "Global inconsistency detected") END IF

RETURN (TRUE, "All consistency checks passed")

END PROCEDURE

IV. Resolution of Consistency Conflicts

When a cross-layer inconsistency is detected, it should be resolved according to the following priority:

Priority rule:

$$\text{Priority}(G_i) > \text{Priority}(G_j) \text{ for } i < j$$

That is, lower-layer rules take priority over upper-layer rules.

V. Conflict Resolution Procedure:

PROCEDURE ResolveInconsistency(conflict)

// Identify the layers involved in the conflict layers = IdentifyConflictLayers(conflict) lower_layer = min(layers) upper_layer = max(layers)

// Resolve according to priority IF CanResolveByRevising(upper_layer) THEN ReviseUpperLayer(upper_layer, conflict) ELSE IF MustRevise(lower_layer) THEN // Lower-layer revision requires a stricter procedure InitiateLowerLayerRevision(lower_layer, conflict) ELSE // Cannot be resolved, report the error ReportUnresolvableConflict(conflict) END IF

END PROCEDURE

VI. Institutionalization of Consistency Maintenance

Conflict reportingReceive and handle consistency conflict reportsConflict Resolution Committee
Revision coordinationCoordinate cross-layer revisionsProtocol Stack Management Committee

§16.3 Comparison of the Protocol Stack with Traditional Governance

§16.3.1 Comparison with Hierarchy

I. Basic Characteristics of Hierarchy

Definition 16.3.1 (Hierarchy)

Hierarchy is a governance model characterized by the distribution of power and authority along a ranking structure, in which superiors have the power of command and control over subordinates.

Core characteristics of hierarchy:

CharacteristicDescription
Authority rankingAuthority is distributed by rank, with superiors above subordinates
Chain of commandDecisions are transmitted top-down through the chain of command
Division of dutiesEach level has a clear division of duties
Accountability mechanismSubordinates are accountable to superiors

II. Similarities between the Protocol Stack and Hierarchy

SimilarityHierarchyProtocol Stack
Layered structurePower layeringFunctional layering
Superior-subordinate relationSuperiors command subordinatesLower layers constrain upper layers
Division of dutiesDuties are clear at each levelFunctions are clear at each layer

III. Differences between the Protocol Stack and Hierarchy

Table 16.10 Differences between the protocol stack and hierarchy

DimensionHierarchyProtocol Stack
Meaning of layersPower ranksFunctional layers
Direction of constraintSuperiors constrain subordinatesLower layers constrain upper layers
Distribution of flexibilitySuperiors are more flexibleUpper layers are more flexible
Revision mechanismSuperiors decide revisionEach layer has a revision procedure
Direction of accountabilitySubordinates are accountable to superiorsUpper layers are accountable to lower layers for consistency

Key Difference One: Direction of Constraint

In hierarchy, the direction of constraint is top-down: superiors impose constraints on subordinates, and subordinates must obey the commands of superiors.

$$\text{Hierarchy}: \text{Upper} \xrightarrow{\text{constrains}} \text{Lower}$$

In the protocol stack, the direction of constraint is bottom-up: lower layers impose constraints on upper layers, and upper layers must operate within the lower-layer constraint framework.

$$\text{Protocol Stack}: \text{Lower} \xrightarrow{\text{constrains}} \text{Upper}$$

Key Difference Two: Distribution of Flexibility

In hierarchy, superiors are usually more flexible than subordinates, because superiors possess greater decision-making power.

$$\text{Hierarchy}: \text{Flexibility}(\text{Upper}) > \text{Flexibility}(\text{Lower})$$

In the protocol stack, upper layers are more flexible than lower layers, because upper-layer rules can be adjusted within the lower-layer constraint framework.

$$\text{Protocol Stack}: \text{Flexibility}(\text{Upper}) > \text{Flexibility}(\text{Lower})$$

Although the two appear the same in the distribution of flexibility, their meanings differ: the flexibility of hierarchy comes from power, while the flexibility of the protocol stack comes from functional positioning.

Key Difference Three: Revision Mechanism

In hierarchy, revision is usually decided by superiors and executed by subordinates.

$$\text{Hierarchy}: \text{Revision} = \text{Decision}(\text{Upper})$$

In the protocol stack, each layer has an independent revision procedure, and lower-layer revision requires a stricter procedure.

$$\text{Protocol Stack}: \text{Revision}(L_i) = \text{Procedure}_i(\text{Proposal}, \text{Assessment}, \text{Consensus})$$

IV. Advantages and Limitations of Hierarchy

Table 16.11 Advantages and limitations of hierarchy

AdvantagesLimitations
High decision-making efficiencyInsufficient flexibility
Clear responsibilityLimited innovation
Low coordination costInformation distortion
Strong execution capacityPoor adaptability

V. Advantages of the Protocol Stack over Hierarchy

Protocol Stack AdvantageExplanation
Greater stabilityLower-layer constraints provide a stable foundation
Better flexibilityUpper layers can be flexibly adjusted within constraints
Stronger traceabilityThe rules of each layer can be traced back to lower-layer bases
Better fault toleranceThe rollback mechanism supports error correction

§16.3.2 Comparison with Network Governance

I. Basic Characteristics of Network Governance

Definition 16.3.2 (Network Governance)

Network Governance is a governance model characterized by multiple relatively independent nodes forming a network through horizontal linkages, with decisions reached through negotiation and coordination.

Core characteristics of network governance:

CharacteristicDescription
PolycentricityThere is no single center of authority
Horizontal linkageNodes interact through horizontal linkages
Negotiated decision-makingDecisions are reached through negotiation and coordination
Flexible adaptationThe network structure can be flexibly adjusted

II. Similarities between the Protocol Stack and Network Governance

SimilarityNetwork GovernanceProtocol Stack
DistributedPower is distributed across multiple nodesFunctions are distributed across multiple layers
NegotiabilityDecisions are reached through negotiationUpper-layer rules are negotiably revisable
FlexibilityThe network structure is adjustableUpper-layer rules are adjustable

III. Differences between the Protocol Stack and Network Governance

Table 16.12 Differences between the protocol stack and network governance

DimensionNetwork GovernanceProtocol Stack
Structure typeHorizontal networkVertical hierarchy
Source of constraintNegotiated consensusLower-layer rules
Source of stabilityRelational stabilityLower-layer stability
Coordination mechanismHorizontal coordinationInter-layer interfaces
Conflict resolutionResolution through negotiationLower-layer priority

Key Difference One: Structure Type

Network governance is a horizontal structure, with equal horizontal relations between nodes.

$$\text{Network Governance}: \text{Node}_i \leftrightarrow \text{Node}_j \text{ (horizontal)}$$

The protocol stack is a vertical structure, with constraining and constrained vertical relations between layers.

$$\text{Protocol Stack}: L_i \xrightarrow{\text{constrains}} L_{i+1} \text{ (vertical)}$$

Key Difference Two: Source of Constraint

In network governance, constraints come from negotiated consensus, with no preset constraint framework.

$$\text{Network Governance}: \text{Constraint} = \text{Consensus}(\text{Nodes})$$

In the protocol stack, constraints come from lower-layer rules, and upper layers must operate within the lower-layer constraint framework.

$$\text{Protocol Stack}: \text{Constraint}(L_{i+1}) = \text{Rules}(L_i)$$

Key Difference Three: Source of Stability

The stability of network governance comes from the stability of relations between nodes, and changes in relations may cause network instability.

$$\text{Network Governance}: \text{Stability} = f(\text{RelationshipStability})$$

The stability of the protocol stack comes from the stability of lower-layer rules, and lower-layer rules provide a stable foundation for upper layers.

$$\text{Protocol Stack}: \text{Stability} = f(\text{LowerLayerStability})$$

Large space for innovationUnclear responsibility
Strong inclusivenessInsufficient stability

§16.3.3 The Unique Positioning of the Protocol Stack

I. Positioning of the Protocol Stack: A Synthesis of Hierarchy and Network Governance

The protocol stack attempts to synthesize the advantages of hierarchy and network governance while avoiding the limitations of both.

Table 16.14 The synthetic positioning of the protocol stack

DimensionHierarchyNetwork GovernanceProtocol Stack
StructureVertical ranksHorizontal networkVertical functional layers
ConstraintSuperiors constrain subordinatesNegotiated constraintLower layers constrain upper layers
FlexibilitySuperiors flexibleFully flexibleUpper layers flexible
StabilityAuthority stabilityRelational stabilityLower-layer stability
RevisionDecided by superiorsDecided through negotiationLayered procedures

II. Unique Characteristics of the Protocol Stack

Characteristic One: Functional Layers Rather Than Power Ranks

The layers of the protocol stack are functional rather than power-based. The distinction of each layer is based on functional positioning, not the magnitude of power.

$$\text{Protocol Stack Layers} = f(\text{Function}) \neq f(\text{Power})$$

Characteristic Two: Lower-Layer Constraint Rather Than Superior Command

The constraints of the protocol stack come from lower-layer rules, not superior commands. Lower-layer rules have normative binding force, not command binding force.

$$\text{Protocol Stack Constraint} = \text{NormativeConstraint}(L_{i-1}) \neq \text{Command}(\text{Superior})$$

Characteristic Three: Negotiated Revision Rather Than Unilateral Decision

The revision of the protocol stack proceeds through a negotiation procedure, not a unilateral decision. Each layer has the right to participate in revision.

$$\text{Protocol Stack Revision} = \text{NegotiatedRevision} \neq \text{UnilateralDecision}$$

Characteristic Four: Rollbackable Rather Than Irreversible

The protocol stack supports rollback; when a problem arises in the rules, one can roll back to a previous version. This contrasts with the irreversibility of traditional governance models.

$$\text{Protocol Stack} \models \text{Rollbackability}$$

III. Applicable Scenarios for the Protocol Stack

Based on the above unique characteristics, the protocol stack is particularly applicable to the following scenarios:

ScenarioReason for Applicability
Cross-subject governanceFunctional layers avoid power disputes
Long-term governanceLower-layer stability provides a long-term foundation
Governance under uncertaintyRollback supports error correction
Governance of plural valuesNegotiated revision accommodates plural values

IV. Deep Analogy between the Protocol Stack and TCP/IP

The success of the TCP/IP protocol stack provides an important inspiration for the protocol stack methodology:

Table 16.15 Inspiration of TCP/IP's success for the protocol stack

TCP/IP ExperienceInspiration for the Protocol Stack
Layered design reduces complexityGovernance problems can also be handled in layers
Interface standardization promotes interoperabilityInter-layer interface standardization promotes coordination
Lower-layer stability supports upper-layer innovationStable normative principles support institutional innovation
The end-to-end principle maintains flexibilityThe Principle of Upper-Layer Flexibility maintains adaptability

V. Theoretical Contributions of the Protocol Stack Methodology

The contributions of the protocol stack methodology to governance theory include:

  1. A new governance model: it proposes a third governance model distinct from hierarchy and network governance
  2. Unity of stability and flexibility: it achieves the unity of stability and flexibility through layered design
  3. A traceability framework: it provides a systematic framework for the traceability of rules
  4. A fault-tolerance mechanism: it introduces a rollbackable fault-tolerance mechanism

Formal statement:

$$\neg\text{Applicable}(\text{ProtocolStack}) \Leftarrow \text{DecisionTime} < \text{Threshold}_{fast}$$

Examples:

SituationDecision Time RequirementApplicability

Situation Three: Single-Subject Decision-Making

When decisions are made by a single subject, the multi-layer negotiation mechanism of the protocol stack may be too complex and does not apply.

$$\neg\text{Applicable}(\text{ProtocolStack}) \Leftarrow |\text{DecisionMakers}| = 1$$

Multi-party negotiationMultiple subjectsApplicable

Situation Four: Deterministic Problems

When a problem is highly deterministic, the rollback mechanism of the protocol stack may be an unnecessary overhead and does not apply.

Formal statement:

$$\neg\text{Applicable}(\text{ProtocolStack}) \Leftarrow \text{Uncertainty} < \text{Threshold}_{low}$$

Examples:

SituationDegree of DeterminacyApplicability

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

As the opening of Part Five, "Institutional Design," this chapter establishes the theoretical foundation of the protocol stack methodology. The core conclusions are as follows:

Conclusion One: The Conceptual Foundation of the Protocol Stack

The protocol stack is a hierarchically organized governance framework that draws on the design ideas of the network protocol stack and organizes governance rules into multiple layers. The protocol stack of this work includes five layers:

LayerNameContentRevision Difficulty
L₀Physical Constraint LayerThermodynamic laws, information-theoretic boundsNon-revisable
L₁Ontological-Epistemological Layerthe New Three Views (NC, NL, NK)Extremely difficult to revise
L₂Normative Principle LayerRecursive freedom, negentropy responsibility, reversibilityDifficult to revise
L₃Institutional Design LayerProtocol stack architecture, tribunal, IRBRevisable
L₄Operational Protocol LayerIndicators, procedures, formsEasily revisable

The analogy from network protocols to governance protocols is structural rather than isomorphic; the governance protocol stack must handle special problems such as value judgments, subjecthood, and normativity.

Conclusion Two: The Five Major Characteristics of the Protocol Stack

The protocol stack has five core characteristics:

CharacteristicFormal StatementFunction
Layering$\mathcal{G} = \bigcup_{i=0}^{n} G_i$Functional separation
Constraint propagation$G_i \models \text{Constraint}(G_{i-1})$Normative constraint
Revision difficulty gradient$\text{RevDiff}(G_i) > \text{RevDiff}(G_j)$ for $i < j$
Stability foundation
Interface standardization$\text{Interface}(G_i, G_{i+1}) = \langle \text{Input}, \text{Output}, \text{Protocol} \rangle$Inter-layer coordination
Rollbackability$\text{Rollback}(G_i, v_n \rightarrow v_{n-1})$Fault-tolerance capability

These five characteristics are interrelated: layering is the foundation, constraint propagation and the revision difficulty gradient are the unfolding of layering, interface standardization supports inter-layer coordination, and rollbackability is the comprehensive guarantee of the first four characteristics.

Conclusion Three: The Four Design Principles of the Protocol Stack

The design of the protocol stack follows four principles:

PrincipleCore RequirementRealization Mechanism
Principle of Layer SeparationFunctional separation of each layerFunctional boundary definition, institutionalization of responsibilities
Principle of Lower-Layer ConstraintUpper layers must not violate lower layersConstraint inspection procedure, violation handling procedure
Principle of Upper-Layer FlexibilityUpper layers maintain flexibilityParametric design, exception clauses, negotiated revision
Principle of Cross-Layer ConsistencyLayers remain consistentConsistency inspection, conflict resolution procedure

The four principles form an organic whole: layer separation is the foundation, lower-layer constraint and upper-layer flexibility are requirements of two directions, and cross-layer consistency is an integrative requirement.

Conclusion Four: The Unique Positioning of the Protocol Stack

The protocol stack is a synthesis of hierarchy and network governance, with four unique characteristics:

CharacteristicDifference from HierarchyDifference from Network Governance
Functional layersNot power ranksNot a horizontal network
Lower-layer constraintNot superior commandNot negotiated constraint
Negotiated revisionNot unilateral decisionHas a stable foundation
RollbackableNot irreversibleHas a clear procedure

The protocol stack is particularly applicable to cross-subject, long-term, uncertainty, and plural-value governance scenarios.

Conclusion Five: The Applicable Conditions of the Protocol Stack

The applicability of the protocol stack depends on four dimensions:

DimensionApplicable ConditionInapplicable Condition
Foundational constraintsStable foundational constraints existLack of stable foundational constraints
Time spanLong-term governanceRapid decisions needed
Subject pluralityMultiple subjectsSingle-subject decision-making
UncertaintyDeep uncertaintyDeterministic problems

Interstellar civilization governance and global climate governance are highly applicable to the protocol stack methodology, while routine corporate operations are lowly applicable.

[1] The OSI reference model was formally published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in 1984, numbered ISO 7498. The model divides network communication into seven layers and has become an important reference framework for network protocol design.

[2] The TCP/IP protocol stack is the foundational protocol system of the Internet, developed by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in the 1970s. Unlike the seven-layer OSI model, TCP/IP adopts a four-layer model: network interface layer, network layer, transport layer, and application layer.

[3] The "end-to-end principle" (End-to-End Principle) is an important principle of network design, proposed by Saltzer, Reed, and Clark in 1984. The principle advocates placing complex functions at network endpoints rather than the network core, in order to maintain the simplicity and flexibility of the network.

[4] Research on hierarchy as an organizational form can be traced back to Max Weber's theory of bureaucracy. In Economy and Society, Weber systematically elaborated the characteristics of bureaucracy, including the hierarchical system, rule orientation, and professional division of labor.

[5] The concept of Network Governance arose in the 1990s, with representative scholars including R.A.W. Rhodes and Mark Bevir. Network governance emphasizes polycentricity, horizontal coordination, and negotiated decision-making.

[6] The concept of Adaptive Governance originates from complex adaptive systems theory and emphasizes governance through learning and adaptation under conditions of uncertainty. Representative scholars include Carl Folke and Brian Walker.

[7] The concept of Multi-level Governance was proposed by Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks in the 1990s, initially used to analyze European Union governance and later extended to broader governance research.

[8] The concept of Experimentalist Governance was proposed by Charles Sabel and Jonathan Zeitlin and emphasizes governance through experimentation, learning, and iteration.

[9] This chapter's exposition of the protocol stack methodology draws on the layered architecture design ideas of software engineering, in particular the principle of "Separation of Concerns."

[10] The concept of Rollbackability draws on the rollback mechanism in database transaction management and the version rollback function of software version control systems (such as Git).

Node NumberNode NameCore ConclusionLocation
16.1-AThe analogy basis of the protocol stackThe governance protocol stack draws on the layered design idea of the network protocol stack, but must handle special problems such as value judgments, subjecthood, and normativity§16.1.1
16.1-BThe five major characteristics of the protocol stackThe protocol stack has five core characteristics: layering, constraint propagation, revision difficulty gradient, interface standardization, and rollbackability§16.1.2
16.1-CThe five major advantages of the protocol stackThe protocol stack has five major advantages: unity of stability and flexibility, traceability, modular revision, fault tolerance, and auditability§16.1.3
16.2-APrinciple of Layer SeparationThe Principle of Layer Separation requires functional separation of each layer, defended by the three reasons of complexity management, specialization, and maintainability§16.2.1
16.2-BPrinciple of Lower-Layer ConstraintThe Principle of Lower-Layer Constraint requires that upper-layer rules must not violate lower-layer constraints, realized through the hierarchical constraint structure and the inspection procedure§16.2.2
16.2-CPrinciple of Upper-Layer FlexibilityThe Principle of Upper-Layer Flexibility requires maintaining flexibility under the premise of satisfying lower-layer constraints, realized through parametric design, exception clauses, and the negotiated revision procedure§16.2.3
16.2-DPrinciple of Cross-Layer ConsistencyThe Principle of Cross-Layer Consistency requires consistency among the layers, realized through the consistency inspection procedure and the conflict resolution mechanism§16.2.4
16.3-AComparison with HierarchyThe key differences between the protocol stack and hierarchy lie in the direction of constraint, the source of flexibility, and the revision mechanism§16.3.1
16.3-BComparison with Network GovernanceThe key differences between the protocol stack and network governance lie in the structure type, the source of constraint, and the source of stability§16.3.2
16.3-CThe unique positioning of the protocol stackThe protocol stack is a synthesis of hierarchy and network governance, with four unique characteristics: functional layers, lower-layer constraint, negotiated revision, and rollbackability§16.3.3
16.4-AApplicable situationsThe protocol stack applies to situations in which stable foundational constraints exist, long-term stability is needed, multiple subjects are involved, and deep uncertainty exists§16.4.1
16.4-BInapplicable situationsThe protocol stack does not apply to situations lacking stable foundational constraints, requiring rapid decisions, involving single-subject decision-making, or involving deterministic problems§16.4.2
16.4-CApplicability assessmentApplicability assessment proceeds through a four-dimensional scoring procedure; interstellar civilization governance and global climate governance are highly applicable§16.4.3

Footnotes

Chapter 16 Footnotes

[1] The OSI reference model was formally published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in 1984 as ISO 7498. The model divides network communication into seven layers and has become an important reference framework for network protocol design.

[2] The TCP/IP protocol stack is the foundational protocol suite of the Internet, developed by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in the 1970s. Unlike the seven-layer OSI model, TCP/IP adopts a four-layer model: the network interface layer, the network layer, the transport layer, and the application layer.

[3] The "End-to-End Principle" is an important principle of network design, proposed by Saltzer, Reed, and Clark in 1984. The principle advocates placing complex functions at the network endpoints rather than in the network core, so as to preserve the simplicity and flexibility of the network.

[4] The study of hierarchy as a form of organization can be traced back to Max Weber's theory of bureaucracy. In Economy and Society, Weber systematically set out the characteristics of bureaucracy, including hierarchy, rule orientation, and professional division of labor.

[5] The concept of network governance emerged in the 1990s, with representative scholars including R.A.W. Rhodes and Mark Bevir. Network governance emphasizes polycentricity, horizontal coordination, and negotiated decision-making.

[6] The concept of adaptive governance derives from complex adaptive systems theory and emphasizes governance through learning and adaptation under conditions of uncertainty. Representative scholars include Carl Folke and Brian Walker.

[7] The concept of multi-level governance was proposed by Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks in the 1990s, initially for the analysis of European Union governance and later extended to governance research more broadly.

[8] The concept of experimentalist governance was proposed by Charles Sabel and Jonathan Zeitlin and emphasizes governance through experimentation, learning, and iteration.

[9] The exposition of the protocol stack methodology in this chapter draws on the ideas of layered architecture design in software engineering, in particular the principle of "Separation of Concerns."

[10] The concept of rollbackability draws on the rollback mechanisms of database transaction management and the version-reversion functions of software version control systems (such as Git).

The Protocol-Stack Architecture: Layers L₀–L₄Chapter 17

Detailed Protocol Stack Architecture: Layers L₀-L₄

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 16 established the theoretical foundation of the protocol stack methodology, clarifying the concept, characteristics, design principles, and applicable conditions of the protocol stack. The task of this chapter is to concretize this methodological framework, detailing the content specifications, revision procedures, and inter-layer relations of each layer of the protocol stack.

The five layers of the protocol stack (L₀-L₄) constitute the complete governance architecture of this work from physical constraints to operating procedures. Each layer has its specific functional positioning, content specification, and revision conditions. This chapter will unfold this architecture layer by layer, transforming the protocol stack from an abstract methodology into an operable institutional framework.

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The core task of this chapter is to transform the New Three Views from a theoretical framework into an institutional architecture. The position and role of the New Three Views in the protocol stack are as follows:

$$\text{the New Three Views} \xrightarrow{\text{institutionalization}} L_1 \xrightarrow{\text{constraint}} L_2, L_3, L_4$$

Specifically:

  • NC (the New Cosmological View) → institutionalization of the cosmological view at the L₁ layer → constrains the Principle of Recursive Freedom at the L₂ layer
  • NL (the New View of Life) → institutionalization of the view of life at the L₁ layer → constrains the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility at the L₂ layer
  • NK (the New View of Cognition) → institutionalization of the view of cognition at the L₁ layer → constrains the Principle of Reversibility at the L₂ layer

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer the following fundamental questions:

Core Question One: What physical constraints does the L₀ layer contain? Why are these constraints non-revisable? Core Question Two: How are the New Three Views institutionalized at the L₁ layer? What conditions does revision of the L₁ layer require? Core Question Three: How are the three normative principles institutionalized at the L₂ layer? How are prohibited red lines set? Core Question Four: What is the concrete content of the L₃ and L₄ layers? How is flexible revision achieved? Core Question Five: How is consistency maintained among the layers? How are conflicts resolved?

VI. Boundary Statement

All content of this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Conceptual prototype stage: the protocol stack architecture designed in this chapter is at the TRL 2 stage, applicable to academic research and thought experiments
  2. Open revision: the protocol stack architecture itself is revisable, following its own versioning principle
  3. Non-mandatory: before the indicator system matures, the content of this chapter should not serve as a mandatory basis for decision-making
  4. Cultural sensitivity: institutional design needs to consider applicability across different cultural backgrounds

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • If the reader is concerned with the physical foundations, it is suggested to focus on §17.1
  • If the reader is concerned with the institutionalization of the New Three Views, it is suggested to focus on §17.2
  • If the reader is concerned with the operationalization of normative principles, it is suggested to focus on §17.3
  • If the reader is concerned with concrete institutional design, it is suggested to focus on §17.4 and §17.5
  • If the reader is concerned with systemic consistency, it is suggested to focus on §17.6

§17.1 The L₀ Layer: The Physical Constraint Layer

§17.1.1 Thermodynamic Constraints

I. Positioning of the L₀ Layer

The L₀ layer is the lowest layer of the protocol stack, containing inviolable physical laws and natural regularities. These constraints are not man-made rules but the way the universe itself operates. Any governance framework must operate within these constraints, otherwise it will face physical impossibility.

Definition 17.1.1 (L₀ Layer)

The L₀ layer is the physical constraint layer of the protocol stack, containing all physical laws and natural regularities that governance frameworks must observe.

Formal statement:

$$L_0 = \{c \mid c \text{ is a physical law or natural constraint}\}$$

Characteristics of the L₀ layer:

CharacteristicDescriptionFormal Statement
UniversalityApplies to all physical systems$\forall s \in \text{PhysicalSystems}: s \models L_0$
InviolabilityCannot be violated by any means$\neg\exists a: a \vdash \neg L_0$
Non-revisabilityDoes not change by human will$\text{Revision}(L_0) = \emptyset$

II. The First Law of Thermodynamics: Conservation of Energy

Constraint 17.1.1 (Conservation of Energy)

In any isolated system, energy can neither be created nor destroyed, but can only be transformed from one form to another.

Formal statement:

$$\Delta U = Q - W$$

where $U$ is the internal energy of the system, $Q$ is the heat absorbed by the system, and $W$ is the work done by the system on its surroundings.

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Energy cannot arise from nothingAny civilizational activity requires energy input
Energy cannot vanish into nothingEnergy use necessarily produces consequences
Energy transformation involves lossEfficiency is always less than 100%

III. The Second Law of Thermodynamics: The Principle of Entropy Increase

Constraint 17.1.2 (Principle of Entropy Increase)

In any isolated system, entropy never decreases. Spontaneous processes always proceed in the direction of increasing entropy.

Formal statement:

$$\Delta S_{\text{universe}} \geq 0$$

For reversible processes the equality holds; for irreversible processes it is strictly greater than zero.

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Entropy spontaneously increasesThe maintenance of order requires continuous energy input
Irreversible processes generate entropyMany actions have irreversible consequences
Negentropy has a costThe maintenance of complexity requires resource input

Relation between the second law of thermodynamics and the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility:

The second law of thermodynamics is the physical foundation of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP). Life and civilization, as negentropic organizations, depend for their persistence on obtaining a negentropy flow from the environment.

$$\text{NL-2}(\text{negentropic organization}) \xleftarrow{\text{physical foundation}} \text{the second law of thermodynamics}$$

IV. The Third Law of Thermodynamics: Absolute Zero Is Unattainable

Constraint 17.1.3 (Absolute Zero Is Unattainable)

It is impossible to cool a system to absolute zero through a finite number of steps.

Formal statement:

$$\lim_{T \to 0} S = S_0$$

where $S_0$ is the entropy of the system at absolute zero; for a perfect crystal $S_0 = 0$.

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
The perfect state is unattainableAny system has inherent imperfection
The limiting state requires infinite resourcesThe cost of pursuing extreme goals tends to infinity

§17.1.2 Information-Theoretic Constraints

I. Basic Constraints of Information Theory

Information theory reveals the fundamental limits of information processing, and these limits are binding on any intelligent system (including governance systems).

Constraint 17.1.4 (Non-negativity of Information Entropy)

Information entropy is always non-negative, and is zero only in the determinate case.

Formal statement:

$$H(X) = -\sum_{i} p_i \log p_i \geq 0$$

The equality holds if and only if there exists some $i$ such that $p_i = 1$.

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Uncertainty cannot be eliminatedFully determinate prediction is impossible
Information acquisition has a costReducing uncertainty requires resource input

Constraint 17.1.5 (Channel Capacity Limit)

Any channel has a maximum transmission rate; exceeding this rate will inevitably produce errors.

Formal statement:

$$C = \max_{p(x)} I(X; Y)$$

where $C$ is the channel capacity and $I(X; Y)$ is the mutual information.

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Communication rate has an upper limitInformation transmission has physical limits
Transmission above capacity produces errorsInformation overload degrades decision quality

Constraint 17.1.6 (Data Processing Inequality)

Data processing cannot increase the amount of information.

Formal statement:

$$I(X; Y) \geq I(X; Z) \text{ if } X \to Y \to Z$$

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Processing does not increase informationDecision quality is limited by the quality of the original information
Information is lost in transmissionMulti-layer decision-making involves information decay

II. Relation between Information-Theoretic Constraints and the New View of Cognition

Information-theoretic constraints are the physical foundation of the New View of Cognition (NK), in particular the support for NK-3 (deep uncertainty).

$$\text{NK-3}(\text{deep uncertainty}) \xleftarrow{\text{physical foundation}} \text{information-theoretic constraints}$$

Landauer's Principle: The Thermodynamic Cost of Information Erasure

Constraint 17.1.7 (Landauer's Principle)

Erasing one bit of information generates at least $k_B T \ln 2$ of heat.

Formal statement:

$$Q_{\min} = k_B T \ln 2 \approx 2.87 \times 10^{-21} \text{ J at } T = 300K$$

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Information erasure has a costForgetting and resetting are not free
Computation has a thermodynamic costInformation processing consumes energy

§17.1.3 Causal Structure Constraints

I. Basic Constraints of Causation

Causal structure is the basic organizational mode of the universe, and any governance framework must respect the basic constraints of causation.

Constraint 17.1.8 (The Law of Causality)

A cause precedes its effect in time, and an effect cannot influence its cause.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Cause}(A, B) \Rightarrow t_A < t_B$$

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Causation has temporal orderDecisions must be based on available information
Effects cannot change causesThe past cannot be changed

Constraint 17.1.9 (The Speed-of-Light Limit)

The speed of information transmission cannot exceed the speed of light.

Formal statement:

$$v_{\text{signal}} \leq c$$

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Information transmission has delayInterstellar communication involves significant time lag
Instantaneous coordination is impossibleDistributed decision-making is necessary

Impact of the speed-of-light limit on interstellar governance:

Earth-Mars (closest)3 minutes6 minutesSignificant delay
Earth-Mars (farthest)22 minutes44 minutesReal-time coordination difficult
Nearest star4.2 years8.4 yearsReal-time coordination impossible

Constraint 17.1.10 (Causal Closure)

The evolution of physical systems is determined by physical causes, with no supernatural intervention.

Formal statement:

$$\forall e \in \text{PhysicalEvents}: \exists c \in \text{PhysicalCauses}: \text{Cause}(c, e)$$

Constraints on governance:

Constraint ContentGovernance Implication
Physical causal closureGovernance must be realized through physical means
No supernatural interventionOne cannot rely on miracles or supernatural forces

II. Relation between Causal Structure Constraints and the New Cosmological View

Causal structure constraints are the physical foundation of the New Cosmological View (NC), in particular the support for NC-2 (process ontology).

$$\text{NC-2}(\text{process ontology}) \xleftarrow{\text{physical foundation}} \text{causal structure constraints}$$

§17.1.4 Non-Revisability of the L₀ Layer

I. Argument for Non-Revisability

The non-revisability of the L₀ layer is the cornerstone of protocol stack design. This non-revisability is not man-made but derives from the essential characteristics of physical laws.

Argument One: The Universality of Physical Laws

Physical laws apply to all physical systems and do not change with the observer, place, or time.

$$\forall s, t, l: \text{PhysicalLaw}(L) \Rightarrow s \models L \text{ at } t \text{ in } l$$

Argument Two: The Inviolability of Physical Laws

Physical laws cannot be violated by any means. Any phenomenon alleged to violate a physical law is either a measurement error, or a misunderstanding of the law, or the discovery of new physics (in which case the old law is revised into an approximation of the new law).

$$\neg\exists a: a \vdash \neg L_0$$

Argument Three: The Objectivity of Physical Laws

Physical laws do not depend on human will, belief, or decision. Humans can discover physical laws but cannot create or modify them.

$$L_0 \perp \text{HumanWill}$$

II. The Boundary of Non-Revisability

Although the L₀ layer is non-revisable, our knowledge of the L₀ layer is revisable.

Definition 17.1.2 (The Epistemological Boundary of the L₀ Layer)

The L₀ layer itself is non-revisable, but our statement of the L₀ layer ($\hat{L}_0$) is revisable.

$$L_0 \text{ (ontology)} \neq \hat{L}_0 \text{ (epistemology)}$$

Table 17.2 The ontological-epistemological distinction of the L₀ layer

AspectContentRevisability
OntologyPhysical laws themselvesNon-revisable
EpistemologyOur statement of physical lawsRevisable (with scientific progress)

III. Scientific Revolutions and the Revision of the L₀ Layer Statement

Scientific revolutions in history have led to revisions of the statement of physical laws:

Scientific RevolutionOld StatementNew StatementRelation
Relativity revolutionNewtonian mechanicsRelativistic mechanicsLow-speed approximation
Quantum revolutionClassical mechanicsQuantum mechanicsMacroscopic approximation
Thermodynamic revolutionCaloric theoryStatistical mechanicsParadigm replacement

IV. Procedure for Revising the L₀ Layer Statement

When a major change in scientific consensus occurs, the statement of the L₀ layer needs to be revised accordingly.

PROCEDURE L0StatementRevision(new_scientific_consensus)

// Step 1: verify scientific consensus IF NOT VerifyScientificConsensus(new_scientific_consensus) THEN RETURN REJECT("Scientific consensus not established") END IF

// Step 2: assess impact impact = AssessImpactOnUpperLayers(new_scientific_consensus)

// Step 3: update the L₀ statement L0_statement_new = UpdateL0Statement(new_scientific_consensus)

// Step 4: cascade update the upper layers IF impact.requires_upper_layer_revision THEN CascadeRevision(L0_statement_new) END IF

// Step 5: record the change RecordRevision(L0_statement_old, L0_statement_new, justification)

RETURN SUCCESS

END PROCEDURE

§17.2 The L₁ Layer: The Ontological-Epistemological Layer

§17.2.1 Institutionalization of the New Cosmological View

I. Positioning of the L₁ Layer

The L₁ layer is the ontological-epistemological framework layer of the protocol stack, containing the core propositions of the New Three Views. The L₁ layer is based on the physical constraints of the L₀ layer, but contains interpretive and conceptual components. The L₁ layer provides the ontological and epistemological foundation for the normative principles of the L₂ layer.

Definition 17.2.1 (L₁ Layer)

The L₁ layer is the ontological-epistemological framework layer of the protocol stack, containing the core propositions of the New Three Views (the New Cosmological View, the New View of Life, the New View of Cognition).

Formal statement:

$$L_1 = \text{NC} \cup \text{NL} \cup \text{NK}$$

where NC is the set of propositions of the New Cosmological View, NL is the set of propositions of the New View of Life, and NK is the set of propositions of the New View of Cognition.

II. Core Propositions of the New Cosmological View

The New Cosmological View contains three core propositions:

Proposition NC-1 (Relational Ontology)

The basic constituent unit of reality is not independently existing entities but the relations between entities.

Formal statement:

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{U}: \text{Properties}(x) = f(\text{Relations}(x))$$

Proposition NC-2 (Process Ontology)

The basic mode of existence of reality is not static states but dynamic processes.

Formal statement:

$$\forall x \in \mathcal{U}: \text{State}(x, t) = g(\text{Process}(x, t-\Delta t, t))$$

Proposition NC-3 (Participatory Universe)

The observer is not a bystander of the universe but a participant in the universe's evolution.

Formal statement:

$$\forall o \in \mathcal{O}, \exists e \in \mathcal{E}: \text{Observe}(o, e) \Rightarrow \text{Modify}(o, e)$$

III. Institutionalization of the New Cosmological View

The institutionalization of the New Cosmological View means transforming NC-1, NC-2, and NC-3 into operative principles in the governance framework.

Table 17.4 Institutionalization of the New Cosmological View

PropositionInstitutionalized ContentOperative Principle
NC-1Relational assessmentWhen assessing an action, the influence of the relational network must be considered
NC-2Processual assessmentWhen assessing an action, dynamic processes and long-term evolution must be considered
NC-3Participative assessmentWhen assessing an action, the feedback effects of observation and intervention must be considered

Institutionalization of NC-1: Relational Assessment

Institutional Rule 17.2.1 (Relational Assessment Rule)

Any major decision must undergo a relational assessment, identifying the decision's influence on the relational network.

Assessment procedure:

PROCEDURE RelationalAssessment(decision)

// Step 1: identify related entities entities = IdentifyRelatedEntities(decision)

// Step 2: map the relational network relation_network = MapRelationNetwork(entities)

// Step 3: assess relational impacts FOR EACH relation IN relation_network: impact = AssessRelationImpact(decision, relation) RecordImpact(relation, impact) END FOR

// Step 4: comprehensive assessment overall_impact = AggregateRelationalImpacts()

RETURN overall_impact

END PROCEDURE

Institutionalization of NC-2: Processual Assessment

Institutional Rule 17.2.2 (Processual Assessment Rule)

Any major decision must undergo a processual assessment, considering the decision's dynamic evolution and long-term consequences.

Assessment procedure:

PROCEDURE ProcessualAssessment(decision)

// Step 1: define time horizons time_horizons = [short_term, medium_term, long_term]

// Step 2: simulate dynamic evolution FOR EACH horizon IN time_horizons: trajectory = SimulateEvolution(decision, horizon) RecordTrajectory(horizon, trajectory) END FOR

// Step 3: identify critical turning points critical_points = IdentifyCriticalPoints(trajectories)

// Step 4: assess long-term consequences long_term_consequences = AssessLongTermConsequences(trajectories)

RETURN (trajectories, critical_points, long_term_consequences)

END PROCEDURE

Institutionalization of NC-3: Participative Assessment

Institutional Rule 17.2.3 (Participative Assessment Rule)

Any major decision must undergo a participative assessment, considering the feedback effects of the decision-maker's observation and intervention on the system.

Assessment procedure:

PROCEDURE ParticipativeAssessment(decision, decision_maker)

// Step 1: identify feedback loops feedback_loops = IdentifyFeedbackLoops(decision, decision_maker)

// Step 2: assess observation effects observation_effects = AssessObservationEffects(decision_maker)

// Step 3: assess intervention effects intervention_effects = AssessInterventionEffects(decision)

// Step 4: comprehensive feedback assessment overall_feedback = IntegrateFeedbackEffects( feedback_loops, observation_effects, intervention_effects )

RETURN overall_feedback

END PROCEDURE

§17.2.2 Institutionalization of the New View of Life

I. Core Propositions of the New View of Life

The New View of Life contains three core propositions:

Proposition NL-1 (Cross-Substrate Life)

The essence of life is functional and does not depend on a specific material substrate.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Life}(x) \Leftrightarrow [\text{Metabolism}(x) \land \text{SelfMaintenance}(x) \land \text{Information}(x)]$$

Proposition NL-2 (Negentropic Organization)

Life is a negentropic process, depending on the acquisition of a negentropy flow to maintain ordered structure.

Formal statement:

$$\forall l \in \mathcal{L}: \text{Persist}(l) \Rightarrow \dot{N}(l) > 0$$

where $\dot{N}(l)$ is the negentropy flow of the living being $l$.

Proposition NL-3 (Continuum of Consciousness)

Consciousness is not a binary presence or absence but a graded continuum.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Consciousness}: \mathcal{E} \to [0, 1]$$

II. Institutionalization of the New View of Life

Table 17.5 Institutionalization of the New View of Life

PropositionInstitutionalized ContentOperative Principle
NL-1Cross-substrate subjecthoodSubjecthood is not limited to carbon-based life
NL-2Negentropy responsibility frameworkSubjects bear a maintenance responsibility for negentropy sources
NL-3Consciousness degree assessmentThe weight of moral consideration correlates with the degree of consciousness

Institutionalization of NL-1: Cross-Substrate Subjecthood

Institutional Rule 17.2.4 (Cross-Substrate Subjecthood Rule)

The recognition of subjecthood is not based on the material substrate but on functional characteristics.

Subjecthood recognition procedure:

PROCEDURE SubjectStatusRecognition(entity)

// Step 1: assess metabolic function metabolism_score = AssessMetabolism(entity)

// Step 2: assess self-maintenance function self_maintenance_score = AssessSelfMaintenance(entity)

// Step 3: assess information-processing function information_score = AssessInformationProcessing(entity)

// Step 4: comprehensive assessment IF metabolism_score >= threshold_m AND self_maintenance_score >= threshold_s AND information_score >= threshold_i THEN RETURN SUBJECT_STATUS_GRANTED ELSE RETURN SUBJECT_STATUS_PENDING END IF

END PROCEDURE

Institutionalization of NL-2: Negentropy Responsibility Framework

Institutional Rule 17.2.5 (Negentropy Responsibility Framework Rule)

All entities with subjecthood bear a maintenance responsibility for negentropy sources; the degree of responsibility is related to capability, benefit, and impact.

Responsibility allocation formula:

$$\text{NRP}_i = \alpha \cdot \text{Capability}_i + \beta \cdot \text{Benefit}_i + \gamma \cdot \text{Impact}_i + \text{Baseline}$$

where $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$, and Baseline is the minimum responsibility of all subjects.

Institutionalization of NL-3: Consciousness Degree Assessment

Institutional Rule 17.2.6 (Consciousness Degree Assessment Rule)

The weight of moral consideration should correlate with the degree of consciousness, assessed through the UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale).

III. Relation between the Degree of Consciousness and Moral Weight:

$$\text{MoralWeight}(e) = f(\text{UCS}(e))$$

where $f$ is a monotonically increasing function, whose specific form will be discussed in detail in Chapter 7.

§17.2.3 Institutionalization of the New View of Cognition

I. Core Propositions of the New View of Cognition

The New View of Cognition contains four core propositions:

Proposition NK-1 (Participatory Cognition)

Cognition is not a passive reflection of the external world but an active interaction between the subject and the world.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Know}(s, p) \Rightarrow \text{Participate}(s, p)$$

Proposition NK-2 (Social Knowledge)

Knowledge is a social achievement, depending on social validation and community recognition.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Knowledge}(p) \Rightarrow \text{SocialValidation}(p)$$

Proposition NK-3 (Deep Uncertainty)

In complex systems, fundamental cognitive limits exist; certain uncertainties cannot be eliminated by more information.

Formal statement:

$$\exists \mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{U}: \forall I: \text{Uncertainty}(\mathcal{S} | I) > \epsilon$$

Proposition NK-4 (Negotiability of Knowledge)

Cognitive standards and the boundaries of knowledge are negotiable rather than fixed.

Formal statement:

$$\forall \text{standard} \in \mathcal{S}: \text{Negotiable}(\text{standard})$$

II. Institutionalization of the New View of Cognition

Table 17.6 Institutionalization of the New View of Cognition

PropositionInstitutionalized ContentOperative Principle
NK-1Participatory decision-makingThe decision process should include the participation of stakeholders
NK-2Social validation procedureMajor knowledge claims require social validation
NK-3Acknowledgment of uncertaintyDecisions must explicitly acknowledge and handle deep uncertainty
NK-4Negotiated revision mechanismCognitive standards and rules can be revised through negotiation

(i) Institutionalization of NK-1: Participatory Decision-Making

Institutional Rule 17.2.7 (Participatory Decision-Making Rule)

Major decisions should include the participation of stakeholders; the degree of participation correlates with the scope of the decision's impact.

Grading of the degree of participation:

Scope of Decision ImpactDegree of ParticipationMode of Participation
Local impactConsultationSolicitation of opinions
Regional impactNegotiationMulti-party negotiation
Global impactCo-decisionJoint decision-making
Interstellar impactFull co-decisionFull participation

(ii) Institutionalization of NK-2: Social Validation Procedure

Institutional Rule 17.2.8 (Social Validation Procedure Rule)

Major knowledge claims (in particular knowledge claims that influence governance decisions) require a social validation procedure.

Social validation procedure:

PROCEDURE SocialValidation(knowledge_claim)

// Step 1: expert review expert_review = ExpertReview(knowledge_claim)

// Step 2: peer review peer_review = PeerReview(knowledge_claim)

// Step 3: public discussion public_discussion = PublicDiscussion(knowledge_claim)

// Step 4: comprehensive assessment validation_result = IntegrateValidation( expert_review, peer_review, public_discussion )

RETURN validation_result

END PROCEDURE

(iii) Institutionalization of NK-3: Acknowledgment of Uncertainty

Institutional Rule 17.2.9 (Acknowledgment of Uncertainty Rule)

All major decisions must explicitly acknowledge and handle deep uncertainty, and must not feign certainty.

Uncertainty handling procedure:

PROCEDURE UncertaintyAcknowledgment(decision)

// Step 1: identify sources of uncertainty uncertainty_sources = IdentifyUncertaintySources(decision)

// Step 2: classify uncertainties FOR EACH source IN uncertainty_sources: IF IsReducible(source) THEN reducible_uncertainties.add(source) ELSE irreducible_uncertainties.add(source) END IF END FOR

// Step 3: formulate response strategies FOR EACH uncertainty IN irreducible_uncertainties: strategy = DevelopRobustStrategy(uncertainty) RecordStrategy(uncertainty, strategy) END FOR

// Step 4: record the uncertainty statement uncertainty_statement = GenerateUncertaintyStatement( reducible_uncertainties, irreducible_uncertainties, strategies )

RETURN uncertainty_statement

END PROCEDURE

(iv) Institutionalization of NK-4: Negotiated Revision Mechanism

Institutional Rule 17.2.10 (Negotiated Revision Mechanism Rule)

Cognitive standards and governance rules can be revised through a negotiation procedure; revision must satisfy the requirement of procedural legitimacy.

Negotiated revision procedure:

PROCEDURE NegotiatedRevision(rule, layer)

// Step 1: proposal proposal = SubmitRevisionProposal(rule)

// Step 2: identification of stakeholders stakeholders = IdentifyStakeholders(rule)

// Step 3: negotiation consensus = Negotiate(proposal, stakeholders)

// Step 4: constraint check IF NOT ConstraintCheck(consensus, layer) THEN RETURN ReviseProposal(consensus) END IF

// Step 5: implementation ImplementRevision(consensus)

RETURN SUCCESS

END PROCEDURE

§17.2.4 Revision Procedure of the L₁ Layer

I. Particularity of L₁ Layer Revision

Revision of the L₁ layer is more possible than that of the L₀ layer but still requires an extremely strict procedure. Revision of the L₁ layer may trigger cascading revisions of the L₂, L₃, and L₄ layers.

I. Trigger Conditions for Revision

Revision of the L₁ layer may be triggered by the following situations:

Trigger ConditionDescriptionExample
Change in the L₀ layerRevision of the L₀ layer statement necessitates adjustment of the L₁ layerNew physical discoveries change the understanding of the universe
Internal contradictionA contradiction is found among L₁ layer propositionsAn NC proposition conflicts with an NL proposition
Empirical refutationEmpirical evidence is inconsistent with L₁ layer propositionsDiscovery that consciousness is indeed binary
Conceptual improvementA better conceptual framework emergesA more precise statement of relational ontology

II. Revision Procedure

PROCEDURE L1Revision(revision_proposal)

// Step 1: verification of trigger conditions trigger = ValidateTriggerCondition(revision_proposal) IF trigger == INVALID THEN RETURN REJECT("Invalid trigger condition") END IF

// Step 2: L₀ consistency check IF NOT L0ConsistencyCheck(revision_proposal) THEN RETURN REJECT("Inconsistent with L0") END IF

// Step 3: internal consistency check IF NOT InternalConsistencyCheck(revision_proposal) THEN RETURN REJECT("Internal inconsistency") END IF

// Step 4: impact assessment impact = AssessImpactOnUpperLayers(revision_proposal)

// Step 5: expert deliberation expert_review = ConveneExpertPanel(revision_proposal) IF expert_review.recommendation != APPROVE THEN RETURN REJECT(expert_review.reason) END IF

// Step 6: broad consultation consensus = BroadConsultation(revision_proposal, impact) IF consensus.level < SUPERMAJORITY THEN RETURN REJECT("Insufficient consensus") END IF

// Step 7: implement the revision ImplementL1Revision(revision_proposal)

// Step 8: cascade update CascadeRevisionToUpperLayers(revision_proposal, impact)

// Step 9: record RecordL1Revision(revision_proposal, justification)

RETURN SUCCESS

END PROCEDURE
