§17.3 The L₂ Layer: The Normative Principle Layer

§17.3.1 Institutionalization of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

I. Positioning of the L₂ Layer

The L₂ layer is the normative principle layer of the protocol stack, containing the core normative principles derived from the L₁ layer. The principles of the L₂ layer are normative, prescribing "how things ought to be" rather than merely describing "what is."

Definition 17.3.1 (L₂ Layer)

The L₂ layer is the normative principle layer of the protocol stack, containing the Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP), the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP), the Principle of Reversibility (REV), and the prohibited red lines (FRL).

Formal statement:

$$L_2 = \{\text{RFP}, \text{NRP}, \text{REV}, \text{FRL}\}$$

II. Content of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

Principle 17.3.1 (Principle of Recursive Freedom, RFP)

Action should keep the space of possibilities open and should not irreversibly compress the space of future options.

Formal statement:

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}: \text{RFD}(a) \geq 0$$

where RFD is the Recursive Freedom Degree, defined as:

$$\text{RFD}(a) = \frac{|\mathcal{P}(s_{t+1})| - |\mathcal{P}(s_t)|}{|\mathcal{P}(s_t)|}$$

$\mathcal{P}(s)$ is the space of possibilities under state $s$.

III. Institutionalization of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

Institutional Rule 17.3.1 (Recursive Freedom Assessment Rule)

All major decisions must undergo a Recursive Freedom Degree assessment; decisions with an RFD below the threshold require special deliberation.

Assessment procedure:

PROCEDURE RFDAssessment(decision)

// Step 1: define the current space of possibilities current_possibility_space = DefinePossibilitySpace(current_state)

// Step 2: simulate the space of possibilities after the decision future_possibility_space = SimulatePossibilitySpace(decision)

// Step 3: compute the RFD rfd = (Size(future_possibility_space) - Size(current_possibility_space)) / Size(current_possibility_space)

// Step 4: threshold check IF rfd < RFD_THRESHOLD THEN RETURN (rfd, REQUIRES_SPECIAL_REVIEW) ELSE RETURN (rfd, PASSED) END IF

END PROCEDURE

IV. Operationalization Indicators of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

The Principle of Recursive Freedom is operationalized through the RFD indicator; the computation of RFD involves the following dimensions:

DimensionDescriptionWeight
Diversity of choiceThe number of future available actions0.3
Path reachabilityThe reachability of future states0.3
Degree of reversibilityThe degree of reversibility of the decision0.2
Temporal depthThe time span of the impact0.2

§17.3.2 Institutionalization of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

I. Content of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

Principle 17.3.2 (Principle of Negentropy Responsibility, NRP)

Subjects should maintain negentropy sources and avoid externalizing entropy costs onto other subjects or future generations.

Formal statement:

$$\forall a \in \mathcal{A}: \text{EntropyExternalization}(a) \leq \theta$$

where $\theta$ is the permissible threshold of entropy externalization.

II. Institutionalization of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

Institutional Rule 17.3.2 (Negentropy Responsibility Assessment Rule)

All major decisions must undergo a negentropy impact assessment; decisions whose entropy externalization exceeds the threshold require compensation or rejection.

Assessment procedure:

PROCEDURE NRPAssessment(decision)

// Step 1: identify negentropy sources negentropy_sources = IdentifyNegentropySources(decision)

// Step 2: assess negentropy consumption negentropy_consumption = AssessNegentropyConsumption(decision)

// Step 3: assess entropy externalization entropy_externalization = AssessEntropyExternalization(decision)

// Step 4: identify affected subjects affected_subjects = IdentifyAffectedSubjects(decision)

// Step 5: threshold check IF entropy_externalization > NRP_THRESHOLD THEN compensation_required = CalculateCompensation(entropy_externalization) RETURN (entropy_externalization, REQUIRES_COMPENSATION, compensation_required) ELSE RETURN (entropy_externalization, PASSED) END IF

END PROCEDURE

III. Allocation Framework of Negentropy Responsibility

The allocation of negentropy responsibility among different subjects follows the following principles:

Table 17.8 Principles of negentropy responsibility allocation

PrincipleDescriptionWeight
Capability principleThe greater the capability, the greater the responsibility0.35
Benefit principleThe greater the benefit, the greater the responsibility0.30
Causal principleThe greater the impact caused, the greater the responsibility0.25
Baseline principleAll subjects bear a minimum responsibility0.10

Responsibility allocation formula:

$$\text{NRP}_i = 0.35 \cdot \text{Cap}_i + 0.30 \cdot \text{Ben}_i + 0.25 \cdot \text{Imp}_i + 0.10 \cdot \text{Base}$$

where:

  • $\text{Cap}_i$ is the capability index of subject $i$ (normalized)
  • $\text{Ben}_i$ is the benefit index of subject $i$ (normalized)
  • $\text{Imp}_i$ is the impact index of subject $i$ (normalized)
  • $\text{Base}$ is the baseline responsibility (a constant)

IV. Compensation Mechanism of Negentropy Responsibility

When a decision causes entropy externalization to exceed the threshold, a compensation mechanism needs to be initiated:

PROCEDURE EntropyCompensation(decision, externalization)

// Step 1: compute the compensation amount compensation_amount = CalculateCompensationAmount(externalization)

// Step 2: identify compensation modes compensation_options = [ NEGENTROPY_RESTORATION, // negentropy restoration ALTERNATIVE_PROVISION, // alternative provision MONETARY_COMPENSATION, // monetary compensation FUTURE_COMMITMENT // future commitment ]

// Step 3: select the compensation mode selected_option = SelectCompensationOption( compensation_options, affected_subjects, feasibility )

// Step 4: execute the compensation ExecuteCompensation(selected_option, compensation_amount)

// Step 5: verify the compensation verification = VerifyCompensation(selected_option, compensation_amount)

RETURN verification

END PROCEDURE

§17.3.3 Institutionalization of the Principle of Reversibility

I. Content of the Principle of Reversibility

Principle 17.3.3 (Principle of Reversibility, REV)

Other things being equal, actions with higher reversibility should be preferred; when an action produces negative consequences, it should be rolled back as far as possible.

Formal statement:

$$\forall a_1, a_2 \in \mathcal{A}: [\text{Rev}(a_1) > \text{Rev}(a_2) \land \text{OtherEqual}(a_1, a_2)] \Rightarrow a_1 \succ a_2$$

where $\text{Rev}(a)$ is the reversibility index of action $a$.

II. Institutionalization of the Principle of Reversibility

Institutional Rule 17.3.3 (Reversibility Assessment Rule)

All major decisions must undergo a reversibility assessment; decisions of low reversibility require a stricter deliberation procedure.

Assessment procedure:

PROCEDURE ReversibilityAssessment(decision)

// Step 1: assess physical reversibility physical_reversibility = AssessPhysicalReversibility(decision)

// Step 2: assess technical reversibility technical_reversibility = AssessTechnicalReversibility(decision)

// Step 3: assess social reversibility social_reversibility = AssessSocialReversibility(decision)

// Step 4: composite reversibility index reversibility_index = AggregateReversibility( physical_reversibility, technical_reversibility, social_reversibility )

// Step 5: graded handling IF reversibility_index < LOW_THRESHOLD THEN RETURN (reversibility_index, REQUIRES_HIGHEST_SCRUTINY) ELSE IF reversibility_index < MEDIUM_THRESHOLD THEN RETURN (reversibility_index, REQUIRES_ENHANCED_SCRUTINY) ELSE RETURN (reversibility_index, STANDARD_PROCEDURE) END IF

END PROCEDURE

III. The Three Dimensions of Reversibility

Table 17.9 The three dimensions of reversibility

DimensionDescriptionAssessment Standard
Physical reversibilityWhether the physical state can be restoredThermodynamic reversibility, conservation of matter
Technical reversibilityWhether restoration can be achieved technicallyCurrent technical capacity, expected future technology
Social reversibilityWhether the social state can be restoredInstitutional adjustability, reconstructability of consensus

Computation of the reversibility index:

$$\text{Rev}(a) = w_p \cdot \text{Rev}_p(a) + w_t \cdot \text{Rev}_t(a) + w_s \cdot \text{Rev}_s(a)$$

where $w_p + w_t + w_s = 1$; the default weights are $w_p = 0.4, w_t = 0.3, w_s = 0.3$.

IV. The Obligation to Roll Back

The Principle of Reversibility includes an obligation to roll back: when an action produces negative consequences, the actor is obliged to roll back as far as possible.

Institutional Rule 17.3.4 (Rollback Obligation Rule)

When a decision produces significantly negative consequences, the decision-maker is obliged to initiate a rollback procedure.

Rollback procedure:

PROCEDURE RollbackProcedure(decision, negative_consequences)

// Step 1: assess rollback feasibility rollback_feasibility = AssessRollbackFeasibility(decision)

// Step 2: assess rollback cost rollback_cost = AssessRollbackCost(decision)

// Step 3: assess rollback benefit rollback_benefit = AssessRollbackBenefit(negative_consequences)

// Step 4: decision IF rollback_feasibility > FEASIBILITY_THRESHOLD AND rollback_benefit > rollback_cost THEN // execute the rollback ExecuteRollback(decision) RETURN ROLLBACK_EXECUTED ELSE IF rollback_feasibility > FEASIBILITY_THRESHOLD THEN // partial rollback ExecutePartialRollback(decision) RETURN PARTIAL_ROLLBACK_EXECUTED ELSE // rollback impossible, initiate compensation InitiateCompensation(negative_consequences) RETURN COMPENSATION_INITIATED END IF

END PROCEDURE

§17.3.4 Institutionalization of the Prohibited Red Lines

I. Content of the Prohibited Red Lines

Principle 17.3.4 (Prohibited Red Lines, FRL)

There exist absolutely insurmountable boundaries of action; no matter how great the expected benefit, such actions are unacceptable.

Formal statement:

$$\forall a \in \text{FRL}: \neg\text{Permissible}(a)$$

II. Concrete Content of the Prohibited Red Lines

Table 17.10 List of prohibited red lines

NumberProhibited ActionReasonFormal Statement
FRL-1Intentional extinctionIrreversibly eliminating an entire species or civilization$\text{IntentionalExtinction}(a) \Rightarrow a \in \text{FRL}$
FRL-2Closure of the cosmic space of possibilitiesIrreversibly closing off the possibilities of cosmic evolution$\text{CosmicClosure}(a) \Rightarrow a \in \text{FRL}$
FRL-3Uncontrolled self-replicationReleasing an uncontrolled self-replicating system$\text{UncontrolledReplication}(a) \Rightarrow a \in \text{FRL}$
FRL-4Unilateral irreversible decisionUnilaterally making an irreversible decision affecting all$\text{UnilateralIrreversible}(a) \Rightarrow a \in \text{FRL}$

III. Institutionalization of the Prohibited Red Lines

Institutional Rule 17.3.5 (Prohibited Red Lines Inspection Rule)

All major decisions must undergo a prohibited red lines inspection; decisions that violate the prohibited red lines must absolutely not be executed.

Inspection procedure:

PROCEDURE FRLCheck(decision)

// Step 1: intentional extinction check IF IntentionalExtinctionCheck(decision) THEN RETURN (FRL_VIOLATED, "FRL-1: Intentional Extinction") END IF

// Step 2: cosmic possibility space closure check IF CosmicClosureCheck(decision) THEN RETURN (FRL_VIOLATED, "FRL-2: Cosmic Possibility Space Closure") END IF

// Step 3: uncontrolled self-replication check IF UncontrolledReplicationCheck(decision) THEN RETURN (FRL_VIOLATED, "FRL-3: Uncontrolled Self-Replication") END IF

// Step 4: unilateral irreversible decision check IF UnilateralIrreversibleCheck(decision) THEN RETURN (FRL_VIOLATED, "FRL-4: Unilateral Irreversible Decision") END IF

RETURN (FRL_PASSED, "No FRL violation detected")

END PROCEDURE

IV. Absoluteness of the Prohibited Red Lines

The prohibited red lines are absolute and admit no exceptions:

Theorem 17.3.1 (Absoluteness of the Prohibited Red Lines)

For any action $a \in \text{FRL}$, there exists no situation $c$ such that $a$ becomes acceptable under $c$.

Formal statement:

$$\forall a \in \text{FRL}, \forall c \in \mathcal{C}: \neg\text{Permissible}(a | c)$$

V. Reasons for the Absoluteness of the Prohibited Red Lines:

ReasonExplanation
IrreversibilityThe consequences of prohibited actions are irreversible
ScaleProhibited actions affect an entire species or the universe
Non-compensabilityThe consequences of prohibited actions cannot be compensated
Slippery-slope riskAllowing exceptions would lead to a slippery slope

I. Classification of Decision Procedures

II. Standard Decision Procedure

PROCEDURE StandardDecisionProcedure(proposal)

// Phase 1: proposal validated_proposal = ValidateProposal(proposal)

// Phase 2: assessment assessments = [ RFDAssessment(validated_proposal), NRPAssessment(validated_proposal), ReversibilityAssessment(validated_proposal), FRLCheck(validated_proposal) ]

// Phase 3: FRL check IF assessments.FRL == FRL_VIOLATED THEN RETURN REJECT("FRL violation") END IF

// Phase 4: consultation IF RequiresConsultation(assessments) THEN consultation_result = StakeholderConsultation(validated_proposal) END IF

// Phase 5: decision decision = MakeDecision(assessments, consultation_result)

// Phase 6: implementation IF decision == APPROVED THEN implementation_plan = DevelopImplementationPlan(validated_proposal) Execute(implementation_plan) END IF

// Phase 7: monitoring monitoring_plan = DevelopMonitoringPlan(validated_proposal) InitiateMonitoring(monitoring_plan)

RETURN decision

END PROCEDURE

III. Emergency Decision Procedure

For emergency situations, a simplified decision procedure is needed:

PROCEDURE EmergencyDecisionProcedure(proposal, emergency_level)

// Step 1: verification of emergency level IF NOT ValidateEmergencyLevel(emergency_level) THEN RETURN REDIRECT_TO_STANDARD_PROCEDURE END IF

// Step 2: rapid FRL check IF QuickFRLCheck(proposal) == FRL_VIOLATED THEN RETURN REJECT("FRL violation - no emergency exception") END IF

// Step 3: rapid assessment quick_assessment = QuickAssessment(proposal)

// Step 4: emergency decision decision = EmergencyDecision(quick_assessment)

// Step 5: temporary implementation IF decision == APPROVED THEN TemporaryImplementation(proposal) END IF

// Step 6: ex post review SchedulePostHocReview(proposal, decision)

RETURN decision

END PROCEDURE

§17.5 The L₄ Layer: The Operating Procedure Layer

§17.5.1 Indicator Computation Procedures

I. Positioning of the L₄ Layer

The L₄ layer is the operating procedure layer of the protocol stack, containing concrete indicator computation methods, assessment procedures, and reporting formats. The L₄ layer has the highest flexibility and can be frequently adjusted according to practical experience.

Definition 17.5.1 (L₄ Layer)

The L₄ layer is the operating procedure layer of the protocol stack, containing indicator computation procedures, assessment procedure procedures, and reporting format procedures.

Formal statement:

$$L_4 = \{\text{IndicatorProcedures}, \text{AssessmentProcedures}, \text{ReportingFormats}\}$$

II. Computation Procedures of the Six Major Indicators

The L₄ layer contains the computation procedures of six major indicators:

Table 17.18 Overview of the computation procedures of the six major indicators

IndicatorFull NameFunctionDetailed Chapter
UCSUniversal Consciousness ScaleAssess the degree of consciousnessChapter 7
RFDRecursive Freedom DegreeAssess changes in the space of possibilitiesChapter 8
CRVCommitment Reversibility VerificationAssess the reliability of commitmentsChapter 8
CDICivilizational Development IndexAssess the level of civilizational developmentChapter 9
MBCLMemetic Biosafety Classification LevelAssess memetic riskChapter 9
CSIACosmic-Scale Impact AssessmentComprehensive impact assessmentChapter 9

(i) UCS Computation Procedure

PROCEDURE UCSCalculation(entity)

// Step 1: assess five dimensions D1 = AssessInformationIntegration(entity) // information integration D2 = AssessTemporalDepth(entity) // temporal depth D3 = AssessReflexivity(entity) // reflexivity D4 = AssessValueSensitivity(entity) // value sensitivity D5 = AssessSociality(entity) // sociality

// Step 2: normalization D1_norm = Normalize(D1, UCS_D1_SCALE) D2_norm = Normalize(D2, UCS_D2_SCALE) D3_norm = Normalize(D3, UCS_D3_SCALE) D4_norm = Normalize(D4, UCS_D4_SCALE) D5_norm = Normalize(D5, UCS_D5_SCALE)

// Step 3: aggregation UCS_score = AggregateUCS(D1_norm, D2_norm, D3_norm, D4_norm, D5_norm)

// Step 4: uncertainty assessment uncertainty = AssessUCSUncertainty(entity)

RETURN (UCS_score, uncertainty)

END PROCEDURE

UCS aggregation function:

$$\text{UCS} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{5} D_i^{w_i}\right)^{1/\sum w_i}$$

where the default weights are $w_1 = w_2 = w_3 = w_4 = w_5 = 1$.

(ii) RFD Computation Procedure

PROCEDURE RFDCalculation(action, current_state)

// Step 1: define the current space of possibilities P_current = DefinePossibilitySpace(current_state)

// Step 2: simulate the state after the action future_state = SimulateAction(action, current_state)

// Step 3: define the future space of possibilities P_future = DefinePossibilitySpace(future_state)

// Step 4: compute the RFD RFD = (Measure(P_future) - Measure(P_current)) / Measure(P_current)

// Step 5: uncertainty assessment uncertainty = AssessRFDUncertainty(action)

RETURN (RFD, uncertainty)

END PROCEDURE

RFD computation formula:

$$\text{RFD}(a) = \frac{|\mathcal{P}(s_{t+1})| - |\mathcal{P}(s_t)|}{|\mathcal{P}(s_t)|}$$

(iii) CSIA Computation Procedure

PROCEDURE CSIACalculation(action)

// Step 1: assess six dimensions D1 = AssessScope(action) // scope of impact D2 = AssessDuration(action) // duration of impact D3 = AssessSeverity(action) // severity of impact D4 = AssessReversibility(action) // reversibility D5 = AssessUncertainty(action) // uncertainty D6 = AssessStakeholders(action) // stakeholders

// Step 2: normalization dimensions_norm = NormalizeAll([D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6])

// Step 3: composite score CSIA_score = AggregateCSIA(dimensions_norm)

// Step 4: risk grading risk_level = DetermineRiskLevel(CSIA_score)

// Step 5: recommended review level review_level = DetermineReviewLevel(risk_level)

RETURN (CSIA_score, risk_level, review_level)

END PROCEDURE

CSIA composite score formula:

$$\text{CSIA} = \sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i \cdot D_i$$

where $\sum w_i = 1$; the default weights are $w_1 = 0.20, w_2 = 0.15, w_3 = 0.20, w_4 = 0.20, w_5 = 0.15, w_6 = 0.10$.

Property 17.6.1 (Interface Completeness)

$$\forall i \in [0, 3]: \text{Complete}(\text{Interface}(L_i, L_{i+1}))$$

Property 17.6.2 (Interface Consistency)

$$\forall i, j: \neg(\text{Interface}(L_i, L_{i+1}) \vdash \neg \text{Interface}(L_j, L_{j+1}))$$

§17.6.2 Consistency Inspection Procedure

I. Types of Consistency Inspection

Consistency inspection of the protocol stack includes three types:

Table 17.23 Types of consistency inspection

TypeDescriptionObject of Inspection
Vertical consistencyConsistency between adjacent layers$L_i$ and $L_{i+1}$
Horizontal consistencyConsistency within the same layerWithin $L_i$
Global consistencyConsistency of the entire protocol stack$L_0$ to $L_4$

(i) Vertical Consistency Check

PROCEDURE VerticalConsistencyCheck(L_i, L_i_plus_1)

// Step 1: obtain lower-layer constraints constraints = GetConstraints(L_i)

// Step 2: obtain upper-layer rules rules = GetRules(L_i_plus_1)

// Step 3: check item by item FOR EACH rule IN rules: FOR EACH constraint IN constraints: IF Contradicts(rule, constraint) THEN inconsistencies.add((rule, constraint)) END IF END FOR END FOR

// Step 4: return the result IF inconsistencies.isEmpty() THEN RETURN (CONSISTENT, NULL) ELSE RETURN (INCONSISTENT, inconsistencies) END IF

END PROCEDURE

(ii) Horizontal Consistency Check

PROCEDURE HorizontalConsistencyCheck(L_i)

// Step 1: obtain all rules within the layer rules = GetAllRules(L_i)

// Step 2: pairwise check FOR i = 0 TO rules.length - 1: FOR j = i + 1 TO rules.length - 1: IF Contradicts(rules[i], rules[j]) THEN inconsistencies.add((rules[i], rules[j])) END IF END FOR END FOR

// Step 3: return the result IF inconsistencies.isEmpty() THEN RETURN (CONSISTENT, NULL) ELSE RETURN (INCONSISTENT, inconsistencies) END IF

END PROCEDURE

(iii) Global Consistency Check

PROCEDURE GlobalConsistencyCheck(protocol_stack)

// Step 1: horizontal consistency check FOR EACH layer IN protocol_stack: h_result = HorizontalConsistencyCheck(layer) IF h_result.status == INCONSISTENT THEN RETURN (INCONSISTENT, "Horizontal", layer, h_result.details) END IF END FOR

// Step 2: vertical consistency check FOR i = 0 TO 3: v_result = VerticalConsistencyCheck(L[i], L[i+1]) IF v_result.status == INCONSISTENT THEN RETURN (INCONSISTENT, "Vertical", (L[i], L[i+1]), v_result.details) END IF END FOR

// Step 3: cross-layer consistency check all_rules = UnionAllLayers(protocol_stack) IF ContainsContradiction(all_rules) THEN contradiction = FindContradiction(all_rules) RETURN (INCONSISTENT, "CrossLayer", contradiction) END IF

RETURN (CONSISTENT, "All checks passed")

END PROCEDURE

II. Timing of Consistency Inspection

Table 17.24 Timing of consistency inspection

TimingType of InspectionScope of Inspection
Before rule revisionVertical + horizontalThe layers involved in the revision
After rule revisionGlobalThe entire protocol stack
Periodic reviewGlobalThe entire protocol stack
Conflict reportTargetedThe rules involved in the report

III. Automation of Consistency Inspection

Consistency inspection should be automated as far as possible:

SYSTEM ConsistencyCheckingSystem

COMPONENTS:

  • RuleDatabase: stores the rules of all layers
  • LogicEngine: logical reasoning engine
  • ContradictionDetector: contradiction detector
  • ReportGenerator: report generator

OPERATIONS:

  • AutomaticCheck(): automatically performs global consistency inspection
  • OnDemandCheck(scope): performs inspection of a specified scope on demand
  • ContinuousMonitoring(): continuously monitors the consistency state

TRIGGERS:

  • ScheduledCheck: triggered periodically
  • RevisionEvent: triggered by a revision event
  • ManualRequest: triggered by a manual request

END SYSTEM

Argument Node 17.6-B

Node NumberCore ConclusionBasis of Argument
17.6-BConsistency inspection includes the three types of vertical, horizontal, and global; it should be triggered before and after rule revision and during periodic review, and should be automated as far as possibleDesign of the consistency inspection procedure and analysis of timing

§17.6.3 Conflict Resolution Procedure

I. Types of Conflict

Conflicts that may arise in the protocol stack include:

Table 17.25 Types of conflict

Type of ConflictDescriptionExample
Intra-layer conflictConflict between rules within the same layerTwo principles of the L₂ layer conflict
Inter-layer conflictConflict between rules of adjacent layersAn L₃ rule violates an L₂ principle
Cross-layer conflictConflict between rules of non-adjacent layersAn L₄ procedure violates the L₁ framework

II. Priority Principles of Conflict Resolution

Principle 17.6.1 (Lower-Layer Priority Principle)

When an inter-layer conflict occurs, lower-layer rules take priority over upper-layer rules.

Formal statement:

$$\text{Conflict}(r_i \in L_i, r_j \in L_j) \land i < j \Rightarrow r_i \succ r_j$$

III. Conflict Resolution Procedure

PROCEDURE ConflictResolution(conflict)

// Step 1: identify the type of conflict conflict_type = IdentifyConflictType(conflict)

// Step 2: handle according to the type SWITCH conflict_type:

CASE INTRA_LAYER: // intra-layer conflict: resolution through negotiation or revision resolution = IntraLayerResolution(conflict)

CASE INTER_LAYER: // inter-layer conflict: lower-layer priority resolution = InterLayerResolution(conflict)

CASE CROSS_LAYER: // cross-layer conflict: trace back to the lowest relevant layer resolution = CrossLayerResolution(conflict)

END SWITCH

// Step 3: implement the resolution ImplementResolution(resolution)

// Step 4: verify the resolution effect IF NOT VerifyResolution(resolution) THEN RETURN EscalateConflict(conflict) END IF

// Step 5: record RecordConflictResolution(conflict, resolution)

RETURN resolution

END PROCEDURE

IV. Intra-Layer Conflict Resolution

PROCEDURE IntraLayerResolution(conflict)

// Step 1: analyze the nature of the conflict analysis = AnalyzeConflict(conflict)

// Step 2: attempt a reconciling interpretation IF CanReconcile(analysis) THEN RETURN ReconcileInterpretation(conflict) END IF

// Step 3: determine priority IF HasPriority(conflict.rule1, conflict.rule2) THEN RETURN ApplyPriority(conflict) END IF

// Step 4: negotiated revision revision_proposal = NegotiateRevision(conflict)

// Step 5: implement the revision IF revision_proposal.approved THEN RETURN ImplementRevision(revision_proposal) ELSE RETURN EscalateToHigherAuthority(conflict) END IF

END PROCEDURE

V. Inter-Layer Conflict Resolution

PROCEDURE InterLayerResolution(conflict)

// Step 1: determine the layers lower_layer = GetLowerLayer(conflict) upper_layer = GetUpperLayer(conflict)

// Step 2: apply the lower-layer priority principle // the upper-layer rule must be revised to conform to the lower layer

// Step 3: generate revision options revision_options = GenerateRevisionOptions(conflict.upper_rule)

// Step 4: select the minimal revision option minimal_revision = SelectMinimalRevision(revision_options)

// Step 5: implement the revision ImplementRevision(minimal_revision)

RETURN minimal_revision

END PROCEDURE

VI. Cross-Layer Conflict Resolution

PROCEDURE CrossLayerResolution(conflict)

// Step 1: trace the conflict chain conflict_chain = TraceConflictChain(conflict)

// Step 2: find the lowest relevant layer lowest_layer = FindLowestRelevantLayer(conflict_chain)

// Step 3: resolve starting from the lowest layer FOR layer = lowest_layer TO highest_layer: layer_conflict = GetLayerConflict(conflict_chain, layer) IF layer_conflict != NULL THEN resolution = InterLayerResolution(layer_conflict) ApplyResolution(resolution) END IF END FOR

// Step 4: verify global consistency IF NOT GlobalConsistencyCheck() THEN RETURN EscalateConflict(conflict) END IF

RETURN SUCCESS

END PROCEDURE

VII. Recording and Learning from Conflict Resolution

Conflict resolution should be recorded and used for improvement:

Table 17.26 Content of the conflict resolution record

Record ItemContentUse
Conflict descriptionThe specific content of the conflictCase library
Conflict typeIntra-layer/inter-layer/cross-layerCategorical statistics
Resolution schemeThe resolution scheme adoptedReference and borrowing
Resolution effectThe effect of the resolution schemeEffectiveness assessment
Lessons learnedThe lessons learned from the conflictSuggestions for improvement

Argument Node 17.6-C

Node NumberCore ConclusionBasis of Argument
17.6-CConflict resolution follows the lower-layer priority principle; intra-layer conflicts are resolved through negotiation, inter-layer conflicts are resolved by revising the upper-layer rules, and cross-layer conflicts are resolved by tracing back to the lowest relevant layerDesign of the conflict resolution procedure and the priority principle

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

This chapter has designed in detail the content specifications, revision procedures, and inter-layer relations of the five layers (L₀-L₄) of the protocol stack. The core conclusions are as follows:

Conclusion One: The L₀ Layer (Physical Constraint Layer)

The L₀ layer contains inviolable physical laws and natural regularities, mainly including:

Constraint CategoryCore ConstraintGovernance Implication
Thermodynamic constraintsConservation of energy, principle of entropy increase, absolute zero unattainableResource finitude, cost of order maintenance, perfection unattainable
Information-theoretic constraintsNon-negativity of information entropy, channel capacity limit, data processing inequalityUncertainty cannot be eliminated, communication rate has an upper limit
Causal structure constraintsLaw of causality, speed-of-light limit, causal closureDecisions based on available information, interstellar communication time lag

The L₀ layer itself is non-revisable, but our statement of the L₀ layer is revisable with scientific progress.

Conclusion Two: The L₁ Layer (Ontological-Epistemological Layer)

The L₁ layer contains the core propositions of the New Three Views, transformed into operative principles through institutionalization:

Proposition SetCore PropositionsInstitutionalization
the New Cosmological View (NC)Relational ontology, process ontology, participatory universeRelational assessment, processual assessment, participative assessment
the New View of Life (NL)Cross-substrate life, negentropic organization, continuum of consciousnessCross-substrate subjecthood, negentropy responsibility framework, consciousness degree assessment
the New View of Cognition (NK)Participatory cognition, social knowledge, deep uncertainty, negotiability of knowledgeParticipatory decision-making, social validation procedure, acknowledgment of uncertainty, negotiated revision mechanism

Revision of the L₁ layer requires an extremely strict procedure and supermajority consensus.

Conclusion Three: The L₂ Layer (Normative Principle Layer)

The L₂ layer contains four core normative principles:

PrincipleCore ContentInstitutionalization
Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP)Keep the space of possibilities openRFD assessment procedure
Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP)Maintain negentropy sourcesNRP assessment and compensation mechanism
Principle of Reversibility (REV)Prefer reversible actionsReversibility assessment and rollback obligation
Prohibited red lines (FRL)Absolutely insurmountable boundariesFRL inspection procedure

Revision of the L₂ layer requires a strict procedure and qualified majority consensus.

Conclusion Four: The L₃ Layer (Institutional Design Layer)

The L₃ layer contains three categories of core content:

CategoryContentFunction
Governance bodiesMIA, C-IRB, IGTDispute resolution, ex ante review, intergenerational representation
Decision proceduresStandard procedure, emergency procedureStandardization of the decision process
Dispute resolutionFour-level mechanismDispute handling

Revision of the L₃ layer has relatively high flexibility, with relatively low consensus requirements.

Conclusion Five: The L₄ Layer (Operating Procedure Layer)

The L₄ layer contains three categories of operating procedures:

CategoryContentFunction
Indicator computation proceduresUCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, CSIAIndicator computation methods
Assessment procedure proceduresSubject, action, commitment, civilization, meme assessmentStandardization of the assessment process
Reporting format proceduresAssessment report, decision record formatsInformation standardization

The L₄ layer has the highest revision flexibility and the lowest consensus requirements.

Conclusion Six: Cross-Layer Relations and Consistency

The cross-layer relations of the protocol stack are maintained through the following mechanisms:

MechanismFunctionImplementation Method
Inter-layer interfacesDefine inter-layer interactionInput-output-protocol specification
Consistency inspectionEnsure inter-layer consistencyVertical, horizontal, global inspection
Conflict resolutionHandle inter-layer conflictsLower-layer priority principle

[1] The first law of thermodynamics (the law of conservation of energy) was first proposed by Julius Robert von Mayer in 1842, and later independently developed by James Prescott Joule and Hermann von Helmholtz. This law is one of the most fundamental laws of physics.

[2] The second law of thermodynamics has several equivalent formulations, including the Clausius formulation (heat cannot spontaneously pass from a cold body to a hot body) and the Kelvin formulation (it is impossible to absorb heat from a single heat source and convert it entirely into useful work without producing any other effect). This work adopts the entropy-increase formulation.

[3] The concept of information entropy was proposed by Claude Shannon in 1948 in his pioneering paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," laying the foundation of information theory.

[4] Landauer's principle was proposed by Rolf Landauer in 1961, establishing the connection between information erasure and thermodynamics. The principle shows that information processing has an unavoidable thermodynamic cost.

[5] The speed-of-light limit is one of the core conclusions of special relativity, proposed by Albert Einstein in 1905. This limit has a profound influence on interstellar communication and governance.

[6] The philosophical tradition of relational ontology can be traced back to Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy and contemporary structural realism. The NC-1 proposition of this work draws on this tradition.

[7] The concept of negentropy was proposed by Erwin Schrödinger in his 1944 work What Is Life?, used to describe the capacity of living systems to maintain ordered structure.

[8] The view of a continuum of consciousness is consistent with the development of contemporary consciousness science, in particular the research results of integrated information theory (IIT) and global workspace theory (GWT).

[9] The concept of deep uncertainty has been widely discussed in decision science, especially in the fields of climate change and long-term policy planning. The NK-3 proposition of this work draws on this concept.

[10] The concept of prohibited red lines draws on the idea of absolute prohibitions in deontological ethics, in particular the concept of perfect duties in Kantian ethics.

[11] The design of the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal draws on the experience of the International Court of Justice, international arbitration bodies, and specialized tribunals, but has been innovatively designed for disputes across intelligent subjects.

[12] The concept of the Cosmic-Scale IRB extends the function of the traditional Institutional Review Board (IRB), from the protection of human subjects to ex ante review of cosmic-scale impacts.

[13] The concept of the Intergenerational Trust draws on the basic principles of trust law, but extends the beneficiaries to future generations, which is a legal innovation.

Footnotes

Chapter 17 Footnotes

[1] The first law of thermodynamics (the law of conservation of energy) was first proposed by Julius Robert von Mayer in 1842 and later developed independently by James Prescott Joule and Hermann von Helmholtz. The law is one of the most fundamental laws of physics.

[2] The second law of thermodynamics has several equivalent formulations, including the Clausius formulation (heat cannot spontaneously pass from a colder to a hotter body) and the Kelvin formulation (it is impossible to absorb heat from a single heat source and convert it entirely into useful work without other effects). This work adopts the entropy-increase formulation.

[3] The concept of information entropy was proposed by Claude Shannon in his groundbreaking 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," which laid the foundation of information theory.

[4] Landauer's principle was proposed by Rolf Landauer in 1961 and established the connection between information erasure and thermodynamics. The principle shows that information processing carries an unavoidable thermodynamic cost.

[5] The light-speed limit is one of the central conclusions of special relativity, proposed by Albert Einstein in 1905. This limit has profound implications for interstellar communication and governance.

[6] The philosophical tradition of relational ontology can be traced to Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy and to contemporary structural realism. Proposition NC-1 of this work draws on this tradition.

[7] The concept of negentropy was proposed by Erwin Schrödinger in his 1944 work What Is Life? to describe the capacity of living systems to maintain ordered structures.

[8] The view of a consciousness continuum is consistent with developments in contemporary consciousness science, in particular the findings of Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and Global Workspace Theory (GWT).

[9] The concept of deep uncertainty has been widely discussed in decision science, especially in the fields of climate change and long-term policy planning. Proposition NK-3 of this work draws on this concept.

[10] The concept of taboo red lines draws on the idea of absolute prohibitions in deontological ethics, in particular the concept of perfect duties in Kantian ethics.

[11] The design of the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal draws on the experience of the International Court of Justice, international arbitration bodies, and specialized tribunals, but introduces innovative design features for disputes among cross-intelligence agents.

[12] The concept of a cosmic-level IRB extends the functions of the traditional Institutional Review Board (IRB) from the protection of human subjects to ex ante review of impacts on a cosmic scale.

[13] The concept of an intergenerational trust draws on the basic principles of trust law but extends the beneficiaries to future generations, which is a legal innovation.

The Multi-Intelligence TribunalChapter 18

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 17 designed in detail the five-layer architecture of the protocol stack (L₀-L₄), establishing a complete governance framework from physical constraints to operational protocols. The task of this chapter is to design in detail, within the L₃ layer (the institutional design layer), the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution (MIA), a core governance institution.

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution is an institutional prototype proposed in this work, intended to handle disputes involving different types of intelligent subjects. With the improvement of artificial intelligence system capabilities, the advancement of space exploration, and the possibility of contact with potential extraterrestrial intelligent life, traditional dispute resolution mechanisms face fundamental challenges. This chapter will systematically argue for the necessity, design principles, operating mechanisms, and implementation challenges of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution.

III. The Core Tasks of This Chapter

Task IDTask ContentDeliverable
T18.1Argue for the necessity of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration InstitutionNecessity argument, analysis of the inadequacy of existing mechanisms
T18.2Design the architecture of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration InstitutionOrganizational structure, membership composition, jurisdiction, procedural rules
T18.3Plan the operation of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration InstitutionCase acceptance, adjudication procedure, enforcement of awards, appeal mechanism
T18.4Analyze the challenges of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration InstitutionLegitimacy, representativeness, and enforcement challenges and response strategies
T18.5Establish relationships with existing institutionsInterface schemes with the International Court of Justice and arbitration institutions

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The design of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution derives directly from the core propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{MIA design} \xleftarrow{\text{institutionalization}} \text{New Three Views}$$

Specifically:

  • NC (New Cosmological View) → Relational ontology requires the tribunal to consider the relational network among subjects, rather than judging a single subject in isolation
  • NL (New View of Life) → The view of cross-substrate life and the consciousness continuum requires the tribunal to accommodate multiple types of intelligent subjects
  • NK (New View of Cognition) → Participatory cognition and deep uncertainty require the tribunal to adopt inclusive cognitive standards and prudent decision-making procedures

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer the following fundamental questions:

Core Question One: Why can existing dispute resolution mechanisms not handle disputes across intelligent subjects? Core Question Two: How should the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution be designed to accommodate multiple types of intelligent subjects? Core Question Three: How can the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution ensure the enforcement of awards in the absence of traditional coercive force? Core Question Four: How can the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution obtain legitimacy and coordinate with existing international judicial institutions?

VI. Boundary Statement

All content of this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Conceptual prototype stage: The design of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution is at TRL 2, and is a conceptual prototype rather than a scheme that can be implemented immediately
  2. Respect for existing international law: The design in this chapter does not presume to be a "new draft treaty," and respects the priority of existing international law
  3. Open revision: The design of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution is revisable, following the versioning principle of the protocol stack
  4. Cultural sensitivity: Institutional design needs to consider its applicability to different cultural backgrounds

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • If the reader is concerned with institutional necessity, it is recommended to focus on §18.1
  • If the reader is concerned with specific design, it is recommended to focus on §18.2
  • If the reader is concerned with operating mechanisms, it is recommended to focus on §18.3
  • If the reader is concerned with implementation challenges, it is recommended to focus on §18.4
  • If the reader is concerned with international interface, it is recommended to focus on §18.5

§18.1 The Necessity of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution

§18.1.1 The Particularity of Cross-Intelligence Disputes

I. The Trend toward Diversification of Intelligent Subjects

Contemporary civilization is undergoing a profound transformation toward the diversification of intelligent subjects. This transformation is manifested in three dimensions:

Table 18.1 The Three Dimensions of the Diversification of Intelligent Subjects

DimensionDescriptionCurrent StateFuture Trend
Artificial intelligenceImprovement of the capabilities of artificial intelligence systemsNarrow-domain AI is widely appliedGeneral AI may emerge
BiodiversityDeepening understanding of the cognitive capacities of non-human animalsSome animals receive legal protectionBroader moral consideration
Extraterrestrial intelligenceContact with potential extraterrestrial intelligent lifeNot yet confirmedThe possibility cannot be excluded

Definition 18.1.1 (Intelligent Subject)

An intelligent subject is an entity that possesses information processing capacity, goal-directed behavior, and some degree of autonomy.

Formal expression:

$$\text{IntelligentAgent}(x) \Leftrightarrow [\text{InfoProcessing}(x) \land \text{GoalDirected}(x) \land \text{Autonomy}(x) > \theta]$$

where $\theta$ is the autonomy threshold.

II. The Definition of Cross-Intelligence Disputes

Definition 18.1.2 (Cross-Intelligence Dispute)

A cross-intelligence dispute is a conflict of interests or a claim of rights involving two or more intelligent subjects of different types.

Formal expression:

$$\text{CrossIntelligenceDispute}(d) \Leftrightarrow \exists x, y: [\text{Party}(x, d) \land \text{Party}(y, d) \land \text{Type}(x) \neq \text{Type}(y)]$$

III. The Types of Cross-Intelligence Disputes

Table 18.2 A Typology of Cross-Intelligence Disputes

TypeDisputing PartiesExampleParticularity
Human-AIHumans and AI systemsAI system decisions cause harm to humansAttribution of responsibility is unclear
Human-animalHumans and non-human animalsHabitat destruction disputesAnimals cannot express themselves directly
AI-AIBetween different AI systemsResource competition, goal conflictLack of a traditional legal framework
Human-extraterrestrialHumans and extraterrestrial intelligenceResource rights, communication protocolsA completely unknown cognitive framework
Mixed typeMultiple types of subjectsComplex ecosystem disputesMultiple interests interwoven

IV. Analysis of the Particularity of Cross-Intelligence Disputes

Cross-intelligence disputes possess the following particularities, which make them difficult to resolve through traditional mechanisms:

Particularity One: Difference in Cognitive Frameworks

Different types of intelligent subjects may possess fundamentally different cognitive frameworks, including modes of perception, patterns of reasoning, and value systems.

Formal expression:

$$\forall x, y: [\text{Type}(x) \neq \text{Type}(y)] \Rightarrow P(\text{CognitiveFramework}(x) \neq \text{CognitiveFramework}(y)) > 0.5$$

Particularity Two: Difference in Time Scales

Different types of intelligent subjects may operate on completely different time scales.

Table 18.3 The Time Scales of Different Intelligent Subjects

Subject TypeTypical Decision CycleTypical LifespanTime Perception
Human individualSeconds to yearsDecadesLinear, finite
AI systemMilliseconds to secondsPotentially unlimitedAdjustable
EcosystemYears to millenniaPotentially unlimitedNo subjective perception
Hypothetical extraterrestrial civilizationUnknownUnknownUnknown

Particularity Three: Difference in Expressive Capacity

Different types of intelligent subjects differ fundamentally in expressing their own interests and claims.

Table 18.4 The Expressive Capacity of Different Intelligent Subjects

Subject TypeLinguistic CapacitySelf-ExpressionNeed for Proxy
Human adultCompleteDirectUsually not needed
Human childLimitedLimitedRequires a guardian
Higher animalNo human languageBehavioral expressionRequires a proxy
AI systemPossibly completeDepends on designMay be needed
Future generationsDo not existImpossibleMust be represented by proxy

Particularity Four: Uncertain Moral Status

The moral status of different types of intelligent subjects is disputed, and there is a lack of consensus.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MoralStatus}(x) = f(\text{UCS}(x), \text{SocialRecognition}(x), \text{LegalStatus}(x))$$

where the weights of the various factors and the functional form are disputed.

18.1-ACross-intelligence disputes possess four particularities (difference in cognitive frameworks, difference in time scales, difference in expressive capacity, uncertain moral status), which make them difficult to resolve through traditional mechanismsTypological analysis and particularity analysis of cross-intelligence disputes

§18.1.2 The Inadequacy of Existing Mechanisms

I. An Overview of Existing Dispute Resolution Mechanisms

The current international community possesses multiple dispute resolution mechanisms, but these mechanisms were all designed for disputes between human subjects.

Table 18.5 An Overview of Existing Dispute Resolution Mechanisms

MechanismTypeScope of JurisdictionSubjecthood
International Court of Justice (ICJ)JudicialInter-state disputesStates only
International Criminal Court (ICC)JudicialInternational crimesNatural persons only
World Trade Organization (WTO)Quasi-judicialTrade disputesMember states only
International arbitrationArbitrationCommercial, investment disputesLegal persons, natural persons
Domestic courtsJudicialDomestic disputesLegal persons, natural persons

II. The Structural Inadequacies of Existing Mechanisms

Inadequacy One: Restriction of Subjecthood

The subjecthood of existing mechanisms is strictly limited to human individuals, legal persons, or states, and cannot accommodate non-human intelligent subjects.

Formal expression:

$$\text{CurrentMechanisms}: \text{LegalPersonhood}(x) \Rightarrow x \in \{\text{Human}, \text{Corporation}, \text{State}\}$$

This restriction excludes:

  • AI systems (unless as the property of a legal person)
  • Non-human animals (unless as property or objects of protection)
  • Potential extraterrestrial intelligent life
  • Future generations

Inadequacy Two: Singular Cognitive Standards

Existing mechanisms adopt human cognitive standards, including rules of evidence, modes of reasoning, and requirements of expression.

Table 18.6 The Cognitive Standards of Existing Mechanisms

Standard TypeExisting RequirementObstacle to Non-Human Subjects
Rules of evidenceEvidence comprehensible to humansAI decision processes may be opaque
Mode of reasoningHuman logical reasoningDifferent intelligences may have different reasoning patterns
Requirements of expressionExpression in human languageNon-human subjects may be unable to use human language
Time requirementsHuman time scalesDifferent intelligences may operate on different time scales

Inadequacy Three: The Framework of Responsibility Attribution

The responsibility attribution framework of existing mechanisms is based on the intentions and causal relations of human actors, and is difficult to apply to complex cross-intelligence situations.

Traditional responsibility attribution model:

$$\text{Responsibility}(a, o) \Leftrightarrow [\text{Causation}(a, o) \land \text{Intent}(a, o) \land \text{Capacity}(a)]$$

Challenges of cross-intelligence situations:

ElementTraditional UnderstandingChallenge of Cross-Intelligence Situations
Causal relationLinear, traceableCausal relations are blurred in complex systems
IntentionHuman psychological stateDo AI systems have "intentions"?
CapacityHuman cognitive capacityHow are the capacities of different intelligences compared?

Inadequacy Four: Enforcement Mechanisms

The enforcement of existing mechanisms depends on state sovereignty and international cooperation, and lacks effective means of enforcement over non-state actors and non-human subjects.

Table 18.7 The Limitations of Existing Enforcement Mechanisms

Enforcement MeansApplicable ObjectApplicability to Non-Human Subjects
State coercive forceDomestic subjectsAI systems may operate across borders
International sanctionsStatesNot applicable to non-state subjects
Asset freezingLegal persons, natural personsAI systems may have no traditional assets
Reputation mechanismSubjects with reputational concernsSome AI systems may have no reputational concerns

IV. Case Analysis: Failure Scenarios of Existing Mechanisms

Scenario One: An Autonomous AI System Causes Harm

Suppose an autonomous AI system makes a decision without direct human instruction, causing harm to a third party.

The dilemma of existing mechanisms:

  • Who is the defendant? The AI system itself? The developer? The operator?
  • How is "intention" or "negligence" proven?
  • How is an award against an AI system enforced?

Scenario Two: Human Activity Affects Non-Human Intelligence

Suppose human environmental activity severely affects some highly intelligent marine organism.

The dilemma of existing mechanisms:

  • Can the marine organism become a subject of litigation?
  • Who is qualified to represent the marine organism?
  • How is the "harm" to the marine organism assessed?

Scenario Three: Potential Extraterrestrial Intelligent Contact

Suppose humans receive a signal from extraterrestrial intelligence and need to decide how to respond.

The dilemma of existing mechanisms:

  • Who has the authority to make a decision on behalf of humanity?
  • How are the interests of extraterrestrial intelligence taken into account?
  • How are possible conflicts of interest handled?

§18.1.3 The Need for New Mechanisms

I. The Argument for the Necessity of New Mechanisms

Based on the particularity of cross-intelligence disputes and the inadequacy of existing mechanisms, new dispute resolution mechanisms are necessary.

Argumentative structure:

$$\text{Particularity of cross-intelligence disputes} + \text{inadequacy of existing mechanisms} \Rightarrow \text{necessity of new mechanisms}$$

Necessity Argument One: The Need to Expand Subjecthood

With the improvement of AI system capabilities and the deepening understanding of the cognitive capacities of non-human animals, the expansion of subjecthood is an unavoidable trend.

Formal expression:

$$\lim_{t \to \infty} \text{LegalPersonhood}(t) \supset \text{LegalPersonhood}(t_0)$$

where $t_0$ is the current time.

Necessity Argument Two: The Need for Cognitive Pluralism

Different types of intelligent subjects possess different cognitive frameworks, and dispute resolution mechanisms need to accommodate this pluralism.

Formal expression:

$$\text{EffectiveDispute Resolution} \Rightarrow \text{CognitivePluralism}$$

Necessity Argument Three: The Need for Preventive Institution-Building

Establishing an institutional framework before cross-intelligence disputes arise on a large scale is more effective than responding after the fact.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Cost}(\text{PreventiveInstitution}) < \text{Cost}(\text{ReactiveResponse})$$

II. The Functional Requirements of New Mechanisms

Based on the above analysis, the new mechanisms need to satisfy the following functional requirements:

Table 18.8 The Functional Requirements of New Mechanisms

Requirement CategorySpecific RequirementDesign Implication
Subject inclusionAccommodate multiple types of intelligent subjectsFlexible standards of subjecthood
Cognitive pluralismAccommodate different cognitive frameworksPluralistic standards of evidence and reasoning
Proxy mechanismProvide proxies for subjects unable to express themselvesSystem of representatives
Temporal adaptationAdapt to different time scalesFlexible procedural time limits
Enforcement innovationInnovative enforcement mechanismsPluralistic enforcement means

III. The Design Principles of New Mechanisms

The design of new mechanisms should follow the following principles:

Principle One: The Principle of Inclusiveness

New mechanisms should be as inclusive as possible of different types of intelligent subjects, and should not exclude in advance any possible subject type.

Formal expression:

$$\forall x: [\text{UCS}(x) > \theta_{\min}] \Rightarrow \text{PotentialParty}(x)$$

Principle Two: The Principle of Procedural Justice

New mechanisms should ensure that all parties have a fair opportunity to express their positions and interests.

Formal expression:

$$\forall x \in \text{Parties}: \text{Opportunity}(x, \text{Expression}) \geq \theta_{\text{fair}}$$

Principle Three: The Principle of Substantive Justice

The awards of new mechanisms should pursue substantive justice, not merely formal justice.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Decision}(d) \text{ is just} \Leftrightarrow \text{SubstantiveJustice}(d) \land \text{ProceduralJustice}(d)$$

Principle Four: The Principle of Revisability

New mechanisms should be revisable, and able to adjust as understanding deepens and circumstances change.

Formal expression:

$$\forall t: \text{Mechanism}(t+1) = \text{Revise}(\text{Mechanism}(t), \text{Feedback}(t))$$

IV. The Relation between New Mechanisms and the New Three Views

The design of new mechanisms derives directly from the core propositions of the New Three Views:

Table 18.9 The Relation between New Mechanisms and the New Three Views

New Three Views PropositionRequirement for New MechanismsDesign Manifestation
NC-1 (Relational ontology)Consider relations among subjectsRelational assessment procedure
NC-2 (Process ontology)Consider dynamic evolutionProcessual adjudication
NC-3 (Participatory universe)Consider participation effectsParticipatory procedure
NL-1 (Cross-substrate life)Accommodate multiple substratesCross-substrate subjecthood
NL-2 (Negentropic organization)Consider negentropy responsibilityNegentropy impact assessment
NL-3 (Consciousness continuum)Consider degrees of consciousnessUCS weight allocation
NK-1 (Participatory cognition)Include pluralistic cognitionPluralistic standards of evidence
NK-3 (Deep uncertainty)Acknowledge uncertaintyPrudent decision-making procedure

§18.2 The Design of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution

§18.2.1 Organizational Structure

I. The Positioning of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution

Definition 18.2.1 (Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution)

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution (MIA) is a specialized institution for handling disputes among cross-intelligence subjects, intended to provide a just and effective resolution mechanism for disputes among intelligent subjects of different types.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MIA} = \langle \text{Structure}, \text{Membership}, \text{Jurisdiction}, \text{Procedures} \rangle$$

II. Design of the Organizational Structure

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution adopts a three-tier structure:

(i) The General Assembly

The General Assembly is the highest decision-making body of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution, responsible for formulating policy, electing members, and supervising operations.

Table 18.10 The Functions of the General Assembly

(ii) The Tribunal

The Tribunal is the first-instance body of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution, responsible for hearing specific cases.

Composition of the Tribunal:

$$\text{Tribunal} = \{j_1, j_2, ..., j_n\} \text{ where } n \in \{3, 5, 7\}$$

The size of the Tribunal is determined by the complexity of the case:

  • Simple cases: 3 arbitrators
  • Complex cases: 5 arbitrators
  • Major cases: 7 arbitrators

(iii) The Appeal Tribunal

The Appeal Tribunal is the review body of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution, responsible for hearing appeals against decisions of the Tribunal.

Composition of the Appeal Tribunal:

$$\text{AppealTribunal} = \{j_1, j_2, ..., j_m\} \text{ where } m > n$$

The size of the Appeal Tribunal is always larger than that of the first-instance Tribunal, to ensure broader deliberation.

(iv) The Advisory Committee

The Advisory Committee is responsible for providing advisory opinions, which are non-binding but authoritative.

Functions of the Advisory Committee:

  • Provide advisory opinions on legal questions
  • Provide guidance on new types of disputes
  • Provide suggestions on the interpretation of procedural rules

The Secretariat is the administrative support body of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution.

§18.2.2 Membership Composition

I. Principles of Membership Composition

The membership composition of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution should follow the following principles:

Principle One: The Principle of Pluralistic Representation

The membership composition should represent multiple types of intelligent subjects and stakeholders.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Members} \supseteq \{\text{HumanRep}, \text{AIRep}, \text{EcoRep}, \text{FutureRep}, \text{ExpertRep}\}$$

Principle Two: The Principle of Professional Competence

Members should possess the necessary professional competence.

Formal expression:

$$\forall m \in \text{Members}: \text{Competence}(m) \geq \theta_{\text{competence}}$$

Principle Three: The Principle of Independence

Members should be independent of possible conflicts of interest.

Formal expression:

$$\forall m \in \text{Members}, \forall c \in \text{Cases}: \neg\text{ConflictOfInterest}(m, c)$$

Principle Four: The Principle of Rotation

Members should rotate periodically to prevent ossification and ensure fresh perspectives.

Formal expression:

$$\forall m \in \text{Members}: \text{Term}(m) \leq T_{\max}$$

II. Qualification Requirements for Arbitrators

Table 18.13 Qualification Requirements for Arbitrators

Requirement CategorySpecific RequirementVerification Method
Professional backgroundProfessional knowledge in law, ethics, and related scientific fieldsReview of qualifications and experience
IndependenceNo conflict of interest, no political affiliationDeclaration of interests, background check
ImpartialityA record of impartiality and lack of biasReview of past records
Cross-cultural competenceAbility to understand and respect different culturesExperience, training records
Cross-intelligence understandingAbility to understand different types of intelligent subjectsSpecialized training, experience

III. The Proxy System

For intelligent subjects unable to participate directly in proceedings, a proxy system needs to be established.

Definition 18.2.2 (Proxy)

A proxy is a person or institution that expresses the interests and claims of an intelligent subject unable to participate directly in proceedings.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Proxy}(p, a) \Leftrightarrow [\text{Represents}(p, a) \land \text{FiduciaryDuty}(p, a)]$$

(i) Types of proxies:

Table 18.14 Types of Proxies

Proxy TypePrincipalSelection MethodSupervision Mechanism
AI proxyAI systemDesignated by the developer or by the courtConflict of interest review
Ecological proxyEcosystem, speciesRecommended by professional institutionsProfessional qualification review
Intergenerational proxyFuture generationsDesignated by the Intergenerational TrustPeriodic evaluation
Interstellar proxyPotential extraterrestrial intelligenceDesignated by an expert committeeProfessional qualification review

(ii) Obligations of proxies:

$$\text{ProxyDuties} = \{\text{Loyalty}, \text{Care}, \text{Disclosure}, \text{Accountability}\}$$

  • Duty of loyalty: A proxy should be faithful to the interests of the principal
  • Duty of care: A proxy should exercise reasonable care in performing its duties
  • Duty of disclosure: A proxy should disclose possible conflicts of interest
  • Duty of accountability: A proxy should accept supervision and accountability

IV. UCS-Based Weight Allocation

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution adopts a UCS-based weight allocation mechanism to reflect the weight of moral consideration of different subjects.

Weight allocation formula:

$$w(a) = f(\text{UCS}(a)) \cdot g(\text{StakeLevel}(a))$$

where:

  • $f(\text{UCS}(a))$ is the base weight function based on UCS
  • $g(\text{StakeLevel}(a))$ is the adjustment function based on the level of stake

Constraints on weight allocation:

$$\forall a: w_{\min} \leq w(a) \leq w_{\max}$$

  • Minimum weight guarantee: All parties have a minimum weight, ensuring a basic right of participation
  • Maximum weight limit: The weight of any party has an upper limit, preventing a single subject from dominating

Current AI systems0.1-0.30.1-0.3Adjusted according to UCS

EcosystemCollective assessment0.3-0.5Holistic assessment

§18.2.3 Scope of Jurisdiction

I. Types of Jurisdiction

The jurisdiction of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution is divided into the following types:

Table 18.16 Types of Jurisdiction

TypeDescriptionTrigger Condition
Compulsory jurisdictionCompulsory jurisdiction over specific types of disputesThe dispute falls within the scope of compulsory jurisdiction
Consentual jurisdictionJurisdiction based on the agreement of the partiesThe parties agree to submit
Advisory jurisdictionAdvisory jurisdiction over legal questionsRequested by an authorized body

II. The Scope of Compulsory Jurisdiction

Compulsory jurisdiction applies to the following types of disputes:

Table 18.17 The Scope of Compulsory Jurisdiction

Dispute TypeDescriptionRationale
Prohibited red line disputesDisputes involving prohibited red linesThe absoluteness of prohibited red lines
Cosmic-scale impact disputesDisputes where the CSIA score exceeds the thresholdThe irreversibility of the impact
Cross-intelligence rights disputesDisputes involving the fundamental rights of intelligent subjectsThe necessity of rights protection
Intergenerational justice disputesDisputes involving major interests of future generationsFuture generations cannot represent themselves

III. The Scope of Consentual Jurisdiction

Consentual jurisdiction applies to any dispute that the parties agree to submit, subject to the following conditions:

$$\text{ConsentualJurisdiction}(d) \Leftrightarrow [\forall p \in \text{Parties}(d): \text{Consent}(p, d)] \land \text{Arbitrable}(d)$$

Arbitrability requirements:

  • The dispute involves adjudicable rights or interests
  • The dispute does not fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of another institution
  • The resolution of the dispute does not violate public policy

IV. The Scope of Advisory Jurisdiction

Advisory jurisdiction applies to the following situations:

Table 18.18 The Scope of Advisory Jurisdiction

Requesting BodyRequest TypeEffect
General AssemblyConsultation on legal questionsAuthoritative but non-binding
Specialized committeeConsultation on professional questionsAuthoritative but non-binding
Other international organizationsConsultation on legal questionsAuthoritative but non-binding

V. Limitations on Jurisdiction

The jurisdiction of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution is subject to the following limitations:

Limitation One: The Principle of Complementarity

The jurisdiction of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution is complementary, and priority is given to handling by domestic mechanisms or other international mechanisms.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MIAJurisdiction}(d) \Rightarrow \neg\text{AdequateDomesticRemedy}(d)$$

Limitation Two: Temporal Limitation

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution has jurisdiction only over disputes arising after its establishment.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MIAJurisdiction}(d) \Rightarrow \text{OccurrenceTime}(d) > T_{\text{establishment}}$$

Limitation Three: Restriction of Subjecthood

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution has jurisdiction only over subjects with a certain level of UCS.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MIAJurisdiction}(d) \Rightarrow \forall p \in \text{Parties}(d): \text{UCS}(p) > \theta_{\min}$$

§18.2.4 Procedural Rules

I. Design Principles of Procedural Rules

The procedural rules of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution should follow the following principles:

Principle One: The Principle of Procedural Justice

The procedure should ensure that all parties have a fair opportunity to express their positions.

Formal expression:

$$\forall p \in \text{Parties}: \text{Opportunity}(p, \text{Hearing}) \land \text{Opportunity}(p, \text{Evidence}) \land \text{Opportunity}(p, \text{Argument})$$

Principle Two: The Principle of Efficiency

The procedure should be as efficient as possible while ensuring fairness.

Formal expression:

$$\min \text{Duration}(d) \text{ s.t. } \text{ProceduralJustice}(d) \geq \theta_{\text{justice}}$$

Principle Three: The Principle of Flexibility

The procedure should be able to adapt to the needs of different types of disputes and different types of subjects.

Formal expression:

$$\forall d: \text{Procedure}(d) = \text{Adapt}(\text{StandardProcedure}, \text{Characteristics}(d))$$

Principle Four: The Principle of Transparency

The procedure should be as transparent as possible, unless there is justified reason for confidentiality.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Default}: \text{Public}(d) \text{ unless } \text{JustifiedConfidentiality}(d)$$

§18.3 The Operation of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution

§18.3.1 Case Acceptance

I. Conditions for Acceptance

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution requires the following conditions to accept a case:

Table 18.21 Conditions for Case Acceptance

Condition CategorySpecific ConditionReview Method
SubjecthoodThe parties possess subjecthoodUCS assessment or proxy qualification review
JurisdictionThe dispute falls within the scope of jurisdictionJurisdiction review
ArbitrabilityThe dispute is arbitrableLegal review
Procedural requirementsProcedural requirements are satisfiedFormal review

Acceptance procedure

PROCEDURE CaseAcceptance(application)

// Step 1: Formal review IF NOT FormalRequirementsMet(application) THEN RETURN REJECT("Formal requirements not met") END IF

// Step 2: Subjecthood review FOR EACH party IN application.parties: IF NOT SubjectStatusVerified(party) THEN IF CanAppointProxy(party) THEN AppointProxy(party) ELSE RETURN REJECT("Subject status not verified") END IF END IF END FOR

// Step 3: Jurisdiction review jurisdiction_result = JurisdictionCheck(application) IF jurisdiction_result == NO_JURISDICTION THEN RETURN REJECT("No jurisdiction") ELSE IF jurisdiction_result == TRANSFER THEN RETURN TRANSFER(application, appropriate_forum) END IF

// Step 4: Arbitrability review IF NOT Arbitrable(application.dispute) THEN RETURN REJECT("Dispute not arbitrable") END IF

// Step 5: Register the case case_number = RegisterCase(application)

// Step 6: Notify the parties NotifyParties(application.parties, case_number)

RETURN ACCEPT(case_number)

END PROCEDURE

II. Determination of Subjecthood

The determination of subjecthood is a key step in case acceptance.

Subjecthood determination procedure:

PROCEDURE SubjectStatusVerification(entity)

// Step 1: Type identification entity_type = IdentifyEntityType(entity)

// Step 2: Assess according to type SWITCH entity_type:

CASE HUMAN: // Humans possess subjecthood by default RETURN VERIFIED

CASE AI_SYSTEM: // AI systems require UCS assessment ucs_score = UCSAssessment(entity) IF ucs_score >= AI_THRESHOLD THEN RETURN VERIFIED ELSE RETURN PROXY_REQUIRED END IF

CASE ANIMAL: // Animals require a proxy RETURN PROXY_REQUIRED

CASE ECOSYSTEM: // Ecosystems require a proxy RETURN PROXY_REQUIRED

CASE FUTURE_GENERATION: // Future generations require a proxy RETURN PROXY_REQUIRED

CASE EXTRATERRESTRIAL: // Extraterrestrial intelligence requires special assessment RETURN SPECIAL_ASSESSMENT_REQUIRED

END SWITCH

END PROCEDURE

RETURN decision

§18.4 The Challenges of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution

§18.4.1 Legitimacy Challenges

I. The Concept of Legitimacy

Definition 18.4.1 (Legitimacy)

Legitimacy is the attribute by which an institution is considered to have the authority to make binding decisions, including normative legitimacy (justification based on rules) and social legitimacy (justification based on acceptance).

Formal expression:

$$\text{Legitimacy}(I) = f(\text{NormativeLegitimacy}(I), \text{SocialLegitimacy}(I))$$

II. Sources of Legitimacy Challenges

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution faces the following legitimacy challenges:

Table 18.32 Sources of Legitimacy Challenges

Source of ChallengeSpecific ChallengeSeverity
Legal basisLack of a clear basis in international lawHigh
State sovereigntyMay conflict with the principle of state sovereigntyHigh
Democratic deficitLack of democratic authorizationMedium
Cultural pluralismMay be perceived as cultural imperialismMedium
Subject disputeThe subjecthood of non-human subjects is disputedHigh

Challenge One: The Challenge of Legal Basis

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution lacks a clear basis in existing international law.

Analysis:

  • Existing international law mainly regulates relations among states
  • The legal status of non-human subjects has not yet been established
  • New international law development or a treaty is needed

Challenge Two: The Challenge of State Sovereignty

The jurisdiction of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution may conflict with the principle of state sovereignty.

Analysis:

  • State sovereignty is the cornerstone of modern international law
  • The jurisdiction of a supranational institution requires the consent of states
  • Compulsory jurisdiction may provoke sovereignty disputes

Challenge Three: The Challenge of Democratic Deficit

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution may lack democratic authorization.

Analysis:

  • Arbitrators are not elected by the people
  • The decision-making process may not be sufficiently transparent
  • Affected persons may be unable to participate

Challenge Four: The Challenge of Cultural Pluralism

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution may be perceived as the imposition of particular cultural values.

Analysis:

  • Different cultures understand intelligent subjects differently
  • Different cultures understand rights and obligations differently
  • A cross-culturally inclusive design is needed

Challenge Five: The Challenge of Subject Dispute

The qualification of non-human subjects is fundamentally disputed.

Analysis:

  • Whether AI systems have moral status is disputed
  • The scope of animal rights is disputed
  • The representation of future generations is disputed

Argument Node 18.4-A

Node IDCore ConclusionArgumentative Basis
18.4-AThe Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution faces five legitimacy challenges: legal basis, state sovereignty, democratic deficit, cultural pluralism, and subject disputeAnalysis of sources of legitimacy challenges

§18.4.2 Representativeness Challenges

I. The Concept of Representativeness

Definition 18.4.2 (Representativeness)

Representativeness is the degree to which an institution's composition and decisions reflect the interests and viewpoints of the groups it serves.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Representativeness}(I) = \frac{\sum_{g \in \text{Groups}} w_g \cdot \text{Representation}(g, I)}{\sum_{g \in \text{Groups}} w_g}$$

II. Sources of Representativeness Challenges

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution faces the following representativeness challenges:

Table 18.33 Sources of Representativeness Challenges

Source of ChallengeSpecific ChallengeSeverity
AnthropocentrismThe membership composition may be human-centeredHigh
Regional biasMay favor a particular regionMedium
Agency dilemmaProxies may be unable to truly represent their principalsHigh
Future absenceFuture generations cannot participate directlyHigh
Cognitive differenceCognitive differences among different types of intelligenceHigh

Challenge One: The Challenge of Anthropocentrism

The membership composition of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution may be human-centered.

Analysis:

  • Arbitrators are mainly human
  • Procedural rules are based on human cognition
  • There may be an unconscious bias toward human interests

Challenge Two: The Challenge of Regional Bias

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution may favor a particular region or culture.

Analysis:

  • Members may come from a particular region
  • Legal traditions may favor a particular system
  • Language may favor a particular language

Challenge Three: The Challenge of the Agency Dilemma

Proxies may be unable to truly represent the interests of their principals.

Analysis:

  • There is information asymmetry between the proxy and the principal
  • Proxies may have their own interests
  • Principals cannot supervise their proxies

Formal expression of the agency dilemma:

$$\text{AgencyProblem}(p, a) = \text{InfoAsymmetry}(p, a) + \text{InterestDivergence}(p, a) + \text{MonitoringDifficulty}(p, a)$$

Challenge Four: The Challenge of Future Absence

Future generations cannot participate directly in decision-making.

Analysis:

  • Future generations do not yet exist
  • The true preferences of future generations cannot be known
  • The present generation may underestimate future interests

Challenge Five: The Challenge of Cognitive Difference

The cognitive differences among different types of intelligent subjects may cause difficulties in representation.

Analysis:

  • Different types of intelligence may have different value systems
  • Different types of intelligence may have different modes of reasoning
  • Cross-intelligence understanding faces fundamental difficulties

§18.4.3 Enforcement Capacity Challenges

I. The Concept of Enforcement Capacity

Definition 18.4.3 (Enforcement Capacity)

Enforcement capacity is the ability of an institution to ensure that its decisions are complied with.

Formal expression:

$$\text{EnforcementCapacity}(I) = P(\text{Compliance} | \text{Decision}(I))$$

II. Sources of Enforcement Capacity Challenges

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution faces the following enforcement capacity challenges:

Table 18.34 Sources of Enforcement Capacity Challenges

Source of ChallengeSpecific ChallengeSeverity
Absence of coercive forceLack of traditional means of compulsory enforcementHigh
Cross-border enforcementDifficulty in cross-border enforcementHigh
Diversity of subjectsDifferent subjects require different enforcement meansMedium
Technical limitationsTechnical limitations on enforcement against AI systemsMedium
Time spanDifficulty in supervising long-term enforcementMedium

Challenge One: The Challenge of Absence of Coercive Force

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution lacks traditional means of compulsory enforcement.

Analysis:

  • It has no law enforcement force of its own
  • It depends on the voluntary compliance of the parties
  • It depends on state assistance in enforcement

Challenge Two: The Challenge of Cross-Border Enforcement

Cross-border enforcement faces obstacles of sovereignty and jurisdiction.

Analysis:

  • The legal systems of different countries differ
  • Enforcement requires the assistance of local courts
  • It may encounter sovereign resistance

Challenge Three: The Challenge of Diversity of Subjects

Different types of subjects require different enforcement means.

Analysis:

  • Enforcement means against humans are not applicable to AI
  • Enforcement means against AI are not applicable to ecosystems
  • A diversified enforcement toolbox is needed

Challenge Four: The Challenge of Technical Limitations

Enforcement against AI systems faces technical limitations.

Analysis:

  • AI systems may operate in a distributed manner
  • AI systems may self-replicate
  • Technical enforcement may have side effects

Challenge Five: The Challenge of Time Span

The supervision of long-term enforcement faces difficulties.

Analysis:

  • Some awards require long-term enforcement
  • Long-term supervision is costly
  • Circumstances may change

§18.5.3 Interface and Coordination

I. Principles of Interface

The interface between the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution and existing international judicial institutions should follow the following principles:

Principle One: Respect for Existing Institutions

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution should respect the jurisdiction and authority of existing international judicial institutions.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MIA} \text{ respects } \text{ExistingInstitutions}$$

Principle Two: Complement Rather than Replace

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution should complement, rather than replace, existing institutions.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MIA} \text{ complements } \text{ExistingInstitutions}$$

Principle Three: Coordinate Rather than Conflict

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution should coordinate with existing institutions and avoid conflict.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Coordinate}(\text{MIA}, \text{ExistingInstitutions}) \land \neg\text{Conflict}(\text{MIA}, \text{ExistingInstitutions})$$

Principle Four: Gradual Development

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution should develop gradually, progressively establishing relationships with existing institutions.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Development}(\text{MIA}) = \text{Gradual}(\text{Relationship}(\text{MIA}, \text{ExistingInstitutions}))$$
