Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

This chapter designed in detail the complete framework of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution. The main conclusions are as follows:

Conclusion One: The Necessity Argument

Cross-intelligence disputes possess four particularities (difference in cognitive frameworks, difference in time scales, difference in expressive capacity, uncertain moral status), and existing dispute resolution mechanisms possess four structural inadequacies (restriction of subjecthood, singular cognitive standards, inapplicable framework of responsibility attribution, absence of enforcement mechanisms); therefore, new cross-intelligence dispute resolution mechanisms are necessary.

$$\text{Particularity of cross-intelligence disputes} + \text{inadequacy of existing mechanisms} \Rightarrow \text{necessity of new mechanisms}$$

Conclusion Two: Organizational Structure

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution adopts a three-tier structure:

LevelInstitutionFunction
Decision-making levelGeneral AssemblyHighest decision-making
Adjudication levelTribunal, Appeal Tribunal, Advisory CommitteeCase adjudication
Support levelSecretariat, Specialized CommitteesAdministrative and professional support

Conclusion Three: Membership Composition

The membership composition of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution follows four principles:

PrincipleContent
Pluralistic representationRepresent multiple types of intelligent subjects
Professional competencePossess necessary professional competence
IndependenceIndependent of conflicts of interest
RotationPeriodic rotation

and establishes a proxy system and a UCS-based weight allocation mechanism.

Conclusion Four: Scope of Jurisdiction

The jurisdiction of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution is divided into three categories:

TypeScope
Compulsory jurisdictionProhibited red line disputes, cosmic-scale impact disputes, cross-intelligence rights disputes, intergenerational justice disputes
Consentual jurisdictionDisputes that the parties agree to submit
Advisory jurisdictionConsultation on legal questions

Conclusion Five: Procedural Rules

The procedural rules of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution follow four principles:

PrincipleContent
Procedural justiceEnsure fair opportunity
EfficiencyEfficient on the premise of fairness
FlexibilityAdapt to different disputes and subjects
TransparencyAs public as possible

Conclusion Six: Operating Mechanisms

The operation of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution includes four segments:

SegmentContent
Case acceptanceReview of subjecthood, jurisdiction, arbitrability, procedural requirements
Adjudication procedureFive stages: preparation, written, oral, deliberation, decision
Enforcement of awardsPluralistic enforcement mechanisms
Appeal mechanismAppeals based on statutory grounds

Conclusion Seven: Challenges and Responses

The Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution faces three categories of challenges:

Challenge CategorySpecific ChallengeResponse Strategy
LegitimacyLegal basis, state sovereignty, democratic deficit, cultural pluralism, subject disputeGradual legal development, respect for sovereignty, enhanced participation, cross-cultural inclusiveness
RepresentativenessAnthropocentrism, regional bias, agency dilemma, future absence, cognitive differenceInstitutional correction, regional balance, proxy supervision, intergenerational trust, cognitive pluralism
Enforcement capacityAbsence of coercive force, cross-border enforcement, diversity of subjects, technical limitations, time spanPluralistic mechanisms, international coordination, tailored schemes, technical capacity, long-term supervision

Conclusion Eight: Relationship with Existing Institutions

The relationship between the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution and existing international judicial institutions is complementary and cooperative:

Relationship TypeContent
With the International Court of JusticeComplementary relationship, coordination mechanism to handle overlapping jurisdiction
With arbitration institutionsComplementary and cooperative, borrowing procedural experience
Interface principlesRespect, complementarity, coordination, gradualness

Preview of Subsequent Chapters

This chapter established the complete framework of the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution. Subsequent chapters will continue to develop the institutional design:

ChapterThemeRelation to This Chapter

Chapter 21From Theory to PracticeThe implementation path of the MIA

[1] The proxy representation system borrows from the agency system in civil law and the trustee system in trust law, but has been innovatively designed for non-human subjects. The traditional agency system requires the principal to have legal capacity, whereas the proxy representation system of this work extends to intelligent subjects unable to express themselves.

[2] The detailed design of the UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) is given in Chapter 7. The UCS is a multidimensional consciousness assessment tool, including five dimensions: degree of information integration, temporal depth, reflexivity, value sensitivity, and sociality.

[3] The detailed content of the prohibited red lines (FRL) is given in Chapter 14 and Chapter 17. The prohibited red lines include four categories of absolutely prohibited actions: deliberate extinction, closure of cosmic possibility space, uncontrollable self-replication, and unilateral irreversible decisions.

[4] The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, established under Article 92 of the Charter of the United Nations. The jurisdiction of the ICJ is limited to inter-state disputes, which is its fundamental difference from the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution.

[5] The main legal framework for international arbitration includes the 1958 Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York Convention) and the arbitration laws of various countries. The New York Convention provides the legal basis for the cross-border enforcement of international arbitral awards.

[6] The principle of complementarity borrows from the jurisdictional design of the International Criminal Court. Under the Rome Statute, the jurisdiction of the ICC is complementary, and is exercised only when domestic judicial systems are unwilling or unable genuinely to carry out an investigation or prosecution.

[7] The agency problem is a classic problem in economics and law, referring to the problems arising between a proxy and a principal due to information asymmetry and misaligned interests. The proxy supervision mechanism of this work aims to alleviate this problem.

[8] The reputation mechanism is one of the important means of enforcing international law. In an international society lacking compulsory enforcement force, reputational cost is an important factor inducing actors to comply with rules.

[9] The gradual legal development path borrows from the historical experience of the development of international law. Many rules of international law have undergone a development process from academic discussion to soft law and then to hard law, such as the development of international human rights law and international environmental law.

[10] The detailed design of the Intergenerational Trust is given in Chapter 19. The Intergenerational Trust is a specialized institution representing the interests of future generations, and forms institutional complementarity with the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution.

[11] The detailed design of CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment) is given in Chapter 9. CSIA is a composite indicator for assessing the cosmic-scale impact of actions, including six dimensions: scope, duration, severity, reversibility, uncertainty, and stakeholder impact.

[12] Technical enforcement refers to the compulsory enforcement of awards through technical means, such as code modification, access restriction, or system isolation for AI systems. This is an innovative extension of traditional enforcement means, but it also faces technical and ethical challenges.

Footnotes

Chapter 18 Footnotes

[1] The institution of proxy representation draws on the institution of agency in civil law and the institution of trusteeship in trust law, but introduces innovative design features for non-human agents. Traditional agency requires that the principal possess legal capacity, whereas the proxy representation institution of this work extends to intelligent agents that cannot express themselves.

[2] The detailed design of the UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) is given in Chapter 7. The UCS is a multidimensional tool for assessing consciousness, comprising five dimensions: degree of information integration, temporal depth, reflexivity, value sensitivity, and sociality.

[3] The detailed content of the taboo red lines (FRL) is given in Chapters 14 and 17. The taboo red lines comprise four categories of absolutely prohibited actions: deliberate extinction, closure of the cosmic possibility space, uncontrollable self-replication, and unilateral irreversible decisions.

[4] The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, established under Article 92 of the Charter of the United Nations. The jurisdiction of the ICJ is limited to disputes between states, which is the fundamental difference between it and the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal.

[5] The main legal framework for international arbitration includes the 1958 Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (the New York Convention) and the arbitration laws of individual states. The New York Convention provides the legal basis for the cross-border enforcement of international arbitral awards.

[6] The principle of complementarity draws on the jurisdictional design of the International Criminal Court. Under the Rome Statute, the jurisdiction of the ICC is complementary, being exercised only when national judicial systems are unwilling or unable genuinely to conduct investigations or prosecutions.

[7] The agency problem is a classic problem in economics and law, arising between principals and agents as a result of information asymmetry and divergent interests. The agent monitoring mechanisms of this work are intended to mitigate this problem.

[8] The reputation mechanism is one of the important means of enforcing international law. In an international society lacking coercive enforcement power, reputational cost is an important factor inducing actors to comply with rules.

[9] The path of gradual legal development draws on the historical experience of the development of international law. Many rules of international law have undergone a development process from academic discussion to soft law to hard law, as in the development of international human rights law and international environmental law.

[10] The detailed design of the Intergenerational Trust is given in Chapter 19. The Intergenerational Trust is a specialized institution representing the interests of future generations and forms an institutional complement to the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal.

[11] The detailed design of the CSIA (Cosmic Scale Impact Assessment) is given in Chapter 9. The CSIA is a composite indicator for assessing the cosmic-scale impact of an action, comprising six dimensions: scope, duration, severity, reversibility, uncertainty, and stakeholder impact.

[12] Technical enforcement refers to the enforcement of rulings through technical means, such as code modification of AI systems, access restrictions, or system isolation. This is an innovative extension of traditional enforcement instruments, but it also faces technical and ethical challenges.

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 18 designed in detail the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution (MIA), establishing an ex post adjudication mechanism for handling disputes among cross-intelligence subjects. The task of this chapter is to design two complementary institutions: the Cosmic Institutional Review Board (C-IRB) and the Intergenerational Trust (IGT). The C-IRB is responsible for the ex ante review of major actions, and the IGT is responsible for the proxy representation of the interests of future generations. Together with the MIA, the two form the core organizational set of the L₃-layer institutional design.

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The design of the Cosmic IRB and the Intergenerational Trust derives directly from the core propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{C-IRB} + \text{IGT} \xleftarrow{\text{institutionalization}} \text{New Three Views}$$

Specifically:

  • NC (New Cosmological View) → Process ontology requires ex ante review of major actions, because once an action is initiated it becomes part of the cosmic process
  • NL (New View of Life) → Negentropy responsibility requires protecting the ability of future generations to obtain negentropy flows, which is the theoretical basis of the Intergenerational Trust
  • NK (New View of Cognition) → Deep uncertainty requires prudent decision-making, and the review procedure of the C-IRB embodies this requirement

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer the following fundamental questions:

Core Question One: How can an institution be designed that is able to review actions with cosmic-scale impacts? Core Question Two: How can the interests of future generations, who do not yet exist, be represented in contemporary institutions? Core Question Three: How do the ex ante review body (C-IRB) and the future-generation representation body (IGT) coordinate? Core Question Four: How can these institutional ideas be implemented gradually under real-world political constraints?

VI. Boundary Statement

All content of this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Conceptual prototype stage: The designs of the C-IRB and the IGT are at TRL 2, and are conceptual prototypes rather than schemes that can be implemented immediately
  2. Respect for existing international law: The design in this chapter does not presume to be a "new draft treaty," and respects the priority of existing international law
  3. Open revision: The institutional design is revisable, following the versioning principle of the protocol stack
  4. Cultural sensitivity: Institutional design needs to consider its applicability to different cultural backgrounds

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • If the reader is concerned with the ex ante review mechanism, it is recommended to focus on §19.1
  • If the reader is concerned with the institutionalization of intergenerational justice, it is recommended to focus on §19.2
  • If the reader is concerned with institutional coordination, it is recommended to focus on §19.3
  • If the reader is concerned with implementation feasibility, it is recommended to focus on §19.4

§19.1 The Design of the Cosmic IRB

§19.1.1 The Expansion of the IRB Concept

I. The Concept and Functions of the Traditional IRB

The Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a core institution of modern research ethics, originating from the mid-twentieth-century reflection on ethical issues in human experimentation.

Definition 19.1.1 (Traditional IRB)

A traditional IRB is an institution that reviews the ethical compliance of research involving human subjects, intended to protect the rights, safety, and well-being of research participants.

Table 19.1 The Core Elements of the Traditional IRB

ElementContentLegal Basis
Object of reviewResearch involving human subjectsBelmont Report, Declaration of Helsinki
Review standardInformed consent, risk-benefit ratio, fair selectionNational research ethics regulations
CompositionScientists, ethicists, community representativesInstitutional rules
PowerApprove, modify, reject research protocolsLegal authorization

II. The Historical Evolution of the Traditional IRB

The development of the traditional IRB has gone through three stages:

Table 19.2 The Historical Evolution of the Traditional IRB

StagePeriodLandmark EventCore Concern
Embryonic period1947-1966Nuremberg CodeVoluntary consent
Institutionalization period1966-1991Belmont ReportSystematized principles
Maturity period1991-presentCommon RuleStandardized procedures

III. The Expansion from the Traditional IRB to the Cosmic IRB

The design of the traditional IRB assumed the following conditions:

  1. The impact of research is mainly limited to direct participants
  2. Risks and benefits can be assessed within a reasonable time
  3. Affected persons can give informed consent
  4. The consequences of research are basically reversible

However, certain contemporary and future actions break these assumptions:

Table 19.3 The Breaking of Traditional IRB Assumptions

Traditional AssumptionSituation of BreakExample
Impact limited to participantsImpact expands to the global and even cosmic scaleClimate engineering, transmission of interstellar signals
Timely assessment possibleConsequences persist for generations or longerNuclear waste disposal, gene editing
Informed consent possibleAffected persons do not yet exist or cannot communicateFuture generations, potential extraterrestrial life
Basically reversibleConsequences are irreversible or extremely difficult to reverseSpecies extinction, ecosystem collapse

IV. The Concept of the Cosmic IRB

Definition 19.1.2 (Cosmic IRB)

The Cosmic Institutional Review Board (C-IRB) is an institution that reviews the ethical compliance of actions with cosmic-scale impacts, intended to protect the interests of all intelligent subjects that may be affected (including future generations and potential non-human intelligence).

Formal expression:

$$\text{C-IRB} = \langle \text{Scope}, \text{Criteria}, \text{Composition}, \text{Powers}, \text{Procedures} \rangle$$

where:

  • $\text{Scope}$: scope of review (actions with cosmic-scale impacts)
  • $\text{Criteria}$: review criteria (based on the L₂-layer normative principles)
  • $\text{Composition}$: composition (pluralistic representation)
  • $\text{Powers}$: powers (approve, modify, reject, circuit-break)
  • $\text{Procedures}$: procedures (review process)

V. The Dimensions of Expansion from the Traditional IRB to the Cosmic IRB

Table 19.4 The Dimensions of Expansion of the IRB Concept

DimensionTraditional IRBCosmic IRBRationale for Expansion
Object of reviewResearch on human subjectsActions with cosmic-scale impactsExpanded scope of impact
Protected personsResearch participantsAll intelligent subjectsExpanded scope of subjects
Time horizonDuration of researchDeep time scalesExtended duration of consequences
Spatial scopeResearch siteCosmic scaleExpanded spatial scope of impact
Review standardTraditional ethical principlesL₂-layer normative principlesExpanded normative basis

Argument Node 19.1-A

Node IDCore ConclusionArgumentative Basis
19.1-AThe Cosmic IRB is an expansion of the traditional IRB concept along five dimensions—object of review, protected persons, time horizon, spatial scope, and review standard—and this expansion is a necessary institutional innovation for responding to actions with cosmic-scale impactsAnalysis of the breaking of traditional IRB assumptions and argument for the dimensions of expansion

§19.1.2 The Functions of the Cosmic IRB

I. Definition of Core Functions

The core function of the Cosmic IRB is to conduct ex ante ethical review of actions with cosmic-scale impacts.

Definition 19.1.3 (Cosmic-Scale Impact Action)

A cosmic-scale impact action is an action whose consequences may spatially extend beyond the Earth, temporally persist for multiple generations, and in terms of subjects possibly affect multiple types of intelligent subjects.

Formal expression:

$$\text{CosmicScaleAction}(a) \Leftrightarrow [\text{SpatialScope}(a) > \theta_s] \lor [\text{TemporalScope}(a) > \theta_t] \lor [\text{SubjectScope}(a) > \theta_m]$$

where:

  • $\theta_s$: spatial scope threshold (e.g., beyond the Earth's atmosphere)
  • $\theta_t$: temporal scope threshold (e.g., beyond one generation)
  • $\theta_m$: subject scope threshold (e.g., affecting multiple types of intelligent subjects)

Function One: Ex Ante Review

Ex ante review is the primary function of the C-IRB, intended to assess the ethical compliance of an action before it is implemented.

Formal expression of ex ante review:

$$\text{PreReview}(a) = \text{Evaluate}(a, \text{L}_2\text{Principles}) \rightarrow \{\text{Approve}, \text{Modify}, \text{Reject}\}$$

Trigger conditions for ex ante review:

Table 19.5 Trigger Conditions for Ex Ante Review

Trigger ConditionDescriptionThreshold
CSIA thresholdThe CSIA score exceeds the thresholdCSIA > 0.7
Proximity to prohibited red linesThe action is close to a prohibited red lineFRL distance < 0.2
IrreversibilityThe action is highly irreversibleREV < 0.3
Intergenerational impactThe impact of the action persists for multiple generationsTime span > 100 years
Cross-intelligence impactThe action affects multiple intelligent subjectsNumber of subject types > 2

Function Two: Continuous Monitoring

Continuous monitoring is the second function of the C-IRB, intended to track the implementation process of approved actions.

Formal expression of continuous monitoring:

$$\text{ContinuousMonitoring}(a) = \text{Track}(a, t) \rightarrow \text{Update}(\text{RiskAssessment}(a, t))$$

Content of continuous monitoring:

Monitoring ContentDescriptionFrequency
Implementation progressProgress in implementing the actionPeriodic
Change in riskUpdate of the risk assessmentEvent-triggered
New informationNewly emerging relevant informationContinuous
Stakeholder feedbackFeedback from affected personsPeriodic

Function Three: Circuit-Breaker Triggering

Circuit-breaker triggering is the third function of the C-IRB, intended to activate the circuit-breaker mechanism in emergencies.

Definition 19.1.4 (Circuit-Breaker Mechanism)

The circuit-breaker mechanism is an emergency procedure that forcibly suspends or terminates an action when serious risks are discovered during its implementation.

Formal expression of circuit-breaker triggering:

$$\text{CircuitBreaker}(a, t) = \begin{cases} \text{Halt}(a) & \text{if } \text{Risk}(a, t) > \theta_{\text{critical}} \\ \text{Continue}(a) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Trigger conditions for the circuit-breaker:

Table 19.6 Trigger Conditions for the Circuit-Breaker

Condition TypeDescriptionResponse
Red line touchedThe action touches a prohibited red lineImmediate termination
Sharp increase in riskThe risk assessment sharply deterioratesSuspend review
New evidenceSignificant negative new evidence appearsSuspend review
Urgent request from stakeholdersUrgent request from major stakeholdersSuspend review

Function Four: Advisory Recommendations

Advisory recommendations constitute the fourth function of the C-IRB, intended to provide ethical consultation to decision-makers.

Formal expression of advisory recommendations:

$$\text{Advisory}(q) = \text{Analyze}(q, \text{L}_2\text{Principles}) \rightarrow \text{Recommendation}(q)$$

Types of advisory recommendations:

Consultation TypeDescriptionEffect
Policy consultationRecommendations on policy-makingReference
Technical consultationRecommendations on technological developmentReference
Ethical consultationAnalysis of ethical issuesAuthoritative
Emergency consultationRecommendations on emergenciesPriority handling

19.1-BThe Cosmic IRB has four core functions: ex ante review, continuous monitoring, circuit-breaker triggering, and advisory recommendations; together these four functions constitute complete ethical oversight of actions with cosmic-scale impactsFunction definitions and formal expressions

§19.1.3 The Composition of the Cosmic IRB

I. Composition Principles

The composition of the Cosmic IRB should follow the following principles:

Principle One: The Principle of Pluralistic Representation

The composition of the C-IRB should represent multiple types of stakeholders.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Composition} \supseteq \{\text{Scientists}, \text{Ethicists}, \text{PolicyMakers}, \text{CivilSociety}, \text{FutureRep}, \text{NonHumanRep}\}$$

Principle Two: The Principle of Professional Competence

C-IRB members should possess the necessary professional competence.

Formal expression:

$$\forall m \in \text{Members}: \text{Competence}(m, \text{Domain}(m)) \geq \theta_{\text{competence}}$$

Principle Three: The Principle of Independence

C-IRB members should be independent of possible conflicts of interest.

Formal expression:

$$\forall m \in \text{Members}, \forall a \in \text{Actions}: \neg\text{ConflictOfInterest}(m, a)$$

Principle Four: The Principle of Rotation

C-IRB members should rotate periodically to prevent ossification.

Formal expression:

$$\forall m \in \text{Members}: \text{Term}(m) \leq T_{\max}$$

§19.1.4 Review Procedure

I. Design Principles of the Review Procedure

The review procedure of the Cosmic IRB should follow the following principles:

Principle One: The Principle of Comprehensiveness

The review should comprehensively consider all aspects of the impact of an action.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Review}(a) = \bigcup_{d \in \text{Dimensions}} \text{Evaluate}(a, d)$$

Principle Two: The Principle of Transparency

The review process should be as transparent as possible.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Default}: \text{Public}(\text{Review}(a)) \text{ unless } \text{JustifiedConfidentiality}(a)$$

Principle Three: The Principle of Participation

The review should allow stakeholders to participate.

Formal expression:

$$\forall s \in \text{Stakeholders}(a): \text{Opportunity}(s, \text{Participation})$$

Principle Four: The Principle of Prudence

The review should adopt a prudent attitude under uncertainty.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Uncertainty}(a) \uparrow \Rightarrow \text{Caution}(\text{Review}(a)) \uparrow$$

PROCEDURE PrincipleReview(action)

// Step 1: Prohibited red line check IF TouchesFRL(action) THEN RETURN REJECT("Touches Forbidden Red Line") END IF

// Step 4: Principle of Reversibility check rev_score = EvaluateReversibility(action) IF rev_score < REV_THRESHOLD THEN FLAG("REV concern") END IF

// Step 5: Comprehensive assessment RETURN ComprehensiveAssessment(flags)

END PROCEDURE

§19.1.5 Integration with CSIA

I. The Core Position of CSIA in C-IRB Review

CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment) is the core tool of C-IRB review, providing a quantitative basis for review decisions.

Definition 19.1.7 (CSIA)

CSIA is a composite indicator system for assessing the cosmic-scale impact of actions, including assessment of six dimensions.

Formal definition of CSIA:

$$\text{CSIA}(a) = h(D_1(a), D_2(a), D_3(a), D_4(a), D_5(a), D_6(a))$$

where the aggregation function $h$ may adopt a weighted average or a maximum method:

$$h_{\text{weighted}} = \sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i \cdot D_i$$

$$h_{\text{max}} = \max_{i \in \{1,...,6\}} D_i$$

where $\theta_{\text{fuse}}$ is the circuit-breaker threshold, usually set at 80.

§19.2 The Design of the Intergenerational Trust

§19.2.1 The Expansion of the Trust Concept

I. The Concept of the Traditional Trust

A trust is a legal arrangement in which one party (the settlor) transfers property to another party (the trustee), who manages the property for the benefit of a third party (the beneficiary).

Definition 19.2.1 (Traditional Trust)

A traditional trust is a legal relationship in which the settlor transfers property rights to the trustee, who manages and disposes of the trust property for the benefit of the beneficiary in accordance with the purpose of the trust.

Core elements of the traditional trust:

ElementDescription
SettlorThe person who creates the trust and transfers the property
TrusteeThe person who receives the property and manages the trust
BeneficiaryThe person who enjoys the benefits of the trust
Trust propertyThe property managed by the trust
Purpose of the trustThe purpose for which the trust is created

II. The Expansion from the Traditional Trust to the Intergenerational Trust

The design of the traditional trust assumed the following conditions:

  1. The beneficiary is determinate or determinable
  2. The trust property is definable
  3. The term of the trust is limited
  4. The beneficiary can assert its own rights

However, when future generations are considered, these assumptions are broken:

Table 19.20 The Breaking of Traditional Trust Assumptions

Traditional AssumptionChallenge of the Intergenerational Situation
Determinate beneficiaryFuture generations do not yet exist and cannot be determined
Definable propertyThe "property" to be protected includes abstract concepts such as the space of possibilities and sources of negentropy
Limited termThe Intergenerational Trust requires an indefinite or extremely long term
Beneficiary can assert rightsFuture generations cannot assert their own rights

III. The Concept of the Intergenerational Trust

Definition 19.2.2 (Intergenerational Trust)

The Intergenerational Trust (IGT) is a trust arrangement created by the present generation for the benefit of future generations, in which trustees manage and protect, on behalf of future generations, the resources and the space of possibilities that are crucial to the well-being of future generations.

Formal expression:

$$\text{IGT} = \langle \text{Settlor}, \text{Trustee}, \text{Beneficiary}, \text{TrustProperty}, \text{Purpose} \rangle$$

where:

  • $\text{Settlor}$: settlor (humanity as a whole in the present generation)
  • $\text{Trustee}$: trustee (the Intergenerational Trust institution)
  • $\text{Beneficiary}$: beneficiary (future generations)
  • $\text{TrustProperty}$: trust property (space of possibilities, sources of negentropy, common heritage)
  • $\text{Purpose}$: purpose of the trust (protect the interests of future generations)

IV. The Theoretical Basis of the Intergenerational Trust

The theoretical basis of the Intergenerational Trust comes from the New Three Views:

Table 19.21 The Theoretical Basis of the Intergenerational Trust

New Three Views PropositionSupport for the Intergenerational Trust
NC-2 (Process ontology)Contemporary actions affect future possibilities and require institutional protection
NL-2 (Negentropic organization)Sources of negentropy are limited and require intergenerational distribution
NL-3 (Consciousness continuum)Future generations have moral status, and their interests should be protected
NK-3 (Deep uncertainty)Uncertainty about the future requires prudent intergenerational arrangements

§19.2.2 The Functions of the Intergenerational Trust

I. Definition of Core Functions

The core function of the Intergenerational Trust is to represent the interests of future generations and to protect the resources and the space of possibilities that are crucial to the well-being of future generations.

Function One: Interest Representation

Interest representation is the primary function of the IGT, intended to represent the interests of future generations in contemporary decision-making.

Formal expression of interest representation:

$$\text{InterestRepresentation}(d) = \text{Advocate}(\text{FutureGenerations}, d)$$

Function Two: Asset Management

Asset management is the second function of the IGT, intended to manage and protect assets crucial to future generations.

Formal expression of asset management:

$$\text{AssetManagement}(A) = \text{Preserve}(A) \land \text{Enhance}(A) \land \text{Transmit}(A)$$

Oversight and accountability is the third function of the IGT, intended to supervise the fulfillment of the responsibilities of contemporary actors toward future generations.

§19.2.4 Management of Trust Assets

I. Definition of Trust Assets

The assets of the Intergenerational Trust differ from the property of a traditional trust, and include both tangible and intangible assets.

Definition 19.2.3 (Intergenerational Trust Assets)

Intergenerational Trust assets are the sum of resources, capacities, and possibilities that are crucial to the well-being of future generations.

II. Classification of Trust Assets:

III. Principles of Asset Management

Asset management of the Intergenerational Trust should follow the following principles:

Principle One: The Principle of Preservation and Appreciation

Trust assets should at least maintain their value, and preferably appreciate.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Value}(A, t+1) \geq \text{Value}(A, t)$$

Principle Two: The Principle of Sustainable Use

The use of trust assets should be sustainable and should not impair the ability of future generations to use them.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Use}(A, t) \leq \text{RegenerationRate}(A, t)$$

Principle Three: The Principle of Diversity Protection

The management of trust assets should protect diversity and avoid homogenization.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Diversity}(A, t+1) \geq \text{Diversity}(A, t)$$

Principle Four: The Principle of Reversibility

Asset management decisions should be as reversible as possible.

Formal expression:

$$\forall d \in \text{Decisions}: \text{Reversibility}(d) \geq \theta_{\text{rev}}$$

§19.4.3 Gradual Implementation Path

I. Principles of Gradual Implementation

The implementation of the C-IRB and the IGT should follow the principle of gradualness, proceeding from proof of concept to pilot operation and then to formal operation.

Principle One: From Soft to Hard

Begin with soft law (guidelines, recommendations) and gradually develop into hard law (treaties, regulations).

Formal expression:

$$\text{SoftLaw} \rightarrow \text{HybridLaw} \rightarrow \text{HardLaw}$$

Principle Two: From Small to Large

Begin with small-scale pilots and gradually expand the scope.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Pilot} \rightarrow \text{Regional} \rightarrow \text{Global}$$

Principle Three: From Simple to Complex

Begin with simple functions and gradually add complex functions.

Formal expression:

$$\text{BasicFunctions} \rightarrow \text{IntermediateFunctions} \rightarrow \text{FullFunctions}$$

Principle Four: Adaptive Adjustment

Make adaptive adjustments based on implementation feedback.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Implementation}(t+1) = \text{Adjust}(\text{Implementation}(t), \text{Feedback}(t))$$

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

This chapter designed in detail two complementary institutions—the Cosmic IRB and the Intergenerational Trust. The main conclusions are as follows:

Conclusion One: The Design of the Cosmic IRB

The Cosmic IRB is an expansion of the traditional IRB concept along five dimensions: object of review, protected persons, time horizon, spatial scope, and review standard.

$$\text{C-IRB} = \langle \text{Scope}, \text{Criteria}, \text{Composition}, \text{Powers}, \text{Procedures} \rangle$$

Table 19.50 Key Points of the Cosmic IRB Design

ElementContent
FunctionsEx ante review, continuous monitoring, circuit-breaker triggering, advisory recommendations
CompositionScientists, ethicists, policy experts, citizen representatives, future generation representatives, non-human representatives
Review procedureNine-stage standard flow
Integration with CSIACSIA as the core assessment tool

Conclusion Two: The Design of the Intergenerational Trust

The Intergenerational Trust is an expansion of the traditional trust concept along four dimensions: beneficiary, trust property, term, and assertion of rights.

$$\text{IGT} = \langle \text{Settlor}, \text{Trustee}, \text{Beneficiary}, \text{TrustProperty}, \text{Purpose} \rangle$$

Table 19.51 Key Points of the Intergenerational Trust Design

Trust assetsNatural capital, knowledge capital, possibility capital, negentropy capital
Beneficiary representationPresumption of basic interests, hybrid representation mechanism, fourfold accountability

Conclusion Three: Coordination between the Two Institutions

The division of functions between the C-IRB and the IGT follows the three principles of complementarity, collaboration, and independence.

Table 19.52 Key Points of Coordination between the Two Institutions

Division of functionsThe C-IRB leads review, the IGT leads representation

[1] The history of the Institutional Review Board (IRB) can be traced back to the 1947 Nuremberg Code, which was a response to Nazi human experimentation. The 1964 Declaration of Helsinki further developed the principles of research ethics. The 1979 Belmont Report established the three basic principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice, which became the theoretical basis of the modern IRB.

[2] The detailed design of CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment) is given in Chapter 9. CSIA is a composite indicator for assessing the cosmic-scale impact of actions, including six dimensions: scope of impact, depth of impact, severity of impact, reversibility, uncertainty, and cascade risk.

[3] The circuit-breaker mechanism borrows the concept of the circuit-breaker from financial markets, but applies it to the field of ethical governance. The financial circuit-breaker suspends trading during severe market volatility, while the ethical circuit-breaker suspends or terminates an action when serious risks are discovered.

[4] The trust institution originated in English equity law, initially to circumvent the restrictions of feudal land law. The modern trust has developed into a flexible property management tool, widely applied in wealth succession, philanthropy, and commercial arrangements.

[5] Intergenerational justice is an important topic in political philosophy and ethics. The main theories include Rawls's just savings principle, Parfit's discussion of the non-identity problem, and the contributions of contemporary longtermists.

[6] The non-identity problem, proposed by Derek Parfit, points out that our decisions affect who will exist in the future, and therefore it is difficult to say that our decisions "harm" particular future persons. This work responds to this problem by focusing on the space of possibilities rather than on particular future persons.

[7] The presumption of basic interests borrows from Rawls's concept of "primary goods," namely the basic resources and capacities that people will need regardless of their specific life plans.

[8] The trustee's duty of loyalty and duty of care are core concepts of trust law, requiring the trustee to be faithful to the interests of the beneficiary and to perform duties with reasonable care.

[9] The gradual institutional development path borrows from the historical experience of the development of international law. Many international institutions have undergone a development process from soft law to hard law, and from small scale to large scale.

[10] The institutional design for representing future generations borrows from the "Commissioner for Future Generations" institutions established in countries such as Hungary and Wales, but has been extended and deepened.

[11] The classification of trust assets borrows from concepts such as natural capital, human capital, and social capital, but adds two new categories—possibility capital and negentropy capital—to reflect the theoretical framework of this work.

[12] The joint review mechanism borrows from the practice of cross-departmental joint review in environmental impact assessment, but extends it to cross-institutional and cross-generational situations.

Footnotes

Chapter 19 Footnotes

[1] The history of the Institutional Review Board (IRB) can be traced to the 1947 Nuremberg Code, which was a response to Nazi human experimentation. The 1964 Declaration of Helsinki further developed principles of research ethics. The 1979 Belmont Report established the three basic principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice, which became the theoretical foundation of the modern IRB.

[2] The detailed design of the CSIA (Cosmic Scale Impact Assessment) is given in Chapter 9. The CSIA is a composite indicator for assessing the cosmic-scale impact of an action, comprising six dimensions: scope of impact, depth of impact, severity of impact, reversibility, uncertainty, and cascading risk.

[3] The circuit breaker mechanism draws on the concept of circuit breakers in financial markets, but applies it to the domain of ethical governance. While financial circuit breakers suspend trading during severe market fluctuations, ethical circuit breakers suspend or terminate actions when serious risks are detected.

[4] The trust institution originated in English equity law, initially to circumvent the restrictions of feudal land law. The modern trust has developed into a flexible instrument of property management, widely used in wealth succession, philanthropy, and commercial arrangements.

[5] Intergenerational justice is an important topic in political philosophy and ethics. The main theories include Rawls's just savings principle, Parfit's discussion of the non-identity problem, and the contributions of contemporary longtermists.

[6] The non-identity problem was proposed by Derek Parfit, who pointed out that our decisions affect who will exist in the future, so that it is difficult to say that our decisions "harm" particular future persons. This work responds to the problem by focusing on the possibility space rather than on particular future persons.

[7] The presumption of basic interests draws on Rawls's concept of "primary goods," namely the basic resources and capacities that people will need regardless of their particular life plans.

[8] The trustee's duty of loyalty and duty of care are core concepts of trust law, requiring the trustee to be faithful to the interests of the beneficiary and to discharge the office with reasonable care.

[9] The path of gradual institutional development draws on the historical experience of the development of international law. Many international institutions have undergone a development process from soft law to hard law and from small scale to large scale.

[10] The institutional design of the representation of future generations draws on the institution of the "Commissioner for Future Generations" established in countries such as Hungary and Wales, but extends and deepens it.

[11] The classification of trust assets draws on concepts such as natural capital, human capital, and social capital, but adds two new categories, possibility capital and negentropy capital, to reflect the theoretical framework of this work.

[12] The joint review mechanism draws on the practice of cross-departmental joint review in environmental impact assessment, but extends it to cross-institutional and cross-generational contexts.

Versioned Governance and Rollback MechanismsChapter 20

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 18 designed the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution (MIA), and Chapter 19 designed the cosmic-scale IRB and the Intergenerational Trust (IGT). These institutional designs all face a common challenge: how can institutions retain their adaptability under deep uncertainty? The task of this chapter is to design versioned governance and rollback mechanisms, providing the entire protocol stack with the capacity for dynamic evolution.

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The design of versioned governance and rollback mechanisms derives directly from the core propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{VersionedGovernance} + \text{Rollback} \xleftarrow{\text{institutionalization}} \text{New Three Views}$$

Specifically:

  • NC (the New Cosmological View) → process ontology means that institutions themselves are evolutionary processes and require versioned management
  • NL (the New View of Life) → the adaptability of negentropic organization requires institutions to respond to environmental change
  • NK (the New View of Cognition) → the negotiability of knowledge and deep uncertainty require institutions to be revisable and rollbackable

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer the following fundamental questions:

Core Question One: How can the idea of version control in software engineering be applied to governance institutions? Core Question Two: Under what conditions should an institutional rollback be triggered? Core Question Three: How can versioned governance be integrated with the layered architecture of the protocol stack? Core Question Four: Where are the boundaries of versioned governance? Which situations are non-rollbackable?

VI. Boundary Statement

All content in this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Conceptual prototype stage: The versioned governance mechanism is at TRL 2, a conceptual prototype rather than a mature solution
  2. Technical-metaphorical nature: Concepts borrowed from software engineering require adaptive transformation and cannot be mechanically applied
  3. Physical irreversibility: Versioned governance cannot violate physical laws; the consequences of certain actions are non-rollbackable
  4. Open revision: The design in this chapter is itself revisable

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • Readers interested in conceptual foundations are advised to focus on §20.1
  • Readers interested in technical implementation are advised to focus on §20.2
  • Readers interested in the rollback mechanism are advised to focus on §20.3
  • Readers interested in practical applications are advised to focus on §20.4
  • Readers interested in limitations are advised to focus on §20.5

§20.1 The Concept of Versioned Governance

§20.1.1 From Software Version Control to Governance Version Control

I. Basic Concepts of Software Version Control

Software version control (Version Control) is a core practice in software engineering for managing code changes; it originated in the 1970s and was widely developed during the open-source software movement.

Definition 20.1.1 (Software Version Control)

Software version control is a system that records changes to a file or set of files over time, enabling users to revert to a particular version, compare differences between versions, and manage parallel development in multi-person collaboration.

Core elements of software version control:

ElementDescriptionFunction
Version identificationUniquely identifies each versionTracing, referencing
Change recordRecords the content of each changeAuditing, understanding
Branch managementSupports parallel development pathsExperimentation, isolation
Merge mechanismIntegrates changes from different branchesCollaboration, integration
Rollback capabilityRestores to a previous versionError correction, recovery

II. Historical Evolution of Software Version Control

Table 20.1 Historical evolution of software version control

StagePeriodRepresentative systemCore feature
Local version control1970s-1980sRCSSingle machine, file level
Centralized version control1990s-2000sCVS, SVNCentral server, network collaboration
Distributed version control2005-presentGit, MercurialDistributed, complete history

III. The Analogy from Software to Governance

The success of software version control has inspired attempts to apply its ideas to other domains. Governance institutions and software code exhibit structural similarities:

Table 20.2 Analogy between software code and governance institutions

DimensionSoftware codeGovernance institution
Basic unitCode fileRules, procedures, institutions
Change demandChanges in functional requirements, bug fixesEnvironmental change, problem exposure
Collaboration demandMulti-developer collaborationMulti-stakeholder participation
Quality assuranceTesting, code reviewEvaluation, deliberation
Rollback demandFixing introduced bugsCorrecting failed reforms

IV. The Concept of Governance Version Control

Definition 20.1.2 (Governance Version Control)

Governance version control is the application of the core ideas of software version control to the management of governance institutions, making institutional changes traceable, comparable, and rollbackable, and supporting multi-party collaboration and parallel experimentation.

Formal expression:

$$\text{GovernanceVersionControl} = \langle \text{VersionID}, \text{ChangeLog}, \text{Branching}, \text{Merging}, \text{Rollback} \rangle$$

V. Differences Between Governance Version Control and Software Version Control

Despite the analogy, important differences exist between governance version control and software version control:

Table 20.3 Differences between governance version control and software version control

DimensionSoftware version controlGovernance version control
Object of changeCode textRules, procedures, institutions, behavior
Speed of changeCan iterate rapidlyUsually requires a longer cycle
Difficulty of rollbackUsually technically feasibleMay involve irreversible consequences
Testing methodAutomated testingPiloting, simulation, evaluation
StakeholdersDevelopers, usersMultiple stakeholders
Legitimacy requirementTechnical effectivenessTechnical effectiveness + political legitimacy

VI. Theoretical Foundations of Governance Version Control

The theoretical foundations of governance version control derive from the New Three Views:

Table 20.4 Theoretical foundations of governance version control

New Three Views propositionSupport for governance version control
NC-2 (process ontology)Institutions are evolutionary processes and require versioned management
NK-3 (deep uncertainty)Uncertainty requires institutions to be revisable
NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge)The social nature of knowledge requires collaborative institutional development

Node IDCore ConclusionArgument Basis
20.1-AGovernance version control is the application of the core ideas of software version control (version identification, change records, branch management, merge mechanisms, rollback capability) to the management of governance institutions, but it must take into account the particularities of governance institutions (complex objects of change, high rollback difficulty, legitimacy requirements)Analogical analysis and differential analysis between software version control and governance institutions

§20.1.2 Core Features of Versioned Governance

Feature One: Traceability

Traceability is the foremost feature of versioned governance; it means that every change to an institution has a complete record and can be traced to the reason, content, time, and responsible party of the change.

Definition 20.1.3 (Traceability)

Traceability is the complete historical record of institutional changes, such that the state of the institution at any point in time can be reconstructed and any change can be traced back to its source.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Traceability}(I) \Leftrightarrow \forall t: \text{Reconstructable}(I, t) \land \forall c \in \text{Changes}(I): \text{Traceable}(c)$$

Content of traceability:

Traced contentDescription
Change contentWhat was specifically changed
Change reasonWhy the change was made
Change timeWhen the change was made
Responsible partyWho is responsible for the change
Basis of changeOn what basis it was made
Change impactWhat impact the change produced

Feature Two: Comparability

Comparability is the second feature of versioned governance; it means that different versions can be systematically compared to identify differences and trends of change.

Definition 20.1.4 (Comparability)

Comparability means that institutions of different versions can be compared in a structured way, identifying differences and assessing the direction and magnitude of change.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Comparability}(I) \Leftrightarrow \forall v_1, v_2 \in \text{Versions}(I): \text{Diff}(v_1, v_2) \text{ is computable}$$

Dimensions of comparability:

Comparison dimensionDescription
Structural comparisonChanges in institutional structure
Content comparisonChanges in specific rules
Effect comparisonChanges in implementation effects
Trend comparisonDirection and speed of change

Feature Three: Rollbackability

Rollbackability is the third feature of versioned governance; it means that a previous version can be restored when necessary.

Definition 20.1.5 (Rollbackability)

Rollbackability means that an institution can be restored to a previous version when necessary, undoing unsuccessful changes.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Rollbackability}(I) \Leftrightarrow \forall v \in \text{Versions}(I): \text{Restorable}(I, v) \text{ under certain conditions}$$

Levels of rollbackability:

Rollback levelDescriptionDifficulty
Rule rollbackRestoring the previous rule textLow
Procedure rollbackRestoring the previous procedure designMedium
Institutional rollbackRestoring the previous institutional arrangementHigh
Behavioral rollbackUndoing the consequences of actions already takenExtremely high or impossible

Feature Four: Branchability

Branchability is the fourth feature of versioned governance; it means that parallel paths of institutional experimentation can be created.

Definition 20.1.6 (Branchability)

Branchability means that a branch version can be created from the main version for parallel experimentation, without affecting the operation of the main version.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Branchability}(I) \Leftrightarrow \text{CanCreate}(\text{Branch}(I)) \land \text{Independent}(\text{Branch}(I), \text{Main}(I))$$

Applications of branchability:

Application scenarioDescription
Pilot experimentPiloting a new institution locally
Parallel schemesTesting multiple schemes simultaneously
Regional variationAllowing regional variants
Risk isolationIsolating experimental risk

Feature Five: Mergeability

Mergeability is the fifth feature of versioned governance; it means that the successful experience of branch versions can be integrated into the main version.

Definition 20.1.7 (Mergeability)

Mergeability means that changes from a branch version can be integrated into the main version or another branch, achieving experience sharing and institutional integration.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Mergeability}(I) \Leftrightarrow \text{CanMerge}(\text{Branch}(I), \text{Main}(I)) \land \text{ConflictResolvable}$$

Argument Node 20.1-B

Node IDCore ConclusionArgument Basis
20.1-BVersioned governance has five core features: traceability, comparability, rollbackability, branchability, and mergeability; together these five features constitute the complete capability of versioned governanceDefinitions and formal expressions of each feature

§20.1.3 Advantages of Versioned Governance

Advantage One: Enhanced Adaptability

Versioned governance enhances the institution's capacity to adapt to environmental change.

Mechanism of adaptability enhancement:

$$\text{Adaptability}(I) = f(\text{ChangeCapacity}(I), \text{FeedbackSpeed}(I), \text{RollbackCapacity}(I))$$

Table 20.5 Enhancement of adaptability by versioned governance

Adaptability dimensionTraditional governanceVersioned governance
Speed of changeSlow (requires comprehensive reform)Fast (incremental change)
Feedback integrationDifficult (lacks systematic records)Easy (complete history)
Error-correction capacityWeak (difficult to roll back)Strong (rollbackable)
Experimentation capacityWeak (high risk)Strong (branchable)

Advantage Two: Reduced Risk of Change

Versioned governance reduces the risk of institutional change through branch experimentation and rollback capability.

Mechanism of risk reduction:

$$\text{Risk}(I, \text{Change}) = \text{BaseRisk} \times (1 - \text{RollbackCapacity}) \times (1 - \text{BranchingCapacity})$$

Table 20.6 Reduction of risk by versioned governance

Risk typeTraditional governanceVersioned governance
Failure riskHigh (comprehensive implementation)Low (pilot first)
Irreversibility riskHigh (difficult to roll back)Low (rollbackable)
Conflict riskHigh (one-size-fits-all)Low (allows variants)
Learning costHigh (lacks records)Low (complete history)

Advantage Three: Facilitated Collaboration

Versioned governance facilitates multi-party collaboration through transparent change records and branch management.

Mechanism of collaboration facilitation:

$$\text{Collaboration}(I) = f(\text{Transparency}(I), \text{ParallelWork}(I), \text{ConflictResolution}(I))$$

Table 20.7 Facilitation of collaboration by versioned governance

Collaboration dimensionTraditional governanceVersioned governance
TransparencyLow (changes not transparent)High (complete records)
Parallel workDifficult (frequent conflicts)Easy (branch isolation)
Conflict resolutionDifficult (lacks tools)Easy (merge mechanisms)
Contribution trackingDifficult (incomplete records)Easy (complete attribution)

Advantage Four: Enhanced Accountability

Versioned governance enhances accountability through complete change records.

Mechanism of accountability enhancement:

$$\text{Accountability}(I) = f(\text{Traceability}(I), \text{Attribution}(I), \text{Auditability}(I))$$

Table 20.8 Enhancement of accountability by versioned governance

Accountability dimensionTraditional governanceVersioned governance
Responsibility attributionDifficult (incomplete records)Easy (complete attribution)
Audit capacityWeak (lacks history)Strong (complete history)
TransparencyLowHigh
Learning capacityWeakStrong

Advantage Five: Support for Gradual Evolution

Versioned governance supports the gradual evolution of institutions rather than radical change.

Mechanism of gradual evolution:

$$\text{GradualEvolution}(I) = \sum_{t} \text{IncrementalChange}(I, t)$$

Table 20.9 Support for gradual evolution by versioned governance

Evolution dimensionTraditional governanceVersioned governance
Change granularityLarge (comprehensive reform)Small (incremental change)
Change frequencyLow (periodic)High (continuous)
Change riskHighLow
Learning integrationDifficultEasy

Argument Node 20.1-C

Node IDCore ConclusionArgument Basis
20.1-CVersioned governance has five main advantages: enhanced adaptability, reduced risk of change, facilitated collaboration, enhanced accountability, and support for gradual evolutionMechanism analysis and comparison of each advantage

§20.2 Implementation of Versioned Governance

§20.2.1 Version Identification System

I. Functions of Version Identification

The version identification system is the infrastructure of versioned governance, providing a unique identifier for each version.

Definition 20.2.1 (Version Identification)

Version identification is a symbol system that uniquely identifies a specific version of an institution, enabling versions to be precisely referenced, compared, and traced.

Design principles of version identification:

PrincipleDescription
UniquenessEach version has a unique identifier
OrderlinessThe identifier reflects version order
ReadabilityThe identifier is easy to understand
InformativenessThe identifier carries version information
StabilityOnce assigned, the identifier does not change

I. Semantic Versioning

This work adopts semantic versioning (Semantic Versioning) as its version identification system.

Definition 20.2.2 (Semantic Versioning)

Semantic versioning is a version identification system of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, in which changes to each part carry a specific meaning.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Version} = \text{MAJOR}.\text{MINOR}.\text{PATCH}$$

II. Rules of Semantic Versioning:

Table 20.10 Rules of semantic versioning

Version partChange typeChange example
MAJORIncompatible major changeFundamental change of a core proposition
MINORBackward-compatible feature additionAdding indicators, adjusting weights
PATCHBackward-compatible bug fixCorrecting errors, clarifying wording

III. Extensions of Version Identification

For complex governance institutions, the version identification system may need to be extended:

Table 20.11 Extensions of version identification

Extension typeFormatUse
Pre-release versionMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-alpha.1Identifies a not-yet-officially-released version
Build metadataMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH+build.123Attaches build information
Branch identifierMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-branch.nameIdentifies a branch version
TimestampMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-20250101Attaches time information

IV. Version Identification of Each Protocol Stack Layer

Each layer of the protocol stack adopts an independent version identifier:

Table 20.12 Version identification of each protocol stack layer

LevelVersion identifier formatCurrent versionChange frequency
L₀L0-MAJOR.MINORL0-1.0Extremely low
L₁L1-MAJOR.MINOR.PATCHL1-0.9.0Low
L₂L2-MAJOR.MINOR.PATCHL2-0.9.0Medium-low
L₃L3-MAJOR.MINOR.PATCHL3-0.9.0Medium
L₄L4-MAJOR.MINOR.PATCHL4-0.9.0High

V. Management of Version Identification

SYSTEM VersionIdentificationSystem

COMPONENTS:

  • VersionRegistry: version registry
  • VersionGenerator: version number generator
  • VersionValidator: version number validator

OPERATIONS:

  • GenerateVersion(change_type): generate a new version number
  • RegisterVersion(version, content): register a version
  • ValidateVersion(version): validate the version number format
  • CompareVersions(v1, v2): compare version order
  • GetLatestVersion(): obtain the latest version

RULES:

  • Once assigned, the version number cannot be changed
  • The version number must be monotonically increasing
  • The version number must conform to semantic rules

END SYSTEM

Argument Node 20.2-A

Node IDCore ConclusionArgument Basis
20.2-AThe version identification system adopts semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), providing each protocol stack layer with an independent version identifier and supporting precise reference, comparison, and tracing of versionsVersion identification design principles and semantic versioning rules

§20.2.2 Change Tracking System

I. Functions of Change Tracking

The change tracking system records every change to an institution and provides a complete history of changes.

Definition 20.2.3 (Change Tracking)

Change tracking is a mechanism for systematically recording institutional changes, including the content, reason, time, responsible party, and impact of a change.

II. Structure of a Change Record

Each change should record the following information:

Table 20.13 Structure of a change record

FieldDescriptionNecessity
Change IDUnique identifier of the changeRequired
Version numberVersion number after the changeRequired
TimestampTime of the changeRequired
Change typeAddition/modification/deletionRequired
Change contentSpecific content of the changeRequired
Change reasonReason for the changeRequired
Responsible partyParty responsible for the changeRequired
Approval recordApproval process and resultRequired
Impact assessmentImpact analysis of the changeRecommended
Related changesOther related changesRecommended
Rollback guideHow to roll back this changeRecommended

III. Change Log Format

CHANGELOG FORMAT

[Version number] - Date

Change type

  • Description of change content

Change reason

  • Explanation of reason

Responsible party

  • Information on responsible party

Approval record

  • Approval process

Impact assessment

  • Impact analysis

Rollback guide

  • Rollback steps

Example:

[L2-0.9.1] - 2025-06-15

Modification

  • Adjust the weight parameters in the RFD calculation formula

Change reason

  • Stress testing showed that the original weights produced unreasonable results under extreme scenarios

Responsible party

  • Indicator System Working Group

Approval record

  • 2025-06-10 Working Group proposal
  • 2025-06-12 Expert review passed
  • 2025-06-15 Official release

Impact assessment

  • Affects the RFD calculation procedure at the L₄ layer
  • Calculation manual needs to be updated

Rollback guide

  • Restore the original weight parameters
  • Re-run the affected calculations

IV. Implementation of Change Tracking

SYSTEM ChangeTrackingSystem

COMPONENTS:

  • ChangeLog: change log storage
  • ChangeRecorder: change recorder
  • ChangeQuery: change query interface
  • DiffEngine: difference computation engine

OPERATIONS:

  • RecordChange(change): record a change
  • QueryChanges(criteria): query changes
  • ComputeDiff(v1, v2): compute version differences
  • GenerateReport(period): generate a change report
  • ExportHistory(format): export change history

INTEGRITY_RULES:

  • Change records cannot be deleted
  • Change records cannot be modified (only corrections may be appended)
  • All changes must have an approval record

END SYSTEM

V. Change Classification

Changes are classified by nature and impact:

Table 20.14 Change classification

Classification dimensionCategoryDescription
NatureAdditionAdding new content
ModificationModifying existing content
DeletionDeleting existing content
RefactoringStructural adjustment without functional change
ImpactMajorAffects core functions or principles
ModerateAffects some functions
MinorLimited impact
UrgencyUrgentRequires immediate handling
RoutineHandled by the normal process
PlannedImplemented as planned

§20.2.3 Branch Management System

I. Functions of Branch Management

The branch management system supports the creation of parallel institutional development paths, achieving experimental isolation and risk control.

Definition 20.2.4 (Branch)

A branch is an independent development path derived from the main version, allowing independent changes without affecting the main version.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Branch}(I, t) = \text{Fork}(\text{Main}(I), t)$$

Where:

  • $\text{Branch}(I, t)$: the branch created at time $t$
  • $\text{Fork}$: the derivation operation
  • $\text{Main}(I)$: the main version

II. Branch Types

Table 20.15 Branch types

Branch typeUseLifecycleMerge strategy
Main branchCurrently effective versionPermanentReceives merges
Development branchVersion under developmentMedium-termMerges into main branch
Experimental branchExperimental changesShort-termSelective merge
Pilot branchRegional/domain pilotMedium-termMerge after evaluation
Historical branchArchived historical versionPermanentNot merged
Emergency branchEmergency fixShort-termFast merge

Branch management strategy

STRATEGY BranchManagement

MAIN_BRANCH:

  • Always kept stable and available
  • Only accepts approved changes
  • Is the basis for all other branches

DEVELOPMENT_BRANCH:

  • Derived from the main branch
  • Used to develop new features
  • Merged back into the main branch when complete

EXPERIMENTAL_BRANCH:

  • Derived from the development branch or the main branch
  • Used for high-risk experiments
  • Merged if successful, discarded if not

PILOT_BRANCH:

  • Derived from the main branch
  • Used for pilots in a specific region or domain
  • Merged after successful evaluation

HOTFIX_BRANCH:

  • Derived from the main branch
  • Used for emergency fixes
  • Quickly merged back into the main branch

END STRATEGY

IV. Branch Creation Procedure

PROCEDURE CreateBranch(branch_type, source, purpose)

// Step 1: Validate creation conditions IF NOT ValidBranchType(branch_type) THEN RETURN ERROR("Invalid branch type") END IF

IF NOT SourceExists(source) THEN RETURN ERROR("Source branch does not exist") END IF

// Step 2: Create the branch new_branch = Fork(source) new_branch.type = branch_type new_branch.purpose = purpose new_branch.created_at = NOW() new_branch.created_by = CURRENT_USER

// Step 3: Register the branch RegisterBranch(new_branch)

// Step 4: Log the creation LogBranchCreation(new_branch)

RETURN new_branch

END PROCEDURE

§20.2.4 Merging and Conflict Resolution

I. The Concept of Merging

Merging is the operation of integrating the changes of a branch version into a target version.

Definition 20.2.5 (Merging)

Merging is the operation of integrating the changes of one branch into another branch, such that the target branch contains the changes of the source branch.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Merge}(\text{Source}, \text{Target}) \rightarrow \text{Target}'$$

Where $\text{Target}'$ contains the changes of both $\text{Source}$ and $\text{Target}$.

II. Merge Types

Table 20.16 Merge types

Merge typeDescriptionApplicable scenario
Fast-forward mergeThe target branch moves directly to the source branchThe target branch has no new changes
Three-way mergeMerging based on a common ancestorBoth branches have changes
Squash mergeCompressing multiple commits into oneCleaning up history
Selective mergeMerging only some changesPartial adoption

III. The Concept of Conflict

A conflict occurs when, during a merge, the source branch and the target branch have made different changes to the same content, making automatic merging impossible.

Definition 20.2.6 (Conflict)

A conflict occurs when, during a merge, the source branch and the target branch have made inconsistent changes to the same location, such that the merge result cannot be automatically determined.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Conflict}(S, T) \Leftrightarrow \exists c_1 \in \text{Changes}(S), c_2 \in \text{Changes}(T): \text{Target}(c_1) = \text{Target}(c_2) \land c_1 \neq c_2$$

IV. Conflict Types

Table 20.17 Conflict types

Conflict typeDescriptionResolution method
Textual conflictDifferent modifications to the same textManual selection or editing
Structural conflictInconsistency in structural adjustmentRedesign the structure
Semantic conflictInconsistency at the level of meaningResolution through negotiation
Principled conflictConflict touching on core principlesHigh-level decision

V. Conflict Resolution Strategies

Table 20.18 Conflict resolution strategies

StrategyDescriptionApplicable situation
Priority strategyDecide which side to adopt based on priorityPriorities are clear
Negotiation strategyReach agreement through negotiationBoth sides can negotiate
Hierarchical strategyRefer to a higher authority for decisionConflict is major
Hybrid strategyCombine the changes of both sidesChanges in non-conflicting parts
Deferral strategyTemporarily set aside the conflictTiming is not yet ripe

VI. Merge Procedure

PROCEDURE MergeBranches(source, target, strategy)

// Step 1: Pre-check IF NOT CanMerge(source, target) THEN RETURN ERROR("Cannot merge: prerequisites not met") END IF

// Step 2: Detect conflicts conflicts = DetectConflicts(source, target)

// Step 3: Handle conflicts IF conflicts NOT EMPTY THEN IF strategy = "abort" THEN RETURN ERROR("Conflicts detected, merge aborted") ELSE conflicts = ResolveConflicts(conflicts, strategy) IF conflicts NOT RESOLVED THEN RETURN {status: "conflicts_remaining", conflicts: conflicts} END IF END IF END IF

// Step 4: Execute the merge merged = ExecuteMerge(source, target)

// Step 5: Validate the merge result IF NOT ValidateMerge(merged) THEN RETURN ERROR("Merge validation failed") END IF

// Step 6: Log the merge LogMerge(source, target, merged, strategy)

RETURN {status: "success", result: merged}

END PROCEDURE

§20.3 Design of the Rollback Mechanism

§20.3.1 The Concept and Types of Rollback

I. The Concept of Rollback

Rollback is the core capability of versioned governance; it means restoring an institution to a previous version.

Definition 20.3.1 (Rollback)

Rollback is the operation of restoring an institution from the current version to a target version, undoing some or all of the changes of the current version.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Rollback}(I, v_{\text{current}}, v_{\text{target}}) \rightarrow I'$$

Where $I'$ is the institutional state restored to $v_{\text{target}}$.

II. Types of Rollback

Table 20.19 Rollback types

Rollback typeDescriptionApplicable situation
UndoUndo the most recent changeA single change encounters a problem
RevertRevert to a specified versionNeed to restore to a particular state
ResetReset to the initial stateComplete overturning
Partial rollbackRoll back only part of the changesPart of the changes encounter a problem
Cascade rollbackRollback triggers associated rollbacksChanges are mutually dependent

III. Undo

Undo is the simplest form of rollback, undoing the most recent change.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Undo}(I) = \text{Rollback}(I, v_n, v_{n-1})$$

IV. Cascade Rollback

Cascade rollback means that when a change is rolled back, other changes that depend on it must also be rolled back.

Formal expression:

$$\text{CascadeRollback}(I, c) = \text{Rollback}(I, c) \cup \bigcup_{c' \in \text{Dependents}(c)} \text{Rollback}(I, c')$$

V. The Semantics of Rollback

Rollback is not merely a technical operation; it also involves considerations at the semantic level:

Table 20.20 Semantic levels of rollback

LevelDescriptionDifficulty
Text rollbackRestoring the rule textLow
Procedure rollbackRestoring the operating procedureMedium
Organizational rollbackRestoring the organizational arrangementHigh
Behavioral rollbackUndoing actions already implementedExtremely high or impossible
Cognitive rollbackRestoring the cognitive stateImpossible

Argument Node 20.3-A

Node IDCore ConclusionArgument Basis

§20.3.2 Trigger Conditions for Rollback

I. Types of Trigger Conditions

Rollback should not be triggered arbitrarily; clear trigger conditions are required.

Table 20.21 Types of rollback trigger conditions

TypeDescriptionExample
Effect triggerThe change does not achieve the expected effectIndicators do not improve
Problem triggerThe change produces new problemsSide effects
Feedback triggerStakeholders objectProtest, appeal
Risk triggerThe change brings new risksSafety risk
Timing triggerEnvironmental change makes the change no longer applicableThe conditions have changed

II. Active Trigger Conditions

Active triggering means that the governing subject actively decides to roll back:

Table 20.22 Active trigger conditions

ConditionThresholdResponse
Effect significantly below expectation< 50% of the expected effectEvaluate rollback
Serious negative effects appearHigh severityEmergency rollback
Key indicators deteriorateDeterioration exceeds thresholdEvaluate rollback
Loss of consensusSupport rate falls below thresholdEvaluate rollback
Fundamental environmental changePreconditions no longer holdEvaluate rollback

III. Passive Trigger Conditions

Passive triggering means that rollback is automatically triggered when preset conditions are met:

Table 20.23 Passive trigger conditions

ConditionTrigger mechanismResponse time
Safety threshold breachedAutomatic monitoringImmediate
Deadline reachedScheduled checkAs planned
Dependency failureDependency monitoringImmediate
External requestExternal triggerAs agreed

IV. Trigger Decision Procedure

PROCEDURE EvaluateRollbackTrigger(institution, version)

// Step 1: Collect trigger signals signals = CollectSignals(institution, version)

// Step 2: Evaluate each trigger condition triggered_conditions = [] FOR each condition IN TriggerConditions DO IF EvaluateCondition(condition, signals) THEN triggered_conditions.APPEND(condition) END IF END FOR

// Step 3: Determine priority IF triggered_conditions NOT EMPTY THEN priority = DeterminePriority(triggered_conditions) ELSE RETURN {trigger: FALSE} END IF

// Step 4: Generate a trigger recommendation recommendation = GenerateRecommendation(triggered_conditions, priority)

RETURN { trigger: TRUE, conditions: triggered_conditions, priority: priority, recommendation: recommendation }

END PROCEDURE

Formal expression:

$$\text{TriggerRollback}(I, v) \Leftrightarrow \bigvee_{i} \text{Condition}_i(I, v)$$

V. Emergency Rollback Procedure

In emergency situations, a simplified procedure may be adopted for rapid response:

PROCEDURE EmergencyRollback(institution, target_version)

// Step 1: Rapid assessment IF NOT IsEmergency(institution) THEN RETURN ERROR("Not an emergency") END IF

// Step 2: Authority check IF NOT HasEmergencyAuthority(CURRENT_USER) THEN RETURN ERROR("Insufficient authority for emergency rollback") END IF

// Step 3: Execute rollback ExecuteRollback(institution, target_version)

// Step 4: Notify relevant parties NotifyStakeholders(institution, target_version)

// Step 5: Follow-up procedure ScheduleReview(institution, target_version)

RETURN {status: "emergency_rollback_completed"}

END PROCEDURE

VI. Partial Rollback Procedure

Partial rollback rolls back only part of the changes:

PROCEDURE PartialRollback(institution, changes_to_rollback)

// Step 1: Analyze dependencies dependencies = AnalyzeDependencies(changes_to_rollback)

// Step 2: Determine the rollbackable set rollbackable = DetermineRollbackable(changes_to_rollback, dependencies)

// Step 3: Execute partial rollback FOR each change IN rollbackable DO RollbackChange(institution, change) END FOR

// Step 4: Validate consistency IF NOT ValidateConsistency(institution) THEN RETURN ERROR("Inconsistency after partial rollback") END IF

RETURN {status: "partial_rollback_completed", rolled_back: rollbackable}

END PROCEDURE
