[1] The concept of the theory-policy gap draws on the discussion of the "knowledge-action gap" in policy science. This gap has been widely discussed in fields such as environmental policy and public health policy. See: Nutley, S. M., Walter, I., & Davies, H. T. O. (2007). Using Evidence: How Research Can Inform Public Services. Policy Press.

[2] The concept of policy translation draws on the research tradition of "knowledge translation", especially its application in the fields of medicine and public health. See: Graham, I. D., et al. (2006). Lost in knowledge translation: Time for a map? Journal of Continuing Education in the Health Professions, 26(1), 13-24.

[3] The analysis of the abstraction gap draws on the discussion of "abstract" and "concrete" in philosophy. Abstraction is the process of extracting common features from concrete things, whereas policy-making requires the application of abstract principles to concrete contexts. See: Rosen, G. (2020). Abstract Objects. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

[4] The analysis of the context gap draws on the philosophical tradition of contextualism, which emphasizes the context dependence of knowledge and norms. See: DeRose, K. (2009). The Case for Contextualism. Oxford University Press.

[5] The analysis of the operability gap draws on the discussion of "policy operability" in policy science. Operability refers to the degree to which a policy can actually be implemented. See: Howlett, M. (2011). Designing Public Policies: Principles and Instruments. Routledge.

[6] The analysis of the legitimacy gap draws on the discussion of "legitimacy" in political philosophy, especially the distinction between argumentative legitimacy and democratic legitimacy. See: Peter, F. (2017). Political Legitimacy. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

[7] The classification of policy instruments draws on the classic classification in policy science. Hood (1983) proposed the NATO classification (Nodality, Authority, Treasure, Organization), on the basis of which this work makes adjustments. See: Hood, C. C. (1983). The Tools of Government. Macmillan.

[8] The analysis of regulatory instruments draws on research in regulation theory. Regulation is an important means by which the government intervenes in the market and society. See: Baldwin, R., Cave, M., & Lodge, M. (2012). Understanding Regulation: Theory, Strategy, and Practice (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press.

[9] The analysis of economic instruments draws on the discussion of market-based instruments in environmental economics. Economic instruments influence behavior by changing the incentive structure. See: Stavins, R. N. (2003). Experience with market-based environmental policy instruments. In K.-G. Mäler & J. R. Vincent (Eds.), Handbook of Environmental Economics (Vol. 1, pp. 355-435). Elsevier.

[10] The analysis of informational instruments draws on research in behavioral public policy. Informational instruments influence behavior by providing information and are an important component of "nudge" strategies. See: Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge: Improving Decisions about Health, Wealth, and Happiness. Yale University Press.

[11] The methods of policy impact assessment draw on the practice of Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA). RIA is a policy assessment tool adopted by many countries and international organizations. See: OECD. (2020). Regulatory Impact Assessment. OECD Publishing.

[12] The analysis of policy at the international level draws on research in international law and international relations. The formulation of international policy involves a complex process of international coordination. See: Goldstein, J., et al. (2000). Introduction: Legalization and world politics. International Organization, 54(3), 385-399.

[13] The concept of soft law has been widely discussed in international law. Soft law refers to international documents that do not possess legal binding force but have normative influence. See: Shelton, D. (Ed.). (2000). Commitment and Compliance: The Role of Non-Binding Norms in the International Legal System. Oxford University Press.

[14] The analysis of policy at the national level draws on the tradition of comparative policy research. There are significant differences in the policy-making processes of different countries. See: Howlett, M., Ramesh, M., & Perl, A. (2009). Studying Public Policy: Policy Cycles and Policy Subsystems (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.

[15] The analysis of policy at the organizational level draws on research in organization theory and corporate social responsibility. Corporate policy is an important component of corporate governance. See: Crane, A., et al. (Eds.). (2008). The Oxford Handbook of Corporate Social Responsibility. Oxford University Press.

[16] The analysis of guidelines at the individual level draws on research in professional ethics. Professional codes of ethics are important tools for regulating the behavior of professionals. See: Davis, M. (2002). Profession, Code, and Ethics. Ashgate.

[17] The distinction between academic recommendation and policy decision draws on the discussion of the "science-policy interface" in science policy research. The role of scientists in the policy process needs to be clearly delimited. See: Pielke, R. A. (2007). The Honest Broker: Making Sense of Science in Policy and Politics. Cambridge University Press.

[18] The analysis of democratic procedure draws on research in democratic theory, especially the tradition of deliberative democracy. See: Gutmann, A., & Thompson, D. (2004). Why Deliberative Democracy? Princeton University Press.

[19] The issue of the representation of future generations in democratic procedure is an important topic in the study of intergenerational justice. See: Tremmel, J. C. (Ed.). (2006). Handbook of Intergenerational Justice. Edward Elgar.

[20] The ethical constraints of policy translation draw on the discussion of research ethics and the ethics of science communication. Scholars have specific ethical responsibilities in the policy process. See: Resnik, D. B. (2007). The Price of Truth: How Money Affects the Norms of Science. Oxford University Press.

The core task of Part Six (Policy Translation) is to translate the theoretical framework, indicator system, normative principles, and institutional design established in the first five parts into operable policy recommendations. This chapter (Chapter 21b) has established the general framework of policy translation, and subsequent chapters will further refine the policy guidelines for different actors and the implementation roadmap.

Policy translation is the key link through which this work moves from theory to practice. Without effective policy translation, even the best theory can only remain at the level of academic discussion. But policy translation also has its boundaries—academic recommendation cannot replace democratic procedure, and the validity of theory cannot automatically translate into the legitimacy of policy. This chapter has clarified this boundary, laying the methodological foundation for the subsequent policy recommendations.

Footnotes

Chapter 21-II Footnotes

[1] The concept of the theory-policy gap draws on the discussion of the "knowledge-action gap" in policy science. This gap has been widely discussed in fields such as environmental policy and public health policy. See: Nutley, S. M., Walter, I., & Davies, H. T. O. (2007). Using Evidence: How Research Can Inform Public Services. Policy Press.

[2] The concept of policy translation draws on the research tradition of "knowledge translation," especially its application in medicine and public health. See: Graham, I. D., et al. (2006). Lost in knowledge translation: Time for a map? Journal of Continuing Education in the Health Professions, 26(1), 13-24.

[3] The analysis of the abstraction gap draws on philosophical discussion of "abstract" and "concrete." Abstraction is the process of extracting common features from concrete things, whereas policymaking requires applying abstract principles to concrete situations. See: Rosen, G. (2020). Abstract Objects. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

[4] The analysis of the contextuality gap draws on the philosophical tradition of contextualism, which emphasizes the context-dependence of knowledge and norms. See: DeRose, K. (2009). The Case for Contextualism. Oxford University Press.

[5] The analysis of the operability gap draws on discussion of "policy operability" in policy science. Operability is the degree to which a policy can actually be implemented. See: Howlett, M. (2011). Designing Public Policies: Principles and Instruments. Routledge.

[6] The analysis of the legitimacy gap draws on discussion of "legitimacy" in political philosophy, in particular the distinction between justificatory legitimacy and democratic legitimacy. See: Peter, F. (2017). Political Legitimacy. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

[7] The classification of policy instruments draws on classic classifications in policy science. Hood (1983) proposed the NATO classification (Nodality, Authority, Treasure, Organization); this work adapts it. See: Hood, C. C. (1983). The Tools of Government. Macmillan.

[8] The analysis of regulatory instruments draws on research in regulation theory. Regulation is an important means by which government intervenes in the market and society. See: Baldwin, R., Cave, M., & Lodge, M. (2012). Understanding Regulation: Theory, Strategy, and Practice (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press.

[9] The analysis of economic instruments draws on discussion of market-based instruments in environmental economics. Economic instruments influence behavior by altering incentive structures. See: Stavins, R. N. (2003). Experience with market-based environmental policy instruments. In K.-G. Mäler & J. R. Vincent (Eds.), Handbook of Environmental Economics (Vol. 1, pp. 355-435). Elsevier.

[10] The analysis of information instruments draws on research in behavioral public policy. Information instruments influence behavior by providing information and are an important component of "nudge" strategies. See: Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge: Improving Decisions about Health, Wealth, and Happiness. Yale University Press.

[11] The method of policy impact assessment draws on the practice of Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA). RIA is a policy assessment tool adopted by many states and international organizations. See: OECD. (2020). Regulatory Impact Assessment. OECD Publishing.

[12] The analysis of policy at the international level draws on research in international law and international relations. The formulation of international policy involves a complex process of international coordination. See: Goldstein, J., et al. (2000). Introduction: Legalization and world politics. International Organization, 54(3), 385-399.

[13] The concept of soft law has been widely discussed in international law. Soft law refers to international instruments that are not legally binding but have normative influence. See: Shelton, D. (Ed.). (2000). Commitment and Compliance: The Role of Non-Binding Norms in the International Legal System. Oxford University Press.

[14] The analysis of policy at the national level draws on the tradition of comparative policy research. There are significant differences in the policymaking processes of different countries. See: Howlett, M., Ramesh, M., & Perl, A. (2009). Studying Public Policy: Policy Cycles and Policy Subsystems (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.

[15] The analysis of policy at the organizational level draws on research in organization theory and corporate social responsibility. Corporate policy is an important component of corporate governance. See: Crane, A., et al. (Eds.). (2008). The Oxford Handbook of Corporate Social Responsibility. Oxford University Press.

[16] The analysis of guidance at the individual level draws on research in professional ethics. Codes of professional ethics are important instruments for regulating the conduct of professionals. See: Davis, M. (2002). Profession, Code, and Ethics. Ashgate.

[17] The distinction between academic advice and policy decisions draws on discussion of the "science-policy interface" in science policy research. The role of scientists in the policy process needs to be clearly defined. See: Pielke, R. A. (2007). The Honest Broker: Making Sense of Science in Policy and Politics. Cambridge University Press.

[18] The analysis of democratic procedures draws on research in democratic theory, in particular the tradition of deliberative democracy. See: Gutmann, A., & Thompson, D. (2004). Why Deliberative Democracy? Princeton University Press.

[19] The representation of future generations in democratic procedures is an important topic in the study of intergenerational justice. See: Tremmel, J. C. (Ed.). (2006). Handbook of Intergenerational Justice. Edward Elgar.

[20] The ethical constraints on policy translation draw on discussion in research ethics and the ethics of science communication. Scholars bear particular ethical responsibilities in the policy process. See: Resnik, D. B. (2007). The Price of Truth: How Money Affects the Norms of Science. Oxford University Press.

Chapter Opening Guide

I. Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 21b established the general framework of policy translation, clarifying the translation path, methods, and boundaries from theory to policy. Building on this foundation, the present chapter provides concrete policy guidelines for different types of actors, thereby realizing the "audience differentiation" of policy translation.

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

Policy guidelines for different actors derive directly from the core propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{ActorSpecificGuidelines} \xleftarrow{\text{audience differentiation}} \text{New Three Views}$$

Specifically:

  • NC (the New Cosmological View) → relational ontology requires different actors to bear differentiated responsibilities within the relational network
  • NL (the New View of Life) → the diversity of negentropic organizations requires policy guidelines to adapt to different organizational forms
  • NK (the New View of Cognition) → the distributed nature of knowledge requires different actors to contribute their respective cognitive resources

V. Core Questions

This chapter attempts to answer the following fundamental questions:

Core Question 1: What roles should different types of actors play in the cosmic responsibility framework? Core Question 2: How can policy guidelines suited to the characteristics of different actors be designed? Core Question 3: How should different actors coordinate and cooperate with one another? Core Question 4: How can policy guidelines achieve contextual adaptability while maintaining consistency in principles?

VI. Boundary Statement

All content of this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Nature as academic recommendations: This chapter provides academic policy recommendations, not legally binding policy texts
  2. Primacy of democratic procedure: The actual adoption of any policy must undergo democratic procedure
  3. Context-dependence: Policy recommendations need to be adjusted according to specific contexts
  4. Open revision: The design of this chapter is itself revisable

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • If the reader is a staff member of an international organization, they are advised to focus on §21c.1
  • If the reader is a government official, they are advised to focus on §21c.2
  • If the reader is a corporate manager, they are advised to focus on §21c.3
  • If the reader is a researcher, they are advised to focus on §21c.4
  • If the reader is a member of civil society, they are advised to focus on §21c.5

§21c.1 Policy Guidelines for International Organizations

§21c.1.1 The United Nations and Its Specialized Agencies

I. The Role of the United Nations in the Cosmic Responsibility Framework

As the most universal international organization, the United Nations plays an irreplaceable role in the implementation of the cosmic responsibility framework.

Definition 21c.1.1 (The UN's cosmic responsibility role)

The role of the United Nations in the cosmic responsibility framework is to serve as a global coordination platform that promotes the formation of international consensus on cosmic responsibility principles, norm development, and institution building.

Formal expression:

$$\text{UN\_Role} = \langle \text{Coordination}, \text{NormDevelopment}, \text{InstitutionBuilding} \rangle$$

II. Policy Recommendations for the United Nations General Assembly

Table 21c.1 Policy recommendations for the United Nations General Assembly

Recommendation NumberRecommendation ContentImplementation PathPriority
UNGA-1Adopt a declaration on cosmic responsibility principlesMember state proposal → committee deliberation → General Assembly voteHigh
UNGA-2Establish a working group on cosmic responsibilityEstablished by General Assembly resolutionHigh
UNGA-3Incorporate cosmic responsibility into the sustainable development agendaAmend the SDG frameworkMedium
UNGA-4Promote negotiations for an international convention on intergenerational responsibilityLaunch intergovernmental negotiationsMedium

Detailed Explanation of Recommendation UNGA-1

Recommendation Name: Adopt a declaration on cosmic responsibility principles

Basis for the Recommendation:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology) requires the establishment of a global normative framework
  • NL-2 (negentropic organizations) requires civilization to bear responsibility for maintaining complexity
  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge) requires the formation of consensus through international consultation

Recommendation Content:

It is recommended that the United Nations General Assembly adopt a declaration on cosmic responsibility principles, affirming the following core principles:

  1. The Principle of Recursive Freedom: protect the possibility space of future generations and other intelligent subjects
  2. The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility: bear the responsibility for maintaining cosmic complexity
  3. The Principle of Reversibility: prioritize reversible actions under deep uncertainty

Draft Declaration Framework:

United Nations Declaration on Cosmic Responsibility Principles (Draft Framework)

Preamble

Recognizing that the impact of human activities is extending beyond the Earth... Recognizing the far-reaching implications of new technologies such as artificial intelligence... Recognizing the long-term impact of contemporary decisions on future generations...

Part One: Basic Principles

Article 1 The Principle of Recursive Freedom Article 2 The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility Article 3 The Principle of Reversibility Article 4 The Principle of Intergenerational Equity Article 5 The Principle of Respect for Plural Subjects

Part Two: Implementation Mechanisms

Article 6 International Cooperation Article 7 Capacity Building Article 8 Information Sharing Article 9 Monitoring and Assessment

Part Three: Final Provisions

Article 10 Interpretation Article 11 Review

Implementation Path:

PROCEDURE UNGA_Declaration_Process

// Step 1: Issue introduction (1-2 years) academic_advocacy = AcademicCommunityAdvocacy() member_state_interest = BuildMemberStateInterest()

// Step 2: Working group establishment (1 year) working_group = EstablishWorkingGroup() expert_consultation = ConductExpertConsultation()

// Step 3: Draft drafting (1-2 years) draft = DraftDeclaration(working_group, expert_consultation) member_state_consultation = ConsultMemberStates(draft)

// Step 4: Negotiation and adoption (1-2 years) negotiation = ConductNegotiation(draft, member_state_consultation) final_text = FinalizeText(negotiation) adoption = GAAdoption(final_text)

RETURN adoption

END PROCEDURE

Detailed Explanation of the UNESCO Policy Recommendations

(1) Recommendation UNESCO-1: Incorporate cosmic responsibility into the education agenda

Basis for the Recommendation:

  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge) requires cultivating awareness of cosmic responsibility through education
  • Education is the foundation of long-term normative change

Recommendation Content:

  1. Add a cosmic responsibility dimension to the global citizenship education framework
  2. Develop educational resource packages on cosmic responsibility
  3. Train teachers to conduct cosmic responsibility education
  4. Establish an international exchange network for cosmic responsibility education

(2) Recommendation UNESCO-2: Expand the AI ethics recommendation to include cosmic responsibility

Basis for the Recommendation:

  • UNESCO adopted the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in 2021
  • This recommendation can be expanded to include considerations of cosmic responsibility

Recommendation Content:

  1. Add a "recursive freedom" dimension to AI ethical principles
  2. Add long-term and intergenerational impacts to AI impact assessment
  3. Add representatives of future generations to AI governance mechanisms

§21c.1.2 International Space Agencies

I. The Cosmic Responsibility Role of International Space Agencies

International space agencies hold particular importance in the cosmic responsibility framework, because space activities are the primary pathway for human activities to expand beyond the Earth.

Definition 21c.1.2 (The cosmic responsibility role of international space agencies)

The role of international space agencies in the cosmic responsibility framework is to serve as norm-setters and overseers of space activities, ensuring that space activities conform to cosmic responsibility principles.

Formal expression:

$$\text{SpaceAgency\_Role} = \langle \text{NormSetting}, \text{Oversight}, \text{Coordination} \rangle$$

§21c.1.3 International AI Governance Bodies

I. The Cosmic Responsibility Role of International AI Governance Bodies

With the rapid development of AI technology, the importance of international AI governance bodies within the cosmic responsibility framework has become increasingly prominent.

Definition 21c.1.3 (The cosmic responsibility role of international AI governance bodies)

The role of international AI governance bodies in the cosmic responsibility framework is to ensure that AI development conforms to cosmic responsibility principles, especially the Principle of Recursive Freedom and the Principle of Reversibility.

Formal expression:

$$\text{AIGov\_Role} = \langle \text{Alignment}, \text{Safety}, \text{Ethics} \rangle$$

Detailed Explanation of Recommendation OECD-AI-1

Recommendation Name: Incorporate cosmic responsibility into the OECD AI Principles

Basis for the Recommendation:

  • The OECD adopted the AI Principles in 2019, which have been adopted by the G20
  • These principles can be expanded to include considerations of cosmic responsibility

Recommendation Content:

It is recommended that the following content be added to the OECD AI Principles:

  1. The Principle of Recursive Freedom: the design and deployment of AI systems should protect the possibility space of humans and other intelligent subjects
  2. Long-term impact consideration: the assessment of AI systems should include long-term and intergenerational impacts
  3. Priority of reversibility: under deep uncertainty, reversible AI deployment options should be prioritized

Recommendation Name: Incorporate cosmic responsibility into AI safety standards

Basis for the Recommendation:

  • The international community is discussing the establishment of an international AI safety institution
  • AI safety standards should include considerations of cosmic responsibility

Recommendation Content:

It is recommended that the following cosmic responsibility requirements be incorporated into AI safety standards:

  1. Possibility space assessment: assess the impact of AI systems on the possibility space of humans and other intelligent subjects
  2. Recursive freedom check: verify whether AI systems respect the Principle of Recursive Freedom
  3. Reversibility requirement: require AI systems to be reversible or capable of being shut down
  4. Long-term impact assessment: assess the long-term and intergenerational impacts of AI systems

Detailed Explanation of Recommendation SPACE-1

Recommendation Name: Incorporate CSIA requirements into space law

Basis for the Recommendation:

  • Many countries already have space law or are in the process of formulating it
  • CSIA is a core tool for cosmic responsibility assessment

Recommendation Content:

It is recommended that the following clauses be added to space law:

Article X Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment

  1. For space activities that may produce significant cosmic-scale impacts, a cosmic-scale impact assessment (CSIA) shall be conducted.
  1. The CSIA shall assess the following dimensions:

(a) Scope of spatial impact (b) Depth of temporal impact (c) Severity of impact (d) Reversibility (e) Impact on other subjects (f) Uncertainty

  1. The CSIA report shall be submitted to the competent authority for review and made public.
  1. The competent authority shall decide whether to approve the space activity based on the CSIA results.
  1. The implementing rules of this Article shall be formulated by the competent authority.

  • The EU AI Act and others have already established AI regulatory frameworks
  • The Principle of Recursive Freedom is a core principle of cosmic responsibility

Recommendation Content:

It is recommended that the following clauses be added to AI law:

Article X The Principle of Recursive Freedom

  1. The design, development, and deployment of AI systems shall respect the Principle of Recursive Freedom, that is, protect the possibility space of humans and other intelligent subjects.
  1. AI systems shall not:

(a) irreversibly compress the space of human choices (b) deprive humans of ultimate control over the AI system (c) produce irreversible large-scale negative impacts

  1. High-risk AI systems shall undergo a recursive freedom assessment, assessing their impact on the possibility space.
  1. AI systems that violate the provisions of this Article shall not be placed on the market or used.

ETH-REV-4Establish a reversibility assessment procedureProcedure revisionMedium

Detailed Explanation of Recommendation ETH-REV-1

Recommendation Name: Incorporate cosmic responsibility into ethics review standards

Basis for the Recommendation:

  • Existing ethics review mainly focuses on short-term impacts and direct participants
  • Cosmic responsibility requires consideration of long-term impacts and broader subjects

Recommendation Content:

It is recommended that ethics review bodies add the following cosmic responsibility dimensions to their review standards:

Cosmic Responsibility Dimensions of Ethics Review

  1. Long-term impact assessment
  • What are the long-term impacts of the research/technology?
  • What is the time span of the impacts?
  • Are the long-term impacts predictable?
  1. Intergenerational impact assessment
  • What impact does the research/technology have on future generations?
  • Will it compress the possibility space of future generations?
  • Is there consideration of intergenerational equity?
  1. Reversibility assessment
  • Are the impacts of the research/technology reversible?
  • If negative impacts arise, can they be rolled back?
  • Are there alternative, more reversible options?
  1. Broad subjective impact assessment
  • What impact does the research/technology have on non-human subjects?
  • Have the impacts on ecosystems been considered?
  • Have the impacts on possible AI subjects been considered?
  1. Negentropy impact assessment
  • What impact does the research/technology have on cosmic complexity?
  • Will it lead to irreversible negentropy loss?
  • Is there consideration of negentropy responsibility?

International organizations should play a core role in global coordination, norm development, and institution building.

Preview of Subsequent Chapters

This chapter has provided concrete policy guidelines for different actors, and subsequent chapters will further refine them:

Chapter 21d: Implementation Roadmap and Monitoring Framework

Will design the concrete implementation roadmap and monitoring framework for policy implementation, including:

  1. Short-, medium-, and long-term implementation roadmaps
  2. Milestones and key performance indicators
  3. Monitoring and evaluation framework
  4. Adaptive management mechanisms
  5. Feedback and revision procedures

[1] United Nations General Assembly declarations are an important form of international soft law. Although not legally binding, they have significant normative influence. Historically, many important international norms began as United Nations General Assembly declarations, such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. See: Shelton, D. (Ed.). (2000). Commitment and Compliance: The Role of Non-Binding Norms in the International Legal System. Oxford University Press.

[2] COPUOS (United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space) is the main body responsible for space affairs under the United Nations framework. COPUOS has developed a number of guidelines on space activities, such as the space debris mitigation guidelines and the long-term sustainability guidelines. See: United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs. (2019). Guidelines for the Long-term Sustainability of Outer Space Activities. United Nations.

[3] UNESCO adopted the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence in 2021, the world's first international normative document on AI ethics. This work recommends expanding it on this basis to incorporate considerations of cosmic responsibility. See: UNESCO. (2021). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. UNESCO.

[4] The IAA (International Academy of Astronautics) has developed protocols and declarations on SETI (the search for extraterrestrial intelligence) and METI (the sending of messages to extraterrestrial intelligence). These protocols need to be updated to incorporate considerations of cosmic responsibility. See: Billingham, J., et al. (Eds.). (1999). Social Implications of the Detection of an Extraterrestrial Civilization. SETI Press.

[5] COSPAR (Committee on Space Research) is responsible for formulating planetary protection policy to prevent terrestrial organisms from contaminating other celestial bodies (forward contamination) and extraterrestrial material from contaminating the Earth (backward contamination). See: COSPAR. (2020). COSPAR Policy on Planetary Protection. COSPAR.

[6] The OECD adopted the AI Principles in 2019, which have been adopted by the G20. These principles include inclusive growth, sustainable development, human-centered values, transparency, accountability, and so on. See: OECD. (2019). Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence. OECD.

[7] The GPAI (Global Partnership on AI) is an international AI governance initiative launched by multiple governments, aimed at promoting responsible AI development. See: GPAI. (2020). Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence. GPAI.

[8] The international AI safety institution is a new institution currently under discussion by the international community. The 2023 UK AI Safety Summit proposed the initiative to establish an international AI safety institution. See: UK Government. (2023). The Bletchley Declaration. UK Government.

[9] Intergenerational responsibility clauses in constitutions have precedents in some countries. Article 20a of the German Basic Law provides for the state's responsibility to protect the natural foundations of life, including responsibility toward future generations. See: Tremmel, J. C. (Ed.). (2006). Handbook of Intergenerational Justice. Edward Elgar.

[10] Environmental impact assessment (EIA) is an environmental management tool adopted by many countries. This work recommends adding long-term and intergenerational impact dimensions to EIA. See: Glasson, J., Therivel, R., & Chadwick, A. (2012). Introduction to Environmental Impact Assessment (4th ed.). Routledge.

[11] The standing of future generations has been developed in the judicial practice of some countries. The Supreme Court of the Philippines recognized the standing of future generations in Oposa v. Factoran (1993). See: Oposa v. Factoran, G.R. No. 101083 (Supreme Court of the Philippines, 1993).

[12] Corporate social responsibility (CSR) and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) frameworks provide references for enterprises to bear social responsibility. This work recommends expanding them on this basis to incorporate cosmic responsibility. See: Crane, A., et al. (Eds.). (2008). The Oxford Handbook of Corporate Social Responsibility. Oxford University Press.

[13] Planetary protection is an important ethical and legal requirement of space activities. COSPAR's planetary protection policy classifies missions into different categories and sets different protection requirements. See: Rummel, J. D. (2001). "Planetary Exploration in the Time of Astrobiology: Protecting Against Biological Contamination." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 98(5), 2128-2131.

[14] AI alignment is a core issue in AI safety research, aimed at ensuring that the goals and behavior of AI systems are consistent with human values. See: Russell, S. (2019). Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control. Viking.

[15] The institutional review board (IRB) is the primary mechanism for research ethics review. This work recommends expanding the scope of IRB review to incorporate considerations of cosmic responsibility. See: Shamoo, A. E., & Resnik, D. B. (2015). Responsible Conduct of Research (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.

[16] Deliberative democracy is an important school of democratic theory, emphasizing the formation of public decisions through citizens' deliberation. Citizens' juries, consensus conferences, and the like are concrete forms of deliberative democracy. See: Fishkin, J. S. (2009). When the People Speak: Deliberative Democracy and Public Consultation. Oxford University Press.

[17] Public interest litigation is an important pathway for civil society to participate in environmental governance. Some countries have already established environmental public interest litigation systems. See: Pring, G., & Pring, C. (2009). Greening Justice: Creating and Improving Environmental Courts and Tribunals. The Access Initiative.

[18] Science communication is the process of conveying scientific knowledge to the public. Effective science communication is crucial for cultivating public awareness of cosmic responsibility. See: Bucchi, M., & Trench, B. (Eds.). (2014). Routledge Handbook of Public Communication of Science and Technology (2nd ed.). Routledge.

[19] Global citizenship education is an educational concept promoted by UNESCO, aimed at cultivating students' global awareness and sense of responsibility. This work recommends adding a cosmic responsibility dimension on this basis. See: UNESCO. (2015). Global Citizenship Education: Topics and Learning Objectives. UNESCO.

[20] Multi-stakeholder governance is an important model of global governance, emphasizing the participation of multiple subjects such as governments, enterprises, and civil society. See: Hemmati, M. (2002). Multi-stakeholder Processes for Governance and Sustainability: Beyond Deadlock and Conflict. Earthscan.

Chapter Opening Guide

I. Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 21b established the general framework of policy translation, and Chapter 21c provided specific policy guidelines for different actors. Building on this foundation, this chapter designs the specific implementation roadmap and monitoring framework for policy implementation, completing the "closed loop" of policy translation.

III. Core Tasks of This Chapter

Task No.Task ContentDeliverable
T21d.1Design a phased implementation roadmapFour-phase roadmap
T21d.2Establish a monitoring frameworkMonitoring indicators, data collection, evaluation procedures
T21d.3Design a feedback and adjustment mechanismFeedback collection, problem identification, adjustment decisions
T21d.4Determine success criteria and milestonesShort-, medium-, and long-term success criteria, milestone list

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The implementation roadmap and monitoring framework directly embody the core propositions of the New Three Views:

$$\text{ImplementationFramework} \xleftarrow{\text{operationalization}} \text{New Three Views}$$

Specifically:

  • NC (the New Cosmological View) → process ontology requires the implementation roadmap to have dynamic adaptability
  • NL (the New View of Life) → the persistence of negentropic organization requires the monitoring framework to attend to system health
  • NK (the New View of Cognition) → the revisability of knowledge requires the feedback mechanism to support continuous learning

V. Core Questions

This chapter seeks to answer the following fundamental questions:

Core Question One: How can cosmic responsibility policy recommendations be translated into an actionable implementation roadmap? Core Question Two: How can the progress and effects of policy implementation be monitored? Core Question Three: How can feedback and adjustment be carried out based on monitoring results? Core Question Four: How can success criteria and milestones for policy implementation be defined?

VI. Boundary Statement

All content in this chapter is subject to the following boundary constraints:

  1. Nature as academic recommendation: what this chapter provides are academic implementation recommendations, not a binding implementation plan
  2. Context dependence: the implementation roadmap needs to be adjusted according to the specific context
  3. Acknowledgment of uncertainty: long-term prediction involves fundamental uncertainty
  4. Open revision: the design of this chapter itself is also revisable

VII. Reading Suggestions

  • If the reader is concerned with implementation planning, it is recommended to focus on §21d.1
  • If the reader is concerned with monitoring and evaluation, it is recommended to focus on §21d.2
  • If the reader is concerned with adaptive management, it is recommended to focus on §21d.3
  • If the reader is concerned with success criteria, it is recommended to focus on §21d.4

§21d.1 Implementation Roadmap

§21d.1.1 Phase One: The Foundation Phase (1–3 Years)

I. Strategic Positioning of the Foundation Phase

The foundation phase is the initial stage of cosmic responsibility policy implementation, whose core task is to build the conceptual foundation, form preliminary consensus, and launch pilot projects.

Definition 21d.1.1 (Foundation Phase)

The foundation phase is the first stage of cosmic responsibility policy implementation (1–3 years), whose core task is to build the conceptual foundation, form preliminary consensus, and launch pilot projects, laying the groundwork for subsequent phases.

Formal expression:

$$\text{FoundationPhase} = \langle \text{ConceptBuilding}, \text{ConsensusForming}, \text{PilotInitiation} \rangle$$

The pilot phase is the second stage of cosmic responsibility policy implementation, whose core task is to carry out pilots in selected fields and regions, verify the feasibility of policy recommendations, and accumulate implementation experience.

The pilot phase is the second stage of cosmic responsibility policy implementation (3–7 years), whose core task is to carry out pilots in selected fields and regions, verify the feasibility of policy recommendations, and accumulate implementation experience.

Resource triggerSevere resource insufficiencyScale adjustment
Opportunity triggerEmergence of a major policy windowAcceleration adjustment

III. Adjustment Procedure

PROCEDURE RoadmapAdjustment

// Step 1: Trigger identification trigger = IdentifyTrigger(monitoring_data, environment_scan)

IF trigger IS NOT NULL THEN

// Step 2: Impact assessment impact = AssessImpact(trigger)

// Step 3: Adjustment option design adjustment_options = DesignAdjustmentOptions(trigger, impact)

// Step 4: Stakeholder consultation consultation = ConsultStakeholders(adjustment_options)

// Step 5: Adjustment decision decision = MakeAdjustmentDecision(adjustment_options, consultation)

// Step 6: Adjustment implementation ImplementAdjustment(decision)

// Step 7: Adjustment monitoring MonitorAdjustment(decision)

END IF

END PROCEDURE`

III. Data Collection Procedure

PROCEDURE DataCollection

// Step 1: Determine data needs data_needs = DetermineDataNeeds(indicators)

// Step 2: Identify data sources data_sources = IdentifyDataSources(data_needs)

// Step 3: Design data collection tools collection_tools = DesignCollectionTools(data_sources)

// Step 4: Implement data collection FOR EACH source IN data_sources DO raw_data = CollectData(source, collection_tools)

// Step 5: Data quality check quality_check = CheckDataQuality(raw_data)

IF quality_check.passed THEN validated_data = ValidateData(raw_data) ELSE raw_data = RecollectData(source, quality_check.issues) END IF END FOR

// Step 6: Data integration integrated_data = IntegrateData(validated_data)

// Step 7: Data storage StoreData(integrated_data)

RETURN integrated_data

END PROCEDURE

§21d.2.3 Evaluation Procedures

I. Design Principles of Evaluation Procedures

Evaluation procedures are the key link in converting monitoring data into policy insight.

Definition 21d.2.3 (Evaluation Procedures)

Evaluation procedures are a set of procedures used to analyze monitoring data, assess the progress and effects of policy implementation, and identify problems and opportunities.

Formal expression:

$$\text{EvaluationProcedure} = \langle \text{Analysis}, \text{Assessment}, \text{Identification} \rangle$$

II. Types of Evaluation

Table 21d.34 Types of Evaluation

Evaluation TypePurposeFrequencyMethod
Progress evaluationAssess implementation progressQuarterlyMilestone check, progress comparison
Effectiveness evaluationAssess implementation effectivenessAnnualIndicator analysis, case studies
Impact evaluationAssess long-term impact5 yearsComprehensive assessment, attribution analysis
Process evaluationAssess the implementation processAnnualProcess tracing, stakeholder feedback

III. Progress Evaluation Procedure

PROCEDURE ProgressEvaluation

// Step 1: Collect progress data progress_data = CollectProgressData()

// Step 2: Compare with the plan FOR EACH milestone IN planned_milestones DO actual_status = GetActualStatus(milestone, progress_data) planned_status = GetPlannedStatus(milestone)

variance = CalculateVariance(actual_status, planned_status)

IF variance > threshold THEN flag_issue = TRUE issues.add(milestone, variance) END IF END FOR

// Step 3: Analyze the causes of deviation FOR EACH issue IN issues DO root_cause = AnalyzeRootCause(issue) issue.root_cause = root_cause END FOR

// Step 4: Propose recommendations recommendations = GenerateRecommendations(issues)

// Step 5: Compile the report report = CompileProgressReport(progress_data, issues, recommendations)

RETURN report

END PROCEDURE

IV. Effectiveness Evaluation Procedure

PROCEDURE EffectivenessEvaluation

// Step 1: Collect effectiveness data effectiveness_data = CollectEffectivenessData()

// Step 2: Calculate indicator values FOR EACH indicator IN result_indicators DO indicator_value = CalculateIndicatorValue(indicator, effectiveness_data) indicator.current_value = indicator_value END FOR

// Step 3: Compare with targets FOR EACH indicator IN result_indicators DO target_value = GetTargetValue(indicator) achievement_rate = indicator.current_value / target_value indicator.achievement_rate = achievement_rate END FOR

// Step 4: Comprehensive assessment overall_effectiveness = CalculateOverallEffectiveness(result_indicators)

// Step 5: Identify success factors and barriers success_factors = IdentifySuccessFactors(effectiveness_data) barriers = IdentifyBarriers(effectiveness_data)

// Step 6: Propose recommendations recommendations = GenerateRecommendations(success_factors, barriers)

// Step 7: Compile the report report = CompileEffectivenessReport(effectiveness_data, overall_effectiveness, recommendations)

RETURN report

END PROCEDURE

V. Impact Evaluation Procedure

PROCEDURE ImpactEvaluation

// Step 1: Collect impact data impact_data = CollectImpactData()

// Step 2: Establish the counterfactual counterfactual = EstablishCounterfactual()

// Step 3: Attribution analysis FOR EACH impact_indicator IN impact_indicators DO observed_change = CalculateObservedChange(impact_indicator, impact_data) counterfactual_change = EstimateCounterfactualChange(impact_indicator, counterfactual)

attributed_impact = observed_change - counterfactual_change impact_indicator.attributed_impact = attributed_impact END FOR

// Step 4: Comprehensive impact assessment overall_impact = CalculateOverallImpact(impact_indicators)

// Step 5: Uncertainty analysis uncertainty = AnalyzeUncertainty(impact_indicators)

// Step 6: Compile the report report = CompileImpactReport(impact_data, overall_impact, uncertainty)

RETURN report

END PROCEDURE

PROCEDURE FeedbackCollection

// Step 1: Determine feedback needs feedback_needs = DetermineFeedbackNeeds(evaluation_results, policy_questions)

// Step 2: Design the collection plan collection_plan = DesignCollectionPlan(feedback_needs)

// Step 3: Implement collection FOR EACH source IN feedback_sources DO method = SelectMethod(source, collection_plan) raw_feedback = CollectFeedback(source, method)

// Step 4: Preliminary processing processed_feedback = ProcessFeedback(raw_feedback) feedback_database.add(processed_feedback) END FOR

// Step 5: Integrated analysis integrated_feedback = IntegrateFeedback(feedback_database)

// Step 6: Generate the report feedback_report = GenerateFeedbackReport(integrated_feedback)

RETURN feedback_report

END PROCEDURE

Node No.Core ConclusionArgumentation Basis

§21d.3.2 Problem Identification

I. Importance of Problem Identification

Problem identification is the key link in converting feedback and monitoring data into actionable insight.

Definition 21d.3.2 (Problem Identification)

Problem identification is a set of procedures used to identify policy implementation problems from feedback and monitoring data, analyze the causes of problems, and assess the severity of problems.

Formal expression:

$$\text{ProblemIdentification} = \langle \text{Detection}, \text{Analysis}, \text{Prioritization} \rangle$$

II. Types of Problems

Table 21d.41 Classification of Problem Types

Problem TypeDefinitionExampleIdentification Method
Progress problemImplementation progress deviates from the planMilestone delayProgress monitoring
Effectiveness problemImplementation effectiveness below expectationIndicator not metEffectiveness evaluation
Design problemFlaw in policy designIndicator not applicableFeedback analysis
Resource problemInsufficient or improperly allocated resourcesFunding shortageResource monitoring
Coordination problemInsufficient coordination among actorsDuplicated workProcess evaluation
Environmental problemChanges in the external environmentPolitical changeEnvironmental scanning

III. Problem Identification Procedure

PROCEDURE ProblemIdentification

// Step 1: Data integration integrated_data = IntegrateData(monitoring_data, feedback_data, evaluation_data)

// Step 2: Anomaly detection anomalies = DetectAnomalies(integrated_data)

// Step 3: Problem confirmation FOR EACH anomaly IN anomalies DO is_problem = ConfirmProblem(anomaly)

IF is_problem THEN problem = CreateProblem(anomaly)

// Step 4: Cause analysis root_causes = AnalyzeRootCauses(problem) problem.root_causes = root_causes

// Step 5: Impact assessment impact = AssessImpact(problem) problem.impact = impact

problems.add(problem) END IF END FOR

// Step 6: Problem prioritization prioritized_problems = PrioritizeProblems(problems)

// Step 7: Generate the problem report problem_report = GenerateProblemReport(prioritized_problems)

RETURN problem_report

END PROCEDURE

IV. Problem Priority Assessment

Table 21d.42 Problem Priority Assessment Matrix

Impact LevelHigh UrgencyMedium UrgencyLow Urgency
HighHighest priority (handle immediately)High priority (handle as soon as possible)Medium priority (handle as planned)
MediumHigh priority (handle as soon as possible)Medium priority (handle as planned)Low priority (monitor)
LowMedium priority (handle as planned)Low priority (monitor)Lowest priority (record)

§21d.3.3 Adjustment Decisions

I. Importance of Adjustment Decisions

Adjustment decisions are the key link in converting the results of problem identification into concrete adjustment actions.

Definition 21d.3.3 (Adjustment Decisions)

Adjustment decisions are a set of procedures used to formulate adjustment options, evaluate adjustment options, and make adjustment decisions based on the results of problem identification.

Formal expression:

$$\text{AdjustmentDecision} = \langle \text{OptionGeneration}, \text{Evaluation}, \text{Decision} \rangle$$

II. Types of Adjustment

Table 21d.43 Types of Adjustment

Adjustment TypeDefinitionApplicable SituationDecision Authority
Operational adjustmentAdjust specific operational methodsOperational-level problemsProject team
Tactical adjustmentAdjust implementation strategyStrategy-level problemsExecutive committee
Strategic adjustmentAdjust strategic directionStrategic-level problemsCouncil
Framework adjustmentAdjust the policy frameworkFramework-level problemsGeneral assembly of members

III. Adjustment Decision Procedure

PROCEDURE AdjustmentDecision

// Step 1: Problem analysis problem_analysis = AnalyzeProblem(identified_problem)

// Step 2: Adjustment option generation adjustment_options = GenerateAdjustmentOptions(problem_analysis)

// Step 3: Option evaluation FOR EACH option IN adjustment_options DO feasibility = AssessFeasibility(option) effectiveness = AssessEffectiveness(option) cost = AssessCost(option) risk = AssessRisk(option)

option.score = CalculateScore(feasibility, effectiveness, cost, risk) END FOR

// Step 4: Stakeholder consultation consultation_result = ConsultStakeholders(adjustment_options)

// Step 5: Decision decision_authority = DetermineDecisionAuthority(problem_analysis.level) decision = MakeDecision(adjustment_options, consultation_result, decision_authority)

// Step 6: Decision recording RecordDecision(decision)

RETURN decision

END PROCEDURE

IV. Adjustment Option Evaluation Criteria

Table 21d.44 Adjustment Option Evaluation Criteria

FeasibilityTechnical feasibility, political feasibility, resource feasibility25%
EffectivenessExpected effect of solving the problem30%
CostImplementation cost, opportunity cost20%
RiskImplementation risk, side effects15%
ConsistencyConsistency with core principles10%

III. Continuous Improvement Procedure

PROCEDURE ContinuousImprovement

// Step 1: Improvement plan improvement_plan = DevelopImprovementPlan(adjustment_decision)

// Step 2: Improvement implementation implementation_result = ImplementImprovement(improvement_plan)

// Step 3: Improvement monitoring improvement_monitoring = MonitorImprovement(implementation_result)

// Step 4: Effectiveness evaluation improvement_effect = EvaluateImprovementEffect(improvement_monitoring)

// Step 5: Summarization of lessons learned lessons_learned = SummarizeLessonsLearned(improvement_effect)

// Step 6: Knowledge management UpdateKnowledgeBase(lessons_learned)

// Step 7: Next round of improvement IF improvement_effect.satisfactory THEN StandardizeImprovement(improvement_plan) ELSE next_improvement = PlanNextImprovement(improvement_effect, lessons_learned) END IF

END PROCEDURE

Milestone Achievement Assessment Procedure

PROCEDURE MilestoneAssessment

// Step 1: Collect milestone data milestone_data = CollectMilestoneData(milestone)

// Step 2: Compare against achievement criteria achievement_status = AssessAgainstCriteria(milestone_data, milestone.criteria)

// Step 3: Determine achievement status IF achievement_status.met THEN milestone.status = "Achieved" milestone.achievement_date = current_date ELSE IF achievement_status.partial THEN milestone.status = "Partially achieved" milestone.gap = achievement_status.gap ELSE milestone.status = "Not achieved" milestone.gap = achievement_status.gap END IF

// Step 4: Analyze causes IF milestone.status != "Achieved" THEN root_cause = AnalyzeRootCause(milestone, milestone_data) milestone.root_cause = root_cause END IF

// Step 5: Propose recommendations recommendations = GenerateRecommendations(milestone)

// Step 6: Update the roadmap IF milestone.status == "Achieved" THEN TriggerNextPhase(milestone) ELSE AdjustRoadmap(milestone, recommendations) END IF

RETURN milestone

END PROCEDURE

Chapter Summary

Summary of Core Conclusions

This chapter designed the roadmap and monitoring framework for cosmic responsibility policy implementation; the main conclusions are as follows:

Conclusion One: A Four-Phase Implementation Roadmap

The implementation roadmap is divided into four phases, each with clear goals and key actions.

$$\text{Roadmap} = \langle \text{Foundation}, \text{Pilot}, \text{Expansion}, \text{Maturity} \rangle$$

Table 21d.54 Key Points of the Four-Phase Implementation Roadmap

Foundation phase1–3 yearsConcept building, consensus formation, pilot launch10
Pilot phase3–7 yearsPilot implementation, experience accumulation, evaluation and learning10
Expansion phase7–15 yearsScale expansion, institutional development, international integration10
Maturity phase15 years+Institutional consolidation, normalized operation, continuous improvement10

Conclusion Two: A Four-Level Monitoring Indicator System

The monitoring indicator system includes four levels: input, output, outcome, and impact.

$$\text{MonitoringIndicators} = \langle \text{Input}, \text{Output}, \text{Outcome}, \text{Impact} \rangle$$

Conclusion Three: A Feedback and Adjustment Mechanism

The feedback and adjustment mechanism ensures that policy implementation can adapt to environmental changes and improve continuously.

$$\text{FeedbackMechanism} = \langle \text{Collection}, \text{Identification}, \text{Decision}, \text{Improvement} \rangle$$

[1] The four-phase division of the implementation roadmap draws on the classic framework of policy implementation research. In their pioneering work, Pressman and Wildavsky pointed out that policy implementation is a complex process that needs to be advanced in phases. See: Pressman, J. L., & Wildavsky, A. (1984). Implementation (3rd ed.). University of California Press.

[2] The conceptual construction task of the foundation phase draws on research in the sociology of knowledge. Berger and Luckmann pointed out that social reality is constructed through concepts, and the introduction of new concepts requires a process of institutionalization. See: Berger, P. L., & Luckmann, T. (1966). The Social Construction of Reality. Doubleday.

[3] The design of the pilot phase draws on research on policy experimentation. Heilmann pointed out that policy experimentation is an important pathway for policy innovation, and that risk can be reduced and experience accumulated through pilots. See: Heilmann, S. (2008). Policy Experimentation in China's Economic Rise. Studies in Comparative International Development, 43(1), 1-26.

[4] The institutional development of the expansion phase draws on research on international institutions. Keohane pointed out that the construction of international institutions is a gradual process that needs to develop from soft law to hard law. See: Keohane, R. O. (1989). International Institutions and State Power. Westview Press.

[5] The continuous improvement mechanism of the maturity phase draws on organizational learning theory. Argyris and Schön proposed the concepts of single-loop and double-loop learning; the PDCA+ cycle in this work integrates these concepts. See: Argyris, C., & Schön, D. A. (1978). Organizational Learning: A Theory of Action Perspective. Addison-Wesley.

[6] The roadmap flexible adjustment mechanism draws on research on adaptive management. Holling proposed the concept of adaptive management, emphasizing improvement of management through learning and adjustment under uncertainty. See: Holling, C. S. (Ed.). (1978). Adaptive Environmental Assessment and Management. John Wiley & Sons.

[7] The four-level structure of the monitoring indicator system draws on the Results Chain method. The OECD-DAC evaluation framework divides indicators into four levels: input, output, outcome, and impact. See: OECD. (2002). Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results Based Management. OECD.

[8] The design of the Composite Progress Index (CPI) draws on methods for constructing composite indicators. UNDP's Human Development Index (HDI) is a classic case of a composite indicator. See: UNDP. (1990). Human Development Report 1990. Oxford University Press.

[9] The data collection methods draw on social science research methods. Babbie's research methods textbook provides detailed guidance on methods such as surveys, interviews, and focus groups. See: Babbie, E. R. (2016). The Practice of Social Research (14th ed.). Cengage Learning.

[10] Data quality control draws on research on statistical quality management. Deming's quality management theory emphasizes the importance of data quality to decision-making. See: Deming, W. E. (1986). Out of the Crisis. MIT Press.

[11] The evaluation procedures draw on research on program evaluation. The evaluation research textbook of Rossi, Lipsey, and Freeman provides detailed guidance on evaluation design and implementation. See: Rossi, P. H., Lipsey, M. W., & Freeman, H. E. (2004). Evaluation: A Systematic Approach (7th ed.). Sage.

[12] The attribution analysis of impact evaluation draws on research on causal inference. The econometrics textbook of Angrist and Pischke provides a detailed introduction to causal inference methods. See: Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J. S. (2009). Mostly Harmless Econometrics. Princeton University Press.

[13] The reporting mechanism draws on research on transparency and accountability. Hood pointed out that transparency is a core element of modern governance. See: Hood, C. (2006). Transparency in Historical Perspective. In C. Hood & D. Heald (Eds.), Transparency: The Key to Better Governance? (pp. 3-23). Oxford University Press.

[14] The feedback collection mechanism draws on research on participatory governance. Fung and Wright proposed the concept of "empowered participatory governance," emphasizing the importance of citizen participation to governance quality. See: Fung, A., & Wright, E. O. (Eds.). (2003). Deepening Democracy: Institutional Innovations in Empowered Participatory Governance. Verso.

[15] The root cause analysis of problem identification draws on research on quality management. Ishikawa proposed the cause-and-effect diagram (fishbone diagram) method for analyzing the root causes of problems. See: Ishikawa, K. (1985). What Is Total Quality Control? The Japanese Way. Prentice Hall.

[16] The multi-dimensional evaluation of adjustment decisions draws on research on multi-criteria decision analysis. The decision analysis textbook of Keeney and Raiffa provides detailed methods for multi-criteria decision-making. See: Keeney, R. L., & Raiffa, H. (1993). Decisions with Multiple Objectives. Cambridge University Press.

[17] The PDCA cycle of continuous improvement was popularized by Deming and originates from Shewhart's statistical quality control. This work adds a "learning" link on the basis of PDCA, forming the PDCA+ cycle. See: Deming, W. E. (1986). Out of the Crisis. MIT Press.

[18] Knowledge management draws on research on organizational knowledge management. Nonaka and Takeuchi proposed the SECI model of knowledge creation, emphasizing the transformation between tacit knowledge and explicit knowledge. See: Nonaka, I., & Takeuchi, H. (1995). The Knowledge-Creating Company. Oxford University Press.

[19] The design of success criteria draws on research on performance management. The balanced scorecard method of Kaplan and Norton provides a framework for multi-dimensional performance assessment. See: Kaplan, R. S., & Norton, D. P. (1996). The Balanced Scorecard. Harvard Business School Press.

[20] Milestone management draws on research on project management. PMI's Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK) provides detailed guidance on milestone management. See: Project Management Institute. (2017). A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (6th ed.). PMI.

The policy translation design of Part Six is closely integrated with the One Loop mechanism:

  1. Monitoring triggers rollback: when monitoring indicators show major deviations, this can trigger a roadmap adjustment or a higher-level rollback
  2. Feedback supports learning: the feedback collection and continuous improvement mechanisms support organizational learning and knowledge accumulation
  3. Flexible adjustment maintains adaptability: the flexible adjustment mechanism ensures that policy implementation can adapt to environmental changes
  4. Versioned management: the implementation roadmap and monitoring framework themselves are also revisable and follow the principle of versioned management

Part Six has completed the design of policy translation and prepared the way for Part Seven (stress testing):

  1. Clear objects of examination: the policy translation framework, actor policy guidelines, and implementation roadmap are all objects of examination for stress testing
  2. Clear evaluation criteria: the success criteria and monitoring indicators provide an evaluation benchmark for stress testing
  3. Adjustment mechanisms ready: the flexible adjustment mechanism and continuous improvement mechanism provide procedural support for revisions after stress testing

Part Seven will examine the robustness of the entire theoretical framework through four extreme scenarios (AGI breakthrough, First Contact, ecological tipping point, intergenerational justice crisis), identify weaknesses, and propose revision recommendations.

Volume II Conclusion Volume II Conclusion

I. Core Achievements of This Volume

1.1 The Complete Translation from Principles to Operations

Volume II has accomplished one of the most challenging tasks of this work: translating the abstract normative principles established in Volume I into an operable indicator system, an implementable institutional framework, and actionable policy recommendations. This translation process can be formally expressed as:

$$\text{Volume II} = \mathcal{T}(\text{L}_2 \rightarrow \text{L}_3 \rightarrow \text{L}_4 \rightarrow \text{policy translation layer})$$

where $\mathcal{T}$ represents the "operationalization translation function," which progressively translates the abstract propositions of the normative principle layer (L₂) into the governance architecture of the institutional design layer (L₃) and the specific indicators of the operating procedure layer (L₄), ultimately extending to the implementation pathways of the policy translation layer.

1.2 The Construction of the Six Major Indicator Systems

The core achievement of Part Four (Indicator Systems) is the construction of six major indicator systems, realizing the measurability of the New Three Views propositions:

Table C.2 Correspondence between the Six Major Indicator Systems and the New Three Views

IndicatorFull NameSource PropositionCore Function
UCSUniversal Consciousness ScaleNL-3 (continuum of subjects)Assess the degree of consciousness and moral status of subjects
RFDRecursive Freedom DegreeRFP (Principle of Recursive Freedom)Assess the impact of actions on the possibility space
CRVCommitment Reversibility VerificationNK-2, NK-4 + REVAssess the credibility of commitments
CDICivilizational Development IndexIntegration of the New Three ViewsAssess the level of civilizational development
MBCLMemetic Biosafety Class LevelNK + NRPAssess the risk level of memes
CSIACosmic-Scale Impact AssessmentIntegration of the three principlesAssess the cosmic-scale impact of actions

The design of these six major indicator systems follows three core principles:

Principle One: Anchoring to Normative Principles

Each indicator can be traced back to the normative principles established in Volume I, ensuring the normative foundation of the indicator system:

$$\forall i \in \text{Indicators}: \exists p \in \text{Principles}: \text{Anchor}(i, p)$$

Principle Two: Anti-Goodhart Design

Each indicator adopts a multi-dimensional design to prevent a single indicator from being manipulated:

$$\text{Indicator}_i = f(D_1, D_2, ..., D_n), \quad n \geq 3$$

Principle Three: Cross-Substrate Applicability

Each indicator is designed to be applicable to different types of subjects (humans, AI, hypothetical alien life):

$$\text{Applicability}(i) = \{\text{Human}, \text{AI}, \text{Hypothetical Alien}\}$$

The core innovation of the protocol stack architecture lies in:

  1. Level separation: content of different stabilities is placed at different levels, achieving the unity of "stability of principles" and "flexibility of operations"
  2. Load-bearing constraints: lower levels constrain upper levels, and upper levels must not violate lower levels, ensuring normative consistency
  3. Versioned rollback: each level can be revised while keeping lower levels unchanged, supporting institutional evolution

The design of these institutions embodies the core propositions of the New Three Views:

  • NC-3 (participatory universe) → pluralistic representation and public participation mechanisms
  • NL-3 (continuum of subjects) → representation and rights protection for cross-intelligence subjects
  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge) → versioned governance and rollback mechanism

II. The Transition from Operations to Examination

2.1 The Boundaries of Volume II

Volume II has completed the translation from principles to operations, but this translation itself needs to be examined. All outputs of Volume II are at the "first-generation rough model" stage, with the following boundaries:

Boundary One: The maturity boundary of indicators

All indicators are at the "conceptual prototype" stage (TRL 2) and have not yet undergone large-scale empirical verification:

$$\text{MaturityLevel}(\text{All Indicators}) = \text{ConceptualPrototype}$$

Boundary Two: The idealization boundary of institutional design

The institutional design is a theoretical prototype and needs to be adjusted according to the specific context:

$$\text{InstitutionalDesign} = \text{TheoreticalPrototype} \neq \text{ImplementableBlueprint}$$

Boundary Three: The academic boundary of policy recommendations

The policy recommendations are academic recommendations, whose adoption requires democratic deliberation and feasibility assessment:

$$\text{PolicyRecommendations} = \text{AcademicSuggestions} \neq \text{OfficialPolicy}$$

2.2 The Necessity of Examination

Any normative theory needs to be examined. The outputs of Volume II need to be examined in the following ways:

Examination Method One: Stress Testing

Examine the robustness of the framework through extreme scenarios:

$$\text{StressTest}(\text{Framework}, \text{ExtremeScenario}) \rightarrow \text{RobustnessAssessment}$$

Examination Method Two: International Dialogue

Examine the compatibility of the framework through dialogue with international academic traditions:

$$\text{Dialogue}(\text{Framework}, \text{InternationalTraditions}) \rightarrow \text{CompatibilityAssessment}$$

Examination Method Three: Future Agenda

Identify the development direction of the framework by planning the future research agenda:

$$\text{FutureAgenda}(\text{Framework}) \rightarrow \text{DevelopmentDirection}$$

IV. The Final Positioning of This Volume

4.1 Contributions of This Volume

The core contributions of Volume II can be summarized as follows:

Contribution One: Operationalization translation Translate the abstract normative principles of Volume I into operable indicators, institutions, and policies, achieving the translation "from philosophy to engineering."

Contribution Two: Protocol stack improvement Improve the protocol stack architecture, establish a complete governance framework from physical constraints to operating procedures, and achieve the unity of "stability of principles" and "flexibility of operations."

Contribution Three: Governance institution design Design core governance institutions such as the Multi-Intelligence Arbitration Institution, the cosmic-scale IRB, and the Intergenerational Trust, providing institutional prototypes for cosmic responsibility governance.

Contribution Four: Policy translation Translate the theoretical framework into concrete policy recommendations and implementation pathways, providing a reference for policymakers.

4.2 Limitations of This Volume

Volume II also has clear limitations:

Limitation One: Insufficient empirical verification All indicators and institutional designs are at the conceptual prototype stage and have not yet undergone large-scale empirical verification.

Limitation Two: Tendency toward idealization The institutional design has a tendency toward idealization and needs to be adjusted according to the specific context.

Limitation Three: Political feasibility not assessed The political feasibility of the policy recommendations has not yet been systematically assessed.

Limitation Four: Possible cultural bias The framework may contain cultural bias and requires more cross-cultural dialogue.

4.3 Openness of This Volume

All outputs of Volume II are open and revisable:

$$\text{Openness}(\text{Volume II}) = \text{Revisable} \land \text{Rollbackable} \land \text{Collaborative}$$

This volume invites:

  1. Criticism: criticism of indicators, institutions, and policies is welcome
  2. Improvement: suggestions for improving the framework are welcome
  3. Verification: empirical verification of the framework is welcome
  4. Application: practical application of the framework is welcome

[1] The four-phase division of the implementation roadmap draws on the classic framework of policy implementation research. In their groundbreaking work, Pressman and Wildavsky pointed out that policy implementation is a complex process requiring phased advancement. See: Pressman, J. L., & Wildavsky, A. (1984). Implementation (3rd ed.). University of California Press.

[2] The conceptual construction task of the foundation phase draws on research in the sociology of knowledge. Berger and Luckmann pointed out that social reality is constructed through concepts, and the introduction of new concepts must undergo a process of institutionalization. See: Berger, P. L., & Luckmann, T. (1966). The Social Construction of Reality. Doubleday.

[3] The design of the pilot phase draws on research on policy experimentation. Heilmann pointed out that policy experimentation is an important avenue of policy innovation, and that piloting can reduce risk and accumulate experience. See: Heilmann, S. (2008). Policy Experimentation in China's Economic Rise. Studies in Comparative International Development, 43(1), 1-26.

[4] The institution-building of the expansion phase draws on research on international institutions. Keohane pointed out that the building of international institutions is a gradual process requiring development from soft law to hard law. See: Keohane, R. O. (1989). International Institutions and State Power. Westview Press.

[5] The continuous improvement mechanism of the maturity phase draws on organizational learning theory. Argyris and Schön proposed the concepts of single-loop and double-loop learning; the PDCA+ cycle of this work integrates these concepts. See: Argyris, C., & Schön, D. A. (1978). Organizational Learning: A Theory of Action Perspective. Addison-Wesley.

[6] The flexible adjustment mechanism of the roadmap draws on research in adaptive management. Holling proposed the concept of adaptive management, emphasizing improvement of management through learning and adjustment under uncertainty. See: Holling, C. S. (Ed.). (1978). Adaptive Environmental Assessment and Management. John Wiley & Sons.

[7] The four-tier structure of the monitoring indicator system draws on the Results Chain method. The OECD-DAC evaluation framework classifies indicators into four tiers: inputs, outputs, outcomes, and impacts. See: OECD. (2002). Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results Based Management. OECD.

[8] The design of the Composite Progress Index (CPI) draws on methods of constructing composite indicators. UNDP's Human Development Index (HDI) is a classic case of a composite indicator. See: UNDP. (1990). Human Development Report 1990. Oxford University Press.

[9] The data collection methods draw on social science research methods. Babbie's research methods textbook provides detailed guidance on methods such as surveys, interviews, and focus groups. See: Babbie, E. R. (2016). The Practice of Social Research (14th ed.). Cengage Learning.

[10] Data quality control draws on research in statistical quality management. Deming's theory of quality management emphasizes the importance of data quality for decision-making. See: Deming, W. E. (1986). Out of the Crisis. MIT Press.

[11] The evaluation procedures draw on research in program evaluation. The evaluation research textbook of Rossi, Lipsey, and Freeman provides detailed guidance on the design and conduct of evaluations. See: Rossi, P. H., Lipsey, M. W., & Freeman, H. E. (2004). Evaluation: A Systematic Approach (7th ed.). Sage.

[12] The attribution analysis of impact assessment draws on research in causal inference. The econometrics textbook of Angrist and Pischke provides a detailed introduction to methods of causal inference. See: Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J. S. (2009). Mostly Harmless Econometrics. Princeton University Press.

[13] The reporting mechanism draws on research on transparency and accountability. Hood pointed out that transparency is a core element of modern governance. See: Hood, C. (2006). Transparency in Historical Perspective. In C. Hood & D. Heald (Eds.), Transparency: The Key to Better Governance? (pp. 3-23). Oxford University Press.

[14] The feedback collection mechanism draws on research in participatory governance. Fung and Wright proposed the concept of "empowered participatory governance," emphasizing the importance of citizen participation for the quality of governance. See: Fung, A., & Wright, E. O. (Eds.). (2003). Deepening Democracy: Institutional Innovations in Empowered Participatory Governance. Verso.

[15] The root cause analysis of problem identification draws on research in quality management. Ishikawa proposed the cause-and-effect diagram (fishbone diagram) method for analyzing the root causes of problems. See: Ishikawa, K. (1985). What Is Total Quality Control? The Japanese Way. Prentice Hall.

[16] The multidimensional evaluation of adjustment decisions draws on research in multicriteria decision analysis. The decision analysis textbook of Keeney and Raiffa provides detailed methods of multicriteria decision-making. See: Keeney, R. L., & Raiffa, H. (1993). Decisions with Multiple Objectives. Cambridge University Press.

[17] The PDCA cycle of continuous improvement was popularized by Deming and originated in Shewhart's statistical quality control. This work adds a "learning" step to the PDCA cycle, forming the PDCA+ cycle. See: Deming, W. E. (1986). Out of the Crisis. MIT Press.

[18] Knowledge management draws on research in organizational knowledge management. Nonaka and Takeuchi proposed the SECI model of knowledge creation, emphasizing the conversion between tacit and explicit knowledge. See: Nonaka, I., & Takeuchi, H. (1995). The Knowledge-Creating Company. Oxford University Press.

[19] The design of success criteria draws on research in performance management. The balanced scorecard method of Kaplan and Norton provides a framework for multidimensional performance assessment. See: Kaplan, R. S., & Norton, D. P. (1996). The Balanced Scorecard. Harvard Business School Press.

[20] Milestone management draws on research in project management. PMI's Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK) provides detailed guidance on milestone management. See: Project Management Institute. (2017). A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (6th ed.). PMI.
